Iran sends US ‘seven conditions’ for talks, warns nuclear doctrine could change
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
20:04:43 UTC
05:04:43 KST

President Donald Trump has again raised the possibility of a major new military escalation against Iran while keeping the door open to negotiations, but Tehran is responding with demands of its own. Iranian security chief Mohsen Rezaei said Saturday that Qatar had conveyed Tehran’s conditions to Washington and that Iran was awaiting Trump’s response, while warning that the country’s nuclear doctrine could eventually change.
Trump told Axios on Thursday that he was approaching a major decision over whether to restart large-scale attacks against Iran, asking whether he wanted to “go in and annihilate” the Iranian regime. At the same time, he has publicly said he remains open to diplomacy and has claimed Iran wants a deal. Tehran has disputed that negotiations have resumed and has insisted there will be no talks until its conditions are met.
Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, told Al Jazeera that Tehran remained in contact with mediators in Qatar and Pakistan. He said the three conditions publicly presented for ending the war were an end to fighting “on all fronts,” the release of frozen Iranian assets and an end to the U.S. naval blockade. Reuters independently reported the same three demands.
Iranian reports have referred more broadly to seven conditions communicated to Washington through intermediaries, particularly in connection with reopening the Strait of Hormuz. The complete official list has not been publicly released, though earlier Iranian statements have also demanded sanctions relief and an end to U.S. military pressure.
Rezaei argued that Washington would ultimately have to accept Tehran’s position and said Iran was prepared for what he called a “decisive war.” He also claimed Iran had identified vulnerabilities in the U.S. military and had recently tested an anti-ship missile near an American aircraft carrier. Those claims have not been independently verified.
Rezaei also sharpened Tehran’s nuclear warnings, saying U.S. and Israeli actions could provide grounds for Iran to withdraw from the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty. He said no decision had yet been taken and that Tehran’s next steps would depend on Washington’s conduct.
Iran, he said, remained committed to the religious ruling issued by Ali Khamenei prohibiting nuclear weapons and had not changed its declared nuclear doctrine. But he added that Tehran could not say what would happen in the future, leaving open the possibility of a later shift.
The warning comes amid a renewed confrontation between Tehran and the International Atomic Energy Agency. The IAEA’s Board of Governors this month referred Iran’s nuclear noncompliance to the UN Security Council, saying the agency still lacked access to key sites and information about nuclear material following the attacks on Iranian facilities. Tehran has blamed the U.S. and Israel for creating the situation and continues to say its nuclear program is not intended to produce weapons.
The nuclear and diplomatic standoff is unfolding alongside a major escalation in Yemen, where the Iran-backed Houthis have made rapid gains against forces aligned with the internationally recognized Yemeni government and supported by Saudi Arabia.
The Houthis have seized strategic positions along Yemen’s Red Sea coast and around the Bab al-Mandab Strait, one of the world’s most important maritime chokepoints. Their advances have increased their ability to threaten shipping at the western entrance to the Red Sea at the same time that the Strait of Hormuz remains severely disrupted by the Iran conflict.
Rezaei told Al Jazeera that Iran wanted the Saudi-Houthi fighting to end and said he believed the Houthis were also interested in an agreement with Riyadh. Iran provides extensive support to the group but maintains that the Houthis make their own decisions.
The fighting has meanwhile moved deeper into Saudi territory. On Saturday, the Houthis said they had attacked “sensitive” sites in Riyadh with missiles and drones after flames and a large plume of smoke were seen near the Saudi capital’s main airport. They also claimed an attack on an Aramco facility in Yanbu, a crucial Red Sea oil export hub. Saudi authorities did not immediately confirm what had been struck in Riyadh.
Yanbu has become particularly important because Saudi Arabia has relied on its Red Sea export infrastructure to bypass disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz. But Saudi energy routes have themselves come under growing pressure, including attacks on the kingdom’s East-West pipeline and other infrastructure.
The Houthi offensive has also exposed growing unease in Washington and Gulf capitals about whether Saudi Arabia and its Yemeni allies can reverse the group’s advances.
Multiple U.S. and Gulf sources told CNN that neither Washington nor Riyadh currently has a clear plan for pushing the Houthis back. U.S. intelligence and targeting assistance has increased, but sources expressed doubt that Saudi Arabia could stop the Houthis without additional support.
Former U.S. diplomat Joey Hood told CNN that the Houthi advance in the Red Sea was strengthening the position of Iran’s Revolutionary Guards and complicating any effort to negotiate separately with Tehran. Other regional officials argued that the Yemen front can no longer easily be separated from the wider confrontation with Iran.
A Gulf official summed up the dilemma to CNN: “No one wants to fight alone.” The official said Riyadh would ultimately have to either expand its military campaign or pursue an agreement with the Houthis.
Trump has so far resisted direct U.S. offensive action against the Houthis. CNN reported that Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman asked Trump for U.S. strikes but that the request was rejected, while American assistance has remained focused on intelligence and targeting support. The Washington Post similarly reported that Washington has stopped short of military intervention despite Saudi and Yemeni appeals.
U.S. officials also met Houthi representatives in Oman this month, according to Reuters. Sources said the Houthis reiterated their commitment to the 2025 ceasefire with Washington and said they did not intend to attack American vessels. One Yemeni source said they also pledged not to target Israeli or other commercial vessels, with the exception of Saudi ships. The State Department did not formally confirm the meeting.
The widening regional conflict has also intensified economic pressure in the United States. Oil prices have remained around or above $100 a barrel, while higher gasoline and diesel costs have become an increasingly prominent political issue ahead of the November midterm elections.
Trump has publicly insisted that electoral politics do not determine his Iran policy and has defended higher energy costs as a price worth paying to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon.
Privately, however, The Washington Post reported Saturday that Trump has listened more closely in recent weeks as advisers presented discouraging polling and has indicated in some conversations that he understands the Iran war has contributed to the difficult political environment facing Republicans. One person in frequent contact with Trump disputed that he had accepted responsibility, saying the president instead believes the biggest problem is that his own name will not be on the ballot.
The Post reported that advisers have become more direct with Trump about the political environment and that he intends to increase his involvement in Republican campaigns as the midterms approach. The extent to which the Iran war, oil prices and the widening confrontation in Yemen ultimately shape voter decisions remains uncertain.

Conspiracy theories appear to erode public faith in meritocracy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
20:00:57 UTC
05:00:57 KST

When people buy into conspiracy theories, their faith in the fairness of society begins to erode. New research published in Political Psychology shows that exposure to conspiratorial narratives directly reduces the belief that resources are distributed based on merit, equality, or need. The findings suggest that suspicions of hidden plots foster a deep distrust of institutions, coloring how individuals view the basic rules of social and economic life.
Meritocracy is the idea that society rewards talent and hard work. Many political leaders and cultural narratives lean heavily on this concept to motivate citizens and justify existing economic structures. Alongside equality and need, meritocracy forms the foundation of what psychologists call distributive justice. This term refers to the perceived fairness of how a community divides its wealth, opportunities, and resources.
Public perception of these justice principles dictates how well a society functions. When people believe the system is fair, they are more likely to cooperate and follow the rules. Alternatively, widespread perceptions of injustice can foster resentment and social instability.
Researchers have extensively studied how income disparities and social mobility affect these views. Little research has examined how conspiratorial thinking influences ideas about fairness. Conspiracy theories typically allege that malevolent, secretive groups are orchestrating events for their own benefit. Because these narratives frame elites as exploitative and corrupt, they naturally conflict with the notion of a fair society.
A team of researchers led by Qi Zhao, a psychologist at Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam, set out to test this dynamic. They wanted to know if believing in a conspiracy theory makes people less likely to view the world as fair. The team designed a combination of survey analyses and experiments to see if conspiratorial beliefs alter how people perceive the distribution of resources.
In their first study, the researchers analyzed data from the World Value Survey, a large international dataset. The sample included 90,837 participants across 68 different societies. The researchers looked at survey items measuring beliefs in election fraud conspiracies, such as the idea that rich people buy elections or that television news manipulates voters.
They compared these responses to a question asking whether hard work usually brings a better life. The results showed a consistent negative relationship between conspiracy beliefs and faith in meritocracy. People who endorsed election fraud narratives were less likely to believe that effort leads to success.
This pattern held true regardless of whether a country had a highly democratic government or an authoritarian one. The researchers also accounted for national differences in economic inequality, gross domestic product, and expert ratings of corruption. The link between conspiracy beliefs and diminished faith in meritocracy remained intact across these varied environments.
Because the survey could only show a correlation, the researchers conducted an experiment to test for a causal effect. They recruited 403 participants in the United States for an online study. Half of the participants read a news report about a fictional local government misusing public funds, accompanied by evidence supporting the conspiracy theory. The other half read the same report but with evidence refuting the allegations.
Afterward, participants rated their agreement with statements about how resources were handled in the fictional community. Those exposed to the supporting evidence reported lower belief in meritocracy. They also expressed less belief in the principles of equality, which assumes everyone gets an equal share, and need, which dictates that resources go to those who require them most.
The experiment demonstrated that adopting a conspiracy belief directly lowered perceptions of distributive justice. The researchers also tested potential psychological mechanisms behind this shift. They found that distrust in government acted as a primary bridge, explaining how exposure to the conspiracy theory led to lower ratings of fairness.
The researchers then replicated this experiment with 788 participants in China to see if the effect crossed cultural boundaries. Chinese culture traditionally places a stronger emphasis on equality and need compared to the merit-focused culture of the United States. The scenario in this experiment involved a local government colluding with the media to suppress negative news and control the public.
Just as in the American sample, participants who read evidence validating the conspiracy theory reported lower faith in all three justice principles. They were less likely to believe that the fictional society rewarded hard work, distributed resources equally, or helped those in need. Institutional distrust once again served as the psychological mechanism driving these negative perceptions.
To test whether these dynamics exist outside of civic government, the team conducted a final experiment focused on a corporate workplace. They recruited another 403 American participants and asked them to imagine working for an electronics company. The participants read a rumor that the company’s administration was deliberately hiding the presence of dangerous chemicals to avoid bad publicity.
Similar to the previous experiments, participants received information either confirming or debunking the corporate cover-up. Those in the confirmation group displayed a pronounced drop in their belief that the company operated fairly. They doubted that the administration rewarded good work, treated employees equally, or accommodated worker needs.
The researchers concluded that conspiracy theories degrade trust in administrative bodies, which in turn poisons the perception of fairness in an organizational setting. The effect was especially pronounced for the principles of equality and need. Meritocracy perceptions were also reduced, though they remained slightly more resilient, likely because performance-based rewards are deeply ingrained in corporate structures.
A few caveats apply to how these results translate to the real world. The experiments relied on fictional scenarios to manipulate beliefs, which might not perfectly mirror the deeply entrenched narratives people encounter online or in their communities. Real-world conspiracy theories often tie into long-standing political identities, making them harder to accept or reject based on a single piece of evidence.
The studies focused entirely on conspiracy theories involving powerful institutions like governments and corporate boards. It is unknown if conspiracies targeting marginalized groups or ordinary citizens would have the same effect on perceptions of societal fairness. Future research might explore whether narratives about less powerful groups also erode trust in the broader economic system.
Additionally, while the experiments showed that conspiracy beliefs cause a drop in perceived fairness, the reverse might also happen outside the laboratory. Experiencing genuine unfairness might make people more susceptible to conspiratorial thinking. Examining this cycle could help psychologists understand how institutional distrust deepens over time.
The study, “Not a real meritocracy? How conspiracy beliefs reduce perceived distributive justice,” was authored by Qi Zhao, Jan-Willem van Prooijen, and Giuliana Spadaro.

The moment I knew: On a bike ride, she did a bunny hop over a speed hump – her pure joy for life delighted me
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
20:00:57 UTC
05:00:57 KST

Georgie and I met at a kick-boxing club in London in 2004. We sparred together in a few beginner classes, just hitting soft pads. Although I didn’t pay her too much attention initially, I immediately recognised she was tall, elegant and very good looking.
It wasn’t until the club’s Christmas drinks that things kicked off between us. We started talking and couldn’t stop. We’d both travelled and worked in Latin America, and also loved horses – Georgie had volunteered with a horse-riding business for tourists in Ecuador. The sparks were flying all over the place.
A friend of mine was deejaying at a gay club nearby so we headed there and continued chatting, dancing and flirting. About 2am we found an all-night cafe and talkeduntil daybreak, then went our separate ways. But we planned to meet again.
On my way to our third date, my housemate called saying we’d been burgled. I had to return home and call the police. When I explained this to Georgie she suggested coming to mine instead. When the police finally arrived, many hours later, I introduced myself as one of the occupants. One of the constables asked Georgie who she was. There was this awkward silence – on date three was she my girlfriend? I think we went with “friend”. But she didn’t go home that night.
Things moved quickly from there. One morning in early spring we took a bike ride through a nearby park that had little speed bumps. Like us, our bikes were very different – mine was a lightweight touring bike and hers a hard-tail mountain bike.
I was riding just ahead of her but when I looked back I saw her doing this funky bunny hop over the speed hump. I can picture the jacket she was wearing – dark grey, heavy canvas – and her focus as she flicked her bike over the hump. It was that joie de vivre that delighted me. Her embarrassment when she realised I’d seen was also so very her – wanting to be cool, but so much more than that. This was someone who couldn’t contain her enthusiasm. It crystallised what I loved about her.
After a couple of years of living together in London we moved to Melbourne. She loved the city and fitted right into some sports and footy clubs here. But she found it hard to get work for her niche in sports community development. So she went back to the UK for work and our relationship became long-distance.
Nearly a year later, in 2009, she found out she had breast cancer. She was only 32. Within a fortnight, I gave up my job and moved to the UK to be with her. She absolutely knew I would upend my life to support her at a time it really mattered.
She did recover well initially. A couple of years later we made it back to Australia and this time we both found work that suited us. We also took many great trips – camping in the Northern Territory and Western Australia, cycling trips all over including from Cairns to Cape York.
But a couple of years later she was diagnosed again, and a bit later the cancer metastasised. At the tail-end of 2019 her doctor advised her that she may only have six months to live. It was time for her to head home to the UK and I went with her. It coincided with Covid lockdowns, so we got to spend a tremendous amount of time together in a small town near her family.
Georgie seemed to be improving but then she started to get breathless and her specialists couldn’t work out why. She was in hospital for scans when she had a brain haemorrhage and lapsed into unconsciousness. Two days later, in July 2020, after some intensely moving times in ICU with her family, she died.
I feel so much gratitude for the time we spent together. Just three days before the brain haemorrhage she had cycled to see her GP – so fitting, being active was so important to her. It was her irrepressible energy I loved, and I am a better person for having known her.

When friends become good neighbours: the Melbourne families who transformed one home into three townhouses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
20:00:56 UTC
05:00:56 KST

Melbourne architect Chris Gilbert had run out of eggs. He texted a neighbour and within minutes, he says, their child arrived with some. “Then I made brownies and my kids took some over to the neighbours’ house.”
It sounds like a flashback to a bygone era, but this neighbourly exchange took place this month, at the Davison Collaborative, a novel housing project in the Melbourne suburb of Brunswick. In 2020 the townhouse development replaced one past-its-prime brick veneer house with three architecturally designed three-bedroom family dwellings, trebling the lot’s density and future proofing it “for at least the next 50 years,” says Liam Wallis, from the sustainability focused property development and consultancy company Hip V. Hype.
In 2018, times weren’t so idyllic. Gilbert was bring outbid at auctions week after week. Each Monday he’d arrive despondent at his shared working space with Wallis, and Wallis’ business partner Peter Steele.
Wallis had already been mulling whether pooling resources to redevelop single home lots into multiple dwellings could increase density, while saving families money.
“I said ‘hang on a minute, let’s just do a project. Let’s see if this works. Let’s figure out how hard it is,’” Wallis says.
The collaborative eventually bought a postwar home, owned by the same family for 50 years, at auction. The parents had died and their children were selling. Two years later, the three couples moved in. “And each of those homes were the same size as the original dwelling,” Wallis says.
As Wallis, Gilbert and Steele were moving in, a similar plan was unfolding in another inner-north Melbourne suburb. During lockdowns, a close-knit group of friends and colleagues (with experience in architecture, interior design, project management and a tradie among them) who lived within walking distance of one another in Carlton North, were spitballing ways to parlay their collective professional wisdom (and their finances) into a similar proposition.
Four years later, Sarah Birthisel and her husband, along with couples Sarah Cosentino and Stephen McGarry, and Tanya Smith and Neil Clarke, moved into their tri-townhouse venture, Northcote Townhouses.
Sitting down with Birthisel and Cosentino, the pair are obviously pleased with how things turned out. Knowing such an endeavour wouldn’t be feasible in Carlton North, the group looked to the adjacent municipality of Darebin. Fewer heritage overlays, larger lots and cheaper prices, they explain, made the area far more suitable.
After agreeing on their vision and drafting contracts, the consortium bought a 638 sq metre property that backs on to the Mernda train line in Northcote. Their first order of business was to make their intentions known to other residents on the street. “It was really important to us to connect with our neighbours, to make them aware that this wasn’t going to be something that we would be flipping … That this would be our home, and that resonated really well with the community,” Cosentino says.
Then they went to the council with a strategy that Birthisel says was “very sympathetic to the streetscape and continued the rhythm of the streets”. Development approvals went smoothly and they broke ground in 2022. When it came time to move in, they staggered that process so each couple had some time to settle in.
Cosentino and Birthisel say that while the communal aspects of the arrangement were alluring, each family also wanted a sense of privacy. Two years into their experiment, they feel as if they’ve achieved that.
“I love the security of knowing I’ve got friends at my doorstep. I also equally love that sense of retreat and sanctuary; we could be in the house the whole weekend and feel like we’re not around everyone else at all,” Cosentino says. On the flip side, last summer, they say, was full of plenty of balmy evenings where private gatherings with family and friends spilled into common areas, and impromptu alfresco meals were shared, with their children playing in the communal garden. “Those incidental interactions are so beautiful and bring such a buzz.”
These two projects have been nominated for a slew of awards – the Davison Collaborative was a finalist for the Victorian premier’s design awards, while Northcote Townhouses received a commendation in the Houses awards. While they underline how collectives with the right professional and financial capital can leverage their resources into remarkable housing solutions, they were no small undertaking.
“It’s very difficult for just anyone to do it, unfortunately,” Wallis says. Their project was stalled at planning, and then at the Victorian civil and administrative tribunal (Vcat), for a year. And, like the Northcote venture, the professional experience of the members made all the difference.
In an effort to keep friendships intact, the Davison Collaborative deferred broad spectrum project management to Hip V. Hype because “it’s impossible to run a complex project if you have to go back to someone with every decision, but there are select, important decisions that need collective agreement and so we carved those out [early on],” Wallis says.
For less prepared consortiums, Tim Riley is in the business of filling knowledge gaps. His company Property Collectives has worked on 11 collaborative housing projects around Melbourne and charges a fixed management fee to guide groups of families, friends and occasionally strangers through the process of property development, right through to final fixtures.
He says the kind of people who use his service “aren’t seeing the sort of homes on the market that they would want to live in, at a price point that makes sense to them”.
“There’s an acknowledgment that if we want to create this little co-housing community of 10 or 20 households, we need to do it ourselves.”
While participants often save upwards of $100,000 compared with buying a similar home in a similar area, Riley says these homes are not “capital-A affordable”. But beyond design and financial imperatives, he believes there is something deeper at play.
“I think it is all rooted in a belief that having more meaningful social connections with your neighbours is a really valuable thing to have in life,” Riley says.
“For the young families that are involved, the desire to have a place where their kids are growing up in a supportive community with a range of people in different life stages is really attractive. And similarly for the older generation, they’re not wanting to go to a retirement village, they’re wanting an intergenerational community.”
Riley says his company keeps contracts as standard as possible “so that lenders, builders and the whole ecosystem doesn’t see it as being terribly strange”.
On an interpersonal level, Riley thinks consortiums are most successful when participants share a clear vision. Typically they employ “sociocracy”, which establishes from the outset which decisions need to be unanimous and which require majority approval. Each household has one vote. “And that can reduce a lot of friction through the process.”
The company then walks all participants through a plan of work that has seven decision gates, starting with strategic vision and ending up in operations. He says that “chunking” the herculean task makes the process less daunting. The process from forming the group to moving in takes on average four years.
While no longer a resident of the Brunswick project, Wallis believes every block on Davison Street could easily accommodate similar ventures, turning nine homes into 27.
“We did a bit of an exercise and looked at, within a kilometre radius, how many blocks of land were on laneways in Brunswick with the same attributes as our site. There was something like 500. We could turn 500 family homes into 1,500.
“We don’t need to build 20-level buildings to increase density. We just need to use what we have more effectively.”

Canadians warm to EU ‘associate membership’ proposal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

04:53:55 KST

Canadians warm to EU ‘associate membership’ proposal
From work and study to trade, Canadians see new possibilities in closer ties with the European Union.
Some Canadians are already embracing their newfound European identities after the European Union floated the potential for “associate member” status amid the trade war with the United States.
“Telling my boss I don’t need to show up for work today cuz I’m [European],” an X user joked as talk of closer ties between Canada and the EU spawned a flood of memes about everything from cigarettes for breakfast to generous European vacation time.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Trump says Canada becoming EU ‘associate member’ could be ‘hostile act’
- list 2 of 4UK’s Burnham, Canada’s Carney discuss AI risks, defence cooperation
- list 3 of 4Canada’s Carney welcomes EU’s associated membership proposal
- list 4 of 4Can ‘middle powers’ come together to build a new economic alliance?
“If Canada joins the EU I’m taking [seven] weeks off work next summer,” wrote another user.
Canada is not joining the EU, but the prospect of a new kind of relationship with Europe had been kicking around for days.
It comes after Canada and the US’s trade war broke out as negotiations failed to head off US President Donald Trump’s threatened 50 percent tariffs on nearly $20bn worth of Canadian products, including machinery, textiles and hockey sticks. Back-and-forth retaliatory measures have resulted in both sides slapping new tariffs on each other.
Canadian officials initially pushed back on news reports of the “associate membership” possibility with the EU.
Then, on Wednesday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen made the proposal public. By Thursday, Canada’s own vision was becoming clearer.
Addressing the European Parliament in Strasbourg, Prime Minister Mark Carney welcomed von der Leyen’s ambition, describing what he wanted as an “alliance for the future” spanning critical minerals, defence, artificial intelligence, energy, digital trade, research and financial services.
He also called for making it easier for young Canadians and Europeans to work, study and live on either side of the Atlantic.
“Canada and Europe are each strong,” Carney told EU legislators. “Europe and Canada are stronger together.”
In response to the talks of closer economic relations, Trump threatened to take action against the EU if it moves forward with von der Leyen’s proposal of associate membership for Canada.
“If they do that, if I think it’s at all a hostile act, I will put very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe on many things,” Trump told reporters, calling the proposal “laughable”.
Looking beyond the US
Whatever the partnership is ultimately called, getting closer to Europe appears to have broad support at home.
An Abacus Data survey conducted from September 4 to 9, before the proposal was officially confirmed, found 81 percent of Canadians supported closer integration with the EU while remaining outside the bloc, including making it easier for transatlantic trade, travel, work and study. Eighty percent backed deeper cooperation on foreign policy, defence and economic priorities, up six percentage points since February.
David Coletto, founder and CEO of Abacus Data, said he did not expect those numbers to have shifted significantly now that the conversation has turned to “associate membership”.
He said the support makes more sense against a striking shift in how Canadians view the United States. Positive impressions of the EU have risen to 71 percent, while just 21 percent now have a positive view of the US.
“Canadians overwhelmingly [feel] still angry and a sense of betrayal over how the Trump administration has approached the Canada-US relationship,” Coletto told Al Jazeera.
Flight attendant Donna Gordon welcomes closer ties. She was among several people Al Jazeera spoke to in Nathan Phillips Square in Toronto on Thursday.
She said they made sense given “the state of our negotiations with the United States right now, or lack thereof”. Having travelled frequently to Europe for work, she said she had seen its “efficiency” and “innovation” firsthand.
She was particularly excited about what closer ties could mean for younger Canadians, including greater opportunities to study and work in Europe.
The pull of Europe
For Riyad Choy, that possibility was one of the biggest draws. The Canadian who works for a tech company in New York said greater freedom to live and work in Europe was particularly appealing.
“I would love to have the opportunity,” he said. “I want to be able to have that freedom of movement.”
While older Canadians were more likely to prioritise trade and security, 38 percent of 18-to-29-year-olds polled by Abacus listed study, training and research among their top priorities for a closer EU relationship.
“The thing that most people in Canada and I think a lot of people around the world are just seeking more agency, more control to make choices for themselves,” Coletto said.
For many Canadians, Europe may feel like a natural place to exercise that choice.
Asked which side they had more in common with in terms of values, way of life and outlook on the world, 56 percent chose countries in the EU. Only 16 percent chose the United States.
Peter Van Driel is a hydrogeologist whose father is Dutch Canadian and who previously lived in Germany. He described Canada as culturally “sort of in between” Europe and the United States, pointing to differences in healthcare, gun laws, parental leave and vacation time.
“We’re not as generous as Europe, but more generous than the States,” he said.
But while Van Driel said there was little point trying to please a US administration that was “not being a good partner”, he cautioned against pursuing closer ties with Europe simply as a reaction to Washington.
“I want to see us explore EU partnerships for positive reasons,” he said, pointing to Canada’s natural resources and critical minerals, as well as similarities in education and values.
Defining the relationship
What those partnerships will actually entail, however, remains an open question. The two sides are expected to keep fleshing out the relationship in the coming weeks, including at a Canada-EU summit in Montreal next month.
That uncertainty has given critics room to offer their own interpretations.
Conservative leader Pierre Poilievre framed closer integration as a question of Canadian sovereignty after von der Leyen’s “associate membership” proposal.
“No EU taxes, no EU laws and no EU open-border immigration policies should be imposed on Canadians. Canada must be independent and sovereign. Period,” Poilievre said.
None of those measures have been proposed. There is no indication that Canada would be required to adopt EU taxes or laws, or open its borders under the arrangement being discussed.
But the polling suggests that those critiques may have an audience and that support for closer ties has its limits. While 81 percent backed greater integration while Canada remained outside the EU, support stood at 49 percent when respondents were asked about full membership, with 30 percent opposed and 21 percent unsure.
The partisan gap was wider on full membership: 64 percent of Liberal voters supported it, compared with 33 percent of Conservatives. Yet 70 percent of Conservative voters still backed closer integration while remaining outside the bloc.
Nancy Tung, a retired legal assistant, said Canada had been too reliant on the United States and should “spread its wings”, citing potential benefits for trade, business and international relationships.
She said, however, that she wanted any relationship with Europe to remain an “equal partnership” and wondered what Canada might be expected to contribute financially.
“Do we have to contribute a lot?” she asked. “In the long run, do we have any monetary obligation?”
Narcisse Kakegabon, a band councillor with Long Lake 58 First Nation, also saw potential benefits in finding new markets for Canadian products and minerals, but worried about how the Trump administration might respond.
“You get all the threats from the US, Donald Trump, about there could be consequences for Canada and the EU,” he said. “We really don’t know what’s gonna happen.”

Stop the Bibi bashing and focus on the issues, not the man - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
19:51:12 UTC
04:51:12 KST

To set the record straight, I have never voted for Benjamin Netanyahu or his party, and doubt that I ever will. But he is the prime minister, and I must respect the office he holds. To do otherwise is a blight on democracy.
People who truly believe in democracy must accept the results of an election. They can voice their protests against the policies of the administration, but they should respect the nation’s leaders.
An attack on the leaders contributes to paving the path to anarchy.
I don’t have a clue how many of the stories about Netanyahu are true or false, but I do know that the more he is attacked by Israelis, the more ammunition is given to Israel’s enemies.
Personally, I think he made a mistake in holding off a state commission of inquiry into what led to the horrific events of October 7. Whether he is considered responsible or not is less important than learning where Israel erred, and how not to repeat the same error, which is commonly referred to in Hebrew as the conceptzia.
They’re blaming Netanyahu, they’re blaming Gadi Eisenkot, they’re blaming Benny Gantz, and a whole bunch of others who were part of the decision making process at security meetings over the years.
October 7 didn’t just happen out of the blue. It was a meticulously planned operation. What’’s important is how it developed below the radar of Israel’s intelligence network, not what time Bibi got out of bed.
How is it that Mossad was able to score points in Iran, but missed the train in Gaza?
It’s not as if there were no warning signs. There were, and they were reported – and they were ignored.
Why?
Were there senior officers who objected to female spotters, and thought they should be concentrating on their domestic skills instead of serving in the army?
Or did they simply think that the young women were panicking because they belonged to the so-called weaker sex, and simply treated their warnings as false alarms?
Every possible scenario must be explored, and any commission of inquiry should include mystery writers and film makers whose creative minds will come up with all kinds of possibilities that may not occur to military personnel.
People change as they get older, and Bibi has probably changed a lot since he was a heroic young soldier under the command of Ehud Barak, and the two rescued hostages from a Sabena plane that was hijacked in flight by Palestinian terrorists, as it traveled from Vienna to Tel Aviv. That was more than half a century ago. Even though I totally disagree with Netanyahu politically, I have every confidence that he is no less a patriot today than he was then – though these days, he’s a lot more cautious.
But Barak, whose voice is frequently heard in anti-Bibi circles, is not cautious. It is perfectly legitimate for Barak, a product and former leader of the Left, to challenge policies set by Bibi, a product and current leader of the Right. But Barak should not be attacking Bibi’s character, especially when giving interviews to foreign media.
To do so encourages further character assassination, such as that displayed in the AI-generated judicial reform campaign video released by Bezalel Smotrich, in which he showed Chief Justice Isaac Amit and Attorney-General Gali Baharav-Miara being arrested by police and dragged through the streets. This was so outrageously below the belt that even people on the Right who support judicial reform were outraged.
While I understand what it means to bereaved families to have Bibi either admit to being accountable or having a commission of inquiry decide that he’s accountable, it doesn’t really serve any purpose. It doesn’t bring back the dead. It doesn’t heal the wounded. It doesn’t stop the grief and the mourning.
All it does is remove him from office and provide some temporary satisfaction for people who want to see him suffer as they have suffered.
Then again, it’s a different kind of suffering.
Netanyahu has been trying to make amends in recent weeks, but that may be because of the elections, or simply because he’s had more time to think about the situation and to display a more humane side of his personality.
As there is no likelihood of the establishment of a commission of inquiry before the elections, let us at least look at the issues on which the coalition and the opposition agree and make that the foundation of a temporary truce that could lead to greater solidarity in the future. There will still be disputes, but there are disputes within political parties, not just between opposing parties. However, disputes do not need to be violent or disrespectful.
The idea is for each side to understand where the other is coming from and where it hopes to go.
There are people on both sides who do dialogue with each other, just as there are Israelis and Palestinians who are not only neighbors but friends with different opinions.
We need to accept that others do not have to think as we do. The marketplace of different ideas can lead to many great things.
While we continue our internal squabbles, the enemy perceives us as weak. This was among the many theories of what prompted the Hamas attack. Israel’s national unity was crumbling from within – a factor that may have indicated the time was ripe for an external assault.
We dare not make that mistake again. Avoiding it starts with new rules to the game. Be critical of unjust policies, but don’t attack the leader. In other words, stop the Bibi bashing and focus on the issues, not the man.

NEW YORK – When 10-year-old George Burdynski Jr hopped on his bike on May 24, 1993, near his Maryland home, it was the last time his family saw him.
The disappearance of George, who was also known as Junior, shocked Prince George’s County in Maryland and prompted a large search by law enforcement, including the FBI. Volunteers also joined the search.
But the case languished for more than 33 years.
Now, investigators say they have arrested a 61-year-old man, Joseph Lynch, who has been charged with second-degree murder, rape and other sexual abuse charges in connection with George’s disappearance.
Another person, a 47-year-old man, whom Lynch also sexually assaulted, admitted to beating George to death, authorities said.
That unidentified man has not been charged, the Prince George’s County Police Department said. The county state attorney’s office would not comment on Sept 18.
“We held on to hope for 33 years,” said Virginia Burdynski, George’s sister, at a news conference on Sept 17. “This is not what we prayed for.”
Investigators got a break in the case after a witness, the 47-year-old man, stepped forward in June and said he was with George and Lynch at the time of the boy’s disappearance.
The witness, who was 13 in 1993, lived in George’s neighbourhood.
Lynch physically and sexually assaulted the witness on the day that George disappeared, according to a statement of charges.
On that same day, Lynch forced the witness to sexually assault George while Lynch watched, the statement said.
The witness told investigators he could not direct his anger toward Lynch and instead targeted George, who was younger and smaller, the statement said.
“The witness admitted repeatedly punching and kicking the victim until the victim stopped moving,” the statement said. “The witness recalled observing blood coming from the victim’s head and believed that the victim was dead or had been fatally injured.”
Lynch retrieved a knife, tarp and rope and rolled George inside, the statement said.
Lynch and the witness carried George’s body to a location in Prince George’s County and disposed of him, the statement said.
George’s body has never been found.
“Taken together, the suspect’s actions before, during and immediately after the offences establish that he was an active participant in the continuous course of criminal conduct that resulted in the victim’s death,” the statement said. NYTIMES

Trump says he will create ‘AI Force’ with new ‘AI czar’

United States President Donald Trump has announced he’s creating an “AI Force” and will appoint a new “AI czar” to oversee development of the nation’s artificial intelligence industry.
In a lengthy social media post on Saturday, Trump said he was doing so with a goal of protecting — and advancing — the development of AI, which he described as “the next Industrial Revolution” that would be key to the country’s economic growth. But despite the growing calls for AI to be reined in, Trump’s Saturday announcement reflects his anti-regulatory, pro-growth stance towards a technology he says he believes is key to competing against China.

That is Dhara. What I mean by Dhara is D - disruptive; H - hyper-connectedness; A - asymmetry; R - realignment; and A - autonomy.”“The world is undergoing enormous disruption. Summer of 2026 broke records in Europe, and caused deaths
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
19:47:00 UTC
04:47:00 KST

Summer of 2026 broke records in Europe, and caused deaths
September 19, 2026
The summer (June to August) of 2026 was the warmest in Europe since records began, beating the record set in 2003, according to the Copernicus Climate Change Service,
Not only that, Germany's DWD weather service says that there was an "unprecedented" number of hot days this year. "On average across Germany,there were about 22 hot days with temperatures of at least 30 degrees Celsius and about five very hot days with temperatures of at least 35 degrees Celsius," the DWD wrote in in a press release at the end of August.
The estimated number of heat-related deaths also reached unprecedented levels, with at least 16,300 people dying by the end of August, even if few of them died directly because of the heat, but rather as a consequence of underlying health conditions exacerbated by the heat.
The figures were compiled from a statistical correlation between the number of deaths recorded by Germany's Federal Statistical Office and the temperatures measured by the DWD during a specific period.
Heat-related deaths in Germany are more likely if the average weekly temperature reaches 20 degrees Celsius or more. This is the average of all hourly temperatures recorded in a week, including at nighttime.
This year, the average weekly temperatures in the country rose above the 20-degree mark several times. It was particularly hot at the end of June, when the average weekly temperature reached above 26 degrees between the 22nd and 28th of the month.
Excess mortality during heat waves
Though it is not possible to determine a cause of death using statistics, researchers and medical professionals have a good understanding of how heat affects the human body, and there is widespread consensus that excess mortality during heat waves is possible.
"It was not just the high temperatures on the thermometer that were important, but also how long the heat lasted and the fact that it hardly cooled down at night," said Andreas Matzarakis, professor of environmental meteorology at Freiburg University.
Many people have trouble sleeping on hot nights. Yet, getting enough sleep is important so that the body can recover from the heat and stress of the day.
Matzarakis said that the severity of heat stress was not related solely to air temperatures. Humidity, solar radiation and wind also played a role — and what is known as the 'felt' temperature. He said that humidity and still air could place a heavy strain on the body, even in moderate temperatures.
Underprivileged most vulnerable
The less privileged members of society were also among the most vulnerable, said Martin Röösli, environmental scientist at the Swiss Tropical and Public Health Institute in Basel. "They are more likely to live in homes that are not well insulated or are more likely to work outdoors."
A large proportion of those who died because of the heat probably had only a short life expectancy left, due to their age and medical conditions, but Röösli said that there was a consensus that "some of the deceased could have lived for a long time and were simply in a fragile state at the time of the heat wave."
For Alexandra Schneider, a meteorologist and epidemiologist at the Helmholtz center in Munich in southern Germany, the deaths that occurred during the heat waves were very likely not only because of the "harvesting effect," which describes "how a heat wave causes very vulnerable individuals in particular to die a few days or weeks prematurely."
Had this been the case, there would have been a deficit of mortality in the following weeks, which did not happen. Thus, she believes, a significant proportion of those who died could have lived on for months or even years.
This article was translated from German.

Mecca Alliance will be ‘game-changing platform’: Turkish foreign minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
19:36:29 UTC
04:36:29 KST

The three-nation Mecca Alliance will be a “very game-changing platform,” Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said Saturday, adding that the initiative has reached an advanced stage, with efforts underway to establish its headquarters and assign personnel.
Speaking to Turkish broadcaster NTV on foreign policy issues, Fidan said there is “a very strong will” behind the alliance forged last month between Türkiye, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan, and that Ankara is working to turn this political will into action.
“The Mecca Alliance is really at a good stage. There’s a very strong will that has been put forward. We’re working with all our strength to put this will into action,” Fidan said.
“The Mecca Alliance will be a very game-changing platform,” he added.
Fidan said steps toward the institutionalization of the alliance are underway, particularly work to establish a secretariat envisaged under the agreement and a military headquarters affiliated with it.
He said detailed preparations on both structures have “almost been completed” and that the three countries have reached a common understanding on how they will operate.
According to Fidan, the next stage will be to deploy personnel and make the headquarters operational.
He said that once institutionalization steps are completed, talks could be held with the other two founding countries on admitting new members.
“It is an alliance open to the countries of the region,” he said.
Fidan said the initiative was not intended to create a new regional bloc against other countries but to establish a common defense framework based on regional ownership.
Türkiye’s regional vision, he said, is to bring together as many countries as possible to establish an environment of trust, address regional problems more effectively, and prevent new crises from emerging.
“The basic point of departure for all of this is the search for regional solutions to regional problems,” he said.
Addressing recent attacks by Yemen’s Houthis on Saudi Arabia, Fidan said the issue has existed for roughly a decade, adding that a ceasefire was reached in 2022 before tensions resurfaced following the start of the Gaza conflict.
He said Saudi Arabia’s territorial integrity, sovereignty, and infrastructure had faced serious attacks.
Under the alliance agreement, Fidan said, member countries have responsibilities toward one another as allies.
“We stand in solidarity on this issue,” he said, adding that alliance members are jointly assessing the situation.
Fidan said Türkiye has condemned attacks targeting Saudi Arabia, particularly those directed at Mecca and the country’s oil infrastructure.
He also stressed that Saudi Arabia should remain outside the ongoing dispute between Iran and the US, saying it is not seeking involvement in that confrontation.
“As members of the Mecca Alliance, we are closely monitoring the situation,” he said.
Fidan added that consultations are taking place outside the public eye and said Türkiye would have no difficulty responding if Saudi Arabia had military requirements in certain technical areas.
Asked about criticism from Israel, Iran, India, and Greece that the alliance had remained only “on paper,” Fidan dismissed the claims.
He argued that criticism from those countries itself reflects the significance they attach to the initiative, calling some of the comments attempts at disinformation meant to discredit the alliance.
Fidan also cited Türkiye’s decades of experience in NATO, saying that an alliance should not be judged simply by how frequently its collective defense mechanisms are activated.
He said it was premature to describe the Mecca Alliance as ineffective when the agreement was signed only last month, with institutional steps already moving forward.
Fidan also addressed Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s recent statements targeting Türkiye, saying he is trying to bolster his political fortunes at home and paint himself as indispensable.
“Hostility toward Türkiye is also a product of this. We don’t underestimate it,” Fidan said.
Israel has parliamentary elections just weeks away, on Oct. 27, with polls showing a very close race.
He said Ankara is closely monitoring Netanyahu’s statements, Israel’s policies, and its military cooperation with countries in the region.
Fidan said Türkiye hopes Israel will adopt a foreign policy based on peace, respect and cooperation that would serve both Israel and the wider region.
“Otherwise, it will not only grow increasingly isolated, but will also pay the price itself together with the region,” he said.
Fidan also accused Netanyahu of seeking to create prolonged areas of instability in Syria, following Lebanon and Palestine, in order to strengthen his domestic political position and paint himself as indispensable.
Fidan stressed, however, that Türkiye would act prudently and would not be drawn into what he described as provocations.
Türkiye, he said, does not act alone in the region and maintains partnerships with regional countries.
“Israel is a threat not only to the region but to the world,” Fidan added, referring specifically to the policies pursued by Netanyahu’s government.
He said international concern over those policies is increasingly visible, including among countries traditionally considered close to Israel.
Fidan added that Türkiye hopes the longer-term trajectory of the current regional developments will ultimately favor Palestinians.
On Syria, Fidan said there have been numerous issues requiring close coordination between Ankara and Damascus since December 2024, when the Assad regime fell, including Syria’s reconstruction, unity, territorial integrity, and cooperation with regional countries.
He said Türkiye and Syria had been tasked by their presidents with establishing a joint planning group to closely monitor bilateral projects and other areas of cooperation.
“Whatever happens in Syria and Iraq directly affects Türkiye,” Fidan said, adding that stability, peace, and development in both countries are therefore important for Ankara.
He said he recently reviewed these issues with Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa during a visit to Syria and conveyed messages from Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.
Fidan also said Erdogan and al-Sharaa met on the sidelines of July’s NATO summit in Ankara and discussed regional stability, potential risks, Syria’s integration process, and counterterrorism efforts.
On the process of the dissolution and integration of the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) into the Syrian state and military, Fidan said there is a desire among the parties to move the process forward in a controlled manner.
He described the statements and positions currently being taken by the parties as positive, but said they would need to be followed by concrete steps.
Fidan added that Türkiye is closely monitoring the process through contacts with Syrian security and intelligence institutions, including potential risks and how they are being managed.
Addressing regional tensions linked to Yemen and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, Fidan said there are numerous diplomatic initiatives underway but that these efforts need to produce outcomes acceptable to the relevant parties.
He said there has been a deadlock in negotiations between Iran and the US over the past few months.
According to Fidan, one consequence of the impasse has been the expansion of tensions beyond direct exchanges between the two sides to developments involving Yemen and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
He said the confrontation is becoming increasingly complicated and risks spreading further toward Saudi Arabia.
Fidan said Türkiye is placing particular emphasis on efforts to bring US-Iran negotiations to a conclusion but noted that there is “great distrust” between the two sides.
He said Iran and the US this June reached a common understanding in Pakistan, but difficulties later emerged during implementation of their framework deal.
Both sides, he added, subsequently began interpreting the process differently in ways that served their respective interests.
Fidan said new proposals had been presented to the parties and expressed hope that they would be accepted.
He also warned that the economic consequences of the continuing regional crisis are becoming increasingly difficult for some countries to absorb.
There is a serious bottleneck affecting energy routes, he said, adding that countries such as Türkiye, whose industries and economies depend heavily on imported energy, are facing increasingly significant economic challenges.

Beijing slams new US sanctions against Russia
China has condemned the latest expansion of US sanctions against Russia, including potential tariffs of up to 100% on major buyers of Russian energy, vowing to take “all necessary measures” to safeguard its national interests.
US President Donald Trump signed the sweeping legislation on Friday. Among other measures, the bill authorizes secondary sanctions against the five largest buyers of Russian crude oil and natural gas. It does not explicitly name major importers such as China or India.
Beijing strongly condemned the measure, with a Chinese Commerce Ministry spokesperson saying the country has “always opposed unilateral sanctions that lack the mandate of the UN,” as well as “the imposition of so-called secondary sanctions.”
China has consistently conducted “economic and trade cooperation with other countries on the basis of equality and mutual benefit,” the spokesperson said, adding that such ties are “neither directed at third parties nor subject to interference or coercion by third parties.”
China will closely monitor Washington’s actions and the “follow-up measures” stemming from its latest move. Beijing reserves the right “to take all necessary measures to firmly safeguard [its] national sovereignty and development interests and the legitimate rights and interests of enterprises,” the spokesperson stated while expressing hopes that China and the US will be able to “maintain the stability of economic and trade relations through dialogue and consultation.”
The latest anti-Russian measure was initially proposed by late Republican Senator and Russia hawk Lindsey Graham and Democrat Richard Blumenthal in April 2025. In the year and a half of negotiations, it was significantly watered down, with the originally proposed 500% tariffs on countries that buy Russian energy cut down to 100%, while the actual levy rate can be set below that ceiling, according to the legislation.
Moscow has condemned the additional sanctions as an “unfriendly” move, which was bound to “complicate efforts to find a peaceful settlement in Ukraine,” according to Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov.

Yom Kippur 2026: Does a text message or social media post count as a real apology?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
19:34:12 UTC
04:34:12 KST

Aside from fasting for 25 hours, one of the most challenging requirements of the Day of Atonement is asking forgiveness from someone we hurt or offended in the past year.
“Coming to Yom Kippur and banging on your chest doesn’t do anything. God doesn’t forgive on your behalf. It doesn’t work that way,” said Zev M. Shandalov, a former Chicago pulpit rabbi and an educator, lecturer, author, and community rabbi in Ma’aleh Adumim since 2009.
“We have to go to that person and ask for forgiveness with a heartfelt ‘I’m sorry.’ The struggle today versus, let’s say, just 20 years ago is how that apology should appear.”
Avoiding uncomfortable face-to-face confrontations is easier than ever. We can send texts or voice messages, write emails, or post on social media our requests for forgiveness – mehila, in Hebrew.
Do these modern modes of communication count, or are they just cowardly cop-outs?
Be authentic
Hillel Fuld, a tech columnist and Israel advocate with approximately 750,000 social-media followers, spends a lot of time interacting with people online.
Yet when it comes to apologizing, he said, “sending a text message just doesn’t feel authentic. I get a ton of mass messages before Yom Kippur – Please forgive me, blah, blah, blah – but I don’t do that. If you’re going to ask forgiveness, be authentic about it.”
Fuld said that if he feels the need to beg someone’s pardon, “I don’t care if we’re in the digital age or not – I’m gonna get in my car and go meet that person.”
Shandalov, too, said that “the best option is to physically go to the person asking for forgiveness.” He cited the 12th-century sage Maimonides (Rambam), who wrote that proper repentance requires meeting with the wronged party.
“Of course, the Rambam didn’t have WhatsApp, but he could have said it’s okay to write a letter. But he says no, you have to have an interaction with the person and truly ask for forgiveness,” Shandalov said.
“If that’s not possible, do it in a video chat or phone call. However, sometimes saying ‘I’m sorry’ directly is a very tough thing to do. A voice note is the next best option because at least the recipient can hear the inflection in the sender’s voice.”
He considers the least desirable method to be a “general vanilla message on Facebook that says, ‘To all those whom I might have hurt, I’m sorry.’ There’s no meaning behind that.”
Nobody wants to be a checklist item
A different perspective on mass apology messages is offered by lecturer and author Oriya Mevorach, whose Afarkeset Institute provides educational tools, lectures, and workshops for navigating postmodern and Western culture through a Jewish worldview.
“The problem is not the medium,” she said.
“It’s even a blessing today that we have the opportunity to write something general. In the age of social media, we communicate with so many people – sometimes thousands of people – and we can use the same platform to make amends.”
The problem is that blanket social-media apology posts rarely include the elements necessary to trigger a forgiveness response. Instead, they may be perceived as insulting or insincere.
“What people don’t want to see is that you’re saying sorry as a checklist item. Nobody wants to be a checklist item,” she said.
“When I want someone to ask me for forgiveness, first I would like them to acknowledge what they did wrong; and second, to acknowledge that they know I was insulted or offended by what they did. If a general message would include even just the first part, it’s not that bad,” Mevorach explained.
“If a person would write, for example, ‘I know I often come across as offensive and I sometimes attack people online, and I’m aware of this weakness of mine, and I want to apologize to anyone who was insulted by me,’ I think that’s legit,” she said. “The text must be elaborated enough so people understand we are taking responsibility for a specific action.”
The ideal approach, however, is to send a direct personal message containing “the exact words that the recipient would like to hear.”
Because many of us may have difficulty crafting such a message, she suggests using AI tools such as ChatGPT to help phrase a personalized request for mehila.
Accepting a texted apology
The wording of a texted apology will determine how it is received, Shandalov agreed.
“If you feel the text message that someone sends you is adequate, then accept the apology, say ‘thank you very much,’ and put it behind you,” he counseled.
“But if you can’t accept it, you should respond, ‘Listen, I think this requires more of a discussion. I don’t want to make you feel awkward, but we need to talk about some stuff before I could really give you true forgiveness.’ And that’s fine.”
Jewish tradition stipulates that one is permitted to spurn an apology twice, “because sometimes we can’t forgive something or we don’t think the apology is sincere. By the third time you have to say, ‘Yes, I forgive you.’ If you don’t, you are considered a rasha, a bad person – although it depends on the specific situation,” he added.
According to Shandalov, one must ask for mehila even from a deceased person by vocalizing the apology at the person’s grave.
But as Fuld can attest, it’s certainly preferable to seek forgiveness while the wronged party is still among the living.
Years ago, he got into a heated political discussion with an unknown commenter on his Facebook page. “Unfortunately, I lost my cool and called him a self-hating Jew,” he recalled.
A week later, Fuld was asked by the marketing department of a client company to participate in a phone call pitching the company’s story to a journalist.
“At the end of the conversation, the journalist is like, ‘Okay, fantastic, I’ll write the story. Oh, and Hillel, by the way: Remember the guy you called a self-hating Jew last week on Facebook? That was me.’”
Fuld felt devastated.
“When you’re on the Internet, you don’t put a face to it. Speaking to someone whom I called that name was really upsetting for me. So I apologize profusely, and he’s like, ‘It’s totally cool. I know how the Internet works. We get worked up. Totally fine, all good.’ And that was the end of that.”
A few days later, Fuld was shocked to hear that the journalist had died suddenly and unexpectedly. “I was so grateful that I’d had a chance to make it right with him. The fact that I was able to correct my mistake before he died was of astronomic importance to me.”
The Talmud, said Shandalov, encourages us to emulate God’s attributes. “God is described as mohel v’sole’ah, forgiving and pardoning. So it’s important to understand that granting forgiveness is not just repairing a relationship. It’s a godly act.”

The Haredi Public: A politically responsible voice from Israel's ultra-Orthodox public - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
19:34:05 UTC
04:34:05 KST

Unfortunately, we have gotten used to snarling haredi (ultra-Orthodox) rabbis and politicians who dismiss the concerns of the general Israeli public and disassociate themselves from the burden (actually, the privilege) of running and defending the State of Israel.
By their own admission, all they seek is sinecures for their secluded public, especially the narrowly self-defined Torah/yeshiva “world.”
From this distorted, so-called “Torah perspective,” the task of haredi politicians has been to secure haredi interests against Israeli society and to defend “their people” from “our state” – the “impure” and threatening Zionist state.
Alas, “our” army is not their responsibility. “Our” economy is not their responsibility either. God alone, “their” God, will take care of the bigger picture, along with the beleaguered Israeli taxpayer who pays through his nose and the “suckers” who serve in the Israeli army.
One might have thought that the trauma, suffering, financial deprivation, and household disruption of the past three years in the general Israeli public and in the “Torani” (ardently Torah observant) Religious Zionist community would shock the haredi community out of its crushingly insular shell.
One had hoped that honorable haredi leaders would be stirred toward somewhat increased integration in Israeli society and would nudge forward toward national service in frameworks specially attuned to haredi sensibilities.
One might have imagined great haredi leaders participating in at least one or two of the many funerals for fallen soldiers, or showing up at soldier shiva houses to pay condolences, or quietly taking a minyan (prayer quorum) of their boys late at night to pray at the Mount Herzl military cemetery.
But nada. No movement at the leadership level. Haredi politicians, like the recently deposed MK Moshe Gafni of the Degel HaTorah/UTJ party, spent 40 years insulting and sneering at the secular and Religious Zionist publics and only doubled down on this over the past three years.
Despite October 7, “mainstream” haredi politicians have stuck to the line that “yeshiva boys” (about 100,000 of them) cannot be drafted in any minimal way (whether they are really learning Torah full time or not) or educated any differently.
These leaders are purposefully and devastatingly cut off from the war reality that most Israelis are living. Worse still, they are unflinchingly unfeeling toward the broader public, as their spokesmen unfortunately have made clear.
This is a historic tragedy that has the potential to crash the modern State of Israel, no less, in the Heavens and on earth.
Fortunately, and finally, substantial numbers of haredi Israelis are moving away from this hostile approach. They think for themselves and are seeking alternative political leadership.
They realize that the rejectionist, protectionist posture described above may have been sustainable when the haredi community was a small and embattled minority. It cannot provide a vision for a community rapidly becoming a central pillar in Israeli society. It does not provide a satisfying vision for haredi people themselves.
Enter the Haredi Public party, running for the Knesset for the first time. The new political party begins from a wholly different premise from that of UTJ or Shas: that they, haredi people, are part of the Israeli story.
They do not mean to abandon haredi identity; they believe that haredi Judaism is strong enough to take responsibility for Torah, family, and community, as well as responsibility for sustainable livelihood, defense, civic life, and the future of Israel.
As the visionary chair of the new party’s rabbinic committee, Yehoshua Pfeffer said at the party launch event: “Our initiative means moving from a politics of fear to a politics of hope. It means hope that haredi young people will no longer feel forced to choose between belonging to their community and building a responsible life within the Jewish state.
“It means that the haredi world believes it can grow, mature, and assume a larger and constructive role in strengthening and defending Israel – without losing its soul.
“God did not bring millions of Jews back to the land of our fathers for Israel to fail. Nor did haredi society build its extraordinary world of Torah, family, charity, and community in order to remain forever on the margins of the national story. The next chapter can be different. The question is whether we have the courage to write it.”
The new party, led by its articulate and measured chairman Moti Leitner (a hassidic deputy mayor of Beit Shemesh and a software professional), advocates for protecting those who truly learn Torah full-time while advancing meaningful service for all those who do not, and for giving haredi youth the necessary educational tools to succeed in life and contribute to the Israeli economy and society.
This means working with, not against, the IDF to create haredi service tracks from hesder programs to special brigades and soft military-industrial and civilian-security national service frameworks.
It means rapidly and massively expanding the state-supported haredi school stream that teaches the core curriculum of English, math, science, and civics alongside Torah and Talmud, and which prepares its graduates for potential college study.
Leitner explained that the party was born out of deep conversations with representatives of many haredi communities who felt their voice was not being heard and their needs were not represented within the existing haredi political parties. This includes working haredi people, as well as professionally successful women, haredi immigrants from abroad, and more.
A voice for opportunity and change
These haredim also are horrified by the public and often violent shaming of young haredim who serve in the security force, by campaigns of vilification and terror against even great Torah sages who support cautious change in the haredi world, and by rampant corruption in some haredi municipalities and institutions.
This haredi public also recognizes that too many of its youth are dropping out of schools and feeding the phenomenon of lost street youth without being offered paths that would legitimate a synthesis of haredi identity and professional and national advancement.
Leitner emphasized that the haredi public he represents wants opportunities, not stipends, for haredi young men and women; opportunities to grow and contribute and serve the nation, not to be on the government dole.
The Haredi Public party’s decision to put two women near the top of its Knesset candidate list tells you how bold the new party is. This is unprecedented and long overdue for the haredi public – a breath of fresh air.
The two haredi women in the party – Dr. Nechumi Yaffe (a political psychologist who once worked for the National Security Council) and Ziva Glanz (founder and CEO of the LaShuv olim network) – are impressive leaders.
Rabbi Pfeffer is an intrepid, insightful leader who founded the Iyun Institute at Herut-The Center for Israeli Liberty (formerly the Tikvah Fund), which operates a range of groundbreaking haredi leadership programs and publications.
He is a respected religious court judge, served in the IDF, chairs the public board of Netzah Yehuda, the haredi Nahal brigade, clerked at Israel’s Supreme Court, and is a professor at Hebrew University’s law school.
Pfeffer is truly a model par excellence of a haredi community leader “taking responsibility” for the future of Israel, not shunning and deprecating Israel. I am proud to consider him a close friend!
In fact, I am considering voting for the Haredi Public 40 days from now, even though I do not belong to the ultra-Orthodox community and I dissent from the party platform, which would still give, at least for the next while, a broad exemption from conscription for full-time yeshiva men (not including hesder programs).
This new party – this bold new haredi movement – needs electoral support. Recent polls indicate that it has captured the imagination of the haredi street and the support of about 10% of haredi voters, amounting to about 100,000 voters (or 2.5 Knesset seats), and rising.
This is an astonishing achievement that portends even greater success in the future, but the minimum threshold for election to the Knesset this year will probably be around 150,000 votes (or four seats).
So the new party needs a boost from non-haredi voters who understand the urgency and promise of the Haredi Public and want it to succeed. This will be a worthwhile investment in the long-term health of Judaism and Israeli society!
The writer is managing senior fellow at the Jerusalem-based Misgav Institute for National Security & Zionist Strategy. The views expressed here are his own. His diplomatic, defense, political, and Jewish world columns over the past 30 years are at davidmweinberg.com.
