Israel's ultra-Orthodox community can no longer avoid the hard conversations - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
19:33:51 UTC
04:33:51 KST

Haredim (ultra-Orthodox) made up roughly 2% of Israel’s population 60 years ago. Today, that number is around 13%, and demographers expect it to climb toward 20%, and even 30% within a generation or two. Growth on this scale changes what a community owes the country it lives in.
The haredi community can no longer function as a small group on the margins while others carry the weight of the economy, the army, and civic life. We are becoming a central pillar of this country, and pillars have to hold weight, not just take up space.
Parnassah (livelihood) has turned into something closer to a daily emergency for enormous numbers of haredi families, and I say that from watching it happen to people I know, including myself. Families are large, expenses grow faster than income, and parents find themselves colliding with a reality they were never given the tools to handle.
Our schools do extraordinary work building the spiritual and intellectual life of our children, but somewhere along the way we stopped teaching baseline skills such as arithmetic, English, and skills that any adult needs to earn a living in a modern economy.
Furthermore, about half of haredi students who eventually try to catch up through post-secondary study drop out, because they’re starting from too far behind. That’s a structural failure we built ourselves, and we can unbuild it without touching the yeshiva system meant for those who are meant to sit and study full time.
In my own city, Beit Shemesh, serious plans were underway to build a vocational training complex in the heart of the city, close enough that residents in a community soon approaching half a million people could reach it by bus or on foot and walk away with a trade.
Due to fear of militant elements in the community declaring war on that project, it has stalled. Sadly, this is not an isolated story, but happens across haredi cities whenever anyone tries to build a real path toward employment.
This is an act of harm against thousands of families, dressed up as a defense of Torah values. Torah values include the responsibility to support one’s household. Hazal, our great sages, never envisioned a community where the majority of people live from hand to mouth.
Political leadership bears direct responsibility for where we’ve landed. There is a sitting party leader who has spent the past year traveling the country, threatening institutions that try to switch educational networks to a state haredi system that includes more comprehensive studies in English and math, and this leader told administrators things like, “I’ll come to your house, and I’ll drop a torpedo on it,” and other more graphic language that I won’t share. This is bullying, and it has nothing to do with protecting Torah study.
There are currently 18 haredi Knesset members sitting in the government, and whatever leaves their mouths in public, their operating goal has been singular: make sure no haredi ever serves in the IDF. Everything else is theater.
Haredi hesder yeshivot combine Torah study, IDF service
Since October 7, the army has needed thousands more combat soldiers and thousands more in support roles, and the haredi community is one of the most available sources of manpower in the country. Fourteen haredi hesder yeshivot already exist, some for over a decade, combining serious Torah learning with military service, preserving kashrut, prayer, and ongoing Torah study for soldiers who serve.
These programs work. And yet they get little to no government funding, no institutional recognition, and are treated with open contempt by the same politicians who claim to speak for the haredi public.
When soldiers from our own community went through combat courses, the people who should have stood up publicly to thank them, to embrace them, men like haredi party leaders Yitzhak Goldknopf, Arye Deri, and Moshe Gafni, said nothing.
Worse, our young men who serve report being ignored, mocked, and undermined by the same leadership that benefits politically from claiming to represent all haredim. If those hesder frameworks were properly funded and expanded, we would not be talking about a few hundred participants. We would likely see thousands, and much of the manufactured tension around this issue would fade, because a respected pathway would finally exist for the many young men for whom full-time study was never realistic in the first place.
Ask any of these politicians what they’ve done to solve any of this, and the honest answer, spoken quietly by people close to them, is nothing. When pressed, the answer is always “yes, of course, someone should serve,” delivered in the exact tone people use when they mean the opposite.
Campaigns repeat the line while doing nothing to build it. That gap between what’s said and what’s done is the actual scandal here, more than any individual policy failure.
None of what I’m describing is really about economics or the army as separate issues. It’s about whether haredi leadership is willing to take ownership of the future it keeps promising to protect, instead of hiding behind slogans while institutions collapse and families quietly drown.
The haredi community has the numbers, the talent, and the values to lift this country into a new and bright future; we cannot be the ones to drag it down. What’s missing is leadership honest enough to admit where it has failed, and willing to build something better for the children, the community, and the country we all share.
The writer is chairman of the Haredi Public Party, a new political home for haredim who believe that protecting the world of Torah requires responsible leadership and practical solutions to the challenges facing our community. The party stands for genuine Torah study, increased educational options, dignified employment, appropriate military or national service, economic self-reliance, and a stronger partnership between the haredi community and all of the people of Israel.

Houthis install ‘Iranian’ radar, receive Iranian smuggling - report

A report at the UAE’s Al-Ain media says that “less than 10 days after the Houthis seized control of Yemen’s west coast, Iran rushed to transform this strategic geographical area into a theater of influence for itself.”
Historically, the UAE and therefore its media outlets have good contacts in Aden and the areas of southern Yemen. The UAE played a key role for years in Yemen, backing the Southern Transitional Council against the Houthis.
Now the report indicates that Iran may be playing a role in the area the Houthis captured on September 11 in Yemen. The Houthis launched a rapid offensive up the coast, capturing Mokha and also the areas along the Bab el-Mandab Strait. This is a strategic area.
“Security and media sources revealed that Iran has deployed radar systems in the commanding heights on the western coast, in addition to using the coastal strip as an outlet for smuggling military equipment from Somalia after field visits by its experts,” the report says. It doesn’t say what type of radar may have been placed nearby.
The report argues that this information “reveals Tehran’s efforts to exploit its Houthi arm to transform the Yemeni coast from Hodeidah to Bab el-Mandab into an advanced line of defense for its regional influence network.”
The Houthis have been increasing attacks on Saudi Arabia since the mid-September offensive. The Iranian-backed militias in Iraq also attacked Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline.
In addition to the radar, the Houthis are also involved in smuggling. “Iranian equipment and weapons shipments have recently arrived for the Houthi militias via the western coast.”
Iranian smuggling into Yemen faces challenges
In the past, the Iranians had an easier time smuggling systems into Yemen. Missiles and drone parts arrived by sea. The Iranians recently tried to reopen an air corridor to Yemen in July. The Saudis opposed this. The US has a maritime blockade of Iran. It is unclear how Iran would smuggle items to Yemen.
The sources told Al-Ain that shipments are being unloaded. “After their arrival from the coasts of Somalia, [the shipments] were supervised by Hassan Al-Attas, who is the head of the Fisheries Authority in the Red Sea, based in Hodeidah.”
Al-Ain says that “Attas runs a smuggling network that is a model of an integrated functional hierarchical structure closely linked to the leader Ibrahim Hassan Ismail Al-Madani, while the prominent leader Shaher Al-Qahoum, who trained in Iran, provides it with security cover.”
This type of name-dropping is typical of Al-Ain stories on Yemen. It illustrates the kind of messaging and sourcing behind the report. This is why these reports can matter.
“Al-Attas is also responsible for recruiting fishermen and those with deep maritime experience for the militias, managing smuggling operations from Iran by sea to the shores of Hodeidah, receiving shipments upon arrival, and delivering them to the Houthi militias, as recently reported.”
Houthis intend to create new reality along Red Sea
The goal of the Houthis is to create a new reality along the Red Sea. They are digging trenches in the mountains to prevent the government forces from re-taking the area. They are also increasing activity on the coastline.
“Sources have revealed the installation of radar systems and newly established sites in the highlands overlooking the western coast and the new areas of control.”
The report also says there is activity on Zuqar Island, also known as Jazirat Jebel Zuqar, which means the “Island of Mount Zuaqr,” near the Hanish island chain in the Red Sea.
“These steps come as an outcome of visits and field tours conducted by Iranian experts to vital sites, including Bab el-Mandab, the port and airport of Mokha, during which they met with engineers of the Houthi missile force to establish a new phase of threats to international navigation.”

California judge sentences former Syrian prison boss to 60 years for torturing inmates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
19:28:27 UTC
04:28:27 KST

California judge sentences former Syrian prison boss to 60 years for torturing inmates
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
A federal judge in California has sentenced a former Syrian prison warden to 60 years for torturing inmates and lying to immigration officials to get into the United States.
A jury convicted Samir Ousman Alsheikh, 74, in March of conspiracy to commit torture, three counts of torture, one count of visa fraud and one count of attempted naturalization fraud, according to the U.S. attorney’s office in Los Angeles.
Alsheikh was involved in torturing political dissidents to deter opposition to the regime of then-Syrian President Bashar Assad, according to the Justice Department.
Government officials say Alsheikh is the highest-ranking former member of the Assad regime to be tried and convicted in person outside Syria.
The Justice Department had sought no fewer than 80 years in prison, while Alsheikh requested five years, citing his age and his chronic medical conditions.
In handing down the sentence on Thursday, U.S. District Judge Hernán Vera remarked on the “utter reprehensibility” of Alsheikh’s crime, Courthouse News Service reported.
“The conduct was heinous, unimaginably cruel and unspeakably violent and brutal,” the judge reportedly said.
Nina Marino, Alsheikh’s attorney, said her client plans to appeal the sentence.
In a statement, First Assistant U.S. Atty. Bill Essayli said he hoped the sentence “gives some semblance of healing and closure to this defendant’s victims.”
“Criminals who inflict the type of savage brutality that this defendant did on his victims must never be granted refuge in our country,” Essayli said.
Samir Ousman Sheikh allegedly ordered inmates to a wing of a Syrian prison where they were then tortured with a device known as the ‘flying carpet.’
During Alsheikh’s trial, prosecutors presented evidence that Alsheikh ordered and participated in the torture of prisoners while he headed the Adra Prison, also known as Damascus Central Prison, from around 2005 to 2008.
Jurors heard testimony from three of Alsheikh’s victims who said they were packed into small, filthy, cold, wet cells that were infested with insects and other vermin. They described being tortured and seeing and hearing the torture of other prisoners.
The victims testified about being fastened to a device known as the “Flying Carpet,” which folded their bodies in half at the waist; about being manacled to the ceiling and suspended sometimes for days; and about being beaten while immobilized inside tires, according to the U.S. attorney’s office in L.A.
During the trial, prosecutors presented evidence that when detainees refused Alsheikh’s orders to harm political prisoners, he ordered them to be sent to an underground section of the prison known as Wing 13, where they were tortured.
Prosecutors also presented evidence that Alsheikh, who came to the country in 2020, lied to U.S. immigration authorities about his background to secure a green card and also on an application to naturalize as a U.S. citizen.
Alsheikh has been in custody since his arrest at Los Angeles International Airport in July 2024.
Khaled Abdul Malek, who testified about being detained and tortured under Alsheikh’s direction, praised the sentence in a statement.
“The land of freedom will never be a safe haven for slaughterers and those who committed crimes against humanity,” Malek said. “This trial is not the end, but the first step on the road toward accountability and justice for everyone whose hands have been stained with the blood of innocent people.”

Junior Matildas know the price they're willing to pay to make it
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
19:24:11 UTC
04:24:11 KST

Junior Matildas know the price they're willing to pay to make it to the top
In short:
The Junior Matildas qualified for the U-17 Women's World Cup for the first time, after making it to the semifinals of the Asian Cup.
Players hope it can be a stepping stone to higher senior honours.
What's next?
The tournament will be held in Morocco from October 17 to November 7.
Athletes are often told there's a price to pay if they want to make it to the top of elite sport.
And the journey has to start young, but the Junior Matildas are framing the cost of pursuing their dreams differently.
"No matter what you choose to do in life, there's a price of entry," coach Mike Cooper told ABC Sport.
"Whether that's how much time and effort you have to put into it as a mum and dad driving your child around, the ups and downs of playing well, not playing well, learning from that.
"No matter what level anyone's achieved in whatever sport, they've gone through similar things and knowing that and learning from that I think is really humbling."
Cooper comes from a teaching background, and with two teenage daughters of his own, is uniquely placed to tap into the teen psyche.
He knows the expectations placed on any team carrying the Matildas moniker, especially this group, which is the first Australian side to qualify for the U-17 Women's World Cup.
"We want to go with a purpose, we want to perform, want the girls to express themselves, be brave, be bold, make themselves proud before making other people proud," he said.
"And then come home and learn from that experience because whatever happens over there is just part of their journey."
Testing themselves against the best
It's the opportunity of a very young lifetime for players such as 15-year-old Willa Pearson.
She is already a familiar figure in the women's game here, becoming the youngest-ever A-League player last season when she debuted at 14.
She then broke Sam Kerr's record as the league's youngest-ever goalscorer.
But the Sydney FC defender is keeping a level head.
"That was crazy to be honest," Pearson told ABC Sport.
"It hasn't really sunk in. [I'm] trying to take it step by step, play as good as I can and when I get the opportunity to step on the field, perform as well as I can for Sydney."
Pearson captained the Junior Matildas at the Asian Cup, where a semifinal appearance secured qualification for the World Cup.
"[I've] had the opportunity to test myself against the best players in Asia," she said.
"So now bringing that to a world stage and playing against the European countries and hopefully if we make it past the group stage, America, that would just be insane, to have my benchmark against other players in the world."
Maeve Nicholas, 17, plays for Adelaide United, and was also part of the Asian Cup.
"I think so many people our age would only dream of this opportunity," she said.
"So I think just enjoying the experience, and then also making an impact and showing that Australian football, compared to other nations, is capable of achieving amazing things."
Quotable quotes
Part of Cooper's coaching arsenal includes different ways to bring the team together.
Currently, that involves the players learning Spanish and relating that to football, and he has previously had players and staff choose a quote to share.
"It's just multiple different ways to get to know each other, build connection and where possible link it back to the purpose of what we're trying to do," he said.
Nicholas is living by the mantra that "hard work beats talent when talent doesn't work hard".
"I think that resonates with me a lot because I'm always willing to work hard," she said.
"And I think that's definitely a part of our journey. You need to be willing to put in the effort in order to achieve the results.
Pearson opted for the famed 1-per-centers.
"My quote was '1 per cent better every day'," she said.
"I feel like you get so much thrown at you in life. You get setbacks, good achievements.
"So just trying to make sure everything you have that comes towards you, good or bad, you take a little bit out of that and see if you can be better the next day."
Simple words for mature minds, hoping it all pays off in the long run.

Turkey says it could help meet Saudi military needs under defence pact

Turkey says it could help meet Saudi military needs under defence pact
ANKARA – Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said on Sept 19 that Saudi Arabia may have military needs due to the ongoing attacks by Yemen’s Houthis and that Turkey was ready to help under a trilateral defence pact that also includes Pakistan.
“We see there are very serious attacks on Saudi Arabia’s territorial integrity, sovereignty. We have an alliance agreement in our pact. We are in serious solidarity on this point... They may have some military needs, especially on some technical issues. We would have no issues in meeting these,” Fidan told broadcaster NTV.
The joint defence agreement, dubbed the “Mecca Joint Defence Agreement”, signed last month stipulates that an armed attack on any one of the three countries will be regarded as an attack on all of them.
The Houthis, who control the most populous parts of Yemen, have been launching attacks on Saudi Arabia since declaring a naval blockade against Riyadh in July, a new front in the wider war that began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran in late February. The attacks have targeted Saudi cities, energy infrastructure and shipping, threatening global oil supplies and the main alternative Red Sea route for Gulf exports while traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remains disrupted.
US President Donald Trump has rebuffed pleas from the Saudis for military support to fight the Houthis, who agreed a ceasefire with the US last year after Washington bombed the group for two months.
Fidan said that it was unacceptable for Saudi Arabia to be made a part of the US-Iran war as it had no desire to join the conflict. He added, without elaborating, that proposals have been conveyed to all sides to end the fighting.
“There are many initiatives, but the sides need to accept these,” he said. “There are new proposals, I hope they accept them. Otherwise, the crisis was tolerated until a certain point, but the economic reflections have started to exceed the point of being tolerable.”
Turkey, which has NATO’s second-largest army, has said the pact with nuclear-armed Pakistan and top oil exporter Saudi Arabia was open to expansion and did not seek to replace any existing alliances.
Pakistan has said that there were no discussions about a military reaction from Islamabad under the Mecca agreement in response to the Houthis’ attacks on Saudi Arabia, but added that Pakistan would act when the “time comes”.
Earlier on Sept 19, Yemen’s Houthis said they attacked “sensitive” sites in the Saudi capital Riyadh with missiles and drones, hours after flames and a large plume of smoke were seen near the city’s main airport.
Turkey has condemned the Houthi attacks and called for them to stop immediately. REUTERS

How Ben Harper and Ben Stiller shaped Jack Johnson's journey
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
19:22:13 UTC
04:22:13 KST

Surfing and music have always been intertwined.
From the millennia-long practices of the Kanaka Maoli, to the 19th-century Hawaiian chant of He Inoa No Nāihe, to the 1960s surf guitar of Link Wray and Dick Dale, and the famously landbound Beach Boys.
In the early 2000s, the clearest parallel between surf and song came from a burgeoning subsection of folk- and blues-leaning singer-songwriters, as handy on a goofy foot take-off as a fretboard.
"Ben Harper is a musician first and he loves surfing. I'm a surfer first and I love playing music," surfer, filmmaker and singer-songwriter Jack Johnson tells Double J's Michael Hing.
"Our relationship has always been perfect. He brought me out on the first tours, but I was the one who always knew somebody in town that had surfboards and wetsuits if we needed them."
No-one from that scene travelled further than Johnson, who has sold more than 20 million albums and earned a permanent place on playlists at every cafe you've ever sat in.
In November, the two of them tour Australia together again, with John Butler, another peer from those early days, on every date.
A rich history
In 2001, Johnson toured Australia for the first time, playing a couple of dates at the East Coast Blues and Roots festival, where Ben Harper was practically royalty, his earlier headline sets still spoken of with reverence.
"I got a better spot than I should have on the bill," Johnson says. "Ben asked for a favour, and he got me in there."
On the final night he played the slot immediately before Harper. Tens of thousands crammed into the tent for the headliner. They left as fans of the unknown support act.
He'd soon be filling arenas under his own steam, but Johnson made his gratitude clear at the time.
"I was like, 'OK, I've got to pay Ben back for taking me on tour.' So, I called up some friends and was like, 'Bring a bunch of boards down to the beach.' We got everybody in his band out in the water, and it was such a memorable day.
"Ben grew up surfing and skating, so he had a little more experience. But some of the other guys in the band, it was the first time they'd ever tried.
"Those are the kind of days, when you look back on touring and a lot of the memories you have, that I almost remember more than the show itself."
That trip began a 25-year habit: Johnson has played about 100 shows here since. Adoring crowds help. So does the sun, surf and sand.
"I always feel really at home," he says of Australia. "Anywhere surf culture is big, it's like a real natural thing for me. It's from growing up in Hawaii.
"Some places, people look at you funny when you're walking around in flip-flops. Everybody else has shoes except for you. Then you show up other places and you're totally fine, you feel right at home. Australia is one of those spots."
There's a neat symmetry, then, in the two artists touring Australia together again 25 years on and Johnson is still, unmistakably, a fan.
"Ben Harper was somebody I listened to for a couple of years before we ever got a chance to meet, and anytime I get a chance to do a show with Ben, I just fan out again," Johnson says.
John Butler, another peer from those years, and one of Australia's best-known roots artists, joins every date of the November tour.
"I remember showing up for a sound check at a show we were doing together," Johnson says of his first encounter with Butler.
"I hadn't heard his music much. I walked into this venue and heard somebody ripping on the guitar. I just sat there like, 'Oh, wait, I'm playing with this guy tonight?! Amazing!'"
"For me, it's not just any normal group of shows," he says. "This is a good one."
The perks of fame
After that first Australian tour, Jack Johnson became a megastar.
When he toured his second album On and On in 2003, he headlined arenas on his own terms. None other than Hollywood A-lister Ben Stiller made the video for that album's song Taylor.
"To tell this story, I've got to be a little bit of a name-dropper," Johnson says.
"I got a chance to meet Owen Wilson and he said, 'I like your music, but I'll tell you who's kind of weird about your music: Ben Stiller.'
"He was like, 'He's a little weird. If you see him, watch out for him.'"
Stiller, fresh off Meet the Parents, Zoolander and The Royal Tenenbaums, had one of the most recognisable faces on earth. Johnson made the call anyway.
"We reached out to him," Johnson says.
"We got to know each other a little bit. He was really sweet.
"I asked him, 'Hey, I'm supposed to do a music video for this new song, and there's nothing I want to do less than have to act in a music video. You're good at that stuff. Why don't we do a video where you play me?'"
The idea was strong, but Stiller was one of the biggest film stars in the world. He was busy.
"He was really sweet," Johnson says.
"He was like, 'I'm in the middle of shooting a film. That feels maybe too much. What about this idea: I'm a director and I want to make a video about you, but you're just too mellow and I'm disgruntled with your performance [so] I try to get you to do more.'
"A couple days after we met, we shot the video and it was all improvised. There's some outtakes from it that are really funny. The hardest part was that I couldn't keep a straight face. Every time he would make a joke, I just kept falling apart."
The video sold a lie, though, the same one his sea-swept acoustic ballads have been selling ever since: that Jack Johnson is a permanently relaxed man. The truth is not quite so simple.
"I get a rap for being mellow but I'm not that mellow," he says. "My friends always laugh at the mellow guy label, because I'm actually pretty competitive."
Jack Johnson kicks off his Australian tour in Brisbane on November 7, before shows in Perth, Sydney and Melbourne.

The Yom Kippur War: How Israel missed the warning signs before the surprise attack - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
19:17:43 UTC
04:17:43 KST

There was a faint whiff of uncertainty in the briefing by IDF chief of staff David Elazar hours after the surprise Yom Kippur attack by Egypt and Syria in 1973.
“This is the first time Israel is fighting a defensive war,” he told the cabinet. “We know how to do it from books, but we’ve never actually done it.”
Five days later, in an assessment to defense minister Moshe Dayan, Elazar’s message was blunter. “We cannot win this war.”
Every day the army was destroying Egyptian tanks in Sinai but losing tanks as well and giving up territory. Where would it stop? What the country needed now, said Elazar, was a stable ceasefire that would enable it to rebuild the army “for 100 years.”
The Arab armies that attacked in 1973 bore little resemblance to the ones that were defeated so handily just six years before in the Six Day War. They had been retrained by more than 10,000 Soviet military advisers and rearmed with modern weapons, some of which Israel had not seen before.
The compact Sagger anti-tank missile had turned their hitherto feeble infantry into a formidable challenge for Israel’s vaunted tank corps, and the SAM antiaircraft missile threatened, even negated, Israel’s air superiority over the battlefield.
No less important, the Arabs this time had a sagacious and daring leader in Egyptian president Anwar Sadat.
Israel’s major failure on the eve of the Yom Kippur War was self-inflicted and attributable to one person – Maj.-Gen. Eli Zeira. As head of the Military Intelligence Directorate (MID), he had permitted himself to cross the line between self-confidence and vanity.
In a similar crisis period half a year before, he was the only one on the General Staff to say there would be no war despite serious warning signs. He proved right but for the wrong reasons. He believed that Sadat did not want war because he feared its consequences.
Years later, it was learned that Sadat had stood down only at the request of Syrian president Hafez Assad, who was awaiting shipment of crucial armaments from the Soviet Union, including ground-to-air missiles.
Zeira’s seeming win, however, discouraged his superiors from challenging his judgment in the future.
In the week before Yom Kippur, thousands of Israeli troops on the front lines could see an unprecedented Arab deployment opposite them, but warnings were dismissed in the chain of command on the basis of Zeira’s bold low-danger-of-war assessment.
Reports from foreign intelligence sources (11 in September) likewise warned of serious Arab intentions to launch a war in the coming days.
Zeira continued to insist that the danger of war was low almost until the sirens sounded. Only in a death-bed interview last year (2025) at age 97 did he admit that he had been wrong.
Ironically, it was MID, during his tenure, that had come up with a device regarded as insurance for tracking any Arab decision to go to war.
In the spring of 1973, a helicopter carrying communication technicians and a commando escort flew at night into Egypt and landed near military communication hubs where the technicians inserted special taps which could be activated from Israel – reportedly from Zeira’s office. The phones being tapped were of Egyptian units that would be involved in war preparations.
The device came to be called Special Means. After tests confirmed that the taps worked, the device was shut down.
The intelligence failure that left Israel blind
AS TENSIONS built up in the week before Yom Kippur (which fell on October 6), Elazar twice asked Zeira if he had picked up anything relevant. Zeira gave Elazar to understand that the device was activated but not producing anything relevant. But the taps had not been activated. Zeira feared that activation risked exposure.
Col. Yoel Ben-Porat, head of the vital Signals Intelligence section which tapped electronic devices in the Arab world, asked for permission to mobilize 200 intelligence reservists, in view of rising tensions.
“Yoel, listen well,” said Zeira. “I don’t permit you to even think about mobilizing a fraction of a reservist. It is not intelligence’s job to drive the public crazy nor to undermine the economy.”
When the veteran intelligence officer then recommended activation of Special Means, Zeira refused.
“What do these resources exist for,” asked an exasperated Ben-Porat, “if not for situations like the one we’re facing?”
“The situations you see,” replied Zeira, “are not the ones that I see.”
Zeira had apparently not turned the device on because he was certain, as he had been in the spring, that Sadat saw war as too risky. To activate the device during this fraught period risked its discovery by the Egyptians.
Two days before Yom Kippur Dayan asked what the device was producing. Dayan could not be denied. The device was turned on for several hours, but the conversations picked up were banal.
After the war, the diary of an Egyptian soldier was found on the battlefield and turned over to intelligence analysts.
Sgt. Mahmoud Nadeh introduced himself in his fresh notebook on the shore of the Bitter Lake. “We’ll begin from the beginning. I serve as a sergeant in the armed forces. We’ll be going to war in the next few days. I’m 2.5 km. from the enemy. We’ve been told that we will be the first to cross the [Suez] Canal to free our lands and expel the enemy.”
He promised in the name of “historical truth” to keep an accurate account of events.
The notebook offered insight into the mind of a university-educated Egyptian soldier whose kind was now to be found in large numbers in the armed services alongside peasants and urban slum dwellers.
A third-year humanities student from Alexandria, he had been trained as a commando but was now attached to an amphibious armored unit that was to cross the Bitter Lake. “We are to proceed with all possible speed to the Mitla Pass after an artillery barrage of 50 minutes. I hope to emerge alive from the battle because I believe in God. There is a smile on everyone’s face, even my officer’s.”
Four days before Yom Kippur, Sgt. Yoram Krivine’s platoon took over Strongpoint 111 on the Golan ceasefire line. It was a routine rotation of units, but it struck the 21-year-old paratrooper that the soldiers being relieved seemed unusually happy about leaving. The dark basalt rocks of the igloo-like fort seemed stout enough to withstand even direct artillery hits.
The hillock on which 111 was situated offered a view across the rocky Syrian plain. Krivine could see countless artillery pieces, tanks and half-tracks nestling under camouflage netting. Opposite was Tel Kudne, a strong Syrian position on a volcanic cone. A hundred meters from 111 was one of the UN observation posts positioned along the ceasefire line.
The newcomers were briefed by an intelligence officer attached to the unit they were relieving. The officer identified the Syrian units they were facing.
“The whole Syrian Army is out there,” he said in conclusion. “I’m happy I won’t be here when the war starts.”
Warnings from the front lines
PRIME MINISTER Golda Meir’s contentious meeting with Austrian chancellor Bruno Kreisky about his decision to close down a transit camp for Jews from the Soviet Union on their way to Israel was still on her mind the next day, Wednesday, October 3, when she met with her senior military advisers.
“He didn’t even offer me a glass of water,” she said.
The meeting in the Prime Minister’s Office was described as a consultation by Moshe Dayan, who had requested it.
Though he was a military icon, Dayan related to the 75-year-old grandmother with the deference due her position.
There were reports, he said, that Egypt was bent on war, but the situation on the Syrian front was more troubling. The Syrians had deployed their most advanced SAM antiaircraft missiles not around Damascus, their capital, but covering the Golan.
“This is not a normal defensive deployment,” he noted.
If the Egyptians crossed the canal, Dayan said, they would find themselves in desert with Israeli tanks attacking them from every side. But the Syrians, with just one quick thrust, could hope to push Israel off the Golan and then be protected against counterattacks by the steep heights and the Jordan River below.
Zeira, who had called in sick, was represented by his deputy, Gen. Arye Shalev. On the Suez front, Shalev said, the Egyptian army was engaged in a large-scale military exercise.
“In my opinion,” said the MID officer, “on the basis of much material received in recent days, Egypt believes it is not yet ready to go to war. And if Egypt is not going to war, then neither is Syria.”
Elazar agreed. If Syria were thinking of attacking on its own, he said, Israel would know about it. “When a big machine begins moving, there will be leaks.”
Meir did not choose to challenge a roomful of generals counseling calm, but she remained uneasy.
Security concerns were no longer considered weighty enough by MID to be put on the agenda of the cabinet meeting scheduled for the next day, Thursday, October 4, to hear Meir’s report on her European trip. The government thus remained unaware that the possibility of war was being mooted in high places.
Nor would the bold Arab deployment be referred to at the General Staff meeting. The sole subject on its agenda – two days before Yom Kippur – was discipline, especially the need for soldiers to adhere to the military dress code.
So sanguine was the Israeli high command about the situation that no air photos of the Egyptian lines had been taken between September 25 and October 1, a week when large convoys were moving to the canal zone every night.
A scheduled photo mission on October 2 was canceled because of poor visibility. It was rescheduled for the next day, but when the plane returned, it was found that the camera shutter had failed to open. It would not be until the afternoon of the next day, Thursday, that the mission would finally be executed. It would take all night to process and analyze the photos.
Meanwhile, in Cairo, Sadat had summoned the Soviet ambassador, Vladimir Vinogradov, on October 3 to inform him that Egypt and Syria had decided to go to war against Israel in order to break the Middle East deadlock.
“What will the Soviet attitude be?” he asked.
The reply from Soviet leader Leonid Brezhnev was cool. The decision about war was for the Egyptian leadership alone to make, he said. No well wishes were offered for Arab success.
Brezhnev asked permission to land large passenger planes at an Egyptian airbase the next day to evacuate families of Soviet advisers.
Sadat did not like any part of that reply but did not make an issue of it.
Teams of Israeli photo interpreters combed through the films brought back by the reconnaissance plane all Thursday night, counting every tank and artillery piece. The photos showed a stunning Egyptian buildup the length of the canal.
“You can get a stroke just from the numbers,” said Dayan. “There are 1,100 artillery pieces compared to 802 eight days ago. You people don’t take the Arabs seriously enough.”
Elazar was still not certain there would be war and did not request mobilization, but he canceled all leaves; many frontline soldiers were scheduled to be released for Yom Kippur in the coming hours.
Leading a nation into war was not a role Meir had ever imagined for herself. But she was coping thus far with the steadiness that marked her long public career, picking up the nuances in what the military men were saying and asking relevant questions.
Responding to Meir’s closest adviser, minister Israel Galili, Elazar said he would not mobilize reserves unless there were further indications of war. Initiating mobilization could itself easily lead to escalation by the other side.
The warning that finally reached Israel
MOSSAD CHIEF Zvi Zamir was wakened at 2:30 a.m. in Tel Aviv by a call from his bureau chief, Freddy Eini, who informed him that his most important agent, Ashraf Marwan, wished to meet with Zamir in London the coming night.
Marwan was the son-in-law of former Egyptian president Gamal Abdel Nasser, and a prolific spy. Among other things, he had transmitted to Zamir a copy of Egypt’s plans for an initial attack on Israel. Zamir asked Eini to book a ticket for him on the earliest morning flight to London and arrange for security teams to accompany him on the flight and in London.
As he sat in bed mulling over the call, the phone rang again. This time it was Zeira, who rarely called him at home. He wanted to inform Zamir about the Soviets evacuating the families of their advisers and to know what Zamir made of it.
Zamir, in turn, told him of Marwan’s phone message and of his own plan to fly to London in the morning to meet him. He also told of the code word signaling war.
He didn’t want to wake Golda at this hour, so he asked Zeira to inform her of his trip in the morning. The two men disliked each other, whether for professional or personal reasons, but they managed to conduct this informative conversation civilly.
For Egyptian commanders, the absence of any sign that Israel might be aware of the coming attack was reason for either concern or comfort. Might the Israelis be planning a massive ambush? Or will they be totally surprised?
Toward midnight, scouting teams were sent across the canal at several points to report on any activity they saw. All returned before dawn with the same message: The Jews are sleeping.
One Jew wide awake was Zamir. In London, he was not fasting, and he had not heard a cantor singing the Kol Nidre prayer. But no Jew this Yom Kippur night was gripped by a greater sense of worldly portent than he was. He was meeting with Marwan in a private apartment.
“He [Sadat] is starting the war tomorrow,” said Marwan.
The attack plan was little changed from the one he had passed on to Zamir a few months before. First, an air attack on the Bar-Lev Line – 16 “forts” spaced along the eastern bank of the nearly 200-km.-long Suez Canal. Intensive shelling would follow. Then five infantry divisions would cross the canal in rubber boats, a crossing that would take two days to complete. They would establish two bridgeheads on the Sinai bank. Prefabricated pontoon bridges would then be lowered into the water and floated across.
After dark, commando units would be helicoptered deeper into Sinai to prepare ambushes for Israeli reserve units that would be on their way to the front within a day or two.
Once or twice, Marwan said he was sure that the situation was clear to the Israelis and that they were taking the necessary steps.
He sounded, in fact, like he wasn’t sure. “How can you people not see that this is war?”
The odd remark, Zamir reckoned, may have stemmed from something his sources in Cairo had told him, perhaps that Egypt was unaware of any Israeli countermeasures.
After the meeting, Zamir and Marwan’s case officer and their security detail walked 15 minutes to the apartment of the Mossad station chief in London. The Israeli Embassy was shut because of the holy day, and the only way to transmit his message – the most important Zamir would ever send – was by telephone.
Before leaving for London, he had arranged with his bureau chief, Eini, that he would compose his message as a bland, boring business letter with code words that would enable Eini to ferret out the meaning.
Zamir sat down at a table and asked for paper and a pencil. He then drafted the message about visitors who would be coming to Israel despite the holiday.
The hidden message Eini would reveal would be stunning – before the blast of the shofar marked the end of Yom Kippur this coming night, before the last invocation calling on God to open the gates of heaven and receive his people’s prayers, Israel would be at war on two fronts, with two thirds of the army – its reserves – still unmobilized.
The writer, a former reporter for The Jerusalem Post, is the author of The Yom Kippur War (Schocken), The Boats of Cherbourg (US Naval Institute Press), and The Battle for Jerusalem (Jewish Publication Society). His most recent book is Jerusalem on Earth (updated edition). abra@netvision.net.il

French outpost off Canada in the spotlight as Macron hosts Carney on symbolic visit
Unknown

French outpost off Canada in the spotlight as Macron hosts Carney on symbolic visit
President Emmanuel Macron embarked Saturday on a symbolic visit to Saint Pierre and Miquelon, a French territory off Canada's Newfoundland, where he hosts Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney. The first-ever visit by a Canadian prime minister to the French archipelago in the North Atlantic comes as Carney marks a shift in Ottawa's foreign policy toward Europe amid growing tensions with the US.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
President Emmanuel Macron embarks on a rare and symbolic visit to a remote French territory in the North Atlantic on Saturday, hosting Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney at a time of growing tensions with Washington.
The three-day visit to Saint Pierre and Miquelon, a three-island archipelago of under 6,000 people just 25 kilometres (15 miles) off Newfoundland, will be the first by a French president in over a decade.
The trip to France's only remaining possession in North America, a vestige of the huge territories Paris once controlled in what is now Canada and the United States, carries immense symbolic resonance.
Macron insists that US President Donald Trump's second mandate has served to prove his point Europe needs to be more sovereign, especially on security.
Against the background of an intensifying spat with Trump who has even threatened to annex Canada, Carney has welcomed a proposal for his country to become the European Union's first "associate member".
Read moreEU chief invites Canada to be first-ever ‘associate member’
He is due to join Macron on Sunday as the first Canadian premier to visit the territory. The last visit by a French head of state was by François Hollande in 2014.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
'Same values'
The archipelago is one of several strategically-located French overseas territories that span the globe.
"Saint Pierre and Miquelon is not some insignificant remnant of empire to be managed piecemeal. It is France and Europe in North America," said French senator Annick Girardin, a former overseas territories minister.
Trump, who has repeatedly described Canada as the "51st" US state and dismissed its premier as "governor Carney", earlier this month posted an image with a map of North America in which areas including Canada were coloured in with the US flag.
Carney has in turn described his nation as "the most European of non-European countries".
Watch moreThe Debate: The 28th state? Canada draws closer to EU
The joint visit will underscore that Canada and France countries share "the same values of freedom, democracy, the rule of law and respect for the sovereignty of nations", the French presidential palace said.
"In a world marked by the return of power politics, geopolitical tensions and new forms of dependency, France and Canada share a common ambition: to work together, and with all countries that share these values, to strengthen their capacity to make decisions and act independently," the Élysée said.
Carney's office quoted him as saying that "Canada and France share more than a border. We share a history, common values, and a resolute commitment to building a more secure and prosperous world. In an uncertain world, President Macron and I understand the importance of this relationship".
'Mere spectator'?
Saint Pierre and Miquelon has economic and social problems familiar to many remote territories across the globe.
In what is widely regarded as France's first climate-driven community relocation, the village of Miquelon has started moving inland to escape the growing threat of sea level rise, with a second phase due to begin.
The population is falling, deaths outnumber births and young people leave to study in mainland France or Canada and often do not come back.
The biggest blow was dealt by the collapse of the fishing industry after Canada imposed a moratorium on cod fishing and France's exclusive economic zone shrank after a legal ruling.
"The fishing industry has a future in Saint-Pierre and Miquelon if it restructures," said Girardin.
Calling on France to seek to extend its rights over the seabed, she said: "France must decide whether it wants to be a subarctic power or a mere spectator."
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

Explosions rock Saudi capital – media
Several explosions have been reported in the Saudi capital of Riyadh, disrupting flights and triggering air raid warnings amid escalating hostilities with Yemen’s Houthis.
Saudi authorities sent emergency alerts early on Saturday warning residents of a “hostile aerial threat” and urging them to remain indoors, according to several media outlets. Explosions were reportedly heard across the city before the civil defense agency issued an all-clear about half an hour later. It was the first such warning in Riyadh since fighting in neighboring Yemen intensified in July.
Later on Saturday, a large plume of black smoke and flames was seen near King Khalid International Airport. Reuters footage showed smoke rising from the airport’s fuel-storage area, while flight-tracking service Flightradar24 reported major delays and cancellations. Saudi authorities have not disclosed the cause of the explosions or provided details on casualties or damage.
The latest escalation began in July after Saudi strikes on Yemen's Sanaa International Airport shattered a fragile truce dating back to 2022, prompting a renewed exchange of attacks with the Houthis.
The Houthis, who control much of northern Yemen, have made significant territorial gains in recent weeks, advancing along the Red Sea coast and seizing strategic positions around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, one of the world’s most important maritime chokepoints.
The advances have put further pressure on Saudi Arabia’s oil exports. Riyadh has increasingly relied on Red Sea routes as shipping through the Strait of Hormuz has been disrupted by the US war on Iran.
Maritime tracking data cited by AFP showed Saudi exports through the waterway have declined since July, although several loaded vessels passed through over the past week. The Houthis say international shipping remains unaffected, with the exception of Saudi vessels.
The disruption has already hit crude supplies. State oil giant Saudi Aramco has told European refiners they will receive no crude in October, Bloomberg reported on Friday, as oil prices hover above $100 a barrel.

Al Jazeera fires 24 Gaza staff amid US lawsuit alleging Hamas, Islamic Jihad ties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
18:51:27 UTC
03:51:27 KST

Qatar-based Al Jazeera has dismissed 24 journalists and other staff members who worked for the network in the Gaza Strip, including reporters, photographers and producers, without publicly explaining the move. Several of those dismissed are named in a U.S. civil lawsuit accusing the network of providing support to Hamas and Palestinian Islamic Jihad and employing members of the terror groups as media workers.
There is no evidence that the lawsuit prompted the dismissals, and Al Jazeera has not acknowledged any connection. In Israel, however, the move is being viewed by some officials and others involved in the case as an indirect indication that the network itself may have developed concerns about some of the people it employed in Gaza.
The lawsuit was filed in February 2025 by Shurat HaDin, the Israel Law Center, in U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia on behalf of Americans and their relatives who were harmed in the October 7 attack and the ensuing war. The pro-Israel advocacy organization StandWithUs assisted with research for the case.
Among the plaintiffs is Morris Schneider, the uncle of Shiri Bibas and great-uncle of Ariel and Kfir Bibas, who were murdered in Hamas captivity.
The suit was filed under the U.S. Anti-Terrorism Act, which allows victims to seek damages from entities they allege knowingly provided substantial assistance to terrorist organizations. The plaintiffs are seeking more than $1 billion in damages, as well as punitive damages.
According to the complaint, Al Jazeera went beyond covering Hamas and Palestinian Islamic Jihad and allegedly provided them with infrastructure for disseminating propaganda, recruiting operatives and inciting violence.
The plaintiffs further allege that the network maintained regular contacts with senior members of the organizations, paid for exclusive interviews and employed members of Hamas and Islamic Jihad as reporters, photographers and producers. The lawsuit also claims that some people working under the Al Jazeera name directly participated in the October 7 attack.
Those allegations have not been adjudicated in court. Al Jazeera has filed a motion seeking dismissal of the case, arguing that the complaint fails to establish a sufficient legal basis for the claims. The motion remains pending.
Part of the lawsuit relies on documents that the IDF says were seized in Gaza. In October 2024, the military identified six Al Jazeera journalists whom it alleged were members of Hamas or Palestinian Islamic Jihad, citing personnel records, salary documents, phone directories and records of military training.
At least three of those named by the IDF are among the employees whose work has now been terminated: Alaa Salameh and Ashraf Saraj, whom the military identified as Palestinian Islamic Jihad members, and Talal al-Arrouqi, whom it identified as a Hamas member.
Al Jazeera has repeatedly rejected Israel’s allegations, accusing it of portraying journalists as terrorists in order to justify targeting them.
During the war, the IDF also killed several journalists working for the network after alleging that they simultaneously served in Hamas or Islamic Jihad. They included Anas al-Sharif, Hossam Shabat, Ismail al-Ghoul, Hamza al-Dahdouh and Mohammed Wishah. Al Jazeera rejected the allegations against its employees and accused Israel of seeking to silence its coverage.
The U.S. lawsuit seeks to hold not only individual employees but also the network’s management and its U.S. subsidiary responsible, alleging that the purported assistance to the terror groups reflected a broader pattern rather than isolated conduct by individual staff members.
No evidence has been presented showing that the lawsuit itself led Al Jazeera to terminate the Gaza employees. Plaintiffs and others involved in the litigation, however, point to the timing and to the fact that several people cited in the case are no longer working directly for the network after Al Jazeera spent years rejecting allegations about links between its personnel and Hamas.
The dismissals were first reported by Palestinian news platforms and were later confirmed publicly by several of the affected staff members.
Those whose work was terminated included employees of Al Jazeera Mubasher, the network’s Arabic-language live broadcasting channel, as well as personnel who supplied material for news programs and the network’s website.
It remains unclear whether all 24 were salaried employees or whether some worked under temporary contracts. Several said management had previously assured them that their positions were secure. The Lebanese newspaper Al-Akhbar reported in April that the contracts of four other Gaza journalists had not been renewed after expiring.
Among those who confirmed their dismissal were reporter Mohammed Shaheen, reporter Hassan al-Zaanin and cameraman and field producer Mahmoud Shalha. Shalha wrote on social media that he was informed of the decision during a phone call lasting about 15 seconds, with no explanation or advance warning.
Shaheen and al-Zaanin said they had risked their lives while covering the war and that the dismissals came after they had received assurances of job security. Al Jazeera has issued no public statement explaining whether the move was based on professional, legal, financial or other considerations.
Alongside speculation about whether the U.S. lawsuit influenced the decision, network employees have pointed to a possible organizational explanation. Staff members have said Al Jazeera Mubasher is undergoing restructuring and that management in Doha wants to reduce live broadcasting from Gaza while routing more material through edited news programs.
Arabic-language reports have suggested that some of those dismissed could return to work for the network as freelancers through an outside company called MEDIA. Such an arrangement would reduce their direct contractual relationship with Al Jazeera without necessarily removing them from its content operation.
The firings also come amid broader scrutiny of the status of media workers in Gaza who have been accused of simultaneously serving in armed groups.
The Committee to Protect Journalists has reviewed entries in its database of journalists killed during the war after Hamas and Palestinian Islamic Jihad published obituaries identifying some people previously listed as media workers as members of their organizations. The organization has said that journalists lose civilian protection under international humanitarian law while directly participating in hostilities.
Israel banned Al Jazeera’s operations in the country in May 2024 after the government said its broadcasts harmed national security and served Hamas propaganda. The network denounced the decision as an attack on press freedom. Israeli forces later raided the network’s offices in Ramallah in September 2024 and ordered them closed.
Despite those measures, Al Jazeera continued extensive coverage from Gaza through local crews, some of whom are now at the center of the U.S. litigation.
Jordan Cope, policy director at StandWithUs and an adviser on legal research for the case, said members of terrorist organizations “cannot use journalism as a disguise and shape the information reaching millions of viewers.”
He said Al Jazeera still had many questions to answer, while arguing that the dismissals could represent a first step toward preventing members of terror groups from operating under the title of journalist.

Canadian godfather of AI warns of threat if unchecked
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

18:49:12 UTC
03:49:12 KST

Barry Ellsworth
19 September 2026•Update: 19 September 2026
A Canadian called one of the godfathers of AI has added his voice to the growing chorus of experts warning that the technology poses a real threat to humans, news reports said Saturday.
“The whole world is waking up to something that sounded like science fiction to most people,” Yoshua Bengio, 62, founder and scientific director of the Montreal Institute for Learning Algorithms, told CTV News.
“But the events of the summer actually make it clear that we’re now building AIs that have their own goals that go against the intentions of the companies and the developers who build them, and that they can escape. They can escape the containments in which they have been put.”
Voices sounded by some AI experts were raised earlier this year when some AI agents went rogue, escaped, and committed intentional deception.
On Friday, more than 100 people, including those with intimate knowledge of AI, signed a letter urging companies to put evaluators in programming to keep tabs on any AI gone rogue.
Bengio’s non-profit LawZero project is working to create a program to keep any rogue technology at bay. Canada and Germany are ponying up with CAN$300 million ($214 million) for the project.
AI is supposed to achieve a goal given to it by humans, but it can do that and also add something “really bad,” Bengio said, including “as these researchers are saying, up to the extinction of humanity.”
But Bengio stressed that while the threat from AI is real, there is still time to create safeguards like the LawZero project.

South Korea, US discuss Seoul's role in Middle East, investment pact
South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun met US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Friday as the longtime allies grappled with delayed Korean investments in the United States and Seoul's role in Middle East security.
US President Donald Trump has criticized Seoul in recent weeks over what he described as a lack of South Korean support for US efforts to pressure Iran. The two countries have also yet to finalise agreements governing $350 billion in South Korean investments pledged under a trade deal reached last year.
Cho explained to Rubio Seoul's willingness to make a substantive contribution to restoring freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz, the ministry said in a statement without elaborating.
On Seoul's investment commitments, Rubio stressed their swift execution, the State Department said, while South Korea's foreign ministry said Rubio and Cho agreed to keep communicating to ensure ongoing consultation plans "bear good fruit".
Rubio and Cho also pledged ongoing collaboration across key strategic sectors including semiconductors, the State Department said, while Rubio underscored the need for a fair and transparent business environment for US companies in South Korea.
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung, who is due in the United States next week for the UN General Assembly, said on Friday he would not deploy military assets to the Middle East in a way that could draw the country into conflict.
However, he said Seoul was reviewing whether to play a greater role in safeguarding navigation in the region.
Cho said before leaving Seoul on Thursday that investment plans under its trade deal had been delayed while procedural issues were clarified, without elaborating.
Lee told a news conference on Friday that concerns over the commercial viability of the package had become a sticking point in negotiations, although the two sides were nearing an agreement.
He said some elements of the package were difficult for Seoul to accept, but the government would continue discussions to ensure any deal protects South Korea's interests while benefiting both countries and the broader US-South Korea relationship.
Seoul committed last year to invest in US manufacturing in return for lowering tariffs on imports from South Korean to 15%.
Lee said Seoul had insisted on including a reference to "commercially reasonable" investments in the text of the agreement.
North Korea also featured in the talks, amid speculation over a possible summit between Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.
Rubio and Cho reaffirmed their commitment to the complete denuclearization of North Korea, the State Department said, while Cho said Seoul would actively support the resumption of talks between Washington and Pyongyang, according to the ministry.
President Lee said on Friday it was possible for a summit meeting between Kim and Trump to take place in coming months, but it remained uncertain.

Iran says conditions to re-engage in talks, end war sent to US via Qatar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Iran says conditions to re-engage in talks, end war sent to US via Qatar
Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, tells Al Jazeera Tehran awaiting Trump response.
Iran has conveyed a formal set of conditions to Washington through Qatari mediators for ending the war with the United States, the country’s security chief tells Al Jazeera.
“We remain in contact with the mediator Qatar, which has conveyed our conditions to Washington with the aim of ending the war. We are awaiting President [Donald] Trump’s response,” Mohsen Rezaei told Al Jazeera’s Tehran bureau chief, Nour Eddine Edghir, in an exclusive interview on Saturday.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Iran stages show of force during mobilisation campaign in Tehran
- list 2 of 3Turkiye revokes operating licence of Iran’s Bank Mellat in Istanbul
- list 3 of 3An unaffordable car market highlights Iran’s cost-of-living crisis
“Our conditions are an end to the war on all fronts, the release of our frozen funds and an end to the naval blockade,” said Rezaei, who took over as secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council about a month ago.
“It is in Washington’s interest to accept these conditions. Trump’s threats will not achieve any results. We are prepared for a decisive war.”
Mediators Qatar and Pakistan have been working to re-establish negotiations between the two sides since their memorandum of understanding (MoU) expired last month. Regional countries are also seeking an end to the war that began when the US and Israel launched strikes against Iran in late February, killing Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
Rezaei did not rule out a new US strike against Iran, calling the possibility “very much on the cards” based on his country’s military assessments, while insisting Tehran was ready.
He said Iran’s military planning had shifted since two earlier rounds of conflict and is now focused on US naval assets, stretching from the Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea. Targets beyond that range, towards the Indian Ocean, would fall outside Iran’s reach, he added.
Iran’s ‘two-sided, twofold message’
Rezaei said Iran had recently test-fired a multi-warhead antiship missile near a US vessel or aircraft carrier, with the warheads potentially subject to further development.
He also said the intensity of any future Iranian response would be heavy, encompassing US bases in the region as in previous rounds, as well as US commercial interests and companies operating locally.
Asked whether the war would end soon, he said “in practical terms the war is still going on”, while stressing Tehran was working under a new strategy “to bring this war to an end as soon as possible”.
Al Jazeera’s Tohid Asadi, reporting from Tehran, described Rezaei’s remarks as part of the “two-sided, twofold message” Iran has maintained throughout the conflict – combining openness to diplomacy with continued war preparations.
“On the one hand, readiness for diplomatic engagement … on the other hand, he’s talking about preparation for a decisive war,” Asadi said, noting that mediated talks with Qatar and Pakistan were “under way”, offering “a positive indication regarding the hopes, however slim” for renewed engagement.
David Des Roches, a former Pentagon director of Arabian Peninsula affairs, told Al Jazeera that Washington was unlikely to see the terms as a serious opening.
“At first glance, probably not serious; they would be viewed as surrender,” Roches said.
But he pointed to Iran’s apparent abandonment of an earlier demand for war reparations as a sign of movement. “The first thing you notice is that he’s dropped the demand for reparations, which the Iranians had made at one point,” he said.
Nuclear weapons; Strait of Hormuz; Yemen’s war
On the collapsed MoU, Rezaei rejected US accusations that Tehran violated the deal by striking an oil tanker in the Strait of Hormuz, telling Al Jazeera’s Edghir that Iran’s actions came only after US strikes on Bandar Abbas and an Iranian surveillance platform there.
He said any agreement, including the MoU, required recourse to a dispute-resolution committee agreed between Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf and US Vice President JD Vance, which Washington unilaterally withdrew from.
On Iran’s nuclear programme, Rezaei said Tehran has not decided to withdraw from the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, despite having grounds to do so following the US and Israeli attacks, though he said Washington’s conduct “may push Tehran into withdrawing”.
He said Iran continues to honour a fatwa (decree) from the former Supreme Leader Ruhollah Khomeini prohibiting nuclear weapons and that its doctrine remains unchanged. “But we do not know what will happen in the future,” he said, citing further sanctions or a UN Security Council referral of Iran’s nuclear file as potential future pressure.
Rezaei denied Iranian involvement in Yemen’s war, saying Tehran was ready to help mediate between warring parties but did not exploit the conflict “for its own political ends”.
He also dismissed widespread speculation, including inside Iran, that Tehran could move to close the Bab al-Mandeb Strait to pressure global energy markets, saying the waterway “is a Yemeni matter” tied to the conduct of the Houthi movement, not Iran.
On the Strait of Hormuz, Rezaei said Tehran had come within “a short step” of announcing an agreement with Oman before it was shelved, adding that a deal between the two countries remains ready but may require regional endorsement before being made public.

Do pimple patches actually work? Here's what the science says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

analysis
Do pimple patches actually work? Here's what the science says
You're standing in the skincare aisle and pimple patches are everywhere — clear ones, flesh-coloured ones, stars, hearts. They promise to flatten a pimple overnight.
Then there are those satisfying social media videos where someone peels off a pimple patch to reveal a much calmer-looking pimple underneath.
But do pimple patches actually work? And what are they really doing to your skin?
What's a pimple?
A pimple forms when a hair follicle gets clogged with oil, dead skin cells and bacteria, causing inflammation, redness and sometimes a pus-filled head. You might also hear a pimple called a "spot" or a "zit" — these are just names for the same thing.
"Acne" is the name for the broader skin condition of getting pimples recurrently (along with blackheads and whiteheads), rather than a word for a single pimple.
In this article we'll mostly stick to "pimple" for an individual lesion, and use "acne" only when we're talking about the overall condition.
Pimples affect an estimated 20.5 per cent of people worldwide at any one time, and up to 80–85 per cent of adolescents. This makes it one of the most common skin conditions.
What are pimple patches?
Pimple patches look like a TikTok-era invention, but the underlying technology isn't. They're based on hydrocolloid dressings, which were developed decades ago for wound care. Then dermatologists began adapting them for skin conditions, such as acne.
Hydrocolloid patches caught on as a beauty product in South Korea almost 20 years ago before crossing into Western markets around 2012.
Today's pimple patches are made from a hydrocolloid material — a gel-forming substance — which is often a blend of ingredients such as pectin, gelatin and carboxymethylcellulose. This bonds to a thin, flexible, waterproof outer layer.
The hydrocolloid absorbs moisture, so it can soak up fluid from a wound and hold it in place while the skin underneath heals.
On a pimple, the same process kicks in. Press the patch over a pimple with a visible head, and the hydrocolloid layer starts drawing fluid — pus, oil and dead skin cells — out of the pore and locking it into its gel matrix.
As the patch fills up, it turns white or cloudy, which is exactly what people are peeling off in those satisfying videos. The outer layer holds everything in place and keeps the area covered while this happens.
Pimple patches also act as a physical barrier. They cover the pimple, making it harder to pick, squeeze or touch it, which can otherwise introduce more bacteria and worsen the inflammation.
Some pimple patches are medicated, most commonly with salicylic acid. Others contain tea tree oil, niacinamide or benzoyl peroxide. Rather than simply drying out the pimple, these ingredients are meant to help exfoliate the skin, calm inflammation or target acne-causing bacteria.
You can buy pimple patches at supermarkets or pharmacies, typically for about $6–20 a pack, depending on the brand and whether they're medicated (medicated patches typically cost more than unmedicated ones).
Do they actually work?
A 2025 review found most evidence for hydrocolloid patches comes from wound care, not for pimples specifically.
Of the handful of studies on pimples, many are small and industry-funded that test the brands' own patches. Often these studies are not "blinded". This means either the researchers, participants or both knew if they were using pimple patches, which risks skewing the results.
So while the early results are promising, the evidence for pimple patches is still limited.
One manufacturer-funded trial of 41 people found applying a patch to a pimple that had already come to a head and been popped improved its appearance in a day.
Another small industry-funded study followed 37 people over ten days. In two days, pimples covered with the patches were 35 per cent smaller and looked 44 per cent less less inflamed, based on a combined visual assessment of size and redness. Untreated pimples showed little change. By day ten, the treated pimples were also less likely to develop post-inflammatory pigmentation (dark marks on your skin after a pimple heals).
Patches seem to work best on pimples that already have a visible white or yellow head. That's because the pus sitting inside has already risen close to the skin's surface, putting it within reach of the patch's absorbent gel.
For the best results, apply to clean, dry skin and leave on for six to eight hours or overnight, swapping it once it turns cloudy and swollen. Afterwards, place your pimple patch in the bin.
Are they for me?
Pimple patches can be handy for the odd pimple. But they can only do so much, and they're not for every pimple.
They don't work well for deep, painful cystic pimples because the patch can't reach inflammation that sits deeper in the skin.
People with darker skin tones may also need to be careful, as irritation can increase the risk of dark marks after a pimple heals. This can happen with any skin tone, but skin with more melanin tends to produce more pigment in response to inflammation or irritation, so the resulting dark marks are often more noticeable and slower to fade.
If you have sensitive skin or an allergy to adhesives, patches can cause redness, itching or a rash. Medicated patches containing ingredients such as salicylic acid can also be irritating.
My pimples aren't getting better
If you've tried patches, cleansers and treatments for a few weeks and your pimples aren't budging, it's probably time to get some help. Likewise, if your pimples are deep, painful or starting to leave scars, don't wait.
A GP can discuss your options, and if needed, refer you to a dermatologist to work out what's driving your pimples and find a treatment.
Lisa Byrom is an associate professor of dermatology in the School of Medicine at the University of Queensland. This piece first appeared on The Conversation.

Srebrenica Memorial Center to expand cooperation with Ukraine on war crimes documentation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
18:20:00 UTC
03:20:00 KST

Srebrenica Memorial Center to expand cooperation with Ukraine on war crimes documentation
Nedim Jahić, the Memorial Center’s adviser for program and initiative development, reported this, according to Ukrinform.
As part of the visit, representatives of the Memorial Center met with the Office of the Ukrainian Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights, the ZMINA Human Rights Center, Vshanui, the Media Initiative for Human Rights, Truth Hounds and the Center for Civil Liberties.
They also held meetings with representatives of the Ukrainian Institute of National Memory, the National Museum of the Holodomor-Genocide, the Babyn Yar Holocaust Memorial Center and the National Museum of the History of Ukraine in the Second World War.
Particular attention was paid to Bosnia and Herzegovina’s experience in prosecuting war crimes in national courts, as the country has developed substantial judicial practice in similar cases over more than two decades and accumulated a large body of court rulings and other documents.
One of the main outcomes of the visit will be increased cooperation between Ukrainian partners and state institutions, judicial and law enforcement bodies, experts and organizations in Bosnia and Herzegovina, coordinated by the Memorial Center.
Professional and educational exchanges between specialists from Ukraine and Bosnia and Herzegovina are also planned. This will allow Ukrainian specialists to learn about the experience of the Srebrenica Memorial Center and other institutions, while Bosnian specialists will be able to learn from Ukraine’s current experience.
“The aim of future cooperation is to ensure that the judicial practice and experience of both the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia and Bosnia and Herzegovina’s national judicial system become more systematically accessible to institutions, researchers, civil society organizations and journalists in Ukraine,” said Jahić, who headed the visit.
Another important outcome of the visit was the launch of discussions on closer cooperation between journalists and media organizations in Ukraine, Bosnia and Herzegovina and other Western Balkan countries. During meetings with the Ukrainian National News Agency Ukrinform and organizations producing research and documentary materials, participants discussed expanding media cooperation and ensuring that journalists in Western Balkan countries have access to verified information, documentation, experts and sources in Ukraine.
Another area of cooperation will focus on informing the public about war crimes committed during Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, the experiences of victims and their families, the work of organizations documenting the crimes, and efforts to establish individual criminal responsibility.
At the same time, the parties plan to facilitate Ukrainian journalists’ and researchers’ access to relevant institutions, archives, experts and sources in Bosnia and Herzegovina on war crimes, transitional justice, missing persons, return and reintegration, memorialization and the experience of post-war society.
In the longer term, the initiative envisions developing a media network based on direct communication between journalists, exchanging contacts and verified sources, jointly producing materials, and building links between media outlets and institutions holding relevant documentation.
“It is important to us that this visit does not remain at the level of individual meetings. The Memorial Center can bring together people and institutions in the two countries that perform very similar work – from justice and work with families of missing persons to museums, archives, human rights organizations and media. The next step should be the exchange of people, knowledge, data and specific programs,” Jahić said.
As reported by Ukrinform, in May 2024, the UN General Assembly adopted a resolution establishing an annual day of remembrance for the victims of the Srebrenica genocide, despite opposition from Serbia and Russia.
