Breadcrumb
Growing fuel crisis in Sudan brings transport, service stations to near halt
A major fuel shortage in Sudan has triggered a severe transport crisis, with service stations nearly out of gasoline, restricting the movement of civilians, reports said on Saturday.
Siraj al-Din Hamed, who works at a fuel station in Omdurman, told The New Arab that the shortage stems from insufficient fuel at stations and because imported shipments have not yet reached Khartoum.
“The instability of foreign currency prices is directly reflected in the fuel market…some station owners are postponing supply operations waiting to know the new prices or for the price to stabilise,” he explained.
“Locals say that this has had huge repercussions beyond fuel stations and it has affected daily life, such as transport costs, the movement of goods such as fruits and vegetables,” he added.
Fuel prices have soared across the country’s various states, with a parallel market also emerging, where fuel is being sold for around $22.20 per gallon.
Meanwhile, public transport drivers said that some operating service stations are selling a gallon of fuel for $19.
In Khartoum, the shortage has forced people to wait for several hours for buses in order to get around.
Long queues of cars have also formed outside service stations, with one person, Abu Bakr Yassin, telling The New Arab, that he had been waiting since 4:00 AM despite the shortage of fuel at the station.
“All service stations have stopped working, which has also meant that people are now unable to work,” he explained.
A lack of regulations and the absence of authorities has worsened the situation, with no officials at the scene to address the issue and regulate the movement of vehicles, which have been held at a standstill, blocking roads and key areas.
The crisis has prompted many citizens to demand field monitoring teams, for measures to be taken to address the issue, and for sustainable solutions, as the crisis is expected to worsen.
Mohammed Babiker, from Khartoum state, said the fuel crisis has been going on for several days, and that there does not seem to be any tangible solutions.
“Some of the most affected are the low-income citizens,” he said.
According to local media, the Khartoum state government has been working to provide fuel at stations; however, the efforts are yet to solve the shortage.
Meanwhile, the Sudanese Ministry of Energy said the fuel shortage was due to fluctuations and delays in banking applications, which slowed down purchases and lef to a gradual buildup of vehicles at fuel stations.
They also noted that regional conflict, such as geopolitical developments at the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, has increased marine insurance costs, and subsequently higher prices for petroleum products.

UN peacekeeping chief in Lebanon says smooth transition is critical before pull-out

Breadcrumb
UN peacekeeping chief in Lebanon says smooth transition is critical before pull-out
The head of United Nations peacekeepers in Lebanon said on Saturday it was critical to ensure other UN agencies and Lebanese troops could assume the tasks carried out by the force before it begins withdrawing at the end of this year.
Major General Diodato Abagnara of Italy spoke to Reuters in southern Lebanon at a position operated by the UN peacekeeping force known as UNIFIL, which has been monitoring hostilities in southern Lebanon for nearly 50 years.
Since a new war erupted between Israel and Hezbollah in March, the force has also provided security escorts for humanitarian aid convoys to residents in a small cluster of predominantly Christian southern Lebanese towns now encircled by Israeli troops.
Residents in much of the rest of southern Lebanon have been forcibly displaced by Israeli strikes and evacuation orders.
The UN Security Council has ordered UNIFIL to begin withdrawing at the end of 2026, triggering concerns over whether aid deliveries can continue and how the force can transfer its positions to Lebanese troops.
“There are other United Nations entities here in the south, and so what is very important for us (is) to conduct a very smooth transition to different entities, or for the future of a new mission,” Abagnara told Reuters.
He said UNIFIL was already working with the UN’s country team to ensure humanitarian assistance in Israeli-occupied areas and information sharing with the Lebanese army about “sensitive areas (and) how they can manage this situation.”
Abagnara acknowledged that it could be “very difficult” to hand over some of UNIFIL's posts to Lebanese troops given that more than half lie within areas now controlled by Israeli troops.
Diplomats worry UNIFIL’s departure will mean an end to the UN's "eyes and ears" in southern Lebanon.
Abagnara spoke to Reuters at a position overlooking Mansouri, a town where Israeli forces have been carrying out demolitions since ordering residents to leave in June, despite a ceasefire. Reuters reporters could see excavators in the town knocking down trees and multi-storey homes.
Abagnara described demolitions as “another violation” of UN Security Council resolutions on Lebanon. Israel's military has said it is destroying alleged Hezbollah infrastructure across southern Lebanon.
As a US-backed plan for Lebanon's army to disarm Hezbollah and take control of southern Lebanon has stalled, a diplomatic scramble is underway to address the vacuum that will be left by UNIFIL’s withdrawal.
Lebanon wants an extension. Other countries have discussed a new multinational mission, though it remains unclear what kind of mandate it would have.
Abagnara said an extension would be “a great honor” but that without a new Security Council decision, his force would need to stop operating at the end of the year.
“It's not a long time," he said. "The presence of United Nations in the South is very, very essential. And according to me, more now than ever.”

JP Morgan admits it can't forecast end of Iran war due to Trump
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
17:34:40 UTC
02:34:40 KST

Breadcrumb
JP Morgan admits it can't forecast end of Iran war due to Trump's flip-flopping
JP Morgan has said that it is unable to forecast the end of the US war with Iran, in an admission that its own assumptions about the war's dynamics have not held up.
"For the first time since the start of the Iran conflict, we don't have a baseline view. We simply don’t know how to model the endgame," the bank's global commodities team said in a note published on Thursday.
This is because the underlying assumptions about US President Donald Trump's own red lines, which in theory would limit the war's duration, have not held up.
These include $100 oil, $5 a gallon of petrol, and 4% inflation or 5% yields on 10-year Treasuries, US government bonds that it sells to prop up government spending.
"Those constraints gave us an implicit timeline, and we expected that by June there would be some form of agreement to reopen the strait," the note said, adding that all of these have failed to compel the Trump administration to end the war and ensure the Strait of Hormuz reopens.
Since the start of the Iran war, the closure of the Strait of Hormuz has dramatically affected the global commodity market, with 20% of the world's oil and gas entering the global market through the key waterway.
The price of oil has dramatically fluctuated as oil exports slumped at the immediate start of the war, then picked up as alternative export routes were found, including Iraqi exports via land through Syria, Saudi Arabia's diversion through its East-West Pipeline, the UAE's diversion through its Fujairah pipeline, and a US initiative to smuggle out oil via the strait, bypassing Iranian attacks.
Yet, struggles to export oil have continued as Iranian attacks still threaten maritime shipping, and the reignition of the Yemeni civil war sees Houthi attacks against Saudi oil infrastructure.
"With no clear signals from either the US or Iran that they are prepared to de-escalate… the assumption that the disruption is temporary is becoming increasingly difficult to sustain," JP Morgan's note read.
Has Trump and the war affected economic forecasts?
Jamie Brito, the Executive Director in Refining & Oil Markets at Dow Jones Energy, told The New Arab that the situation is "everybody's energy nightmare. What everybody had feared for the last decades came to fruition this year".
"We are on uncharted territory. Every single analyst team is in uncharted territory. It's quite difficult to predict this kind of, you know, extreme scenario," he said.
Brito said his team's forecasts were based on its observations and analysis of trade, oil production, refining, and other key nodes in the market. Many teams look at these nodes for their own forecasts.
He added that key signposts can be used to understand where things may change, including this summer's World Cup in the US, Canada and Mexico, the establishment of the Memorandum of Understanding between the US and Iran in June, as well as the upcoming midterm election in the US, which is the next signpost.
Trump's rhetoric, however, is increasingly being dismissed in forecasts.
"What we are acknowledging, or what people are seeing, I think is the fact that you cannot expect, you cannot wish or anticipate that the political arena is going to be forced to capitulate or to accept some kind of negotiation and ceasefire, because of some political pressure," Brito said.
What does JP Morgan’s admission mean?
Trump's messaging, and that of his administration, has flip-flopped since the start of the outbreak of the war with Iran.
Initially saying the war would be short, his administration fumbled on its justifications for launching the war. It gave differing reasons for launching the war, including aiming to stop Iran from getting nuclear weapons, regime change, and has even threatened to destroy the country despite seeking negotiations with it.
Trump's most recent prediction for the war is that it would end after the midterms.
Neil Quilliam, an associate fellow with Chatham House's Middle East and North Africa Programme specialising in energy policy and geopolitics, told The New Arab that the admission from JP Morgan is less a statement that its team, or the industry, expects the war to get worse or of a worse economic outcome, but that "some of the assumptions underpinning its forecasting framework no longer hold".
"Assumptions that analysts would ordinarily use to construct an endgame have become much less reliable, and may remain so for the remainder of the Trump administration," he added.
Quilliam said that Trump's statements, and the fact that they don't necessarily reflect the administration's policy on the ground, cause an "unusually challenging environment" for businesses and markets to navigate, which make it difficult for forecasters to establish a baseline for investment decisions.
JP Morgan's statement, he said, is more an admission that "the range of plausible outcomes [of the war] has widened while confidence in assigning probabilities to them has collapsed".
"This is an arguably more significant admission. Markets can price known risks. They find it much harder when there is no reliable framework for judging which outcome is most likely," Quilliam said.
This, in turn, has knock-on effects for economic decision-making.
"Business can still plan around a range of scenarios, but attaching confidence to a single base case becomes increasingly difficult when the political decision-making driving the crisis remains so unpredictable."

After the starting gun was fired, the riders set off along the winding dirt track cutting through the rocky landscape, while spectators cheered the course and on rooftops.
The competition culminated in jubilant celebrations, with supporters surrounding the winning jockey and lifting trophies above the crowd.
Arabian horses occupy a special place in Palestinian culture, and horse races and equestrian beauty championships are held across the West Bank, drawing competitors from different towns and villages.
Open land has become becomes increasingly scarce amid expanding Israeli settlement construction in the West Bank, occupied since 1967.
But horse culture still draws Palestinians together, from urban neighbourhoods to rural villages.
For the local community, the race on Sept 18 was more than just about sports. It was aimed at “preserving a form of Arab heritage that our ancestors cherished and that we continue to uphold today,” Abu Awad told AFP.
The event also provided an opportunity for local jockeys who cannot easily participate in international races to showcase their skills, the organiser said.
“Some horses and riders face difficulties travelling to Jordan or abroad,” he said.
Despite the challenges, participants spoke of dreams that stretch beyond the local track.
“My ambition is to travel to Italy to ride horses,” said racer Mohammed Al-Ajlouni. “We ride here now, but for the future, that is what I hope for.” AFP

Araghchi: ME security must be shaped by regional countries, not foreigners
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
17:29:45 UTC
02:29:45 KST

Araghchi: ME security must be shaped by regional countries, not foreigners
TEHRAN — Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has called for a fundamental shift in the international approach to security, urging the world to move away from militarism, foreign intervention and coercion toward sustainable development, respect for national sovereignty, equal application of international law and lasting peace.
Addressing the virtual forum of Global Town Hall 2026 on Saturday, September 19, Araghchi said the Middle East should pursue a security framework shaped by the countries of the region rather than imposed by foreign powers.
The forum, hosted by the Foreign Policy Community of Indonesia (FPCI), was held under the theme “Calling for a Global U-Turn: Recentering Development, Reclaiming Humanity, Restoring Justice in a Crazy World.”
In his address, Araghchi argued that war, intervention, sanctions and the use of force have increasingly become instruments of international policy rather than exceptional measures, raising fundamental questions about the effectiveness of the international system established to prevent war, protect human dignity and uphold justice.
He said decades of foreign intervention, military pressure and successive wars in the Middle East had demonstrated that military intervention does not produce sustainable security and that coercive pressure cannot provide a foundation for lasting peace.
Instead, he argued that the normalization of military force has entrenched cycles of confrontation and conflict.
Gaza and Lebanon: A broader regional pattern
Araghchi pointed to the situation in Gaza as one of the most severe manifestations of a failed approach to regional security.
“What is taking place in Gaza is not merely a humanitarian tragedy,” he said, describing the situation as a test of the international community’s collective responsibility.
He cited the killing of civilians, forced displacement, collective punishment and the destruction of vital infrastructure, and said the absence of effective accountability had allowed the pattern to extend beyond Gaza to Lebanon.
According to the Iranian foreign minister, military force is increasingly being used not as a last resort but as a mechanism for reshaping the region’s political and security landscape.
He warned that when aggression becomes normalized and escalation is institutionalized, destruction can evolve from a consequence of conflict into an instrument for pursuing political objectives.
 
  
Iran war and sovereignty
Araghchi also linked US and Israeli military aggression against Iran to the broader pattern of conflict and the erosion of restrictions imposed by international law.
He characterized the war as “illegal, unjust, aggressive and unprovoked,” and referred to 'a wider record of unpunished aggression,' including targeted assassinations of Iranian officials, threats against political authorities and violations of national sovereignty.
He warned that failure by the international community to respond effectively to such actions would gradually weaken the boundaries established by international law.
Araghchi also referred to the killing of 168 students in Minab, saying the victims should not be reduced to casualty figures.
“Behind each of these lost lives, there was a family, a future, and a life,” he said, asking when the international community would draw a line and say that enough was enough.
‘Multilateralism must be made more effective’
The Iranian foreign minister argued that the erosion of international law would ultimately undermine the credibility of the institutions responsible for upholding it.
If international law is disregarded whenever major powers’ interests are at stake, he said, the international community can no longer credibly speak of the rule of law.
Likewise, he argued that human rights cannot be considered universal if they are treated as inherent rights for some nations but conditional privileges for others.
Araghchi said the inability of international institutions, including the United Nations, to effectively respond to aggression and hold violators accountable would inevitably damage their credibility and legitimacy.
He nevertheless rejected abandoning multilateralism, saying the answer to the shortcomings of the existing international system is to build “genuine, effective and just multilateralism.”
From militarism to development
Araghchi said a genuine global turnaround would require the political will to change the current trajectory of international affairs.
He outlined a shift from militarism to sustainable development, interventionism to respect for national sovereignty, collective punishment to civilian protection, selective accountability to universal justice, and endless wars to lasting peace.
The world, he said, needs a new paradigm in which development is regarded as an integral component of security, national sovereignty is respected and international law is applied equally and without discrimination.
“No political, strategic or geopolitical interest,” he argued, should take precedence over human life.
Iran’s vision for regional security
Turning specifically to the Middle East, Araghchi said sustainable security could not be dictated from outside the region.
“Regional security must belong to the region itself,” he said, arguing that regional countries should be able to discuss their security, stability, development and common future and devise solutions without the intervention of foreign powers.
For Iran, Araghchi said, the position is rooted not merely in theory but in historical experience.
He said Iran believes sustainable regional security should be built through dialogue, confidence-building, cooperation and mutual respect among regional states rather than through the military presence of foreign powers or the imposition of their political will.
‘The time is now’
Araghchi concluded by describing the current international environment as a historic choice between continuing along a path of militarism, intervention, confrontation and recurring wars, or changing course.
He called for development to be returned to the center of the international agenda, human dignity to be placed ahead of power calculations, and justice to be freed from 'monopoly and selectivity.'
He also called for the restoration of credibility to international law, saying the global turnaround he advocated was not a task for an uncertain future.
“Now is the time,” he said.

Costly overhaul fuels fears for Cairo's street kiosks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
17:28:16 UTC

Breadcrumb
Costly overhaul fuels fears for Cairo's street kiosks
Cairo's omnipresent street kiosks, where commuters grab cigarettes, children buy sweets, and residents stop for cold drinks or phone credit, are set for a makeover that some fear could price many small operators out of business.
Authorities in the Egyptian capital this week launched a scheme to standardise thousands of licensed kiosks, giving existing operators three months to adopt a unified design costing between 50,000 and 60,000 Egyptian pounds ($1,000-$1,200), a hefty sum for many small business owners.
The overhaul is the latest in a series of projects reshaping Cairo's urban landscape, which critics say have at times come at the expense of the city's architectural heritage and historic character.
Beneath a clutter of snack packets, soft-drink adverts and hanging cigarette displays in Cairo's leafy Heliopolis district, shopkeeper Moamen Hassan topped up a customer's phone credit as he voiced support for the plan but concern over the price tag.
"We definitely want the city to look better," the 27-year-old told AFP.
"But many kiosk owners in poorer areas won't be able to afford the cost. Some will have no choice but to close."
Cairo Governor Ibrahim Saber described the scheme as an effort to improve the city's appearance and keep pavements clear, and a prototype unveiled downtown offers a glimpse of that vision.
With its cream-coloured exterior, gold lettering and neatly arranged shelves, it stands in stark contrast to the colourfully chaotic kiosks that line Cairo's streets, their metal frames crowned with branded awnings and crammed with everyday goods.
'It makes life easier'
Known locally as the koshk, the compact structures have been part of Cairo's streetscape for generations, tucked between ageing apartment blocks, transport hubs and busy intersections all across the sprawling city.
Often among the first businesses to open each morning and the last to close at night, many have become neighbourhood landmarks.
"I pass by the kiosk almost every day," 19-year-old university student Sabrine Ahmed told AFP. "It makes life easier."
Under the new scheme, kiosks will be fitted with QR codes allowing the public and authorities to access information including licence details and payment records.
The standardised structures, measuring either six or nine metres square, will also include fixtures like electricity meters and fire extinguishers.
The overhaul comes as many Egyptians are still struggling with the fallout from years of sharp currency devaluations and soaring prices.
To ease the burden, authorities say licensed kiosk owners can pay 25 percent upfront, or between 12,500 and 15,000 pounds, with the remainder spread over two years without interest.

Lying to its people, denying its crimes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
17:23:35 UTC
02:23:35 KST

Lying to its people, denying its crimes
Seven months of concealment: the price Americans aren't told, the crimes Iranians won't forget
TEHRAN — Seven months after the United States and Israel launched their war against Iran, a growing body of reporting, congressional scrutiny, military documents and international investigations is exposing a widening gap between Washington’s public narrative of the conflict and the scale of its human, military and financial consequences.
The war began on February 28 with Washington and Tel Aviv presenting the destruction of Iran’s nuclear and missile capabilities as central objectives. President Donald Trump repeatedly said Iran could not be allowed to obtain a nuclear weapon and, immediately after the opening strikes, described the operation as necessary to prevent that outcome.
Yet the premise of an imminent nuclear threat has remained contested. The Arms Control Association noted that, at the time of the February attack, neither Trump nor Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu publicly presented evidence of an ongoing Iranian nuclear-weapons effort, while International Atomic Energy Agency Director General Rafael Grossi said in early March that the agency did not see a structured program to manufacture nuclear weapons.
Trump nevertheless repeatedly suggested that the conflict would be short. In early March, he said that Iran would have had a nuclear weapon had the United States not acted within two weeks, while subsequent reporting documented a series of shifting predictions about when the war would end. By September, the conflict had entered its seventh month.
Against that backdrop, the question increasingly confronting Washington is not simply what the war has achieved, but how much of its human and material cost has been fully disclosed.
Civilian casualties and the Minab investigation
The most consequential challenge to the official narrative concerns the February 28 strike on the Shajareh Tayyebeh school in Minab, southern Iran.
A recent investigation by the United Nations Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran found “reasonable grounds” to believe that the United States committed a war crime in the Minab strike and in a separate attack on a sports complex and residential area in Lamerd. The mission said the two attacks killed at least 178 civilians.
The Minab attack became one of the war’s most devastating incidents, killing many civilians, including more than 100 children. UN findings said the school was a clearly identifiable civilian facility and that US forces had failed to take the necessary measures to establish that it was a legitimate military target.
The significance of the findings goes beyond the death toll. They challenge the explanation that the Minab strike was simply an unavoidable consequence of the fog of war.
A separate investigation reported by Bloomberg has shed further light on the military decision-making that preceded the attack. According to the investigation, Pentagon investigators identified flawed intelligence, outdated imagery and excessive reliance on artificial-intelligence systems as factors that contributed to the strike that killed 123 children.
The emerging picture is therefore one in which the tragedy cannot readily be reduced to a single technical error. Questions have instead been raised about the entire targeting process — from the intelligence entering the system to the human decisions made after it was processed.
For Tehran, Minab has become a symbol of the civilian toll of the war. Internationally, the UN findings have transformed the incident from an Iranian allegation into the subject of a formal international investigation and legal assessment.
Washington, however, has rejected the UN mission's conclusions. The White House and State Department have disputed the findings and questioned the mission's impartiality.
That disagreement does not resolve the underlying issue: whether the full US investigation into Minab should be made public.
Kuhestak: another strike, another demand for answers
The question of transparency has gained renewed urgency following the September 1 strike on a home in Kuhestak, Hormozgan Province, where a wedding gathering was taking place.
Six Democratic senators — Brian Schatz, Patty Murray, Jeanne Shaheen, Jack Reed, Mark Warner and Chris Coons — have called for a “fully and impartially” conducted investigation into the attack.
The lawmakers said reports indicated that four civilians, including women and a child, were killed and more than 60 people wounded, and that weapons experts and visual analysis suggested the strike was caused by a US bomb. They demanded that the Pentagon release its findings to Congress and the American public.
The senators also said Congress had yet to receive the full findings of the Pentagon's investigation into the February 28 Minab strike.
Their intervention is significant because it places the issue of civilian casualties inside the US political system itself. The demand is not coming only from foreign governments or international organizations; members of the Senate are asking the Pentagon to disclose what it knows about the conduct and consequences of American military operations.
The Kuhestak case therefore adds a second, more recent test of Washington's commitment to transparency.
A casualty count under scrutiny
The questions surrounding transparency extend beyond Iranian civilian deaths.
On September 18, The Washington Post reported that more American service members had died during the Iran war than the Pentagon had publicly acknowledged.
Five US officials familiar with the Defense Department's internal casualty accounting told the newspaper that at least 22 US military personnel had died — four more than the number appearing in the Pentagon's public casualty database. A sixth official put the figure at 23, although that person said not all of the additional deaths were directly attributable to combat and involved US personnel deployed in the Middle East during the hostilities.
The same official said three US contractors in the region had also died since combat operations began.
The Pentagon declined to address the discrepancy in the figures, according to the newspaper.
The issue is not merely statistical. The Pentagon's public casualty database serves as the official record of military deaths and provides the public with information about the human cost of US military operations.
The Washington Post reported that, as of September 18, the public database listed 18 US military fatalities since the beginning of the conflict, while more than 820 service members had been wounded.
Discrepancy has therefore raised a basic question: if the Pentagon's internal accounting contains additional deaths, why are they not reflected in the public record?
What the photographs of US bases reveal
Another part of the story has emerged from photographs taken inside American military installations across the Middle East.
CBS News recently obtained photographs from active-duty US service members showing extensive damage at American positions in Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and elsewhere following Iranian missile and drone attacks.
The images included damaged buildings and vehicles at Camp Buehring and Camp Arifjan in Kuwait and severe damage to an E-3 Sentry aircraft at Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia. CBS said the photographs were provided by serving military personnel who spoke anonymously because of military restrictions on the media.
The Pentagon's inspector general has separately reported equipment losses worth up to $3.7 billion, including losses involving nearly 60 aircraft, while recording Iranian attacks on US bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman and Jordan.
The photographs matter because they provide a visual record of damage that is difficult to capture in official statements consisting largely of aggregate figures.
They also complicate the image of an American military campaign conducted with overwhelming protection from retaliation.
One US service member quoted by CBS described the situation in stark terms, saying the damage being inflicted on American bases had not been adequately communicated to the public.
Other reporting has independently documented damage to American aircraft. CBS reported that an A-10 at a US base in Jordan lost a wing in an Iranian strike, while several F-15s sustained damage.
The bill comes to $43.6 billion — and counting
The most tangible measure of the war's cost is financial.
According to an updated estimate from US Central Command provided to Congress, the conflict had cost the United States approximately $43.6 billion by September 3. About $28.1 billion of the total was attributed to expended munitions. The estimate does not include damage to US bases across the region.
The figure represents a substantial increase from the Congressional Budget Office's estimate of approximately $38 billion through August 1.
The CBO has projected that the war could continue adding roughly $3 billion a month, depending on the intensity of military operations.
The most striking element of the new estimate is the cost of weapons. US munitions expenditure rose from approximately $21.7 billion in the earlier CBO calculation to about $28.1 billion in the Central Command estimate.
The financial burden comes alongside pressure on American weapons stocks. The CBO has warned that the conflict has consumed substantial quantities of precision weapons and missile interceptors, potentially creating replenishment challenges for years.
For a war whose stated objective was to remove a strategic threat, the depletion of American military stocks has itself become a strategic concern.
A war is increasingly difficult to measure through official statements
The emerging evidence does not establish that every undisclosed casualty, military loss or omission was deliberately concealed. Some discrepancies may reflect classification rules, changing casualty categories, operational security or the normal lag involved in military investigations.
But the accumulation of discrepancies has become difficult to ignore.
Civilian deaths in Iran have generated UN investigations and congressional demands for disclosure. American military fatalities appear to exceed the numbers contained in the Pentagon's public database. Photographs from US service members reveal damage at bases that was not initially visible in official accounts. Pentagon documents show billions of dollars in equipment and munitions losses, while the overall cost of the war has risen to $43.6 billion.
At the same time, the Trump administration continues to seek additional resources for the military. The administration has proposed a $1.5 trillion defense budget, while also seeking additional funding connected to the Iran war and other defense priorities.
The result is an increasingly difficult contradiction for Washington: the longer the war continues, the harder it becomes to contain its consequences within a simple narrative of a rapid and decisive military operation.
 
 Seven months into the conflict, the central question is no longer only what the United States says happened in Iran.
It is what the accumulating evidence — from UN investigators, American lawmakers, Pentagon documents, US military personnel and American media investigations — says happened after the first bombs fell.
And on that question, the record is becoming considerably larger than the official daily casualty figures, battlefield statements and headline claims of success.

Two years after Lebanon pager bombs, Israel still evades justice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
17:23:20 UTC
02:23:20 KST

Breadcrumb
Two years after Lebanon pager attacks, impunity emboldens Israel to commit further atrocities
In September 2024, Lebanon was in shock after hundreds of pagers and walkie-talkies exploded simultaneously, killing dozens and injuring thousands. Two years later, with rights groups and victims are still calling for justice, as Israeli leaders continue to boast about the attack.
Despite the international outcry and demands that the attack be tried as a war crime, there has been no form of accountability, with suggestions that the attack perhaps emboldened Israel to commit more atrocities.
Israel touted the attack as targeting Hezbollah operatives, however among the dozens killed were at least two children, and numerous others among the thousands of civilians wounded.
"The pager attacks are an unprecedented war crime that received widespread international condemnation," Ghida Frangieh, head of litigation at the Legal Agenda, told The New Arab.
"However, the Israeli perpetrators continue to openly brag about this war crime, and no sufficient measures were taken to ensure they are held accountable."
Following the attack, Israel's Defence Minister Yoav Gallant praised the Israeli army, Shin Bet and the Mossad for "very impressive results".
At the same time, Israeli media has described the attack as an "extraordinary intelligence" and "stunning tactical" success, quoting former intelligence officials and analysts close to the security establishment.
"I think the Israeli military appears to feel emboldened by this impunity," Ramzi Kaiss, a Lebanon researcher at Human Rights Watch, told The New Arab.
"Not only have we seen more recent continuation of similar patterns that were documented before, but have seen just open declarations by the Israeli military and government leaders talking about either boasting about war crimes that have been committed, or speaking openly about their intention to commit further atrocities."
"There's been continuous impunity."
Kaiss explained that while the rights watchdog has documented a range of unlawful attacks and apparent war crimes by Israel, from the deliberate targeting of civilians, including journalists and medical workers, to the unlawful use of white phosphorus and attacks on peacekeepers, there has been no form of accountability.
When asked why, the researcher gave three reasons: the International Criminal Court (ICC) has no jurisdiction over crimes committed on Lebanese territory, the lack of a strong response from Israel's strongest allies and no domestic judicial investigations in the country.
"We've just seen unlawful attacks continue to impact civilians in the end with no restraints," he said.
Frangeih explained that while the Lebanese state filed complaints to the UN Security Council and the International Labour Organisation, it did not conduct a serious national investigation or request an international probe to document the attack, preserve evidence, and build a legal case.
"The Lebanese government can also open accountability pathways for the victims of Israeli war crimes by accepting the jurisdiction of the International Criminal Court over war crimes committed on Lebanese territories, including the pagers attacks," Frangieh said.
She also suggested that victims could consider resorting to foreign courts in countries where they have ties, or based on universal jurisdiction, to ensure that such a horrific crime does not remain unpunished.
Calls to end arms sales
Kaiss is calling for nations that have been funding and arming the Israeli military to suspend arms sales, military assistance, and arms transport immediately, given the well-documented record of war crimes committed by the Israeli military in Lebanon and the Gaza Strip.
"There are choices to be made by states that continue to provide weapons to Israel, whether they're willing to violate international law and, in many cases, their own domestic law, in order to continue arming a military that has been committing war crimes after war crimes, crimes against humanity and acts of genocide," he said.
At the same time, the researcher said the state needs to provide the ICC with the jurisdiction to investigate and prosecute crimes committed on Lebanese territory since October 2023 to date, and to ratify the Rome Statute.
"Lebanon's parliament should pass a law in line with national standards that criminalises war crimes, crimes against humanity, genocide, and provides the judicial authorities with the legal framework to investigate such crimes and document and preserve evidence," Kaiss said.
"I think there are clear steps that can be taken, starting with other states suspending military assistance, and also Lebanese authorities thinking of the needed steps to open pathways to accountability."
The researcher noted that a United Nations assessment team has been on the ground for three months to conduct an impartial, independent documentation of violations of international human law and human rights committed in Lebanon.
"They're here, and they're conducting their own investigation, which is something that did not happen in the last round of escalation hostilities in 2024," Kaiss noted.
Following recent escalation in March 2026 after a shaky ceasefire, thousands of civilians have been killed and over 340,000 displaced, with dozens of villages completely reduced to rubble.
At the same time, the Israeli government and military's intentions in establishing a buffer zone has depopulated and prevented hundreds of thousands of people from returning.

DR Congo expands Ebola vaccination to Ituri, over 3,700 people vaccinated
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
01:16:16 CST
02:16:16 KST

KINSHASA, Sept. 19 (Xinhua) -- Ebola vaccination was expanded Saturday to Ituri Province, the epicenter of the outbreak in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), with more than 3,700 people having received the Ervebo vaccine in the country.
The latest phase comes with the launch of a vaccination study known as BRAVO in Bunia, the capital of Ituri, conducted by Medecins Sans Frontieres (MSF) in collaboration with Congolese health authorities, the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) and other scientific partners.
The study plans to vaccinate about 20,000 frontline workers in Ituri and North Kivu, two provinces most affected by the outbreak, and follow participants over time to assess the potential effect of Ervebo against the Bundibugyo virus.
Ervebo was developed and licensed against the Zaire virus rather than the Bundibugyo virus driving the current outbreak, and whether it can protect humans against the latter has not been established.
Amid the expanding outbreak, the International Coordinating Group on Vaccine Provision approved an initial allocation of 70,000 doses of Ervebo to the DRC in August. Of the total, 50,000 doses were allocated for health and frontline workers, while 20,000 were set aside for a Phase 3 clinical trial designed to assess the vaccine's impact against the Bundibugyo virus.
According to the Africa CDC, 16,520 doses had been received in the DRC as of mid-September. The use of Ervebo had already begun on Aug. 27 under a protocol-governed program targeting people at high risk of exposure. As of Sept. 17, a total of 3,771 people had been vaccinated, including 3,063 in Tshopo Province and 708 in Bas-Uele Province, according to the latest epidemiological update issued Saturday by the DRC government.
BRAVO, which is expected to run for nine to 12 months, including three months of vaccination and at least six months of participant follow-up, marks a further step in efforts to generate evidence on the vaccine's potential effectiveness against Bundibugyo. A separate Phase 3 trial, based on a randomized ring-vaccination strategy, is also planned to more rigorously assess Ervebo's effectiveness.
According to the DRC government, the country has now reported 7,541 confirmed cases, including 3,639 deaths, with an overall case fatality rate of 48.3 percent. A total of 1,823 patients have recovered.
The outbreak, declared in May, has become the largest and deadliest Ebola outbreak ever recorded in the DRC and the second-largest Ebola outbreak globally, after the 2014-2016 West Africa epidemic. ■

TEHRAN, Sept. 19 (Xinhua) -- A senior Iranian security official said Iran has not yet decided whether to withdraw from the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT), adding that any decision on the issue will depend on Washington's behavior.

Jerusalem Biennale turns art into catalyst for post-October 7 healing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
17:10:17 UTC
02:10:17 KST

The Jerusalem Biennale will open its seventh and largest edition on Thursday, bringing a powerful message of resilience to the heart of Israel.
Running through November 12, the city-wide contemporary art experience will span 21 venues across Jerusalem and feature over 250 Israeli and international artists in 42 exhibitions. Entry to the Biennale exhibitions is free, except for select venues that require a standard entry fee.
This year’s theme, De Profundis (From the Depths) – derived from the opening words of Psalm 130 – explores memory, spirituality, and identity in the wake of post-October 7 collective trauma. Founder and creative director Rami Ozeri described the theme as a catalyst for movement, stating that art creates a passage from the personal and collective subconscious toward expression, connection, and light.
The 2026 Biennale features several internationally acclaimed Israeli contemporary artists. Yehudit Sasportas will premiere Mishpat Mokesh (A Mined Sentence) on October 12 at the Tower of David Jerusalem Museum. The video and sound installation reflects her exploration of buried histories, trauma, and the possibility of transformation and healing.
Belu-Simion Fainaru will participate in the central exhibition, Or Chozer (Reflected Light). Hanita Ilan, winner of the 2025 Rappaport Prize, will present a solo exhibition at Hamiffal Gallery.
Exhibitions confront current moment complexities directly
Highlighted exhibitions directly confront the complexities of the current moment. Or Chozer features 20 artists engaging with Mordecai Ardon’s utopian windows, questioning how to sustain a vision of peace amid brokenness.
At the Van Leer Jerusalem Institute, Open Wound brings together 14 Israeli and Diaspora artists to explore the borderless reverberations of October 7.
Alongside the exhibitions, the seven-week program will include gallery discussions, artist and curator talks, guided tours, workshops, performances, and special events. These gatherings give audiences opportunities to engage directly with the artists and ideas behind the artwork, turning the Biennale into a form of communal prayer reaching for renewal and hope.
For more, visit jerusalembiennale.org

We have sinned: After four years of Netanyahu, the 10 Commandments have a path to teshuva - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
17:09:51 UTC
02:09:51 KST

Every Yom Kippur, we confess even to sins we may never have personally committed because Judaism understands moral responsibility as larger than the individual. We bear responsibility for our community, for what is done in its name. And that idea feels urgent in Israel at this time.
After four years of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government, after October 7 and the terrible war that followed it, Yom Kippur offers an opportunity to examine ourselves through the oldest moral code we possess. By the measure of the Ten Commandments, we have much for which to atone.
‘I am the Lord thy God. Thou shalt have no other gods before me’
We have created other gods: nation, power, ideology, and political leaders. Parts of the Israeli Right have turned nationalism from love of country into an object of faith. Loyalty to Israel has too often been confused with loyalty to a government, a political camp, or even a particular man.
‘Thou shalt not make unto thee any craven images’
We have made idols of things. The Land of Israel occupies a profound place in Jewish memory and prayer, yet reverence for it has hardened into a theology of possession in which a hilltop, settlement, or ancient site can acquire greater moral weight than the human beings living there.
Ultranationalism has acquired its own articles of faith, while territory has assumed an almost religious sanctity. The Land of Israel may be holy; it is not God.
‘Thou shalt not take the name of the Lord thy God in vain’
We have attached God’s name to political ambitions and treated them as though they came from beyond politics. Biblical promises are invoked to sanctify policies devised by human beings, transforming disagreements over settlements and sovereignty into questions of faith.
Once a political objective becomes a divine command, compromise becomes apostasy. Taking God’s name in vain surely includes claiming divine endorsement for choices entirely our own.
‘Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy’
Shabbat is one of Judaism’s most beautiful ideas, a sanctuary in time that interrupts work and commerce. Israeli religious politics has transformed that gift into arguments about buses, shops, and what citizens may do between Friday evening and Saturday night, which for many is their only time off.
Rabbinic interpretation deserves respect, but in its zeal to protect the Sabbath, the religious establishment has obscured its simplest instruction: keep it holy. There is nothing in the commandment about electrons or forcing people to walk up stairs or suffer without transport to the beach.
‘Honor thy father and thy mother’
A society honors its parents through the dignity it affords them in old age. Israel is home to a dwindling generation of Holocaust survivors and the men and women who built the state, yet many spend their final years struggling with poverty, loneliness, and inadequate care.
We are adept at memorializing the Jewish past while proving outrageously ungenerous toward elderly Jews still among us. Honor requires food, housing, companionship, medical care, and dignity. Words are cheap, and we have been cheapening this commandment.
‘Thou shalt not murder’
October 7 gave Israel an obligation to defend its citizens, rescue its hostages, and remove the threat posed by Hamas, yet a just purpose still requires scrutiny of the means. The enormous civilian death toll in Gaza should weigh heavily on the Israeli conscience, because Jewish morality cannot measure the value of life according to nationality.
The commandment also reaches the West Bank, where Jewish extremists have attacked Palestinian civilians. Our deepest sin may be the numbness that allows another death to become a statistic.
‘Thou shalt not commit adultery’
Adultery is a betrayal of covenant, and Israel has been unfaithful to the covenant made at its birth. The Declaration of Independence envisioned a Jewish state founded upon freedom, justice, and peace, guaranteeing equality irrespective of religion, race, or sex.
Attacks on institutions, efforts to weaken checks on governmental power, and the treatment of Arab citizens as conditional members of the national community have strained that compact. Israel’s civic covenant, like any covenant, requires fidelity.
‘Thou shalt not steal’
Across the West Bank, Palestinian land has been appropriated through unauthorized outposts, intimidation, and settlement expansion, while ideological settlers have behaved as though biblical attachment confers ownership. The territorial dispute is complicated; the moral principle is simpler. Another person’s property remains his.
Theft also includes public money distributed according to coalition leverage rather than public need. Sinai required only three words: do not steal. In Israel, it seems we will need many words to convince citizens to fix this on October 27.
‘Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbor’
Israeli politics has become saturated with false witness against fellow Israelis. Leftists become traitors, rightists become fascists, protesters become enemies of the state, government supporters become enemies of democracy, and hostage families are assigned sinister motives.
We increasingly choose facts according to political allegiance and treat disagreement as disloyalty. Democracy requires fierce argument while society requires us to recognize those with whom we argue as neighbors. We have allowed the language of treason to consume the language of disagreement.
‘Thou shalt not covet thy neighbor’s goods’
Israeli politics has increasingly entertained fantasies of a Gaza emptied of Palestinians, of mass “voluntary” emigration, and of a territorial problem solved through their disappearance.
Palestinians possess homes, fields, memories, attachments, aspirations, and a sense of peoplehood. Their attachment to this land can coexist with ours. Our tragedy has been the growing conviction on both sides that one people’s attachment invalidates the other’s.
Returning to Jewish life
Yom Kippur does not end with the catalogue of sins. Confession leads toward teshuva, usually translated as repentance, but carrying the deeper sense of return. Judaism asks us to enumerate our failures because it assumes that human beings remain capable of choosing differently. Ashamnu asks us to see ourselves clearly enough to change.
Israel needs such a return: to a Judaism capable of cherishing the Land of Israel without worshiping it, observing Shabbat, each in their way, without coercion, defending Jewish life while grieving innocent non-Jewish life, and arguing passionately without turning fellow citizens into enemies.
The Torah gives us a principle around which to begin: “Love your neighbor as yourself.”
A few verses later it goes further: “The stranger who resides with you shall be as the native among you, and you shall love him as yourself.” Recognizing humanity beyond tribe is neither weakness nor a foreign ideal. It comes from the heart of the tradition whose name we invoke.
There is a Jewish state strong enough to defend itself and humane enough to grieve innocent life, a Jewish tradition secure enough to inspire without coercing, and a democracy mature enough to contain profound disagreement. The country we have become need not determine the country we choose to be.
So what will we do differently?
At the Neila service, as the long day draws toward its end, religious Jews imagine the gates beginning to close. This year Israel should hear both a warning and an invitation. The gates are still open.
The writer is a former Cairo-based Middle East editor and London-based Europe/Africa editor of the Associated Press. He served as chairman of the Foreign Press Association in Jerusalem and authored two books about Israel.

In 'At Work', Bouillon charms in a predictable look at a struggling novelist - review
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
17:09:27 UTC
02:09:27 KST

Fewer than 5% of fiction writers make a living from their writing, a statistic that seems to shock Paul (Bastien Bouillon), the hero of the new French movie At Work, directed by Valérie Donzelli, which opens in theaters throughout Israel on Thursday.
There is little to surprise anyone familiar with the business of writing and publishing in this movie, and how much you enjoy it will depend on how charmed you are by the performance of Bouillon, an appealing actor who has starred in such films as The Count of Monte Cristo and Leave One Day, as Paul.
Paul is obstinate and maddening, or single-minded and noble, depending on how you see it, as he devotes himself to a floundering writing career that devolves into a struggle for financial survival. Paul, who once ran a successful photography business, gave it up a few years ago to devote himself to writing novels.
He has published several books, all of which were critically acclaimed but none of which sold well. Now his editor (Virginie Ledoyen), whose patience is wearing thin, isn't happy with what she's read of his latest book, a memoir about his failed marriage. He has already spent his advance, and she won’t give him any more money.
His career isn’t his only problem. His ex-wife (played by director Donzelli) has just moved to Montreal with their teen children, and apparently, she has a career that helped support him in his writing. Now he must make a living on only a couple of hundred euros a month in royalties.
He rejects his father’s suggestion that he reopen his photography studio; instead, he looks for a part-time job so he can continue writing.
This leads him into the gig economy, and soon he works as a handyman on a site called Jobbers, where desperate people looking for work try to underbid each other, and he takes on difficult, time-consuming jobs for just 18 or 20 euros. Lonely and dehumanized by this grind, he keeps trying to write.
Paul seems to hold grudges against father, wife who left him
All this might have seemed a bit more engaging if it were clearer what drove him to write. He seems to hold obscure grudges against his unsupportive father and the wife who moved away with his kids, but that alone doesn't explain why he walked away from a successful middle-class life, or why he sticks with writing when he doesn’t seem to know what he wants to say.
As I watched, I kept wondering whether the world needed another book about a mean dad or a failed marriage, which is the last thing I imagine the director wanted me to think. Eventually, though, he finds his voice by writing about the humiliations of the gig economy, a subject that is apparently fresh and alluring to the French reading public.
I had a few thoughts on how the French publishing world differs from the American one as I watched, which I know something about. In America, even one book that doesn’t sell well is generally enough to get an author dropped by their publisher, and editors often barely know the writers, let alone meet with them to discuss their progress.
For example, a friend of mine writing her second book has never met her editor; when she asked the editor if they could have coffee, the editor refused, even though they live about five minutes away from each other.
Another friend in New York tried to deliver a finished manuscript to his editor in person a couple of years ago, and the editor’s assistant wouldn't even let him say hello. So when Paul drops off a bundle of handwritten notebooks and his editor has an assistant type it all up so she can read it, I kept thinking how lucky he was – which, again, was probably not what I was meant to think.
Film part of French literary movie tradition
At Work is part of a tradition of French literary movies which are fun if you can find them.
A few of the best are Lost Illusions, an adaptation of the classic Honoré de Balzac novel about an aspiring writer in Paris; Sagan, a biopic about popular novelist Françoise Sagan, who did make a very good living from her fiction; Like a Turtle on Its Back, a comedy about a blocked writer and his supportive wife; and Promise At Dawn, a portrait of the writer Romain Gary and his ambitious mother.

CNN, MS NOW, Politico reporters blocked from White House after Trump ban

CNN, MS NOW, Politico reporters blocked from White House after Trump ban
White House correspondents for CNN, MS NOW and Politico on Saturday were blocked from entering the US president's office and residence a day after President Donald Trump announced he was banning the three media outlets for what he called "fake news" coverage. News organisations and press freedom groups have slammed the move as unconstitutional.
The White House made good Saturday on President Donald Trump's vow to deny CNN, MS NOW and Politico access to the presidential mansion as punishment for reporting what he calls "fake news."
Read moreTrump bans media outlets CNN, MSNOW and Politico from the White House
The three news outlets denounced the ban as a violation of the US constitution and vowed to keep reporting on the US government.
They are expected to take the bans to court to regain access to the White House, fighting back as Trump expands his battle against mainstream news outlets that he detests and routinely slams as crooked.
"The White House belongs to the American people and the decisions made inside are funded with our tax dollars," MS NOW, formerly known as MSNBC, said Saturday on X.
To display this content from X (Twitter), you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
In its own statement, CNN said "we have a right under the US Constitution to do our reporting without hindrance or interference from the government, and this ban is an illegal assault on this fundamental right."
Reached for comment, the White House referred AFP to President Donald Trump's comments Friday announcing the bans.
Badges confiscated
MS NOW White House correspondent Akayla Gardner described how her access badge did not work as she tried Saturday to go through a security checkpoint she routinely uses.
"There was a red beeping light and so the officer asked me to hand over my badge," she said in an on-air play-by-play of the incident.
Betsy Klein of CNN gave a similar account of failing to enter the White House grounds as she does every day.
"There was a group of cameras waiting outside that gate to watch me walk in," she told her network.
Cheyenne Haslett of Politico was also denied entry and the Secret Service confiscated her access pass, editor in chief Jonathan Greenberger said in a note sent to AFP.
Trump did not say what prompted the move but added that "media Outlets shouldn't be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they're covering the President of the United States."
The 80-year-old Republican -- who has long had a fiery relationship with the mainstream media -- warned Friday that other outlets could face a similar fate but did not say which ones.
Both of Trump's White House terms have seen him lash out repeatedly at media whose coverage displeases him.
He has filed multiple defamation suits against news outlets, attacked the press on Truth Social and verbally assaulted several reporters, notably women, including CNN anchor Kaitlan Collins.
But it is rare for US presidents to outright bar news outlets from the White House -- although Trump in his first term banned CNN reporter Jim Acosta, an action which a court subsequently overturned.
Last year, Trump barred The Associated Press from some events because of the news agency's decision to continue using the term "Gulf of Mexico" -- and not the "Gulf of America" as decreed by Trump.
His administration has also put stricter controls on journalists, including taking control of which outlets can cover events as part of the "pool" admitted to small spaces such as the Oval Office and Air Force One.
Trump's surprise announcement on Friday comes at a time when his approval ratings are at record lows and his Republican Party risks losing control of Congress in November's midterm elections.
The war in Iran and rising prices, particularly at the gas pump, are among the factors that have contributed to his sinking political fortunes.
'Press access is not a privilege'
The move drew immediate accusations that it was unconstitutional and would be thrown out by the courts.
An association representing hundreds of journalists who cover the White House on Satruday demanded the restoration of access for banned colleagues, calling the removal unconstitutional.
"Today's action revoking access for journalists from CNN, POLITICO, and MSNOW violates the First Amendment," the White House Correspondents' Association said, urging the Trump administration "to immediately restore our colleagues' access."
"Press access is not a privilege for journalists. It's a right to ensure the American people can be independently informed," advocacy group Reporters Without Borders said Friday, vowing legal action in response.

Germany's defence chief Carsten Breuer chosen to head NATO military committee

02:01:19 KST

Germany’s defence chief Carsten Breuer was elected as the next chair of NATO’s Military Committee. He will take office in July 2027 for a three-year term, serving as the alliance’s top military adviser.
General Carsten Breuer, Germany's chief of defence, was selected on Saturday as the next head of NATO's military committee, the alliance's supreme military authority and a primary advisory body to its political leadership.
Military chiefs from the 32-nation alliance elected Breuer during a meeting in Copenhagen, the current chair, Italian Admiral Giuseppe Cavo Dragone, announced in a post on X.
Breuer will assume the role in July 2027, succeeding Dragone for a three-year term that aligns with NATO's strategic efforts to bolster deterrence against potential Russian aggression by 2029.
Alongside the Supreme Allied Commander Europe (SACEUR), the chairman of the Military Committee is among the most influential figures in NATO. In this role, Breuer will serve as chief military advisor to Secretary-General Mark Rutte and act as the primary bridge conveying recommendations from alliance chiefs of staff to senior political decision-makers.
German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius praised the appointment, stating that Breuer had demonstrated exceptional strategic foresight and played a pivotal role in restructuring the Bundeswehr.
"Now he will bring all his strength and experience to NATO, which faces major, historic challenges," Pistorius said, highlighting an escalating threat from Russia as European partners take greater responsibility for conventional deterrence while the United States broadens its strategic focus to other regions, according to German media.
Breuer, Germany's highest-ranking soldier, has served as Inspector General of the Bundeswehr since March 2023. He previously led the Bundeswehr's Territorial Command, which he established, and gained national prominence directing the Federal Chancellery's COVID-19 crisis staff under Chancellor Olaf Scholz. An army air defence officer who enlisted in 1984, Breuer is married with three children.
A successor to fill his current post as Inspector General has yet to be named.

Victoria Yakusha crafts sculptural jewellery boutique in New York
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
17:00:45 UTC
02:00:45 KST

Victoria Yakusha crafts sculptural jewellery boutique in New York
Ukrainian designer Victoria Yakusha has created a sculptural, almost monochromatic interior for a jewellery brand's flagship boutique in New York City.
Also from Ukraine, the brand Guzema's store in SoHo is its first US flagship and occupies a 1,100-square-foot (102-square-metre) space on Wooster Street.
Victoria Yakusha Studio used her signature minimalist style to design a space that feels calming and curated.
"My work here was closer to that of a sculptor," said founder Victoria Yakusha. "We didn't want the feeling of traditional retail. We wanted something more intimate."
The long, narrow interior is laid out with products presented in recessed niches on both sides, and inside a series of sculptural vitrines running back through the centre.
These monolithic islands are upholstered in dove-grey suede and "rounded like a river stone" to create a soft, serene statement.
The remainder of the decor is slightly lighter in colour, with mineral-toned plaster and matching storage units creating the impression of a single cohesive surface.
In the store window, a series of white hand-sculpted vessels with textured skins and bowl-like tops are used to present Guzema's jewellery in a novel way.
These pieces follow the same visual language as the Sonaih floor lamp from Yakusha's own design brand Faina, which produces furniture, lighting and decor.
"We wanted the jewelry to feel discovered, not just displayed. That's how we came to the idea of the installation," Yakusha said. "Each vessel is hand-sculpted, layer by layer. It's an artwork in itself. It becomes part of the experience, a way of revealing something precious."
At the back of the store is a semi-private consultation area for one-on-one appointments, screened from the main space by a glass-block partition.
Several more Faina designs feature in this salon, including a curved sofa, ottoman and sconce, along with a burnished-metal table and silver tableware by Natalia Criado.
A former fashion editor, Yakusha has opened galleries for her furniture line in both Antwerp and Miami, and earlier designed the interior for Kyiv eatery Istetyka that balances rough and smooth surfaces.
Since Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, she has designed a furniture collection as an homage to her homeland and proposed a museum to preserve threatened Ukrainian cultural heritage.
The photography is by Matthew Williams.

Caribbean nations draft action plan to push UK to redress reparations over slavery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
17:00:14 UTC
02:00:14 KST

Caribbean nations are drawing up a multi-pronged “action plan” with legal options to push the UK into negotiating a decades-long slavery reparations deal, officials at a reparations conference have said.
Leaders in the region are hoping the UK would agree to targeted and constructive negotiation talks at upcoming Commonwealth and UN summits, but they are ready to take the matter to international courts if Britain continues to resist diplomatic options.
Earlier this month, a spokesperson for Andy Burnham reiterated the British government’s long‑held position that “the UK does not and will not pay reparations”.
Ralph Gonsalves, the former prime minister of St Vincent and the Grenadines, said the Caricom Regional Conference on Reparations, which took place this week, hosted by Barbados with the Caricom Reparations Commission (CRC), was key for agreeing a unified strategy to bring Britain to the negotiating table. Gonsalves is now an elder and adviser for the Repair Campaign, a social movement for reparatory justice.
He said that slavery happened over centuries and reparations had to be realistic and set over decades. “We need a concrete, multigenerational plan,” he said.
On the legal options available to the Caribbean, Gonsalves challenged arguments that Britain did not violate historical laws during transatlantic slavery, adding that the UK’s signature on contemporary UN conventions had established a binding legal obligation for reparative justice.
“The fact is that the consequences of slavery fall squarely under the Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination, which obliges states to help address the consequences of native genocide and slavery,” Gonsalves said.
In March this year, 123 nations voted for a landmark UN resolution that described chattel slavery as the gravest crime against humanity. The UK was one of several European countries that abstained from voting in the resolution. But, last month, a UN committee on the elimination of racial discrimination said countries were legally obliged to consider reparations for the transatlantic slave trade and take other measures to address the enduring legacy of racial discrimination.
David Comissiong, the deputy chair of the Barbados National Task Force on Reparations, said the Caribbean nations were considering “several legal strategies”.
“You’ve had Jamaica trying to engage with the national legal judicial system of the UK, the privy council – that is one strategy,” he said, adding that going to the international court of justice for an advisory opinion was another option.
Prof Sir Hilary Beckles, the chair of the CRC, said reparations was a matter of justice, adding that countries in the region were forced to create viable democracies “out of the mess” of colonialism, which was still having an impact today.
“When Jamaica took its petition to the UK, we had to surround that petition with the fact that when Jamaica became independent in 1962, 80% of the black people in Jamaica could not read or write. After 300 years of British colonisation, they moved into independence with 80% illiteracy. How do you build a modern nation, not even a competitive economy, with 80% illiteracy?”
Speaking at the conference, Mia Mottley, the prime minister of Barbados, said the Caribbean had “no desire to bankrupt anybody”.
“But we have a desire for justice,” she said.
Earlier this year, Barbados commissioned a report which showed that Britain stole 25 million years of life and labour through slavery in the country.
She added: “The British government took almost 200 years to repay the debt that it incurred when it paid the slave owners £20m.” Mottley pointed to the fact that Germany paid $95bn (£71bn) to the Jewish community because of the horrors of the Holocaust.
Mottley said that she did not want “anybody to diminish the fact that in this country here, which I have the honour to lead, that from settlement in 1627, 400 years ago next year, for 211 years, not six, people were treated as chattel”.
“If they dared to speak or to do things that were displeasing, their lives and limbs were put at risk. The evidence is clear. What is absent is the will,” she said.

North Korea has fired around 150 ballistic missiles at Ukraine, learning from each one. Same missiles threaten Japan, and Kyiv just shows its speaker what is inside them
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
16:54:59 UTC
01:54:59 KST

Ukraine's Defense Intelligence, also known as HUR, has given Japan's parliament speaker a rare, close look at a North Korean weapon: the components of a ballistic missile Russia fired at Ukraine. Ukrainian officers have shown the parts to Eisuke Mori, speaker of Japan's House of Representatives, during his delegation's visit to Kyiv, HUR says on social media.
Ukraine has become the place where North Korea's missiles are tested in combat and taken apart. Pyongyang has supplied Russia with roughly 150 KN-23 and KN-24 ballistic missiles since late 2023, along with thousands of troops, and Russia has fired scores of them at Ukrainian cities.
Each strike gives Pyongyang combat data that has sharpened its weapons. Showing Japan the components turns that access into a prospect of future deterrence: the same missiles threaten the Asia-Pacific.
Ukraine hands Japan the evidence
Examining missile parts allows analysts to read the missile's technical characteristics, design, and the state of North Korea's arms industry, HUR says. Ukraine has found that the North Korean missiles falling on its cities are built partly from foreign parts, with components traced to companies in Britain, Japan, Switzerland, China, and the US, Radio Free Asia reports, evidence of how Pyongyang skirts sanctions to build them.
The threat reaches the Pacific
HUR frames the demonstration as a shared-security case. North Korean weapons endanger not only Ukraine but Japan and the wider Asia-Pacific, it says, while the Moscow-Pyongyang partnership lets Russia keep waging its war and lets Pyongyang build up its arsenal and refine its weapons.
"Countering this cooperation requires coordinated action by international partners. Sharing intelligence helps better assess common threats and find ways to overcome them," HUR states.
Pyongyang learns from the strikes
North Korea has sent Russia millions of artillery shells, rocket systems, and thousands of troops, and is paid in cash and technology, with one analyst estimating Pyongyang may have earned about $20 billion from the war. In return, the missiles' accuracy has improved as Pyongyang studies how they perform under fire, turning the war into a live proving ground for weapons built to threaten its neighbors.

Thousands protest inaction over climate crisis in Switzerland
LAUSANNE, Switzerland – Several thousand people marched in the Swiss cities of Geneva and Lausanne on Sept 19 to protest government inaction in the face of global warming.
They were answering a call by a coalition of more than a hundred associations and political parties under the common banner: “No 50-degree summers!”
People of all ages took part in the marches, carrying placards with slogans such as “No Planet B” and “We’re cooked!”, AFP journalists noted.
The larger demonstration was at Lausanne, where organisers said at least 8,000 had taken part.
One marcher, 31-year-old union activist Guillaume Matthey, told AFP he hoped this was the start of “a new cycle of widespread popular mobilisation” to put pressure on the country’s political and financial leaders for their lack of response to the climate crisis.
Already in 2024, the European Court of Human Rights ruled that Switzerland was not doing enough to fight climate change – the first time an international court ruled against a country on this matter.
“This is about telling our authorities that it’s really the time to act,” said one marcher in his 60s, Yves Froidevaux.
“We can’t just finance weapons and then not care about the rest of it – that’s not on,” he added.
Vincent Fontannaz, a 47-year-old actor dressed up as a giant drop of water, said: “There’s been a real lack of water this summer.”
“It’s not just about swimming pools, it’s most of all about agriculture – and for our survival in fact,” he added.
One marcher, 55-year-old architect Laurent Guidetti, wore a gas mask made out of plastic bottles. He was one of the lucky ones to have a well-insulated apartment “that stays cool at night”, he said.
This summer, however, he had thought about people who were not so lucky. “It’s going to be very tough for them,” he added.
And even if they got through this summer’s heatwaves, he did not know how they would manage against the higher temperatures expected in future summers.
After the demonstrations on Sept 19, other protests have been called in several Swiss cities in the coming weeks until Oct 2.
Switzerland’s summer heatwaves forced the closure of a nuclear power station and caused record low water levels in Lake Zurich. AFP
