Officials address challenge of election interference
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
16:42:49 UTC
01:42:49 KST

Diplomats from the US, UK and EU yesterday underscored the need to counter electoral interference and cognitive warfare operations ahead of Taiwan’s year-end local elections.
They made the remarks at this year’s Resilient Taiwan for Sustainable Democracy International Forum hosted by the Presidential Office, saying that electoral interference from authoritarian regimes has become a pervasive threat to democratic countries.
British Office Taipei Representative Ruth Bradley-Jones said election interference in Taiwan is the matter that concerns her the most.
Photo: Fang Pin-chao, Taipei Times
Every democratic country is being targeted by electoral interference, a threat that has become ever more severe with the prevalence of the Internet and advances in artificial intelligence, she said.
Taiwan is “nearest to the fire” of electoral interference, and is bearing the brunt of the damage when it can least afford it, she said, adding that Taiwan must urgently shore up its defenses against meddling.
Head of the European Economic and Trade Office Lutz Gullner said foreign information manipulation and interference, disinformation and cognitive warfare are among the most complex threats confronting the modern state.
For democracies that treasure the freedom of speech, these dilemmas pose a common challenge that defies easy answers, Gullner said.
Dealing with cognitive warfare requires an understanding that disinformation is not about exchanging information or communication, but an instrument in the hybrid warfare toolbox to control, influence or destabilize a targeted society, he said.
A coherent counter-narrative, media literacy and the awareness of the happenings in a country’s informational environment together form the answer to neutralizing foreign information manipulation and influence, he said.
Taiwan’s civil society has demonstrated a remarkable facility in the last of these capabilities, and the government would do well to integrate it within an official strategic framework to counter foreign meddling, Gullner said.
American Institute in Taiwan Director Raymond Greene said that democratic governments must use social media platforms and civil society to fight disinformation effectively.
Cooperation with social media platforms is essential, as they possess the tools capable of targeting fake news within the massive amounts of data social media platforms distribute, he said.
Democracies must counter malicious disinformation without trampling on speech and press freedoms, making it crucial for civil society to be in the spotlight of the fight against hostile cognitive warfare, Greene said.
Neutral groups not aligned with a political faction or ideology can have more credibility among members of the public who do not support the ruling party to reject Internet-based political meddling, he said.

Taiwan to impose tougher drug driving penalties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
16:42:48 UTC
01:42:48 KST

The government is set to impose tougher penalties for drug driving, including vehicle confiscation and fines of up to NT$270,000 for drivers who refuse drug tests, after 23 people were killed in drug driving-related incidents in first half of this year, the Ministry of Transportation and Communications said.
President William Lai (賴清德) on Aug. 17 promulgated amendments to the Road Traffic Management and Penalty Act (道路交通管理處罰條例), increasing penalties for drug driving and drug use, Public Transportation and Supervision Division director Hu Ti-chi (胡迪琦) said yesterday.
The amendments include higher fines, license revocation, liability for passengers traveling in the same vehicle, higher fines for driving without a license after revocation, mandatory addiction treatment and vehicle confiscation, he said.
Photo: Taipei Times
The ministry is preparing to implement the revised rules and has announced planned amendments to four related regulations.
Under the previewed amendments, drivers caught driving under the influence of drugs would face penalties based on the type of vehicle they were operating.
For a first offense, motorcycle riders could be fined NT$120,000, while car drivers face a NT$150,000 fine.
For a second offense within 10 years, the fines would increase to NT$210,000 for motorcycles and NT$240,000 for cars.
From the third offense, an additional NT$90,000 would be added to each fine, with no upper limit on the total amount.
Drivers who refuse to take a rapid saliva test would face even steeper penalties, the planned amendments say.
A first refusal would result in a NT$270,000 fine for motorcycle and car drivers. A second refusal within 10 years would raise the fine to NT$450,000, while each subsequent refusal would add another NT$180,000 to the previous penalty, again with no cap.
For drug-driving violations and related offenses resulting in license revocation, authorities could publish the offender’s name and photograph, and suspend the vehicle’s license plates for two years, the planned amendments say.
The new measures would allow vehicles to be confiscated on the spot when a driver is caught driving under the influence of drugs or refuses a drug test, while anyone caught driving while their license is revoked would face an additional NT$80,000 fine, and the vehicle would be impounded.

In hydropowered Bhutan, solar starts to rise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
16:42:46 UTC
01:42:46 KST

Engineer Rinzin Galley stands on a platform overlooking a former military shooting range on the edge of Bhutan’s capital, Thimphu, now home to a field of solar panels.
With abundant waterways, Bhutan has long relied on hydroelectric power to meet its electricity needs and stay carbon negative.
However, demand is growing, and in winter, when rivers run low before the mountain melt arrives, Bhutan already relies on imported Indian electricity.
Photo: AFP
“Solar projects are booming,” said Rinzin, senior engineer at Norion Renewable Energy.
The company’s biggest project to date is the Dechencholing solar farm on former military land, with an installed capacity of 4.45 megawatts (MW).
Dechencholing is one of several solar fields developed in recent years, including the country’s first mega project — Sephu, with capacity of more than 22MW.
That is relatively modest, especially compared with the vast solar fields installed in neighboring China, but it represents a new direction for Bhutan, where hydropower exports account for up to 15 percent of GDP, according to the World Bank.
“Our plans are to develop about 5,000 megawatts,” said Chhewang Rinzin, managing director of Druk Green Power Corp, the country’s generation utility.
Bhutan can generate about 3,700MW from hydro, but that capacity falls by about 80 percent during the winter, he said.
Winter demand has increased to 1,500MW from 400MW, creating a significant shortfall being met by electricity imports from India.
Officials attribute part of the growing demand to a construction boom, but Bhutan has also bet on bitcoin mining to boost revenue. A planned special economic zone known as the Gelephu Mindfulness City is expected to host energy-hungry data centers.
The problem was already clear in 2008, when a goal of generating 10,000MW from hydropower by 2020 was agreed.
However, the plan ran into a series of obstacles, including financing.
“When you’re looking at constructing 10,000 megawatts in hydropower capacity and each megawatt probably costs you about [US]$1.5 million ... for a small economy like ourselves, that’s quite difficult,” Chhewang said.
Solutions have included liberalizing foreign investment rules and increasing solar targets in the energy mix.
The country now aims for 25,000MW by 2040, with solar accounting for one-fifth of that.
Finding sufficient space for projects is challenging given Bhutan’s largely mountainous terrain.
“When we do solar projects on the ground mount, it takes a huge amount of area to get certain capacity,” Rinzin said.
The country’s high altitudes, circuitous routes and roads frequently damaged by landslides pose further problems.
Part of the push has involved training up a corps of solar engineers, including through the De-suung royal skilling initiative.
Norion has trained about 450 De-suung volunteers “to build in-house capacity in the country,” Rinzin said.
Several dozen work at Norion, which has a goal of installing 30MW of solar by next year, much of it on rooftops.
Rooftop solar is now a common sight in Thimphu on government buildings and businesses, but the incentives for individual consumers are still slim.
Electricity is comparatively cheap in Bhutan and installing solar remains expensive.
Om Pradhan, a former minister and ambassador, had long advocated for solar in Bhutan and was keen to install panels at home.
“I thought that firstly it would benefit me personally, in the sense that my electricity bills would go down,” the 79-year-old former minister for trade and industries told reporters. “The second thing is that I’ve always been an advocate for solar power.”
However, the 600,000 ngultrums (US$6,300) it cost him to install the system remains far out of reach for most Bhutanese.
“Many people calculate that if you put that money in the bank, the interest would pay your electricity bills,” he said.

North Korean leader calls for broader military AI use
North Korean leader Kim Jong-un has called for greater use of AI and automation in the country’s offensive and defensive weapons, while urging manufacturers to boost production.
Kim made the remarks while inspecting several defense enterprises Wednesday to Friday, accompanied by senior officials and his influential sister, Kim Yo-jong.
Photos released by state media show him visiting facilities that produce drones and artillery systems, including massive 600 mm multiple launch rocket systems (MLRS).
Known outside North Korea as the KN-25, the system resembles the US-made HIMARS but has evolved beyond a conventional MLRS, effectively functioning as a short-range ballistic missile launcher.
“Our artillery should have the most concentrated and destructive, massive and versatile offensive capability and responsibly perform the two missions of deterring and fighting war,” the North Korean leader said, as cited by KCNA.
Kim also called for broader use of AI in “offensive and defensive combat weapon systems,” as well as improving armor and automation of artillery weaponry, state media reported. He also instructed manufacturing plants to ramp up production and improve the “conditions and environment for production.”
The North Korean leader reportedly “expressed great satisfaction,” finding that most of the plants are meeting the production goals to fulfill the “huge plans” outlined by the Party Central Military Commission, the top military affairs and planning body of the country.
Prior to joining the nuclear club in the mid-2000s, North Korea relied on a vast artillery park for deterrence, as the South Korean capital, Seoul, is within reach of conventional artillery. Pyongyang has recently worked on modernizing and expanding its artillery park, with some of the missile systems in its arsenal also doubling as nuclear delivery systems.

At camp Norway built in Polish forest, NATO trainers admit Ukraine’s army now moves faster than their own
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
16:37:52 UTC
01:37:52 KST

Ukrainian engineers near the front rewrite their drones' software every couple of days. A NATO army needs about six months to push the same update. That gap in speed is the central challenge for the Western trainers working with Ukrainian troops in Poland, who say Ukraine's wartime tempo is exposing how slowly the West moves in peacetime, the Business Insider reports.
Russia's war forces the Ukrainian Army to buy, train, and adapt at a pace peacetime armies are not built for, and its experience is pushing NATO to confront how much its own bureaucracy slows it down.
The alliance has studied that experience without yet fully absorbing it: in an Estonian war game last winter, a ten-person Ukrainian drone team wiped out two NATO battalions in a day.
Now NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte is calling for a large-scale transformation of the West's defense industry so its armies can react faster.
Two speeds meet in Poland
The place where those speeds collided was Camp Jomsborg, a base Norway built in an eastern Polish forest in a matter of months. There, under an operation called Legio, trainers from across northern Europe drill Ukrainian soldiers while the Ukrainians hand their front-line lessons back to NATO.
The camp sits, as its operations officer, a major identified only as John, put it, at "the mental and geographical middle point between war in the east and peacetime mechanism in the West."
A drone update tells the story
Brigadier General Atle Molde, who commands the task force, put the gap in numbers. If a Western drone needs new software, he said, "you have to send it to a Western country or a company, and an update takes six months."
In Ukraine, "they have the engineers sitting close to the front updating every two days, every two weeks, developing software, adapting it to genuine situations."
Molde said he wants to see greater initiative in innovation within Western armies, but to achieve that, "it has to be some major changes that have to be done on all levels when it comes to legislation."

German-Russian relations at freezing point
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
16:34:00 UTC
01:34:00 KST

German-Russian relations at freezing point
September 19, 2026
For many years, Germany and Russia had a perfect partnership.
Russia supplied cheap energy, which helped German industry succeed in exporting its goods worldwide. This partnership began in the early 2000s. On the German side was Chancellor Gerhard Schröder from the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), followed later by Chancellor Angela Merkel of the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU). Their counterpart was Vladimir Putin.
Even when Russia annexed the Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea in 2014, business continued as usual. It was then that the agreement to build Nord Stream 2, a direct gas pipeline between Russia and Germany designed to bypass Ukraine was signed. At the time, other European countries and the US warned that the pipeline would provide Russia with powerful leverage.
The warnings proved to be correct. On February 24, 2022, Russian tanks rolled into Ukraine. German hopes for a stable European order, the democratization of Russia, and the continuation of its lucrative business model were shattered.
How could so many German politicians be so wrong?
"Shortly before the invasion, the widespread view was that there were no rational grounds for an attack on Ukraine, because the economic, military, and political costs to Russia of starting a war would be far too high," Russia expert Mario Baumann of the German Council on Foreign Relations told DW. "People [in Germany] had projected their own rationality onto Russia. They underestimated the regime's imperialist and revisionist ambitions."
After that, nothing in the bilateral relationship was ever the same again. Chancellor Olaf Scholz(SPD) spoke of a Zeitenwende (epochal shift) in foreign and security policy, in the days after the 2022 invasion of Ukraine began.
Since then, the German armed forces have expanded. Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said the following year, "We must become capable of waging war," a statement that critics still say was an escalation of tensions.
Germany ended its decades-long energy dependence on Russia and shut down Nord Stream 2. In September 2022, the pipeline was blown up. The Federal Prosecutor's Office suspects a Ukrainian group was responsible.
A series of EU sanctions have long since reduced Russian-German trade relations to a minimum. Government cooperation in culture, science, and education has also practically ceased to exist.
A new low point
While the German government under Scholz initially hesitated to take dramatic steps on military aid to Ukraine, Friedrich Merz, then the leader of the opposition, stepped up his rhetoric.
"Ukraine must win the war. Russia must lose the war," he said in 2024 as leader of the CDU/CSU parliamentary group in parliament. In 2025, as chancellor, he then spoke of Russia's "economic exhaustion," which the West must "help bring about." But that has yet to materialize. To this day, Russia has shown no serious willingness to compromise.
Meanwhile, Germany is feeling the consequences of its military support for Ukraine. The German government has long suspected Russia of being behind cyberattacks on government agencies and critical infrastructure.
So when an armed drone was discovered and defused in August 2026 at Leipzig Airport close to Ukrainian transport aircraft — which transport a large portion of the military aid to Ukraine — the government was certain: For the first time, it publicly blamed the Kremlin.
A Russian cultural center in Berlin and the Russian consulate in Bonn were closed, which the German government said were being used as espionage centers. Moscow responded by closing the Goethe Institutes and the German consulate in St. Petersburg.
Putin has denied Russian responsibility for the Leipzig incident, calling it a "serious mistake" to blame Moscow, while Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov even described the accusations as the "beginning of a real war." But Baumann says: "We shouldn't give in to the fears being stoked, because they are part of Russia's strategy to weaken Germany and Europe."
AfD wants to resume relations with Russia
The German government is also facing domestic pressure as the far-right Alternative for Germany(AfD) has made gains in regional elections and is rising in the national polls. The AfD would prefer to end support for Ukraine and normalize relations with Russia, including deals on oil and gas. High fuel prices in Germany have only made the issue more explosive.
"German support for Ukraine worries many people," said Sven Leunig, political scientist at the University of Jena in Thuringia, following the election in the neighboring state of Saxony-Anhalt, where the AfD won the September 6 election by a landslide. However, he noted, "it is less a fundamental rejection of the support itself than a reaction born of fear. People want to 'stay out' of the conflict so as not to be drawn into it more deeply themselves."
In the latest ARD Deutschlandtrend survey, 42% of respondents believe military aid to Ukraine has gone too far. "If public support weakens over the long term, the government will eventually have to respond," says Leunig.
Carry on or change course?
So far, the German government is sticking to its course, as Merz made clear once again following the AfD's election victory. But opinions on how to deal with Russia and the war in Ukraine differ not only among politicians but also among political scientists and experts.
Johannes Varwick of Halle University in Saxony-Anhalt believes it is long past time for a change of course: "German and European policy toward Ukraine resembles a mix of platitudes and wishful thinking," Varwick told DW. "It is high time for a course correction, and Germany should exert pressure on Ukraine to move closer to the latest American proposals, which aim for a compromise and could thus possibly bring about a political solution."
Baumann, on the other hand, argues: "Supporting Ukraine remains the best investment for safeguarding German and European interests. The government has recognized this and should stick to this course and continue to communicate it as such." However, it is important that Berlin act in concert with its European partners.
The war in Ukraine has now lasted longer than World War I. And there is no end in sight. Hopes that Russian-German relations will return to the way they used to be seem illusory for the foreseeable future.

If attacked, he said, Iran would respond by striking US military bases and American interests across the region with greater force.
Tensions in the Middle East have heightened after the US and Israel launched large-scale attacks on Iran in February, prompting Tehran to launch missile and drone strikes against US bases across the region.
Pakistan acted as a mediator to defuse tensions, helping reach an agreement between Washington and Tehran in June to end their hostilities. 
The deal later faltered amid disagreements between the two rivals over the Strait of Hormuz.

Fighting between the Houthis and the government forces has reignited after a four-year truce collapsed in July, months into the Middle East war between the United States and Iran.

China advances lunar spacesuit, bed rest research for 2030 moon landing mission
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
00:23:19 CST
01:23:19 KST

TIANJIN, Sept. 19 (Xinhua) -- China has advanced its push for a crewed moon landing by 2030, with its lunar spacesuit and a bed rest experiment for long-term space stays both progressing, the country's astronaut center said on Saturday.
The development of China's moon-landing spacesuit Wangyu, meaning "gazing into the cosmos," is progressing smoothly, with dozens of key technologies now in place, said Zhang Wanxin, an expert at the Astronaut Center of China, at an aerospace medical engineering conference in Tianjin.
Since the development began in 2020, efforts on Wangyu have focused on meeting the demands of complex lunar-surface operations and extreme environmental challenges, Zhang said, noting that the lunar spacesuit is designed to be lightweight, miniaturized, highly efficient and safe.
Beyond spacesuit development, China is also advancing astronaut health research, having completed the "Dixing-3" bed rest experiment to address physiological protection challenges for long-term space stays and crewed lunar landing missions.
According to Qu Lina, a center expert, the experiment began in May this year. Volunteers were divided into different groups and spent 15 or 30 days in bed. During the experiment, they completed daily activities such as eating, washing, sleeping, urinating and defecating while lying in bed.
Results showed that the experiment effectively protects the human bone, muscle and cardiovascular systems, and it will provide technical support for long-term space stays and crewed lunar landing missions. ■

Feature: Tradition, innovation keep wine culture alive in western Poland
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
00:23:18 CST
01:23:18 KST

ZIELONA GORA, Poland, Sept. 19 (Xinhua) -- Wine glasses clinked as visitors moved from stall to stall in the heart of Zielona Gora, sampling sparkling wines and dry whites while hearing the stories behind each bottle.
The scene unfolded during Winobranie, the annual wine harvest festival in Zielona Gora, a western Polish city with a centuries-old winemaking tradition.
Held each September, the festival brings together dozens of vineyards from across western Poland and features concerts, a market, vineyard tours and a colorful parade.
For visitors, Winobranie is a celebration of wine and local culture. For producers, it is also a chance to showcase their wines, meet customers and carry forward a tradition deeply rooted in the region.
Zielona Gora's winegrowing heritage stretches back more than 700 years. The earliest documented record of grape cultivation in the area dates to 1314, while organized harvest celebrations emerged in the 19th century.
In recent decades, family vineyards combine inherited traditions with new techniques, helping drive a revival of winemaking in the region.
Among the pioneers is Stara Winna Gora, a family vineyard founded in 1997 near Zielona Gora and described as the first officially registered vineyard in Poland.
For Zofia Choluj, a wine seller at the vineyard, the key to sustaining the business over decades is passion. She called it "the most important thing."
That passion, she added, extends beyond winemaking itself. The vineyard works with local artists and craftspeople, incorporating their work into the visitor experience and helping promote local culture.
Choluj has also witnessed a broader revival of winemaking in the region. Training and expertise have expanded for small producers, she said, adding that as wine quality and sales have improved, a new generation has shown growing interest in the trade.
At Na Lesnej Polanie Vineyard, Michal Lewandowski is part of that younger generation. His parents planted their first vines in 1999, gradually turning a small family project into an established vineyard.
Lewandowski said the region's climate and long winegrowing history provide a strong foundation for local producers, while growing competition is pushing vineyards to improve their products and develop new styles.
While some vineyards here draw on decades of family history, newer producers are also bringing fresh ideas to Zielona Gora's wine scene.
At Pod Wieza Vineyard, which was envisioned as a relatively small project when Krystian Kurpiel's parents started it about a decade ago, the family has experimented with different winemaking methods, including Georgian-style clay vessels buried underground and the production of sparkling wines.
Since Kurpiel became a full-time winemaker, the vineyard has expanded to about 3.5 hectares. "We always try to make something distinctive from the others," he said.
A larger harvest gives the winery more room to try different winemaking methods, he added. He noted that the Winobranie festival serves as an important platform for local winemakers to engage directly with customers while showcasing Zielona Gora's distinctive wine culture.
"For many families here, winemaking is passed down from one generation to the next. People have come to realize that wine is part of our local culture, and we have to keep it alive," Kurpiel said. ■

Roundup: Hong Kong's 1st five-year plan responds to public aspirations
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
00:23:13 CST
01:23:13 KST

HONG KONG, Sept. 19 (Xinhua) -- The Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (HKSAR)'s first five-year plan for economic and social development (2026-2030) released earlier this week turns the public's key everyday concerns into measurable, deliverable commitments to improve livelihoods across the city.
The five-year plan and the 2026 policy address were both released on Sept. 16. The five-year plan sets out a blueprint for the future, and the policy address focuses on immediate priorities and actionable details.
Housing is the top livelihood concern for Hong Kong residents. The plan clearly sets a public housing construction target of about 196,000 units over the next five years, while pledging to continuously optimize the home-ownership ladder and striving to largely eliminate substandard subdivided units in residential buildings by 2030.
This proactive housing policy is widely seen as a shift in housing supply toward a "results-oriented" governance model, placing greater emphasis on tangible outcomes and real effectiveness.
The Northern Metropolis is regarded as a new engine to resolve Hong Kong's deep-seated livelihood challenges in housing, employment, and youth development. The plan specifies a further upgrade for the Northern Metropolis University Town under the development concept of "One Town, Five Elements." By coordinating five key elements -- education, technology, industry, talent, and urban development, it aims to foster an innovation ecosystem deeply integrating industry, academia, and research.
"Only by expanding space through development can improvements in people's livelihood have lasting momentum," said Holden Chow, a member of the Legislative Council of the HKSAR.
Chow noted that this approach turns Hong Kong into a "super reservoir" for global talent and positions the Northern Metropolis as a strategic hub connecting the mainland and global markets.
Ms. Lau, a Hong Kong resident who has waited three years for public rental housing and currently lives in a subdivided flat in Kowloon Bay, carefully flipped through the housing policy sections after receiving copies of the five-year plan and policy address.
"Whether it is increasing the supply of Light Public Housing or eliminating substandard subdivided units, it gives me hope of moving into public housing sooner," she said.
During the formulation of this inaugural five-year plan, the HKSAR government held a two-month public consultation, receiving over 17,000 views and suggestions across various sectors. Incorporating the public's voices into the top-level design ensures the policies align better with people's needs and sentiment.
Quality healthcare is another livelihood priority. The five-year plan specifies that public hospital beds will increase to approximately 35,000 by 2031, and the cumulative number of beneficiaries of district health centers will reach 1 million within five years, charting a clear path to expand capacity and enhance quality.
Hong Kong's healthcare reform places greater emphasis on "quality enhancement." By promoting all-round, high-quality, and high-standard development of traditional Chinese medicine, advancing the digital transformation of public hospitals, and optimizing medical talent cultivation, the primary healthcare network continues to be strengthened to deliver more continuous, convenient, and affordable healthcare.
Young people are Hong Kong's future. The five-year plan establishes two dedicated youth sections, elevating youth development to a core position in governance. Ranging from expanding development space to supporting them in pursuing their dreams, the plan maps out systematic arrangements for their growth and success.
Through a dedicated task force, Hong Kong will intensify promotion of its academic, scientific research, and international collaboration resources, highlighting both the "Study in Hong Kong" and "Study Tour in Hong Kong" brands. This not only provides quality educational choices for students from home and abroad, but also builds up youth momentum for Hong Kong's future.
Judith Yu, chair of the Hong Kong Chamber of Commerce in China, said that by integrating education, talent, and youth development into a systematic framework, the five-year plan instills greater confidence in the future among all residents, especially the younger generation.
Yu suggested that local industries establish lasting channels for local young people to integrate into and serve the overall national development through internships and engagement across diverse fields such as innovation and technology. ■

China steps up crackdown on fraudulent practices in environmental monitoring
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
00:22:57 CST
01:22:57 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 19 (Xinhua) -- China will intensify efforts to combat fraudulent practices by environmental monitoring agencies, with multiple government departments coordinating enforcement, the Ministry of Ecology and Environment said Saturday.
Minister of Ecology and Environment Huang Runqiu said fraudulent practices by monitoring agencies remain a serious problem. He called for a zero-tolerance approach to safeguard the quality and credibility of environmental monitoring.
The remarks were made at a recent national meeting convened by the ministry and relevant departments to advance the campaign.
According to the ministry, the campaign will be carried out in three stages, including identifying problems across the sector, conducting concentrated rectification, and establishing standardized operations.
Monitoring agencies will be required to conduct self-inspections and draw up lists of identified problems. Authorities will then carry out targeted rectification, handle violations in accordance with the law and provide guidance to ensure corrective measures are fully implemented.
Spot checks and verification will also be strengthened, with authorities targeting inaccurate, omitted or concealed reporting, as well as perfunctory or sham rectification.
The ministry said it will also improve routine supervision by accelerating the rollout of relevant management rules and making good use of the environmental monitoring management and service platform.
China has tightened oversight of environmental monitoring in recent years as the country steadily advances efforts to strengthen environmental protection.
The country's landmark Ecological and Environmental Code, which took effect on Aug. 15, explicitly prohibits practices such as interfering with sampling, substituting samples, altering monitoring conditions, conducting sham monitoring, and tampering with or fabricating records. ■

Feature: Gaza reopens schools for in-person learning after 3-year hiatus
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
00:22:36 CST
01:22:36 KST

GAZA, Sept. 19 (Xinhua) -- After spending much of the past three years in a tent, 12-year-old Osama Abu Al-Subh walked into a school in western Gaza City on Saturday, the first time since Oct. 7, 2023.
For Osama, the most important part was simply being back with his classmates.
For Gaza, face-to-face education, one of the major aspects of normal life, is returning to the strip among the destruction.
Three schools reopened Saturday: a facility run by the UN Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees (UNRWA) in central Gaza's al-Nuseirat camp and two government schools in western and eastern Gaza City. Other students returned to temporary learning sites across the strip.
About 541,000 students in Gaza are benefiting from educational programs, including around 100,000 enrolled in UNRWA schools, according to the Palestinian Ministry of Education and Higher Education.
The ministry offers two tracks: in-person classes for students able to reach schools or designated sites, and virtual learning for those unable to access physical centers.
It plans to gradually expand in-person education through about 700 educational sites across the strip, in addition to 25 temporary schools expected to be delivered soon.
13-year-old Suad Al-Kafarna, originally from Beit Hanoun in northern Gaza, now lives with her family in a displacement camp in al-Nuseirat.
"I hoped the new academic year would represent a restart for education and allow students to study in stable schools rather than repeatedly moving between displacement sites and makeshift learning centers," Suad said.
11-year-old Fuad al-Jarousha was a little disappointed for not being able to attend a proper school like some of his peers.
Due to his family's location and circumstances, Fuad can only attend classes at a temporary learning site near his displacement camp.
His father was killed in an earlier airstrike, leaving Fuad, the eldest of his siblings, with additional responsibilities despite his young age.
"We have to sit on the ground inside tents because of a shortage of chairs and other basic resources," he said, adding that high temperatures make it difficult for them to concentrate.
Still, Fuad keeps attending lessons, hoping to complete his education despite his family's situation.
Gaza-based psychologist Rawan Ahmed told Xinhua that returning to in-person classes could benefit children who have been exposed to years of displacement, disruption, and uncertainty.
"Returning to a classroom allows children to rebuild a sense of routine and stability after years in which their daily lives were repeatedly disrupted," Ahmed said.
"Being physically present with teachers and classmates also gives them opportunities to interact, communicate and feel that they are part of a community again," she added.
The ministry is seeking to expand in-person learning while maintaining virtual education for students who cannot access schools, but the scale of the challenge remains immense.
According to figures from the Hamas-run Government Media Office in Gaza, more than 620,000 students have been deprived of regular schooling, while over 20,000 students have been killed since the outbreak of the war.
The number of school days decreased from 200 days during the 2022-2023 academic year to only 60 days during 2025-2026, while the number of weekly educational sessions decreased from 30 to 12.
The education system also faces shortages of functioning schools, classrooms, furniture, and other basic resources.
Despite the difficult conditions, the education ministry said more students enrolled in the new school year than in the previous one, showing families' commitment to keeping their children engaged in education despite the devastating circumstances.
"I want to study normally again and stay with my classmates," Osama told Xinhua, hoping classes would continue steadily so he could catch up on lost learning. ■

Demonstrators in US form human chain to protest Kennedy Center closure vote
The “Hands Around the Kennedy Center” rally drew thousands after Trump-backed board votes to close the iconic arts venue.
Thousands of protesters formed a human chain around the Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts in Washington DC to contest its closure, amid fears that United States President Donald Trump could make good on his threat to demolish the venerated landmark.
The crowd filled streets in the Foggy Bottom neighbourhood of the capital on Friday evening, bringing traffic to a standstill as demonstrators made their way to the “Hands Around the Kennedy Center” protest. Many carried signs and some wore costumes, while boos rang out when Trump was mentioned during the programme.
At one point, some protesters linked hands around the building, whose marble facade remained partly concealed by scaffolding and tarpaulins.
Among the most iconic buildings on Washington’s Potomac waterfront, the Kennedy Center has become a battleground over Trump’s bid to assert control over the institution since he returned to office last year, replacing its board with his own appointees and installing himself as chairman.
Chris Raleigh, co-founder of Hands Off the Arts, which organised the rally, said in an interview with The Associated Press news agency that he hoped the turnout would show that people were prepared to push back against Trump’s plans for the building.
The demonstration comes just days after the Trump-installed board voted to close the centre for repairs that are expected to last up to two years. That came hours after District Judge Christopher Cooper quashed the board’s latest attempt to restore Trump’s name to the building.
Last December, the new board added Trump’s name to the building’s facade after the Kennedy Center said its Board of Trustees had unanimously voted to rename the institution in his honour.
A federal judge blocked those efforts in May, ruling that the board had exceeded its statutory authority by unilaterally renaming the Kennedy Center and adding Trump’s name to its facade without congressional approval. Congress had designated the centre as a memorial to the late 35th US President John F Kennedy.
In August, the board tried again to inscribe Trump’s name on the building, this time with wording along the lines of “The John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts Restored and Renovated By President Donald J. Trump”.
The federal judge scotched the move in September, ruling that it violated his May injunction.
Trump has since declined to rule out demolishing the building, while a federal judge on Thursday ordered the Kennedy Center to give 30 days’ notice before undertaking any major structural changes, including demolition.
Speaking to reporters in North Carolina on Wednesday, Trump argued that his administration deserved recognition for rescuing the Kennedy Center and that without the repairs, the building risked falling into disrepair and ultimately being forced to shut down.
Raleigh said he, like others, is concerned that Trump could move ahead without first notifying the court.
“Look at the East Wing,” he said. “We got up one morning and there was a giant hole there.”

UK politics increasingly funded by billionaires as mega-donations surge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
16:00:50 UTC
01:00:50 KST

British politics is increasingly being funded by individual billionaires with a wave of mega-donations having flooded into UK political parties over the past two parliaments.
A total of £179m has been donated by wealthy individuals since 2019, research reveals.
The figures from the IPPR thinktank show how big money is playing an ever more influential role in Westminster, with a particular rise in mega-donations of more than £1m.
The research found that contributions from individual donors have accelerated since the Brexit party received £10m from the Thailand-based billionaire Christopher Harborne and the Liberal Democrats were given £8m by David Sainsbury, the supermarket tycoon, who has now returned to Labour.
Between 2001, when donation records began, and 2018, the total donated by individuals giving more than £1m averaged £3.9m a year.
But between 2019 and 2025, that figure rose to £13.1m a year, almost three-and-a-half times as much, and far outstripping what would be expected with inflation.
The research found 72% of all £1m-plus donations from individuals since records began had come since 2019.
Guardian analysis found that in some years, such as 2023, almost £7 out of every £10 in reported private donations to political parties came from wealthy companies or individuals who gave more than £1m in a calendar year.
The figures are likely to raise fresh concerns about the influence of a small groups of wealthy individuals, which have already been heightened since two crypto billionaires, Harborne and Ben Delo, said they had each given £36m to Reform UK this month.
Reform UK has said it is trying to redress the balance as the other parties have taken millions in mega-donations in past years. The Conservatives’ biggest donors include Frank Hester, who gave more than £20m before the 2024 election, and Labour’s Gary Lubner, who has given more than £9m in total.
The IPPR figures draw on Electoral Commission data since 2001 and Transparency International analysis, plus the two record donations of £36m each to Reform UK from Harborne and Delo.
There is increasing concern among Reform UK’s rivals about the issue of donations of more than £1m, with some Labour MPs pushing for a cap of £100,000 or £500,000 a year.
Some Labour members are intending to push the issue at the party’s autumn conference, and proposals for a cap are likely to be tabled when the government’s current elections bill goes to the House of Lords this autumn.
No 10 has been reluctant to include a cap amid opposition from some trade unions who fear it could lead to restrictions on them being able to donate so much in future.
However, the government has recently pledged to deal with the issue of mega-donors having an outsize influence on politics. It has already introduced a cap of £100,000 a year for donations from overseas voters.
Harry Quilter-Pinner, the executive director of IPPR, said: “Something fundamental has changed in how British politics is funded. Million-pound donations were once exceptional. However, since 2019, mega-donor money has become a much bigger part of our political system.
“Reform’s extraordinary fundraising has accelerated that trend, but this is much bigger than one party or two enormous cheques. This is the Americanisation of British politics, where political parties can become dependent on a handful of people with exceptionally deep pockets.
“Britain should draw a clear line. The government should introduce a £100,000 annual cap now and bring it down over time, so that no individual can bankroll a political party simply because they are incredibly wealthy.”
Civil society groups have urged the government to fix the issue for good, after the government said earlier this month a new taskforce would examine the issue of mega-donations.
Dr Susan Hawley, executive director of Spotlight on Corruption, said: “Without urgent action to limit the amount that wealthy individuals can give to political parties, we’re going to continue to see a staggering inflation of money – and the influence it buys – flowing into the coffers of political parties … The taskforce needs to take decisive action to get big money out of our politics in a fair and even-handed way, so that power and influence is returned to ordinary voters, where it belongs.”
At the time of the £72m in donations to Reform UK, Duncan Hames, senior director of policy at Transparency International UK, said the situation with big donations was “completely out of control, and makes an irrefutable case for government to bring forward an annual cap on political donations, and fast”.

====================================================================================================

Learning about the opposing party’s vaccination rate influences health choices
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
16:00:49 UTC
01:00:49 KST

Public health campaigns often rely on broadcasting facts and statistics to encourage healthy habits. People are more likely to express an intent to receive a COVID-19 vaccine after learning that vaccination rates among members of the opposing political party are higher than they previously thought. The findings, published in PLOS One, suggest that public health campaigns highlighting low vaccination rates to urge action might inadvertently discourage people from getting immunized.
In the United States, political affiliation heavily influences healthcare choices. Currently, whether a person identifies as a Democrat or a Republican is a stronger predictor of their COVID-19 vaccination status than their education level, race, or health insurance coverage. Past research indicates that people often judge the severity of the pandemic and the necessity of government interventions through a partisan lens.
Public health officials frequently attempt to change behavior by providing the public with new data. The success of this strategy heavily depends on what the audience already believes. If a person thinks a virus is exceptionally rare, hearing that it actually infects one in five people might prompt them to take precautions. If that same person already assumed the virus infects half the population, the identical statistic might make them feel safer and less likely to act. Researchers refer to this gap between an individual’s preconceived belief and the actual statistic as an information shock.
Researchers Brandyn F. Churchill of American University, along with Xiaoxue Sherry Gao and Rong Rong of the University of Massachusetts Amherst, wanted to test how these information shocks interact with political identity. They specifically wanted to see how learning new facts about the health behaviors of opposing political groups shapes personal medical decisions.
To establish a baseline of actual COVID-19 experiences, the researchers first conducted an initial survey of 200 adults on an online research platform in May 2024. The group consisted of 100 self-identified Democrats and 100 self-identified Republicans. The participants answered questions about their recent experiences with the virus, including whether they had contracted it or sought medical care. They also reported whether they had received a vaccine, experienced side effects, or vaccinated primarily to protect others.
The initial survey revealed that both political groups experienced similar rates of infection. Both groups also sought medical care for the virus at similar frequencies. There was, however, a vast divide in vaccination behavior. Nearly 46 percent of the Democrats reported receiving a recent COVID-19 vaccine, compared to only 28 percent of the Republicans.
Building on these baseline figures, the researchers designed a main experiment in August 2024 involving 579 different participants. This group included 288 Democrats and 291 Republicans, representing a mix of ages and backgrounds.
The researchers asked these individuals to estimate the responses given by the people in the initial survey. Half of the participants were asked to guess the survey answers of their own political party. The other half were asked to guess the answers of the opposing political party.
To ensure participants answered honestly rather than simply expressing a political bias, they were offered a financial bonus. The participants placed digital bets on how a randomly selected person from the first survey had answered the health questions. If their estimates closely matched the actual data, their chances of winning a monetary reward increased.
The estimates revealed widespread misunderstandings about the realities of the disease. Across the political spectrum, participants overestimated how frequently people caught COVID-19 by about 20 percentage points. They also overestimated how often the virus required medical intervention by 22 percentage points.
Both Democrats and Republicans tended to underestimate the prevalence of vaccine side effects. They also underestimated how many people chose to get vaccinated specifically to protect others.
Participants were no better at accurately estimating the behaviors and experiences of their own political party than they were at estimating those of the opposing party. Both groups consistently overestimated how many Republicans were vaccinated against the virus.
After the participants locked in their estimates, a computer program randomly selected one of the five health topics. The program then revealed the actual statistic from the initial survey to the participant. By comparing the participant’s original guess to the newly revealed statistic, the researchers could measure the size and direction of the information shock. Finally, the researchers asked the participants if they intended to receive an updated COVID-19 vaccine within the next twelve months.
Learning the true statistics regarding infection rates, disease severity, or side effects did not alter the participants’ stated plans to get a vaccine. Seeing the true vaccination rates of their own political party also produced no changes in their intentions.
When participants learned the actual vaccination rate of the opposing political party, their behavior shifted. Participants who realized they had underestimated the opposing party’s vaccination rate became more likely to state an intention to get vaccinated themselves. Those who learned they had overestimated the opposing party’s vaccination rate became less likely to seek a vaccine.
The researchers conducted mathematical tests to ensure this relationship was not a statistical fluke. When they swapped the data to pretend the participants had seen a different health statistic, the effect disappeared. When they looked at whether the information changed past vaccination behavior, there was no connection. This adds weight to the idea that the specific information about the opposing party’s current vaccination rate drove the change in their future intentions.
The researchers attribute this pattern to a social pressure model. In this framework, people are more inclined to adopt a health measure when they see others adopting it. When people learn that a group they view as generally opposed to a behavior is actually participating in it, they may feel increased social pressure to follow suit.
The results present a potential hazard for modern public health messaging. Health agencies often try to motivate the public by emphasizing that vaccination rates are falling below optimal levels. Because people generally overestimate how many of their peers are vaccinated, broadcasting low compliance rates serves as a negative information shock. Hearing that few people are getting the shot could reduce social pressure and inadvertently depress vaccination numbers even further.
While the experiment highlights shifts in stated intentions, an expressed intent to receive a vaccine does not guarantee that a person will actually schedule an appointment and get the shot. The researchers did attempt to follow up with the participants four months later to ask if they had received a vaccine. Many of the participants did not respond to the follow-up survey, meaning the researchers could not reliably track how often intentions translated into real-world behavior.
The study design also limits the ability to explain the underlying psychological mechanisms. The data show that participants reacted to the habits of the opposing political party, but the study does not reveal exactly why this specific information proved more persuasive than data about their own peers. The overall number of participants also constrained the researchers’ ability to analyze differences across more specific demographic categories, such as age, race, or income brackets. Future studies will need to investigate the cognitive pathways that make discordant political information so influential in personal medical decisions.
The study, “Partisan differences in healthcare decision-making: Evidence from a vaccine experiment,” was authored by Brandyn F. Churchill, Xiaoxue Sherry Gao, and Rong Rong.

The hall was decorated with white orchids and pine trees, with wreaths from Tung’s widow, Betty Tung Chiu Hung-ping, and their three children placed in front of the altar. She did not attend the vigil, the South China Morning Post learned.

“The mood is solemn and very quiet. Many visitors stay for about half an hour before leaving,” the attendee said, adding that some of Tung’s close friends were allowed into a room to view his body.

Nuclear workforce passes a hundred thousand across sectors
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
17:00:30 BST
01:00:30 KST

The combined civil and defence nuclear sector grew from 83,000 people in 2023 to over 100,000 in 2025, according to early indications from the latest Nuclear Workforce Assessment set out in the annual update to Parliament published this week.
Within that, the Defence Nuclear Enterprise employs over 47,000, with demand expected to grow to around 65,000 by 2030. Organisations signed up to the Nuclear Skills Plan have recruited over 2,000 graduates and over 4,000 apprentices in the first two years of its operation, of whom around 1,300 graduates and around 3,100 apprentices were in defence nuclear.
A joint investment by the Ministry of Defence and the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero will create over 500 PhD positions across eight years, with the first starting this autumn, which the update says will help develop a new generation of experts to push the boundaries of nuclear science.
Eight indirect intervention contracts are being mobilised to support mid-career switchers, improve cross-sector mobility, address regional challenges and work with training providers to ensure supply matches employer demand.
The plan was published by the Nuclear Skills Taskforce in May 2024 and is led jointly by the two departments, backed by government and industry investment including from BAE Systems, Rolls-Royce Submarines, Babcock and EDF.
The update describes the approach as recognising that a collaborative effort bringing together government, industry and academia from across the civil and defence nuclear sectors is essential to meet future skills needs.
Workforce growth at Barrow-in-Furness has been particularly marked, with the update recording that the workforce there has grown by over 1,800 under the current government. BAE Systems’ Barrow shipyard is described as the only facility in the United Kingdom with the infrastructure, site licence and resources to design and build British nuclear submarines.
BAE Systems, the Defence Nuclear Organisation, Babcock and Rolls-Royce Submarines all maintain teams at Barrow, contributing to the Dreadnought and Astute build programmes and the future SSN-AUKUS programme.
Wes Streeting writes that delivery of the Nuclear Skills Plan is “breaking down barriers to opportunity by bringing highly skilled nuclear jobs to regions that have historically faced challenges”.

RAF Servicewoman Makes History by Passing P Company
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
17:00:00 BST
01:00:00 KST

A Royal Air Force officer has made history by becoming the first RAF servicewoman to successfully complete the All Arms Pre Para Selection (AAPPS) course, commonly known as “P Company”. 
 
Flight Lieutenant Alice, an RAF parachuting officer currently serving with 16 Air Assault Brigade Combat Team Headquarters, completed the demanding course in August, earning the coveted maroon beret awarded to those who successfully pass the selection. 
 
AAPPS is designed to test whether military personnel have the physical and mental resilience required to serve in the Airborne Forces. Those who pass are eligible to undertake the parachuting course required to earn their military parachuting wings. 
 
For Flt Lt Alice, however, the achievement was about more than gaining the qualification. 
 
She had already earned her parachuting wings four years ago after completing the RAF Basic Parachuting Course. But having obtained her wings without completing P Company, she wanted to prove to herself that she had truly earned them. 
 
Her journey began with six weeks of intensive “beat up” training at Merville Barracks in Colchester, preparing her for the physical demands of the selection course. 
 
That was followed by three and a half weeks at Catterick, North Yorkshire, where candidates are pushed through a series of arduous tests before facing the final test week. 
 
The course is deliberately designed to challenge candidates physically and mentally, with those taking part required to demonstrate the determination, teamwork and resilience expected of personnel serving in the Airborne Forces. 
 
For Alice, successfully completing the course culminated in the presentation of her maroon beret, a visible symbol of her achievement and her place within the Airborne community. 
 
Only a handful of servicewomen have successfully completed AAPPS, making Alice’s achievement particularly significant. She is the first woman from the RAF to pass the course. 
 
Her success also highlights the increasingly diverse range of personnel serving within Britain’s airborne capability, demonstrating that the demanding selection process is open to those prepared to meet its exacting standards. 
 
For the RAF officer, the significance of the achievement is perhaps best summed up by the personal motivation that drove her through the gruelling weeks of preparation and selection: having already earned the wings, she wanted to prove she deserved them.

Police hiring standards matter. But they alone cannot stop abuse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
15:58:55 UTC
00:58:55 KST

Police hiring standards matter. But they alone cannot stop abuse
Law enforcement in the US needs high hiring standards. But it also needs reform and trust-building in communities.
During a congressional hearing earlier this week, FBI Director Kash Patel defended changes to the bureau’s hiring standards. His testimony came just two weeks after reports surfaced of loosened hiring standards at another law enforcement agency in the US: Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).
As a result, concerns have emerged about a retreat from standards intended to protect the public by offering a baseline of conduct for law enforcement officers. The American public is right to worry. Loose hiring standards can put reckless individuals in positions of power.
But ensuring commitment to higher standards in law enforcement recruitment alone cannot solve the police violence problem in the US.
Individual misconduct
Research on police misconduct, which has considerably expanded in the wake of Black Lives Matter and related movements, offers useful parameters to guide how we approach the question of hiring standards.
Studies have shown that most cases of use of force are concentrated among a relatively small proportion of officers, at least in the limited departments that track such incidents. That means there are officers who are repeat offenders and have the tendency to engage in such misconduct.
So can risk individuals be identified before they are hired?
One study of more than 12,000 police applicants found that specific responses on pre-employment psychological evaluations were associated with subsequent excessive force complaints and complaints alleging racial misconduct.
However, another study of 642 first-year police officers found that markers for anti-social and borderline behaviour could predict the likelihood of engaging only in certain types of abuse – namely sexual misconduct.
There is also research that suggests abusive policing and officers’ psychological wellbeing may be intertwined, and that the harms of misconduct may extend beyond targeted civilians, possibly even to the offending officers themselves.
In a sample of 137 active-duty US police officers, approximately 11 percent self-reported engaging in abusive policing. Abusive policing was associated with greater PTSD symptoms even after accounting for adverse childhood experiences and workplace trauma.
The implication of all this is that hiring standards based on psychological profiling should neither be dismissed as irrelevant nor treated as a fully reliable way to eliminate all future risk. Standards should be evaluated according to what they actually predict, what they exclude, and what risks arise when they are removed.
Structural violence
But improper selection of law enforcement recruits is only part of the problem.
The US has an exceptionally high rate of police violence compared with other wealthy democracies. For example, the rate of police killings is 33.5 per 10 million in the US, compared with 9.8 in Canada, 1.3 in Germany, and 0.5 in England and Wales.
That cannot plausibly be explained simply by whom we happen to hire. American law enforcement gives officers extraordinary authority to detain, search, use force and, in some circumstances, take a life.
Those powers operate within institutions that have repeatedly struggled with racial bias, unnecessary antagonism of marginalised communities, and abuses of authority. There is also inadequate accountability for law enforcement misconduct, including through qualified immunity and other legal protections that can make it difficult to hold officers personally liable for certain constitutional violations.
The problem, in other words, is not simply that some individuals enter policing who should not. It is also the system into which they enter, and the organisational cultures, incentives, and practices that can shape how they use the power they have been given.
Reducing police misconduct requires system-wide reform, including greater accountability not only for individual officers but for the agencies and institutions responsible for policing.
Effective policing depends in part on public cooperation. Global research across dozens of countries has linked perceived fairness, procedural justice and trust in police to people’s willingness to cooperate with law enforcement.
The credibility of hiring standards can be part of trust-building initiatives, but they must also include broader efforts to strengthen trust and legitimacy among marginalised communities by reducing racial profiling, unnecessary uses of force, and inequitable enforcement of laws.
The challenge is not simply to identify the “wrong” candidates and exclude them, but to build institutions in which selection is accompanied by effective training, supervision, and accountability. Ultimately, the institutions entrusted with extraordinary powers have to be structured to protect the people they serve.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

Ritter warns of US economy collapse, NATO vulnerabilities
Unknown

The latest joint X Space hosted by Tehran Times and Sputnik featured former UN weapons inspector and US Marine intelligence officer Scott Ritter, who warned of an impending structural collapse within the American economic system driven by reckless foreign policies and soaring energy costs, while dismantling Western war narratives and exposing deep-seated military vulnerabilities across the United States and NATO.
Sputnik Question: Donald Trump stated last week that he is not happy about Ukrainian strikes against Russian energy infrastructure and wants them to stop because they are destabilizing to the global economy. Given that these attacks were enabled by intelligence from the CIA and tech companies like Google, Palantir, and Starlink, what explains his decision to explicitly oppose these strikes?
Scott Ritter Answer: Attempting to get into the mind of Donald Trump is impossible, as the Russian government has officially characterized him as emotionally unstable. He is currently under a tremendous amount of economic pressure driven by the rising price of oil, which he views as a primary indicator of American economic health. The price of oil and diesel is rising as a direct result of his own policies, which increases ground shipping costs and transfers those expenses directly to the American consumer. As James Carville famously warned Bill Clinton in 1992, "it's the economy, stupid"—making economic performance the primary concern for American voters.
 
 Trump knows very little about the specific operational details or goals of the conflicts he initiates; for instance, he took America to war in Iran based on a briefing by Benjamin Netanyahu and the head of the Mossad. When he authorized the CIA to pressure Vladimir Putin, he did not understand what the CIA actually does—specifically that it has trained Ukrainian forces since 2014 for cross-border operations, assassinations, and long-range drone strikes. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent explicitly noted that the administration's goal is to collapse the Russian economy by targeting its energy infrastructure. While Trump may enjoy seeing war-porn briefings of burning Russian refineries, he fails to realize the global economic impact. Because Russia had to halt diesel exports to prioritize domestic consumption for harvesting machinery and trucking, a global diesel shortage emerged, pushing US diesel prices above $6 per gallon. Trump understands these economic consequences because high fuel prices severely threaten his party at the upcoming November midterm elections.
Sputnik Question: What has been the response in the US establishment to Russia's retaliation strikes against Ukrainian ports, logistics warehouses, and rail infrastructure, and to what extent has this changed the calculus in Washington?
Scott Ritter Answer: Statements made by senior US government officials closely conform to narratives produced by Ukrainian intelligence regarding heavy Russian casualties and limited Russian military capacity. US intelligence analysts regularly produce reports that validate official policy postures to secure promotions and bonuses rather than providing accurate assessments. American policymakers genuinely believed that Ukrainian drone strikes would collapse Russia's economy, induce long gas lines, trigger a "Moscow Maidan," and lead to regime change before the September 20 parliamentary elections.
 
 However, Russia's retaliatory actions exposed Western intelligence claims as a narrative constructed on lies. Consequently, there is silence among critical decision-makers in Washington because they have no effective counter to these realities. Ukraine is completely bankrupt, unable to pay its soldiers or buy weapons, and seizing frozen Russian assets would end Europe's economy. Ultimately, if economic strain and supply chain disruptions ruin Christmas for American families, voters will severely punish incumbent politicians on election day.
Tehran Times Question: How much of the media campaign regarding the contract between the United States and Venezuela for access to oil is true, and will it solve the economic problems facing the US economy?
Scott Ritter Answer: It is not true at all. Venezuelan oil fields have been maintained haphazardly over many years, with many fields shut down, requiring an extraordinarily expensive and lengthy infrastructure restoration before oil can flow meaningfully. Trump's pressure on American oil companies will not generate significant income or produce substantial oil quantities beyond current levels, making the initiative a policy fantasy. Furthermore, the Strategic Petroleum Reserve of the United States has been exhausted with no capacity to recharge it. Simultaneously, Saudi Arabia is becoming a non-functioning oil producer due to repeated attacks by Houthi forces and Iraqi militias, threatening broader global energy instability. Trump's claim that Venezuelan oil will act as a quick solution represents pure fantasy rather than fact.
Tehran Times Question: How long can the United States economy tolerate this situation and the economic pressures caused by these wars?
Scott Ritter Answer: The United States maintains an illusion of economic stability by printing money excessively and relying on financial smoke and mirrors. The country operates under record-high budget deficits, while government bond yields rising above 5% divert a massive portion of GDP toward paying growing national debt. Leading economic analysts project a major economic crisis emerging around January. While the US may manage to fake it through one more cycle, a structural collapse of the American economic system remains inevitable. Furthermore, efforts by China to establish pro-Yuan trade agreements with Gulf Arab nations threaten to erode the dominance of the petrodollar.
Sputnik Question: Polish Foreign Minister Sikorski claimed that NATO could easily defeat Russia in a conventional war due to overwhelming air power; based on US and Israeli air force operations over Iran, does NATO possess overwhelming air superiority over Russia?
Scott Ritter Answer: NATO has nothing close to air superiority. Establishing air superiority requires generating sustained combat sorties, which demands well-maintained aircraft, fuel, ammunition, active airfields, and functional airborne command and control networks. In any conflict with Russia, NATO's command and control infrastructure would be disabled on day one by advanced Russian electronic warfare. NATO forces have spent two decades operating in undefended airspace dropping guided munitions, but their system failed when applied against Iran, where 39 days of operations failed to inflict a decisive blow.
 
 Furthermore, NATO member states suffer from severe operational unpreparedness; for instance, Germany cannot get 80% of its aircraft off the ramp due to lack of maintenance and training. The F-16 fighter jets transferred to Ukraine were expired aircraft requiring complete refurbishment. Additionally, NATO lacks the required forward airfields, ramp space, fuel storage, and ammunition reserves, all of which would be destroyed on day one, while long-range Russian interceptors would disrupt aerial refueling tankers.
Sputnik Question: Setting aside traditional aviation, how does the rest of NATO compare to Russia in terms of drone and missile capabilities?
Scott Ritter Answer: NATO nations, including Germany, possess zero national air defense capacity. NATO stripped its own air defense inventory to supply Ukraine, whose air defense network was subsequently dismantled by Russian suppression operations. Utilizing drones alone, Russia retains the capability to darken European skies and destroy selected targets without effective opposition. Following the US withdrawal from the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces (INF) Treaty, Russia deployed long-range Iskander-1000 missiles and advanced cruise missiles capable of striking across Europe. Russia maintains sufficient conventional power to destroy NATO's military infrastructure, defense manufacturing, and command centers without utilizing nuclear weapons, granting it total escalatory dominance. While a nuclear exchange would result in the absolute destruction of Europe, Russia maintains survival capabilities, though Moscow seeks peaceful security arrangements rather than conflict with NATO.
Tehran Times Question: How much truth is there to the 60 Minutes interview with the American pilot who was reportedly rescued after his fighter jet was targeted by Iranian air defenses over Iran?
Scott Ritter Answer: While taking the active-duty colonel's service at face value, significant unanswered questions surround whether the event was an authentic rescue or a scripted narrative. The United States suffered a direct conventional defeat against Iranian forces, who executed a superior plan and drove US forces out of strategic installations. Unlike conflicts in Vietnam or Afghanistan where political will decayed, US forces were directly out-maneuvered and beaten in conventional engagement by Iran. To counter this precedent and satisfy the public need for a hero, the Department of Defense collaborated with 60 Minutes to present a scripted narrative to the American public.

Young Palestinian rescued after third Gaza building collapses in four days
A young Palestinian man narrowly escaped death on Saturday after he was pulled out from the rubble of a partially collapsed building by Civil Defence crews in Gaza City.
The incident is the third of its kind just four days, with emergency services stating that the Israeli onslaught since 2023 has left the majority of the enclave's buildings at risk of collapsing.
The Gaza Civil Defence issued a statement saying they were able to “extract a young man, in good condition, after part of a building collapsed on him”. The man’s name and age were not given.
The Civil Defence also did not provide further details on the extent of damage caused by the building falling, or the number of families it housed.
On Wednesday, 21 Palestinians, including 12 children and 5 women were killed, and 45 others were wounded after the al-Saada building collapsed in an industrial area located west of Gaza.
The Civil Defence said at the time that around 100 people, including around 50 children, were living in the building before it collapsed.
On Friday, five Palestinian children were also injured after a residential building partially collapsed in the Sabra neighbourhood of Gaza City, Mahmoud Bassal, a spokesperson for the Civil Defence, said.
Since the ceasefire announced in October, Israel has continued with demolishing buildings and killing civilians.
However, the fierce bombardment throughout the war and restrictions on aid and vital resources such as excavation tools and building equipment, has also meant that thousands of families are forced to live in unstable and dilapidated homes.
Gaza’s Ministry of Health said that there have been at least 61 deaths related to building collapses, noting that there is also a shortage of shelters due to the entire population being displaced.
Many of the buildings have damaged foundations, which result in cracks and parts of the building falling off. However, families have little option but to stay in these dangerous environments due to overcrowding and poor conditions in shelters.
Last week, following a building collapse west of Gaza City, a group of representatives from local tribes and families held a protest against US President Donald Trump's self-styled 'Board of Peace', shedding light on the dire humanitarian situation and the dangers many civilians face due to the lack of appropriate housing.
Dozens of buildings have continued to collapse, with Palestinian governmental institutions repeatedly calling on international UN bodies to allow shelter supplies into Gaza.
Many organisations have also raised concerns over the coming winter months, and the flooding of tents and expected deaths due to the severe cold, amid a lack of vital supplies and proper healthcare.
Israel’s war on Gaza has killed over 73,000 Palestinians since 2023, in what rights groups and UN experts have determined to be a genocide.

Defender Media: Ukraine’s battle-tested drone makers reach no top slot in Pentagon’s $1.1 billion Drone Dominance program, but some Ukrainian technology wins anyway
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
15:46:39 UTC
00:46:39 KST

Ukraine's battle-tested drone makers did not win a single top slot in the Pentagon's latest drone contest. But some Ukrainian technology won anyway, competing quietly under the names of Western partners, The Defender Media reports.
The Pentagon's $1.1 billion Drone Dominance program does not allow direct purchases from Ukrainian firms, which must set up a US legal entity to bid.
The Ukrainians who competed under their own names were hampered by export licenses, the hunt for non-Chinese components, and visa issues, and none of the four cracked the top five in either category.
American firms sweep the top slots
The Pentagon picked five winners each in two categories, long-range strikes out to 15 kilometers and close-in assault. Eric Schmidt's Perennial Autonomy topped the long-range field with its Hornet drone, on 80.1 points, and Neros led the close-in category with 88.1. Neros already supplies Ukraine with 6,000 of its Archer FPV drones.
The rest of the winners, from ORQA's US arm to XTEND and ModalAI, were American as well. All will receive Pentagon supply contracts, with order sizes to be set later.
Ukrainians win under other flags
The Ukrainian firms that announced their entries, F-Drones, General Chereshnya, Grim Tech, and Stellarion, all missed the cut, though General Chereshnya had reached the program's second round earlier in the year.
Bureaucracy tripped the open entrants
Stellarion laid out what went wrong. Getting export permits and moving hardware took so long that integrating American parts, including warheads, and adapting the finished system on schedule became "complicated," its representatives said.
Finding NDAA-compliant, non-Chinese components ate up more time, and visa delays kept its specialists from fixing technical problems on site.
Firms that missed the top five can enter later rounds: a Gauntlet 2.5 contest for bomber drones is set for October, and a third phase begins in February 2027, with missions built to test control of several drones at once.
