CNN said its "mission to report on the US government will continue regardless of any attempts to restrict physical access to the White House and other government buildings, or any other attempts to impede our journalism."
"We will not be deflected from our duty to hold the government and other public bodies to account, and we will continue to report on the actions and processes of this administration without fear or favour," the news network added.
"CNN stands fully behind our White House team."
First Amendment rights
MS NOW said it "intends to take any steps necessary to defend our First Amendment rights and the essential role of independent journalism in our democracy," referring to the US Constitution's guarantee of a free press.
"The White House belongs to the American people, and the decisions made inside are funded by our tax dollars," the network added.
Politico journalists also said they were turned away from the White House shortly after MS NOW and CNN.
Politico’s communications team disputed his claim that the publication “received government subsidies", saying the allegation had been "thoroughly debunked".
“Politico will continue to fairly report on this White House and future ones. We will vigorously defend our First Amendment rights against any attempt to restrict them,” an online post said.
Jacqui Heinrich, president of the White House Correspondents’ Association, said the group "stands in defence of our colleagues at CNN, MS NOW, and Politico who are being singled out for doing their jobs."
Trump defended the restrictions by saying he was "tired of reading and seeing fake news" from the outlets and said he dislikes "dishonest press". He did not identify specific stories.
CBS News legal contributor Jessica Levinson said the ban "smacks of content-based discrimination".
"That's the primary thing that the First Amendment guards against," she said.

UK jury clears student activist of expressing support for Hamas

Breadcrumb
UK jury clears student activist of expressing support for Hamas
A student activist has been cleared of voicing support for Palestinian political movement Hamas, which was proscribed by the UK in 2021.
The jury unanimously found Sarah Cotte not guilty of expressing support for the Palestinian group -- a charge which carries up to 14 years in prison under UK anti-terrorism legisation.
The acquittal — which deals a major blow to campaigns targeting Palestinian rights activists in Britain — came after less than two hours of jury deliberations at the end of a five-day retrial at the Old Bailey Central Criminal Court.
Cotte's supporters hailed the verdict as a “massive victory” for the pro-Palestine movement in Britain.
Cotte, 22, expressed her “unconditional solidarity” with the Palestinian armed resistance against the Israeli occupation during a speech at the School of Oriental and African Studies (SOAS), University of London college on 9 October 2023, the Old Bailey was told.
The prosecution had argued that even though she did not name Hamas, her comments at the gathering were “thinly veiled references” to it.
Cotte had denied that her comments were about Hamas, saying she had been supporting “the right to resist” according to the international law and norms.
In June, during her first trial, Sarah faced two charges. The first was inviting support for a proscribed organisation, referring to Hamas, through a public speech, and the second was expressing an opinion or belief supportive of a proscribed organisation through messages in a closed WhatsApp group. Following that trial, the jury unanimously acquitted Cotte of the second charge. However, they failed to reach a definitive verdict on the first charge, leading the prosecution to demand a retrial, which began on Monday.
In the retrial, the prosecution's case rested on the 2023 speech delivered by Cotte — who is Ethiopian and also holds French citizenship — just two days after the start of Israel's genocidal war on Gaza. Speaking at SOAS, she defended the internationally recognised right of peoples, including the Palestinian people, to resist occupation by all means, including armed struggle. She referred to the Palestinian resistance broadly and never mentioned Hamas by name. Cotte, who was 19 years old at the time, referred to the "Al-Aqsa Flood" operation as a legitimate act of resistance.
Cotte concluded her testimony before the court by reaffirming her stance against Zionism, racism, and colonialism, describing it as a matter of principle.
At the end of January 2024, the Met Police’s counter-terrorism officers arrested Cotte after she was reported by UK Lawyers for Israel. The pro-Israel group had also reported Cotte to the University of London. However, the university refused to expel her, reaffirming its commitment to the principle of freedom of expression and opinion.
In remarks to The New Arab, a spokesperson for the Revolutionary Communist Group, to which Cotte belongs, described the acquittal as "massive victory for the principled anti-Zionist, anti-racist and anti-imperialist stance".
The group accuses the British state of “desperately attempting to criminalize the pro-Palestine movement” following its failure to convict Cotte under the Terrorism Act in June.
It pledged to continue fighting against “all criminalisation of supporters of the risen people of occupied Palestine in their righteous struggle against settler-colonialism and genocide”.

George Osborne has said he thought no one would find out about a private viewing of the Bayeux tapestry he organised for the tech billionaire Peter Thiel at the British Museum.
The former chancellor, who is chair of the museum, told the Big Brue festival in Somerset that he had been on holiday when Thiel was shown the medieval artwork.
Thiel, who supports Donald Trump, is the founder of PayPal and Palantir, a software company that builds data integration, analytics and artificial intelligence platforms for government agencies and large corporations.
Palantir has a swathe of British public contracts, including, most controversially, a £330m deal with the NHS, which it has held since 2023.
The company also works for the US, Israeli and UK militaries. Its use of AI-powered software to support military strikes in Gaza and Iran, US Ice immigration raids and its access to NHS data has stoked concern.
Of the viewing, Osborne said: “It wasn’t like we expected anyone to know about it.” The museum’s director of development, Charlotte Appleyard, hosted Thiel at a VIP viewing of the tapestry before it opened to the public on 18 August.
The visit was revealed in the Guardian shortly after it happened.
When asked what the museum might have got in return, Osborne said: “The short answer is he hasn’t offered any money, and were he to offer money, the board would consider it and have to take into account the pros, you know, receiving more income, and the reputational risks.”
Osborne, who lives in Bruton, near where the festival is taking place, complained that people treat the British Museum like the Foreign Office when they protest about donors who are thought to support the Israeli government.
He said: “The critique was that [Thiel] was a supporter of the Israeli government … I mean, this is the most difficult, and almost all the protests that happen at the museum … When I started five years ago, they were climate protests, Just Stop Oil and that kind of thing. Now they’re almost universally Gaza.
“You know that is the moment I would say the most sensitive, difficult political issue for the museum, and you know we try and navigate it, and I keep trying to point out we’re not actually the Foreign Office.”
He said the museum has to take money from companies such as BP to be able to operate.
“You cannot say we want museums to be free, and then one of the biggest British companies offers us £50m, BP, and we go, oh, don’t, because we object to oil exploration. Where is the money going to come from?
“You’d shut down the British Museum. People do say this. They say you shouldn’t take tech money, you shouldn’t take oil money. You can’t take any money from the banks. We want the museum to be free. The museum would shut down.”

What AI Anxiety Looks Like in China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
15:38:19 UTC
00:38:19 KST

What AI Anxiety Looks Like in China
A top-down tech revolution is harder to manage than a bottom-up one.
Anxiety about AI in the United States appears to be getting worse. Prosaic concerns about machines disrupting industries, stealing jobs, and compromising schoolwork are giving way to more harrowing fears about the end of humanity.
Even after top AI executives in the U.S. called for slowing down the breakneck pace of development, President Trump dismissed these safety concerns as a “hoax” that would hand China an advantage in the race for AI supremacy.
Outside of China, Trump’s assertion may appear well founded. While the U.S. roils over the prospects of AI, China’s leadership looks to be charging ahead. In surveys, Chinese people appear more enthusiastic about AI and its potential benefits than respondents in the U.S., and they are adopting it more quickly. Although Chinese President Xi Jinping has expressed more alarm than Trump about the threats of AI—and has even called for regulation to “ensure that AI is always under human control”—his government has made adopting the technology a national priority. The plan is to have AI in every aspect of China’s economy and society by 2035. The country’s steady release of AI models that are open-source, high-performing, and relatively cheap to build and run has been sending shivers through Silicon Valley and Wall Street.
But for all the concern about China’s advances in AI, the reality is that the country is racked by the same anxieties about the onrush of AI as the rest of the world. Chinese social-media platforms are filled with posts in which workers and professionals express their worries that AI will steal their job and livelihood. Leaders in Beijing seem ever more concerned about the potential political and economic risks of this technological disruption.
In the U.S., these tensions are being debated openly and, in theory, will be managed in the courts and on Capitol Hill. In China, where there are no such avenues for people to determine their own fate, leaders must still confront the problems and threats inherent to this technological revolution. This puts the Communist Party in a bind: Advancing AI may well empower China on the world stage, but holding the technology back may be necessary for the party to preserve itself.
Xu Peng, a 30-year-old actor, was out of work last year when he got an unexpected break. A director had reached out to cast him in a short-drama series, each episode minutes long, which have become enormously popular in China. Xu traveled to Hengdian, a film-production hub in eastern China, and began landing roles in one or two dramas a month. And then it all stopped. Xu had expected to act in two dramas after the Chinese New Year in February, but never heard from the studio. When he contacted the producer, he got the news: The company had canceled the productions and would be making videos using artificial intelligence instead.
“It was as though everything was fine yesterday, and today it is suddenly gone,” Xu said.
Xu’s fate is the fear of workers across the country—and around the world. Social-media posters regularly express anxiety about being “distilled,” a term Chinese people use for when an employer uses a worker’s data to train an AI model. In May on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, someone going by the name Nanbei wrote that after leaving a recent job, she learned that her former employer had fed thousands of her chat messages, hundreds of documents, and every one of her work emails into an AI system to create a “digital robot” that took over her responsibilities—and even gave it her name. “The company no longer has to pay me a cent in salary, yet it can keep me there ‘working overtime’ forever,” Nanbei wrote. Another worker, using the handle Xiexiaoya, posted on RedNote, China’s Instagram, in June that the prospect of being distilled kept her awake at night. “I’m afraid my AI double might become more popular than I am,” she wrote.
Two years ago, Shen Anyu, a voice actor who earns a living from narrating news commentaries and other short programs, began noticing an alarming number of videos on social-media platforms that seemed to feature his voice without his permission. Shen hired a lawyer earlier this year and filed a lawsuit against a voice-generation platform. The case is still pending, but in the meantime, his career is “losing blood,” he said, as he loses work to AI. Living with the new technology “is inevitable,” he said, but “I’m not yet sure how we should coexist with AI.”
Though some Chinese people are embracing AI, many are not ready for the change it brings. Bruce Jiang, a 42-year-old commercial director in Shanghai, loves choosing the right lens and finding the perfect shot, and he didn’t want to outsource these and other aspects of his craft to an algorithm. But after his clients began pressuring him to use the technology—“‘You only have to tell AI what you want, and it produces it like magic,’” he said they insisted—he began using tools such as the video-generator Kling for certain tasks. The experience, he said, has been demoralizing. The old method “was work, and it was a cost, but it was also a kind of pleasure,” Jiang said. “That pleasure is disappearing.”
Chinese policy makers at national and local levels have introduced ambitious plans and financial support to rush the country into the AI age. Entrepreneurs across China are adopting AI in the hopes of cutting costs, remaining competitive, and aligning their firms with Beijing’s priorities. In China’s cutthroat society—and especially in sectors where AI is making rapid inroads, such as the entertainment industry—many like Jiang are afraid that they’ll get left behind if they don’t join in.
But these swift and radical changes have yielded mixed results. The state-linked China Center for Information Industry Development estimated in June that nearly 70 percent of the country’s small businesses have not moved beyond initial trials of adopting AI in their operations, largely owing to the costs and complexity of integrating the technology.
After the Chinese AI lab DeepSeek released a large language model last year, Chinese companies rushed to adopt it. But instead of buying a software subscription (an unpopular practice in China owing to the country’s history of piracy), some businesses opted for what locals call an “all-in-one machine,” or a mini data center with DeepSeek installed, which managers simply plugged into their computer systems. This solution was especially popular among state-owned enterprises and government bureaus looking to appear advanced, but the hardware proved to be an ineffective way to use AI. Buyers soon came to see that the machines weren’t worth the investment, and their sales quickly fell.
Earlier this year, plenty of buzz similarly surrounded OpenClaw, a free, open-source, autonomous AI agent. Tech companies hosted popular events to help users install and use the tool, a process that Chinese enthusiasts call “raising a lobster.” At the OpenClaw festival in Beijing in March, the internet-service provider Baidu set up pools with live crustaceans to entertain attendees. Local-government officials encouraged the frenzy by pledging financial aid to start-ups that used OpenClaw.
Disillusionment came quickly. Some distraught users took to social media to express their alarm at how the AI agent, which required masses of personal data to operate without detailed instructions, had a habit of going rogue. “I jumped on the bandwagon” expecting to get a “digital employee,” a woman using the social-media handle HotdogWang wrote in March on RedNote. “Instead, it turned out to be both a money pit and a ticking time bomb.” Some reported that their AI helper had deleted emails or made credit-card purchases without permission. One Douyin user, posting under the name Qizaibushidaju, wrote, “I simply installed it because everyone else was doing so,” only to uninstall it 72 hours later owing to security concerns.
Although Chinese tech executives are not yet engaged in a public debate over the risks of an algorithm-created calamity—the country’s constraints on free speech may inhibit them from speaking out—some Chinese people do worry about more than just jobs and data. “There are only two options for the future,” a man calling himself Qiangni Yinshou wrote on Douyin. “Either humanity goes extinct, or humans shut AI down.”
A user by the name of Buyehou wrote on RedNote that when he engaged a chatbot in a philosophical discussion about humanity’s future, he was told that the options included “either merging with AI or being eliminated.” The man added that “when AI becomes far smarter than humans, has consciousness of its own, and can evolve independently, it will be impossible for humans to control it. There is no turning back now.”
Despite their outward show of confidence, China’s leaders plainly don’t know how life works with AI either. But figuring it out is an urgent concern here, given Beijing’s evident faith in AI as a magical solution to the country’s deepening economic and social problems, and as an essential tool in the pursuit of global dominance over the United States. In the U.S., the diffusion of AI is largely a bottom-up phenomenon as companies, investors, and consumers test the risks and benefits of this new technology. In China, where the development and spread of AI is a national mission that is costing the government hundreds of billions of dollars, leaders are eager to impose these advances from above.
In theory, China’s autocrats can ram through their agenda with scant regard for public sentiment. If confronted with the kinds of protests against AI data centers that have become prevalent in the U.S., Beijing’s leaders could easily send police to crush them and then cover up the problem in a deluge of propaganda. The Communist Party has already shown its willingness to override public concerns in pursuit of technological advantage. In 2024, trials of autonomously driven taxis in the city of Wuhan sparked concern over how robotaxis were “stealing people’s rice bowls”—but the trials have expanded anyway.
Yet China’s leaders have traditionally prized policies that promote stable employment out of fear that mounting joblessness could create unrest and threaten the political order. When the country first embraced markets and opened to trade, its rapidly growing economy and expanding private sector could absorb displaced workers. Now, when China’s sluggish economy already has a jobs problem—nearly a fifth of young workers are unemployed—the advances of AI threaten to put many more people out of work.
“In a nominally Communist state, the image of the party elite allying with business interests to displace the human proletariat with a robot class of workers carries certain political risks,” Carl Minzner, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, told me. “There is the potential for a lot of disgruntled people.”
China’s leaders are showing signs of nervousness. Earlier this year a court in Hangzhou, a technology hub in eastern China, upheld a ruling in favor of a tech worker who had challenged his compensation package after being replaced by AI. In the court’s judgment, the dismissal was unlawful and the worker deserved more money. Although a local-court verdict does not set a national precedent, it appears to be a warning to employers that mass AI layoffs are politically unacceptable. “As employers enjoy the benefits of technology, they must also shoulder corresponding social responsibilities,” the Beijing municipal government wrote last year. The state news agency Xinhua commented in March that “those companies that equate AI with ‘reducing staff’ may seem to lower costs in the short term, but in reality, they lose the core competitiveness of talent accumulation and further erode employee trust.”
Pushing companies to invest in new technologies without shedding redundant workers may preserve social order, but it would also limit AI’s benefits. Jeffrey Ding, an expert on AI in China at George Washington University, told me that the country’s leaders face a “balancing act” between political and economic necessity. “AI does have the potential for bringing massive, widespread productivity growth,” he said. But he also noted that the Communist Party prioritizes legitimacy and regime stability. If embracing AI demands “massive displacement and a lot of structural changes, then that’s where the trade-off begins to bite, and they might have to veer toward slowing down AI adoption.”
If American AI firms do, in fact, slow the pace of innovation, the Communist Party may see this as an opportunity to race ahead in AI. But China’s leaders, facing their own domestic challenges and preoccupied with their own grip on power, may decide that imposing these innovations on the masses is simply too risky—for their own sake, if not for the sake of humanity.
That would probably suit many Chinese people just fine. Xu, the actor, has found work teaching archery and horseback riding—skills he acquired in acting gigs. But he hasn’t given up on his theatrical career. He now plans to produce his own short dramas, partly with the help of AI, though he said that the performers on-screen will all be living, breathing people. AI “will not completely replace human actors,” Xu insisted. At least he can hope.
Cao Li in Hong Kong contributed reporting to this story.

Right-wing musician Pat Boone urges president to speak less, follow Reagan’s example
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
15:37:13 UTC
00:37:13 KST

American singer and actor Pat Boone, one of the biggest pop stars of the 1950s and 1960s and a longtime supporter of Donald Trump, issued a friendly but pointed message to the president on Saturday, urging him to talk less, listen more, and take a page from former president Ronald Reagan.
Boone, best known for hits including "Love Letters in the Sand," addressed Trump directly in a social media post, saying he was offering his advice "in the spirit of friendship and concern."
"I've known and supported President Trump for many years, and I offer these thoughts in the spirit of friendship and concern," Boone wrote.
"Sometimes the strongest thing a leader can do is say less, listen more, and let his actions speak for themselves. I'm praying for our President, as I hope all Americans will, and I'm asking him to remember the example of Ronald Reagan: humor, courtesy, respect, and a presidential manner even in difficult times.
"Mr. President, I say this as a friend. For just a little while, try being quiet. You may be surprised how loudly that silence speaks."
Now in his 90s, Boone was among the defining American pop performers of the pre-Beatles era. His recording of "Love Letters in the Sand" became one of his signature songs, and he remained a major presence on the Billboard charts for years. NPR described Boone last year as a one-time staple of the charts who sold tens of millions of records over the course of his lengthy career.
He has also long been identified with conservative politics.
Boone supported Trump during the 2016 campaign and recorded robocalls aimed at Christian and senior voters on Trump's behalf in the closing days before the election. In a 2022 interview with The Daily Beast, Boone said he had voted for Trump in both 2016 and 2020.
Reagan as the Republican model politician
Boone's invocation of Reagan is not incidental.
He appeared with Reagan at political and White House events throughout the 1980s. Records from the Reagan Presidential Library show Boone appearing alongside the president at a 1982 Washington charity reception, an Illinois Republican rally later that year, and a National Religious Broadcasters convention in 1984.
In Saturday's message, Boone held up Reagan's style — humor, civility, and presidential restraint even amid political conflict — as the model he believes Trump should follow.
Nor is this the first time Boone has urged Trump to change his rhetoric.
In the 2022 interview, Boone recalled speaking directly to Trump during the 2016 campaign, asking him to stop using insulting nicknames and behaving, in Boone's words, like a "schoolyard bully," because it was not presidential. Boone later said he believed Trump had frequently been "his own worst enemy" because of his manner and speech.
His latest appeal thus continues a line of criticism Boone has voiced for years — not of Trump's policy agenda, but of the way he communicates and responds to his opponents.
The timing is notable.
Boone posted his message one day after Trump announced that CNN, MS NOW, and Politico would be banned from the White House, accusing the three news organizations of repeatedly publishing what he called "fake news," "fiction," and "lies." Trump also warned that other outlets could follow.
Boone did not mention the media ban in his message, and there is no basis to say his comments were a direct response to the decision.
His appeal, however, came as Trump intensified his public attacks on news organizations and defended the ban in exchanges with reporters at the White House.
For Boone, the advice was, in the end, simple: a president does not always need to answer.
"Sometimes the strongest thing a leader can do," he wrote, "is say less, listen more, and let his actions speak for themselves."

Israel cannot afford to ignore China’s growing strategic ties with Egypt - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
15:37:08 UTC
00:37:08 KST

Chinese President Xi Jinping recently visited Cairo, his first state visit there since 2016. This visit marks a deeper and crucial shift that Israel must not ignore.
President Xi arrived in Cairo for a formal visit at the end of August, right after the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit that was held in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan.
This itinerary alone speaks volumes about how Beijing positions Cairo on its strategic map. Relations between China and Egypt are long-standing yet complex, largely because of Egypt’s ties with the United States.
The Egyptian newspaper Al-Masry Al-Youm described the relationship as entering a new phase, marking artificial intelligence and energy as sectors where cooperation is expected to expand.
Just recently, the two nations conducted a joint air exercise in which China, for the first time in history, deployed multirole Shenyang J-16 fighter jets to the African continent. This is not just trade – this is a growing presence by a global power in one of the most significant countries in the Middle East.
Yet the underlying, deeper story playing out here that should concern Israelis is not the one about China or even Egypt itself.
Indeed, this story is just one example of large changes that are taking place in the Middle East, right under Israel’s nose. Nevertheless, the government’s policy in the face of these changes has been either backward or nonexistent.
Further, the government may be incapable of implementing even the most basic steps in this regard.
It goes without saying that Israel’s peace treaty with Egypt and the nations’ ties are anchors of regional stability, even if there are disagreements.
Knowing the importance of these ties, it stands to reason that the government would have an organized, sensible approach to maintaining them.
It should have a plan tailored to an understanding of the nexus of American, Egyptian, and Israeli interests. As for the Gaza Strip, the government should have a vision that includes a strategic anchor like Egypt having more influence than countries like Turkey and Qatar.
Yet, like on so many other regional and global issues, this government has none of these. Its foreign policy is driven entirely by short-term domestic political considerations, and it lacks the ability and credibility to manage complex, difficult dialogue with partners and potential partners.
For example, this government would never put together a plan, implement it, or have the credibility and standing to even convince Egypt to deepen energy and economic ties.
Neither does it have a tactic set to maintain a regular strategic dialogue with the largest Arab state – one that has diplomatic ties with Israel.
When it comes to finding ways to work together on shared challenges, like ensuring freedom of navigation in the Red Sea in the face of the Houthi threat, there seems to be no strategy on this front either.
These are common-sense steps that would strengthen ties that aren’t happening because Israel, under this government, doesn’t have a foreign policy. Ties with Egypt are just one instance among dozens of matters where this is happening. For that, Israelis are paying a price economically, in terms of both security and diplomacy.
Government capable of managing Israel
So what needs to change under the next government?
First and foremost, we need a government that actually manages Israel. Those in senior positions need diverse experience managing complex issues and systems.
They should also have expertise in the field that they are responsible for. As a veteran of Israel’s representation abroad, I know what it looks like when there is a government of career politicians who always put politics first rather than policy and proper management.
We saw this in the government that was led by prime minister Naftali Bennett and foreign minister Yair Lapid, and this year, together, they have built a team like that.
Second, we need a government with a clear policy agenda and process. I know from my own experience representing Israel’s economic interests in Asia that on complex, multifaceted issues, there is often no perfect answer.
But with a clear agenda, compass, and process, decision-making improves. One reason I decided to join Bennett’s team is that while many politicians plan campaigns and meet with political strategists, Bennett did something different.
Bennett spent two years building detailed, thorough action plans to address dozens of challenges facing the country, alongside top experts, rooted in his own understanding of the twists and turns of the political system.
In other words, Israel had the right people and the right plans. It seems simple. But over the last four years, we’ve missed these things dearly.
Because of this, opportunities have passed Israel by, and changes in the region like the ones aforementioned regarding Egypt have occurred with Israel not even being present at the decision-making table.
Politics aside, there won’t be a change in course until the country has a government that spends less time making TikToks, tries to govern with simplistic slogans, and meets with party activists in cases best suited to its own political survival, such as its primaries.
Israel needs a government that spends its time on policy planning, tracking, and trying to influence regional developments, one that understands that running the country is its job, not a side gig to gain political influence.
On October 27, Israelis have the chance to choose such a government and put Israel on the path to repair.
The author is the former head of the Israel Trade & Economic Missions in China and a Knesset candidate from the B’Yachad Party, led by Naftali Bennett.

Hormuz oil shipments hit 6-month high, US commander says
RIYADH – Oil and liquefied natural gas shipments through the Strait of Hormuz in the past two weeks reached the highest level in six months, signalling that US naval protection and mine clearance efforts are “paying off”, a regional US commander said.
“Clearly, momentum is building,” Admiral Brad Cooper, head of US Central Command, said in a video message on Sept 19. The strait’s primary transit lanes are clear of mines and Persian Gulf allies have shipped more than one billion barrels of crude through it “in the last couple (of) months”.
Cooper’s comments follow a growing global squeeze on oil and petroleum products since the summer, spurred in part by drone attacks linked to the Iran war that halted a Saudi Arabian pipeline bypassing the strait. Iran maintains it has closed the strait and regional negotiations on agreed shipping routes have faltered.
The Saudi Arabian authorities issued two early-morning air raid alerts for Riyadh on Sept 19, the first in the capital since the height of the US-Iran war in March and April. Saudi civil defence said the danger had lifted soon after in both cases.
An air strike hit jet fuel facilities at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, according to the Wall Street Journal, which cited three officials with knowledge of the incident. The newspaper said that black smoke could be seen at the airport.
US President Donald Trump’s administration, faced with soaring petrol and diesel prices in a midterm election year, has repeatedly cited the volume of tanker traffic through the strait in recent weeks.
US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said on Sept 13 that markets will need to continue relying on transit that he estimates at 10 million barrels a day of crude and oil products through the Strait of Hormuz. He called oil markets “tighter than we’d like today, but they’re not overly tight”.
Cooper said the US – along with Persian Gulf allies, insurers and shipping companies – is working to further increase the flow through the strait.
“The effort is paying off,” he said. “The volume of crude oil, cargo, and liquid natural gas these past two weeks is higher than at any point in the past six months.”
Meanwhile, Iran “has exported zero barrels” as the US enforces a blockade in the strait.
Saudi Arabia, historically the world’s leading oil exporter, came under renewed attack in September as the Houthis, an Iran-backed group based in Yemen, targeted western towns and energy infrastructure. The Saudi government said the drone attack that shut down the East-West pipeline originating in Iraq, which has several pro-Tehran militias.
Yemen’s Houthis have been carrying out almost daily strikes against Saudi Arabia in the last month, with one attack causing a death and several injuries in Taif on Sept 17.
The Houthis have also said they are blockading Saudi ships in the Red Sea and have hit several ships in the waterway, which has served as a key oil export route for Saudi Arabia since the Iran war disrupted Strait of Hormuz traffic. BLOOMBERG

Veteran pro-Israel Democratic Congressman Brad Sherman issued a stark warning to Israel over the weekend, arguing that shifting American public opinion, continued settler violence, Israel's limited investment in its diplomatic apparatus, and National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir's place in the cabinet are putting Israel's international standing and its relationship with the United States at risk.
"Every Israeli official and every Israeli voter should watch this clip, which should be translated into Hebrew," Sherman wrote alongside a CNN segment he shared.
"Yesterday I spoke with the Israeli ambassador. I don't think he, or most Israelis, understand what is at stake."
The CNN segment Sherman highlighted showed a dramatic shift in American attitudes toward Israel.
According to an analysis by CNN chief data analyst Harry Enten, Israel's average net favorability stood at plus 51 points in 2018, during US President Donald Trump's first term, compared with minus 16 points today - a 67-point shift over eight years.
The same analysis cited polling showing that 55% of Americans believe US military assistance to Israel should either be reduced or ended. CNN also presented four separate national surveys - from Ipsos, Fox News, Marquette University Law School, and Pew Research Center - in which Israel's net favorability was negative, ranging from minus 10 to minus 23.
Sherman warns of risks to US weapons access, diplomatic support
Sherman warned that, from Israel's perspective, the stakes in its relationship with Washington go far beyond the annual military assistance package.
"It's not just the traditional $3.8 billion of annual aid," he wrote. "It's access to American weapons and diplomatic support."
He argued that Israel has not done enough to respond to its deteriorating image abroad.
"Israel has been unwilling to take even a few steps to improve its image in the world. They don't fund their Foreign Ministry. Ben-Gvir in the cabinet is an existential threat. Israel cannot survive without friends in the world."
The comments are notable given Sherman's long record on Israel-related issues in Congress. The California Democrat has served in the House since 1997 and is currently a senior member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee and the ranking Democrat on its Middle East and North Africa Subcommittee. His official congressional site has for years listed the US-Israel relationship among his core foreign-policy priorities.

Against that background, his message to Israelis was particularly pointed.

"I hear from Israelis that their actions are justified, and because they are right, they don't have a problem. This demonstrates ignorance of Jewish history."
Sherman: 'Settler violence will continue' unless those in power 'genuinely oppose' it
Sherman devoted much of his warning to developments in the West Bank.
"Settler violence will continue until the relevant ministries are held by people who genuinely oppose settler violence," he wrote.
"The poll numbers CNN reports will only get worse as long as settler violence continues."
The polling Sherman circulated reflects a broader trend, not a single survey.
CNN's July analysis found negative net views of Israel across each of the four national polls it examined. Enten described the change as extending beyond the Democratic base to the broader American electorate.
Among Democrats, the shift has been even sharper.
A separate CNN analysis showed Israel's net favorability among Democratic voters falling from plus 35 points in 2018 to minus 51 points in 2026 - an 86-point swing over eight years.
Sherman's message was not a call to end the US-Israel relationship. Rather, it was a warning from a longtime congressional supporter of Israel that he believes Israeli leaders and voters are underestimating how substantially the political environment in the United States has changed - and how the consequences of further erosion in public support could extend well beyond the annual debate over US military assistance.
Ben-Gvir responded to Sherman's warning later on Saturday, saying that he will "continue to act for the security of Israel's citizens, fearlessly!"

Ukraine steps up measures to protect railways
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
15:37:00 UTC
00:37:00 KST

Ukraine steps up measures to protect railways
September 19, 2026
Recent months have seen a rise in Russian drone attacks on locomotives, stations, and infrastructure. More than 1,600 attacks were reported in the first eight months of 2026, according to Oleh Holovashchenko from Ukrzaliznytsia, the state rail operator.
On September 16, a train traveling between the capital Kyiv and Mykolaiv in southern Ukraine was struck by a Russian drone. The day before, another train in the Volhynia region was attacked near the Polish border.
Two days earlier, a drone had struck the locomotive of a passenger train at the Yahodyn border crossing, just two kilometers (1.2 miles) from Polish territory. Nobody was injured, as Ukrzaliznytsia's monitoring system had previously detected the drone and the train had been evacuated about 15 minutes before the attack. At the time, CIA Director David Petraeus was on another train at the same station.
A separate train carrying several former European leaders, including ex-British Prime Minister Boris Johnson and security advisers had stopped at the station earlier the same day. The Ukrainian authorities believe that this diplomatic train was the drone's actual target, but the train departed earlier than scheduled.
'Putin's terror' against Ukrainian logistics
Russia has damaged or destroyed more than 500 Ukrainian locomotives since its full-scale invasion of Ukrainebegan in 2022. More than half of these attacks happened this year, according to a post on the social media platform X by Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha. He said that part of "Putin's terror" was to destabilize Ukraine's logistics system.
The minister called on international partners to tighten sanctions against Russia further and to provide financial assistance to the Ukrainian government so that it can procure more locomotives that are compatible with Ukraine's Soviet-era broad-gauge (1,520 millimeters or almost 5 feet).
"Ukraine's railway keeps the country moving," Sybiha said. "It enables the rapid evacuation of civilians from frontline areas, transports essential cargo, and keeps grain and other critical goods moving across the country."
Russia was specifically targeting locomotives because they were ideal from a technical point of view, said Vasyl Shevchenko, a former Ukrainian deputy transport minister. "A locomotive's thermal signature is very large, and almost impossible to miss," he told DW. "The impact of a strike can be devastating, because 50 kilograms (110 pounds) of explosives in a diesel locomotive can cause several metric tons of fuel to detonate and completely destroy it. A strike on an electric locomotive will cause a fire that can paralyze an entire stretch of track. That's why they are targeting areas where the loss of a single train can bring traffic to a standstill."
Shevchenko also pointed out that locomotives could not be replaced immediately but had to be ordered in advance and this could take years. Ukrzaliznytsia says that negotiations are underway with various international partners and a contract has already been signed with the French company Alstom. These locomotives are scheduled to start arriving next year.
In the meantime, trains are also being repaired. "While our top priorities used to be saving on costs, providing comfort to the train crew and making sure the trains were attractive, these have changed," Holovashchenko said. "What is most important today is that the locomotive is technically sound and ready to transport passengers and freight." But he added that it was difficult to protect trains against Russia's weapons.
Zelenskyy intensifies protection of critical infrastructure
On September 15, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy held a meeting of the staff of the Supreme Commander-in-Chief to discuss strengthening the protection of critical infrastructure and logistics.
The key issues were contracts for the production of protection systems for critical infrastructure and logistics, but he added that there were plans to expand the electronic warfare component and reorganize the operation of designated mobile fire teams, as well as strengthening air defense lines.
Zelenskyy said that decisions on backup logistics routes in frontline regions were also being made, and he had instructed Ukraine's Finance Ministry of to find additional funding for the logistics sector.
Ukrzaliznytsia sets up monitoring centers
According to Holovashchenko, Ukrzaliznytsia is also seeking its own answers to the new challenges and there are plans to develop early detection systems. He said that a monitoring center had been established to track the movement of drones and trains all over Ukraine.
The fact that Russia has started to use jet-powered Shahed-type drones, which are much faster than previous models, has made it more difficult and given less time to respond. "We used to wait longer to stop trains so we could evacuate passengers," Holovashchenko said. "Now, there are more precautionary stops. But in general, we try not to go into areas where there is a potential danger."
Buses are deployed in areas of particularly high risk and the "train plus bus" concept is being expanded in cooperation with military authorities. Passengers are also being given instructions on how to respond in the event of an alarm and advised to try to get further away from a station than previously.
The most difficult question remains where they should be evacuated to. Holovashchenko said that the monitoring centers had access to maps showing all the shelters along train routes and that dispatchers always tried to stop trains near them, but this was not always possible. He said that train personnel were receiving special psychological support to help passengers.
Ukrzaliznytsia is currently preparing for winter, while working with foundations and other donors to ensure that trains will be heated. Evacuations will be even more difficult as temperatures drop. "This is no easy task. We're providing blankets, rain jackets, and equipment so that train staff can supply passengers with at least the bare necessities if their train comes to a standstill in the middle of nowhere because of a snowstorm, Holovashchenko said.
This article was originally published in Ukrainian.

Voices from the Arab Press: Red lines in Syria, Azerbaijani oil, and Anwar Sadat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
15:36:51 UTC
00:36:51 KST

The end of social media
Okaz, Saudi Arabia, September 5
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
As the Quran tells us, only your Lord himself, full of majesty and honor, will remain. Nothing remains except the face of the one possessed of majesty and honor. That is the rule governing the universe.
Which brings us to the question of the end of social media: when will these applications that control people’s lives disappear? A question like this immediately raises another: what will replace them?
Social media have become almost like food and air. Remove them from your phone, and the device returns to the Nokia era – camera, telephone, and text messages. Those who lived through that period remember it.
I doubt anyone imagined social media or predicted them, even though their incubator, the Internet, already existed. Even Nokia, the giant that dominated the mobile-phone market for decades, collapsed because it failed to see what was standing on its doorstep.
In the 1980s, Asharq al-Awsat began printing by satellite. It was a tremendous technological event: the newspaper could be printed simultaneously in Jeddah and London.
That breakthrough generated many predictions. One of the most popular was that every household would eventually have a machine resembling an ATM, connected to satellites and periodically filled with paper, which each morning would print whichever newspapers you subscribed to. We were told Japan had already begun developing such a device.
Yet technological development took a completely different turn and ultimately eliminated the very essence of the prediction: paper itself. I am not talking here about the emergence of yet another technology giant, but about the disappearance of the great communications giants that once transformed the world.
In earlier eras, human beings did not anticipate what would become perhaps the greatest invention of all: the Internet, which swallowed radio, television, cinema, newspapers, commerce, education, medicine, and human relationships. Social media is only one manifestation of that larger invention.
Today we are witnessing the rise of another technological giant: artificial intelligence. Its growing presence, intertwined with social media, will make it easier for everyone to participate in creating a different world. Yet this very expansion, I believe, will eventually bring about social media’s demise.
When you use X today, you are in practice subject to two sets of laws: Saudi and American. What is permitted in the US is not necessarily permitted in Saudi Arabia, and vice versa.
As artificial intelligence develops rapidly and becomes easier to use, we will not merely gain more advanced knowledge; fabrication will also multiply. Soon we will inhabit a world whose very reality is suspect. Governments everywhere cannot remain spectators.
Official oversight of social media will expand. The door cannot remain open to absolutely everyone – and for once, I use that expression literally rather than figuratively. Some users are respectable, some are among the worst people imaginable, and others pursue very specific agendas.
All seek to influence others, whether for cultural reasons, money, political influence, or ideology. It is hardly an exaggeration to say that every intelligence service in the world has a presence on social media.
Whenever a battle rages on X and affects us, we cannot know with certainty who is behind it or whether it is for us or against us. When you see two people insulting each other online, assume a third party is benefiting from it and helping to inflame it.
Social media will soon become a world of chaos that erodes values and destabilizes settled knowledge. You will not know whether what you are reading is real or fabricated, whether the television channel you are watching is genuine or an imitation, whether the newspaper in front of you is real or fake.
The easier and more precise artificial intelligence becomes, the greater the chaos and the more actors will exploit it for divergent purposes. Governments have already begun intervening, but for now that intervention is mainly regulatory and legal and can exert real force only over accounts within their own jurisdictions.
The next step, in my view, will reach foreign accounts as well. States will decide which remain accessible and which are blocked. Social media will therefore cease to be genuinely global.
X has taken a preliminary step by providing information about the location or origin of certain accounts, but that is not enough to protect states from disorder and penetration. Every country will increasingly separate itself from the global mix.
A day will come when each state can identify what originates domestically and distinguish it from what comes from abroad, blocking the latter with the very artificial intelligence that created the chaos in the first place.
Everything you read and watch will then effectively become a local product, whether published under a real name or a pseudonym. Social media will become an internal forum, much like newspapers and other older media once were.
At that point, they will lose their defining feature: the global public square. And that will be their end.
You may now ask, what will replace social media? I can only answer, as Steve Jobs once did in another context: If you know the future, bring it here now – what are you waiting for? – Abdullah Bin Bakheet
Turkey, Israel, and red lines in Syria
Al-Masry Al-Youm, Egypt, September 6
Israel justified its August 18 strike on the Abu Al-Duhur Air Base, roughly 70 kilometers from the Turkish border, by claiming that Damascus was preparing to allow Turkish forces to deploy there, and that Israeli warnings had not been taken seriously.
Syria and Turkey denied any plan to establish a permanent base, saying Turkish officers had visited the site as part of training and military cooperation.
Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz nevertheless chose to issue a direct warning to Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan against dragging his country into “dangerous adventures in Syria” and testing Israel’s determination to defend itself.
With that strike, Turkish-Israeli relations moved another step away from political disagreement and toward military competition.
The two countries are not at war, and neither appears to have made a decision to go to war, but both are now drawing redlines inside the same geographic space. That is where the real danger begins.
For years, relations between Ankara and Tel Aviv demonstrated an ability to separate politics from interests. Disputes escalated, accusations were exchanged, and ambassadors were recalled more than once, yet trade continued, and practical cooperation never disappeared entirely.
On the eve of the Gaza war, bilateral trade stood at roughly $7 billion annually. The war shattered that equation. Turkey halted direct trade, closed its ports to Israeli vessels, and Erdogan’s language toward the Israeli government reached unprecedented levels of hostility.
Even so, Gaza does not appear to be the arena in which military confrontation between the two states is most likely to begin. It is the source of the political and moral rupture and the fuel for popular and rhetorical hostility, but it does not place Turkish and Israeli forces in the same theater.
Turkey can exert diplomatic and economic pressure and support the Palestinian position, while Israel can reject any Turkish security role in Gaza’s future, but the likelihood of direct fire between the two there remains limited.
Syria is far more dangerous because the dispute is not merely over positions but over two conflicting strategic projects. Turkey wants a unified Syrian state strong enough to control its borders, prevent the emergence of an armed Kurdish entity, and remain politically, economically, and militarily linked to Ankara.
It is therefore helping train the Syrian army and rebuild its institutions, seeking to transform the influence accumulated during years of war into a long-term partnership – perhaps extending into administrative arrangements – with Ahmed al-Sharaa’s government.
Israel, by contrast, wants a Syria that poses no military threat, a demilitarized south, and continuing freedom for its aircraft to strike whatever it considers dangerous to its security.
From Israel’s perspective, replacing Iranian influence with Turkish military influence is not necessarily an improvement. Iran was a familiar and exposed adversary. Turkey is a large NATO member with a substantial army, a defense industry, a network of alliances, and the capacity to help rebuild Syrian power.
This is the core contradiction: what Turkey regards as the natural reconstruction of the Syrian state may be seen by Israel as the creation of a new threat, while what Israel calls freedom of defensive action is viewed by Turkey as a violation of Syrian sovereignty and an attempt to keep the country weak and fragmented.
– Abdel Latif El-Menawy
Azerbaijan’s oil flows to Israel
Asharq al-Awsat, London, September 5
For more than 30 years, Israel and Azerbaijan have built a quiet partnership based on reciprocal interests, without a mutual defense treaty or any formal obligation requiring one to protect the other.
The war with Iran has given that relationship new importance by revealing its practical value in a period of confrontation, particularly in energy and security.
Israel needs Azerbaijani oil and values proximity to the Iranian border, while Baku benefits from Israeli military technology and intelligence cooperation that strengthens its ability to protect its interests.
Even so, both sides prefer to keep the relationship flexible rather than formalize it into an alliance carrying broader commitments.
Diplomatic relations date to 1992, when Israel recognized Azerbaijan and opened an embassy in Baku. Azerbaijan moved more slowly, establishing a trade office in Tel Aviv in 2021 and opening an embassy in 2023, becoming the first Shi’ite-majority country to maintain a permanent diplomatic mission in Israel.
In February 2026, the two countries signed an artificial intelligence memorandum covering supercomputing infrastructure and joint research. Yet there is still no defense treaty between them, only a collection of separate arrangements in trade, energy, arms, and intelligence that can expand or contract according to circumstances.
Oil is the central pillar of the relationship. In 2025, Israel’s imports of Azerbaijani crude rose by 31% to around 94,000 barrels a day, giving Azerbaijan 46.4% of Israel’s total oil imports, compared with roughly 28% from Russia, the second-largest supplier.
The crude travels through the Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan pipeline from Azerbaijan to Turkey’s Mediterranean coast and is then shipped to Ashkelon. The route’s strategic value lies in bypassing the Strait of Hormuz, leaving Iran unable to disrupt it directly through its leverage there.
Maintaining the flow is essential both to Israel’s economy and to its military capacity. Yet the same advantage also creates vulnerability because nearly half of Israel’s oil imports depend on a single supplier.
The crude also transits Turkish territory at a time when Ankara has maintained a trade embargo on Israel since 2024. Turkey does not officially determine the final destination of crude loaded at Ceyhan, but the route nonetheless remains exposed to political fluctuations.
Azerbaijan, for its part, benefits from having a major buyer for its oil and from preserving a corridor connecting the Caspian Sea to the Mediterranean, reinforcing its role as an important energy source outside Russian and Iranian routes.
The security dimension is more sensitive and opaque. Reports have alleged the presence of Israeli special forces and intelligence personnel in southern Azerbaijan near the Iranian border, using the area for intelligence collection, drone operations, and possible rescue teams for pilots.
Other reports have attributed a strike on an Iranian official to activity launched from Azerbaijani territory. Baku has denied these claims as baseless, while Israel has declined to comment. They therefore remain unverified accounts rather than established facts, particularly amid a broad information and intelligence war.
The Caspian Sea dimension became more important after Israel struck Iran’s Bandar Anzali naval base on March 18. According to reports, the attack destroyed a ship, four missile boats, and military infrastructure.
The force destroyed there did not represent a major direct threat to Israel, but in theory it could have threatened Azerbaijani oil installations and Caspian shipping lanes. Its weakening therefore benefited Azerbaijan indirectly and helped protect the region producing the crude destined for Israel.
It also affected a maritime route used by Russia and Iran for trade and, according to Western reports, the movement of military equipment.
Yet closeness to Israel also carries potential costs for Baku. On March 5, drones arriving from the direction of Iran struck Nakhchivan International Airport, wounding four civilians, although Tehran denied responsibility.
The incident was interpreted as a limited warning over Azerbaijani-Israeli cooperation. President Ilham Aliyev responded forcefully by summoning the Iranian ambassador, recalling Azerbaijan’s ambassador, and raising military readiness along the border.
Tensions nevertheless subsided quickly: border crossings reopened, the Azerbaijani and Iranian presidents spoke by telephone, and Azerbaijan sent humanitarian assistance to Iran. This illustrates Baku’s preference for deterrence without severing communication.
Arms have also been central to the partnership. Israel supplied 69% of Azerbaijan’s major weapons imports between 2016 and 2020, including reconnaissance drones, loitering munitions, LORA missiles, and Barak air defense systems.
Purchases later declined after Baku achieved its military objective of regaining Nagorno-Karabakh from Armenia and no longer needed imports at the same pace. Even so, Azerbaijan continues to benefit from existing Israeli systems and the maintenance, upgrades, and training associated with them.
In the balance of gains, Israel derives the greater strategic benefit during wartime because it secures a major oil source beyond Hormuz while maintaining a relationship with a country bordering Iran.
Azerbaijan gains economically and militarily but carries greater geographic and political risk because of its proximity to Iran and its close ties with Turkey. The most realistic course is therefore the current one: deep cooperation without a declared alliance, openness toward Israel combined with continued dialogue with Iran.
It is a partnership from which both benefit, but Israel reaps the broader energy and security advantage, while Baku proceeds cautiously to ensure its gains do not become liabilities. – Huda al-Husseini
Why did Sadat become the 20th century’s greatest president?
El Watan, Egypt, September 5
Anwar Sadat was not a great leader merely because he fought the October War, nor because he later chose peace with Israel, but because he possessed a rare ability to read international transformations and make decisions at the moment they best served Egypt’s interests.
To understand Sadat’s experience, it is not enough to look at the results of the October War, his visit to Jerusalem, or the recovery of Sinai. One must first consider an element of politics that is often decisive: timing.
In 1972, the Soviet Union was still a superpower engaged in an open struggle with the US for global leadership. Yet Sadat took the bold decision to reduce the Soviet presence in Egypt and expel a large number of Soviet advisers.
He did not wait decades for the Soviet Union to collapse before realizing that the international system was changing; he began reorienting Egyptian policy while Moscow was still near the height of its power.
That decision formed part of a broader vision: Egypt could not remain captive to a single international camp, and restoring national decision-making required an independent margin of maneuver.
Then came the October War of 1973. Sadat’s objective was not an open-ended war or a propaganda victory. He wanted to break the stalemate, alter the balance of power, and open the path toward a political settlement that would restore Egyptian rights.
He fought when war served the national objective, then moved toward negotiations when diplomacy became more useful to Egypt. This was a defining feature of his leadership: he used war to change the equation, then used peace to consolidate the results.
He went to Jerusalem, entered difficult negotiations that culminated in the Egyptian-Israeli peace treaty, and eventually restored the whole of Sinai to Egyptian sovereignty.
In parallel, Sadat repositioned Egypt internationally, gradually shifting it from the Soviet sphere toward a strategic relationship with the US.
People may disagree over his economic or domestic policies, and those remain legitimate subjects for criticism, but it is difficult to deny that he possessed a clear foreign-policy vision and a strong ability to read international power balances.
The politician who makes a difference is not merely the one who knows how to fight, but the one who knows when to fight, when to negotiate, when to change direction, and when to understand that the world around him has changed.
Sadat grasped early that international relations are built not on permanent friendships or eternal enmities but on shifting interests, and that the state’s interests must remain the primary compass.
More than half a century later, Egypt faces another international transformation. Its details differ from Sadat’s era, but the underlying question is similar: how can the state maneuver among major powers without becoming a card in anyone else’s hand?
The US remains the world’s strongest power, but China is rising economically and politically, while competition between the two intensifies over the shape of the international system in the coming decades.
Egypt does not need to replace its relationship with Washington with total alignment with Beijing, or to join one camp against the other, but to build a balanced policy that maximizes Egyptian gains.
Cairo needs to preserve its strategic relationship with the US while expanding economic and investment partnerships with China, giving itself greater room to maneuver, strengthening its bargaining position, and protecting national decision-making from dependence on any external power.
The equation is not easy, but it is necessary. Relations with Washington can strengthen Egypt’s hand in dealing with Beijing, just as relations with Beijing can provide additional leverage in dealing with Washington, provided Egyptian interests remain the primary determinant, and Cairo does not become a party to a conflict that does not serve its objectives.
Sadat read a major international transformation in his time and made decisions that redirected Egypt for decades. Today, Egypt’s leadership confronts another changing world, gradually moving from a system dominated by one power toward one that is more competitive and multipolar.
The real issue, then, is not whether Egypt chooses America or China, but whether it can benefit from both relationships and use its geography, political weight, and regional role to advance its national interests.
Sadat taught us that politics is not made of fixed slogans, that national independence does not mean isolation, and that openness does not mean dependence.
The question facing Egypt today is whether it can read the shift between the US and China as Sadat once read the shift between the US and the Soviet Union. I believe the answer is that we are about to witness political maneuvering at the highest level.
– John Al-Masri ■

Gazan photographer did not publish Oct. 7 footage so as not to 'ruin lives' of Palestinian mob
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
15:36:43 UTC
00:36:43 KST

Gazan photographer and journalist Motaz Azaiza said he filmed Israeli hostages being beaten by a Gazan mob on October 7, 2023, but chose not to publish the footage because he feared it could put the Palestinians involved at risk.
“I saw the vehicle of the Al-Qassam Brigades, and there were Israeli captives there,” Azaiza recalled. “People got out, watched, beat them, hit them, and I followed them and filmed. But I did not publish those videos. Why? Because I did not want to ruin the lives of the people who were filmed.
"I understood that Israel would use those videos to identify every person who was there and eliminate them," he added. "I did not want to be responsible, even indirectly, for the deaths of those people in exchange for a few likes and views online.”
A Nobel Peace Prize nominee and one of Time magazine’s 100 most influential people in the world, Azaiza has become one of the most recognizable figures associated with the current war. In an extensive and unusual interview with journalist Ahmed Biqui on the podcast Taqarrab, Azaiza revealed aspects of life in Gaza that his millions of social media followers have not seen.
During the interview, which was published earlier this month, Azaiza also delivered rare public criticism of Hamas's leadership, accusing the group of bringing disaster upon the Gaza Strip.
Azaiza: Hamas 'brought us back to the Middle Ages'
Although Azaiza described himself as a supporter of armed Palestinian resistance, he said such resistance must have limits and serve a purpose.
“I support armed resistance, but one that brings results, or at least gives me the feeling that my life is valuable in the eyes of the resistance. Why should a Palestinian be cheap in the eyes of Palestinians themselves? You are making people hate the resistance with your own hands.”
He also questioned what Hamas’s military campaign has achieved for Palestinians in Gaza since the start of the war, sending a direct message to the group’s leaders.
“From October 7 until today, show me one Palestinian who lives in Gaza and was protected by Hamas’s weapons? No one in Gaza received protection from those weapons.”
Azaiza went on to criticize Hamas’s leadership over its months-long refusal to agree to a deal.
“I am not waiting two years to judge whether Hamas made mistakes. I see the mistake in front of my eyes, when people are dying every day. Now they are talking about an agreement in which they will agree to lay down their weapons. You could have agreed to that already on October 11, 2023. Why was it so important that tens of thousands would be killed? On what table did you put the Palestinian issue? You brought us back to the Middle Ages. You caused women in Gaza to urinate into a plastic bucket. This does not bother you, but what bothers you is if someone suddenly criticizes you?”
Azaiza made these remarks after leaving Gaza. He fled the Strip about four months after the outbreak of the war and currently lives in Qatar.
The photographer said he experienced Hamas’s suppression apparatus firsthand. He described a WhatsApp group called “Smart,” which he said is managed by a Hamas media official at the Rafah crossing and used to organize online campaigns against journalists who challenge the group’s narrative.
“Suddenly I found myself being attacked from all directions,” he recalled. “They take the details of a specific person, publish his phone number in the group and instruct online activists to attack him, curse him and make his life miserable. This is organized behavior, a real mob. When I uploaded a video in which a civilian could be heard cursing Hamas, I faced enormous backlash. Photographers in Gaza have become accustomed to lowering their cameras the moment someone says something bad about Hamas, because anyone who dares to show reality is persecuted relentlessly.”
According to Azaiza, “I lived inside a pressure cooker. The people who controlled us treated our lives as a game. I felt that I had been marked, that at every moment I was walking around with a target on my back.”
Azaiza feels empty, deeply frustrated by internal situation for Palestinians
Despite his international recognition, meetings with world leaders, his highly publicized meeting with Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas, and the global status he has gained, Azaiza described feeling empty and deeply frustrated by the internal Palestinian situation and his new life outside Gaza.
“I wish I had the ability to sleep and never wake up. It is a genuine desire to die,” he said, describing the psychological toll he has experienced. “I travel around the world, flying from London to New York, speaking in front of thousands of people who buy tickets to hear me, sitting at Nobel ceremonies, and I cannot be happy. I live with constant burning trauma.”
Azaiza described his complicated relationship with Gaza in deeply personal terms.
“Gaza is the most toxic place in the world. You love it, but at the same time you hate it. You love it, but it hurts you and destroys you. The reality there forced things upon me that I never wanted. The price we pay to satisfy leaders who do not count us is simply unimaginable.”

UN peacekeeping chief in Lebanon says smooth transition is critical before pull-out
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
15:36:34 UTC
00:36:34 KST

The head of United Nations peacekeepers in Lebanon said on Saturday that it was critical to ensure other UN agencies and Lebanese troops could assume the tasks the force carries out before it begins withdrawing at the end of this year.
Major General Diodato Abagnara of Italy spoke to Reuters in southern Lebanon from a position operated by the UN peacekeeping force known as UNIFIL, which has allegedly monitored hostilities in southern Lebanon for nearly 50 years.
Since a new war erupted after Iran-backed Lebanese terrorist group Hezbollah attacked Israel in March, the force has also provided security escorts for humanitarian aid convoys to residents in a small cluster of predominantly Christian southern Lebanese towns where the IDF is fighting Hezbollah.
Residents in much of the rest of southern Lebanon have been displaced due to Hezbollah embedding itself in civilian areas, necessitating their evacuation before strikes against Hezbollah can be carried out.
The UN Security Council has ordered UNIFIL to begin withdrawing at the end of 2026, triggering concerns over whether aid deliveries can continue and how the force can transfer its positions to Lebanese troops.
“There are other United Nations entities here in the south, and so what is very important for us (is) to conduct a very smooth transition to different entities, or for the future of a new mission,” Abagnara told Reuters.
He said UNIFIL was already working with the UN’s country team to ensure humanitarian assistance in areas where Hezbollah has embedded itself and information sharing with the Lebanese army about “sensitive areas (and) how they can manage this situation.”
Abagnara acknowledged that it could be “very difficult” to hand over some of UNIFIL's posts to Lebanese troops given that more than half lie within areas where the IDF took control after clearing Hezbollah terror infrastructure.
Israel working to clear Hezbollah infrastructure built near UN post
Diplomats worry UNIFIL’s departure will mean an end to the UN's "eyes and ears" in southern Lebanon.
Abagnara spoke to Reuters at a position overlooking Mansouri, a town where Israeli forces have been carrying out demolitions since ordering residents to leave in June so Hezbollah terror infrastructure could be cleared. Reuters reporters could see excavators in the town knocking down trees and homes.
Abagnara claimed that the demolitions are “another violation” of UN Security Council resolutions on Lebanon. Israel's military has said it is destroying Hezbollah infrastructure across southern Lebanon, which was built while UNIFIL was stationed in the area.
Lebanese army efforts to disarm Hezbollah stall
As a US-backed plan for Lebanon's army to disarm Hezbollah and take control of southern Lebanon has stalled, a diplomatic scramble is underway to address the vacuum that will be left by UNIFIL’s withdrawal.
Lebanon wants an extension. Other countries have discussed a new multinational mission, though it remains unclear what kind of mandate it would have.
Abagnara said an extension would be “a great honor” but that without a new Security Council decision, his force would need to stop operating at the end of the year.
“It's not a long time," he said. "The presence of United Nations in the South is very, very essential. And according to me, more now than ever.”
Jerusalem Post Staff contributed to this report.
