Wandering cat Kurri covers 15,000 kilometers in two months
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
14:15:00 UTC
23:15:00 KST

Wandering cat Kurri covers 15,000 kilometers in two months
Kurri, adopted from a shelter, has over the years become a travel‑loving wanderer with six summer road trips behind him.
Recently the cat traveled 15,000 kilometers in two months, braving mountain roads, passing through 14 countries and reaching Armenia.
"Kurri was offended with me for three days. Normally he comes to my lap and sleeps next to me at night, but he just ignored me. He was so upset that we were home and not going anywhere anymore. No more daily excitement."
Now nine years old, Kurri came into owner Katri Bagirov's life from a shelter where she volunteered helping cats find new homes. "I was also a foster home for a while. That winter there were many cats in quarantine. Kurri was in the worst condition, so I took him under my care, took him to the vet, and it turned out he had pneumonia. I nursed him back to health and started looking for a home for him. Soon the thought started ticking that maybe I wanted him myself, and we began looking for ways to adopt him," said Bagirov, whose life involved a lot of travel.
"He didn't really fit my lifestyle, but since my mother offered to take care of Kurri when I'm away, the decision was made," she added.
Kurri was not born a travel cat. At first, even a single car ride was a challenge. "I didn't even have the idea back then that a cat could travel like this. I thought he could come with me to the countryside, visit friends and family. I trained him that first spring with a harness, leash and car. It was a huge headache. He got sick easily, he was anxious, had diarrhea. My car was covered in plastic and newspapers before I started training him more consciously," Bagirov recalled. Today Kurri crawls into her travel suitcase with little trouble and is ready to go.
"Nearly three years passed, covid came, we wanted to go on vacation and ruled out any flights. We decided to go by car, and there was nowhere to leave Kurri. We thought he'd come along, and if needed, we'd just turn back. We drove through Germany, France, Spain and Portugal. And I was surprised how much he walked. He walked through entire villages. Small villages, but still," Bagirov laughed.
This year's trip was Kurri's sixth summer road journey. It was the longest so far and, for the first time, took them to the Caucasus. Traveling with Kurri are Katri, Katri's mother and her husband. Travel planning largely revolves around the four‑legged family member.
"We function as a travel group because we are Kurri's people, and all our trips revolve around him. At least in recent years. We choose everything based on Kurri," Bagirov explained.
"In the European Union it's simple: you need to microchip the animal, have a pet passport and a rabies vaccination. Leaving the EU gets a bit more complicated. You need a health declaration, which basically means a stamp in the pet passport confirming the animal is healthy and has had parasite treatment," Bagirov said.
Before confirming accommodation, they check with potential hosts what they think about having a cat stay overnight. "So far the experience has been very positive. Problems have been with larger hotels that have their own rules and conditions. If it's not allowed, then it's not allowed. But smaller accommodations have generally let Kurri into the room. Very surprising. It's much easier to walk in and ask than to search online," Bagirov noted.

Donbas Is More Than a Line on a Map: Lessons From Gettysburg, Normandy, Iwo Jima
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
14:06:00 UTC
23:06:00 KST

The Donbas is often discussed as though it were primarily a territorial question: a section of the map that might be exchanged, conceded or divided as part of a negotiated settlement. That framing misses a fundamental military reality. Terrain is not interchangeable. Some terrain provides such an advantage to the force that controls it that military professionals have a specific term for it: key terrain.
That concept is among the fundamentals of military art taught to young officers. A hill, ridgeline, river crossing or fortified city can matter far beyond its physical size because control of it determines what an army can observe, defend, attack or protect. The US has learned this lesson repeatedly in its own military history, from Gettysburg to Normandy to Iwo Jima. Americans considering the future of Ukraine should remember those lessons before treating the Donbas as simply another line on a map.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
                                                                                                                                                                         
At Gettysburg, Little Round Top was a relatively small piece of ground on the Union Army’s extreme left. On the afternoon of July 2, 1863, Brigadier General Gouverneur K. Warren recognized that the hill was dangerously exposed as Confederate forces moved against the Union flank. Union troops were hurried to the position, including Colonel Strong Vincent’s brigade, with Colonel Joshua Lawrence Chamberlain and the 20th Maine occupying its extreme left. The National Park Service describes Little Round Top as ideally suited for observation, artillery and defense; Union forces ultimately repelled repeated Confederate attacks and retained control of it.
Russia Enlists Yemeni Citizens for War in Ukraine, Ukraine Intel Says
Chamberlain and the 20th Maine became famous for their defense of the flank and their downhill bayonet charge after ammunition ran low. Their achievement has endured in American military culture not because Little Round Top represented valuable real estate, but because losing the position could have exposed the Union flank and altered the tactical situation across the battlefield. The significance of the ground came from what possession of it allowed one army to do to the other.
The same logic was evident on June 6, 1944, when US Army Rangers assaulted Pointe du Hoc during the Normandy invasion. The Rangers scaled cliffs approximately 100 feet high to attack a German artillery position overlooking the invasion area. They were not risking their lives for the intrinsic value of a few acres of Norman coastline. They were attacking terrain from which German forces could threaten the larger Allied operation.
                                                                                                                                                                         
The Marines who fought on Iwo Jima understood the principle as well. Mount Suribachi dominated the southern portion of the island and the exposed ground beneath it. Marine Corps histories describe the mountain as a major tactical obstacle whose capture was necessary before the advance north could proceed securely. The raising of the American flag on its summit became one of the most recognizable images of the Second World War, but the fight for Suribachi began as a military problem: an enemy-held dominant terrain feature overlooking American forces.
Gettysburg, Normandy and Iwo Jima were different battles in different wars, and historical analogies should not be pushed beyond what they can support. The Donbas is not Little Round Top, and Kramatorsk is not Pointe du Hoc. The enduring lesson is more basic: military terrain has value because of what it enables.
That is the lens through which the debate over the Donbas should be viewed. Russia continues to press toward Sloviansk and Kramatorsk, which sit at the center of Ukraine’s remaining defenses in Donetsk Oblast. Reuters recently described control of Donetsk as critical to both sides as Russian forces continue their offensive and Ukraine concentrates major defensive efforts there. A negotiated territorial concession in such an area therefore cannot be evaluated simply by calculating how many square kilometers would change hands. The relevant question is what military position each side would occupy afterward.
Fortifications, urban terrain, transportation networks, observation, maneuver corridors and the geography behind a defensive line all affect the answer. A defensive position built and improved over years cannot necessarily be recreated by drawing another line farther west. Surrendering key terrain can give an adversary through negotiation an operational advantage it has been unable to secure through combat.
This distinction becomes especially important when negotiations are described in the vocabulary of real estate transactions or commercial bargaining. Wars are not commercial transactions, and territory in war is not fungible property. A company negotiating the sale of an asset can often substitute money for ownership. An army surrendering commanding terrain cannot necessarily purchase equivalent geography somewhere else.
There is also a human dimension that makes the analogy to a real estate transaction particularly inadequate. The United Nations has documented increased pressure on residents of Russian-occupied Ukrainian territory to obtain Russian citizenship, restrictions imposed on people without it, penalties for expressions of Ukrainian cultural identity and continuing expropriation of private property. The disposition of occupied territory therefore determines not only where armies stand but also the political and legal conditions under which civilians will live.
None of this means military history dictates a particular diplomatic formula. Political leaders must weigh military realities alongside human costs, economic constraints, alliance considerations and the prospects for a durable peace. But any negotiation that contemplates territorial concessions should begin with an accurate understanding of what is being conceded and what advantage it may provide.
American military history provides a useful way to explain that distinction to an American public. Little Round Top was not important because Abraham Lincoln coveted a hill in Pennsylvania. Pointe du Hoc was not important because Franklin Roosevelt wanted cliffs in France. Mount Suribachi was not important because the United States wanted possession of a volcanic peak. In each case, Americans fought for terrain because of the military consequences of allowing the enemy to control it.
That is the lesson worth remembering as policymakers discuss the Donbas. Before asking whether Ukraine should surrender a piece of territory in exchange for a diplomatic agreement, they should first ask the question an officer would ask while studying a battlefield: What does control of that ground enable?
The answer may determine not merely where this war ends, but the conditions under which another one could begin.
The views expressed in this opinion article are the author’s and not necessarily those of Kyiv Post.

UN peacekeeping chief in Lebanon says smooth transition is critical before pull-out
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
14:03:38 UTC
23:03:38 KST

UN peacekeeping chief in Lebanon says smooth transition is critical before pull-out
NEAR MANSOURI, Lebanon – The head of United Nations peacekeepers in Lebanon said on Sept 19 it was critical to ensure other UN agencies and Lebanese troops could assume the tasks carried out by the force before it begins withdrawing at the end of 2026.
Major-General Diodato Abagnara of Italy spoke to Reuters in southern Lebanon at a position operated by the UN peacekeeping force known as UNIFIL, which has been monitoring hostilities in southern Lebanon for nearly 50 years.
Since a new war erupted between Israel and Iran-backed Lebanese armed group Hezbollah in March, the force has also provided security escorts for humanitarian aid convoys to residents in a small cluster of predominantly Christian southern Lebanese towns now encircled by Israeli troops. Residents in much of the rest of southern Lebanon have been forcibly displaced by Israeli strikes and evacuation orders.
The UN Security Council has ordered UNIFIL to begin withdrawing at the end of 2026, triggering concerns over whether aid deliveries can continue and how the force can transfer its positions to Lebanese troops.
“There are other United Nations entities here in the south, and so what is very important for us (is) to conduct a very smooth transition to different entities, or for the future of a new mission,” Abagnara told Reuters.
He said UNIFIL was already working with the UN’s country team to ensure humanitarian assistance in Israeli-occupied areas and information sharing with the Lebanese Army about “sensitive areas (and) how they can manage this situation”.
Abagnara acknowledged that it could be “very difficult” to hand over some of UNIFIL’s posts to Lebanese troops given that more than half lie within areas now controlled by Israeli troops.
Israel demolishes town near UN post
Diplomats worry UNIFIL’s departure will mean an end to the UN's “eyes and ears” in southern Lebanon.
Abagnara spoke to Reuters at a position overlooking Mansouri, a town where Israeli forces have been carrying out demolitions since ordering residents to leave in June, despite a ceasefire. Reuters reporters could see excavators in the town knocking down trees and multi-storey homes.
Abagnara described demolitions as “another violation” of UN Security Council resolutions on Lebanon. Israel’s military has said it is destroying Hezbollah infrastructure across southern Lebanon.
As a US-backed plan for Lebanon’s army to disarm Hezbollah and take control of southern Lebanon has stalled, a diplomatic scramble is underway to address the vacuum that will be left by UNIFIL’s withdrawal.
Lebanon wants an extension. Other countries have discussed a new multinational mission, though it remains unclear what kind of mandate it would have.
Abagnara said an extension would be “a great honour” but that without a new Security Council decision, his force would need to stop operating at the end of 2026.
“It’s not a long time,” he said. “The presence of (the) United Nations in the south is very, very essential. And according to me, more now than ever.” REUTERS

Turkish authorities have detained more than 200 people in a sweeping investigation into an alleged international investment fraud network that prosecutors say operated from Turkey and defrauded victims around the world of more than $3 billion.
The Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office said the network operated through companies posing as call centers, consulting firms and tourism businesses. Turkish authorities allege that Israeli-linked figures dominated the companies’ ownership and ultimate beneficiary structures, describing some of those behind the operation as “Israeli fraud barons.”
As of Saturday, 201 people had been detained in the investigation, including nine Israeli citizens, according to Turkish reports. One of the Israelis reportedly also holds a Portuguese passport. The investigation involves 248 suspects, with authorities continuing efforts to locate those still at large.
Turkey’s Justice Minister Akın Gürlek announced the operation on Friday. It was carried out by the Interior Ministry, Turkey’s National Intelligence Organization, known as MIT, the Financial Crimes Investigation Board, or MASAK, Istanbul police and Interpol.
According to Turkish prosecutors, the network operated through 29 companies and 44 call centers that presented themselves as legitimate businesses offering consulting, tourism and customer services.
Potential victims were allegedly recruited through advertisements on social media, search engines and websites promising high returns from foreign currency and cryptocurrency investments.
People who responded were connected with representatives who spoke their native language and initially persuaded them to deposit relatively small amounts of money, prosecutors said. They were then shown fictitious profits on trading platforms controlled by the network and encouraged to invest increasingly large sums.
When investors attempted to withdraw their money, they were allegedly told their accounts had been “blocked” and that additional payments, described as taxes or fees to remove the restriction, were required before their funds could be released.
In reality, Turkish authorities allege, the money was never invested and was instead transferred to bank accounts and cryptocurrency wallets controlled by the network outside Turkey. Prosecutors also allege that those running the operation explicitly instructed employees not to defraud Israeli or American citizens.
Among the countries whose citizens were described as major targets were the United Arab Emirates, Britain, Canada, Australia, Ireland, Russia, Singapore, Malaysia, China, Switzerland, Belgium, Sweden and South Korea.
According to findings by MIT cited by Turkish prosecutors, Israeli figures behind the operation began moving their activities to Turkey and other countries after Israel outlawed the binary-options industry in 2017.
Turkish authorities said investigators raided 286 addresses in Istanbul and the southwestern province of Muğla as part of the operation.
Real estate, vehicles, bank accounts and cryptocurrency assets suspected of being linked to the proceeds of crime were seized or frozen. The Interior Ministry said assets worth approximately 1.5 billion Turkish liras, about $31 million, were targeted, including 80 vehicles and 12 properties.
Authorities have not released a comprehensive official breakdown of the suspects’ identities. Turkish reports, however, said 156 of those detained were Turkish citizens and 45 were foreign nationals.
The foreign detainees reportedly include nine Israelis and 11 Pakistanis; two citizens each from Azerbaijan, Syria, Jordan, Ukraine, Thailand, Indonesia and Morocco; and one each from Kazakhstan, the Philippines, Iran, China, Lebanon, the Palestinian territories, Mexico, Egypt, Mozambique, Argentina and Bangladesh.
The nationality figures are based on Turkish reporting and have not been independently confirmed. Turkish authorities have also not publicly identified the Israeli-linked figures they allege controlled the companies or clarified whether those individuals are among the detainees.
Both Gürlek’s initial announcement and subsequent statements by Turkish prosecutors focused on what investigators described as the network’s ownership and ultimate beneficiary structure, saying figures with links to Israel played a dominant role in the companies behind the alleged scheme.

US allies facing five-year delay in missile deliveries – Bloomberg
The US has warned its allies that deliveries of key missile systems are likely to be delayed by several years due to depleted weapons stocks amid the Iran war, Bloomberg reported on Friday, citing sources. The shortage is also complicating EU efforts to support Kiev with desperately needed air defense ammunition, the article says.
In this vein, Germany asked Washington to accelerate deliveries of Tomahawk cruise missiles and ground-based Typhon launchers, but Raytheon is unlikely to fulfill the order within five years because of stock deficits, according to the outlet. Some Eastern European countries have also experienced delays since shortly after the US-Israeli war on Iran began, Bloomberg sources have claimed.
While US President Donald Trump has rejected claims that the Iran war has left the US short of ammunition, the Pentagon has publicly acknowledged the strain. Earlier this week, the Defense Department inspector general reported that heavy weapons expenditure in the Iran campaign “has resulted in strategic inventory shortfalls and revealed industrial base bottlenecks for munitions resupply.”
A separate Congressional Budget Office assessment said that the US had consumed between one-half and two-thirds of its inventory of certain missile-defense interceptors since June 2025, adding that rebuilding those stocks could take at least five years even if production increases.
The apparent squeeze has been a particularly pressing problem for Ukraine, which needs sophisticated foreign interceptors to shoot down Russian missiles targeting its defense-related facilities. The Washington Post reported in May that Kiev was “almost completely out” of PAC-3 interceptors used by Patriot batteries, while US allies in Europe grew increasingly concerned that depleted American stocks could disrupt the PURL program under which they pay Washington to supply weapons to Ukraine.
Vladimir Zelensky admitted last month that Kiev’s backers had supplied only about one-third as many air-defense missiles in 2026 as during the same period in 2025. At the same time, Ukrainian forces on several occasions acknowledged failing to intercept a single Russian missile during overnight strikes.
To address the issue, European leaders are expected to press Trump for more Patriots for Ukraine during UN meetings next week, Bloomberg said. EU officials are also reportedly seeking US licenses that would allow European countries to manufacture Patriot missiles themselves.
Moscow has consistently argued that Western military aid only prolongs the Ukraine conflict without changing its outcome. Earlier this month, Kremlin foreign policy aide Yury Ushakov suggested that the US could help end the conflict sooner by “first and foremost stopping any assistance to Kiev.”

A deadly crash and the perilous history of LA’s news helicopters: ‘The eye in the sky’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
14:00:48 UTC
23:00:48 KST

The whir of news helicopters flying overhead has long been a familiar soundtrack to life in Los Angeles – and the footage they gather of high-speed chases, wildfires and celebrity sightings a fixture of local television.
For nearly 70 years, Angelenos have gotten their news from “the eye in the sky” – from scenes of OJ Simpson’s fleeing white Bronco, the 1992 LA riots and even Madonna’s wedding to Sean Penn.
On Tuesday, one of those news helicopters crashed live on air while covering the collision of an SUV and a city bus, killing journalist Eliana Moreno, pilot George Marciniw and one person on the ground.
The incident has prompted an outpouring of support for the families, and reflection on the sometimes dangerous and uniquely Californian history of helicopter journalism.
The world’s first “Telecopter” debuted in Los Angeles in 1958, after John Silva, chief engineer for KTLA-TV, retrofitted a helicopter into a flying news studio with ultra-light camera equipment that could transmit footage live from the air. An electronics engineer who’d worked as a radar operator during the second world war, Silva was uniquely suited to the task.
Although KTLA had been the first commercially licensed television station in the city, a growing number of competitors in the 1950s made attracting viewers a growing concern.
In a 2002 interview for the Archive of American Television, Silva recalled his inspiration: “If we could build a news mobile unit in a helicopter we could get over it all, get there first, avoid the traffic and get to all the stories before anybody in the competition.”
Over the next decade, the Telecopter would capture scenes from the Bel Air fire, the Baldwin Hills Dam disaster and the Watts riots.
In the 1980s, the married couple Zoey Tur and Marika Gerrard of the Los Angeles News Service would take up the torch of helicopter reporting – capturing footage of the attack on Reginald Denny during the LA riots and OJ Simpson’s white Bronco chase.
“The city was undergoing a truly tumultuous time,” Matt Yoka, the producer of the documentary Whirlybird told KCRW in a 2021 interview. “I think in one sense, the work that Zoey and Marika were doing was simply trying to bring that into the homes of the people of Los Angeles watching the nightly news.”
Spending their days in the sky, Tur and Gerrard were uniquely positioned to capture breaking news. In a 2024 interview with NBC News, Gerrard recalled how she and Tur were flying over the El Toro ‘Y’ interchange when they heard on the scanner that Simpson’s Bronco had been spotted nearby: “So I slid the door of the helicopter open and then pointed the camera down, and lo and behold there was the white Bronco.”
That practicality has made helicopters a crucial tool for news reporters in the vast cities of the US West.
“A news helicopter is more than a flying camera,” Tammy Rose, a helicopter reporter for ABC-13 in Houston, told the Associated Press. “As a reporter aboard the aircraft, I could see the larger scene, communicate with the newsroom, gather information and report live while events were unfolding.”
Yet, since their earliest use, news helicopters have faced real hazards – from mechanical failures to drone and bird strikes.
In 1977, a KNBC helicopter ran out of fuel and crashed after covering a Santa Barbara wildfire, killing cameraman George Spears and pilot Francis Gary Powers, the U-2 pilot who’d survived being shot down during a spy mission in the Soviet Union.
Since 2000, there have been at least eight fatal crashes involving news helicopters in the United States, killing 16 people.
Those crashes led to some reforms, like all Phoenix news stations agreeing to share one helicopter after a 2007 crash – but some former helicopter journalists worry newsrooms turn to the helicopter too quickly.
“Viewers need information about mass riots, natural disasters and building explosions, especially when news crews on the ground can’t reach the sites. But do mundane street closures and beauty shots really serve the public?” former helicopter reporter Thanh Tan wrote in an op-ed for the Seattle Times after a local helicopter crashed in 2014. “Newsrooms should not send crews into the skies just because they can or to vie for viewership.”
After shaky and emotional footage direct from the helicopter appeared to show the crash, NBC Los Angeles confirmed the deaths of journalist Moreno, pilot Marciniw and pedestrian Edy Fernando Gutiérrez Mejía.
“We are coming on the air with heavy hearts tonight because we lost valued friends and colleagues,” NBC Los Angeles anchor Colleen Williams said on air Tuesday. “We are going to take a couple of minutes to think about that, to process, and to regroup.”
Working for Angel City Air, Moreno and Marciniw had provided aerial coverage for NBC4 and Telemundo 52 for years.
Moreno, nicknamed “Eli in the Heli”, had begun working as a helicopter journalist in 2010, after she graduated from Chapman University. A bilingual reporter in her 30s, Moreno was engaged to be married and had recently completed a marathon.
Her colleague, Jonathan Gonzalez, a weekend news anchor and reporter for NBC Los Angeles, told NBC, “she was damn good at what she did.”
In a statement, Moreno’s family said she’d dreamed of being a news reporter since she was 11 years old and that much of her journey into journalism “was made possible by all of you who welcomed her into your homes and onto your screens”.
“We are infinitely proud of her and feel incredibly blessed to have had the privilege of loving her,” they wrote.
Her longtime colleague, pilot Marciniw, was eyeing retirement after more than 30 years as a helicopter pilot when the crash happened, fellow pilot Esteban Jimenez said. “I knew him since the ’90s. He was my instructor at one time; he was my eyes and ears here in LA,” Jimenez said.
Mejía, known by his nickname “Pichi”, was visiting Los Angeles and had arrived in the city only two days prior. According to a cousin, he’d planned to pick up a car and take it home to sell in Cuilapa, a town in south-eastern Guatemala. His family is now working to repatriate his body.
Just weeks before the crash, in her final Instagram post, Moreno had shared her enthusiasm for helicopter reporting. Captioning a photograph from Whiteman airport, Moreno wrote about covering the summer’s wildfires and how aerial footage allowed her to show the path of a growing fire.
“It just goes to show the power that we have from being the eye in the sky,” she said.

New research links specific military branches and officer ranks to elevated ALS risk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
14:00:46 UTC
23:00:46 KST

New research provides evidence that the risk of developing amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or ALS, varies depending on a veteran’s military branch and rank. The findings suggest that those who served in the Air Force, Navy, and Coast Guard, as well as military officers, tend to experience higher rates of the disease compared to Army veterans and enlisted personnel. The research was published in Neurology.
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis is a fatal neurodegenerative condition that slowly destroys motor neurons, the nerve cells in the brain and spinal cord that control voluntary muscle movement. As these cells break down, people gradually lose their ability to walk, speak, eat, and eventually breathe. While genetic factors play a role in who develops ALS, researchers estimate that environmental factors account for a substantial portion of the risk.
Military service is one of the most consistently identified risk factors for the disease. For instance, a 2026 study using the national ALS registry indicated that military veterans not only have a higher risk of developing the disease but also tend to experience a shorter survival time after diagnosis compared to civilians. Despite this established link, scientists still do not know exactly what aspects of military life increase this risk.
The United States military is composed of different branches, each with distinct environments, missions, and occupational hazards. By looking at how ALS rates differ across these branches and ranks, scientists can begin to pinpoint the specific exposures, such as chemical solvents, intense physical exertion, or psychological stress, that might be driving the increased risk. The research was conducted by Andrea L. Roberts, Marc Weisskopf, and their colleagues at the Harvard TH Chan School of Public Health, who aimed to investigate these differences using an exceptionally large dataset of veteran health records.
“We have known for some 20 years that military veterans are at increased risk for ALS compared to non-veterans, but we still don’t understand why,” Weisskopf, a professor of environmental epidemiology and physiology, told PsyPost. “This work was a first step in trying to better understand that by seeing if there are differences in risk between different types of veterans. This kind of thing can help us start to narrow down to what specific things about military service might be increasing ALS risk.”
The researchers analyzed electronic health records from the Veterans Health Administration, focusing on veterans who received care between January 2000 and October 2024. To ensure they were looking at new cases of ALS, they only included veterans who had at least two years of medical history with the hospital system before any ALS diagnosis. The final sample was massive, including over 9.1 million men and nearly 785,000 women. Within this group, the researchers identified 13,935 men and 484 women who developed ALS.
The team categorized the veterans by their branch of service (Army, Navy, Air Force, Marine Corps, Coast Guard, or multiple branches), their rank (enlisted or officer), and the length of their military careers. The researchers then used statistical models to compare the rates of new ALS cases across these groups, adjusting for factors like age, racial identity, and Hispanic ethnicity. Men and women were analyzed separately because military jobs and the resulting environmental exposures often differ by sex.
The results indicated distinct patterns depending on the branch of service. Among men, Army veterans were used as the baseline comparison group. Compared to the Army, men who served in the Air Force had a 29% higher rate of developing ALS. Navy veterans showed a 15% higher rate, and Coast Guard veterans had a 26% higher rate. On the other hand, men who served in the Marine Corps had a 22% lower rate of ALS compared to Army veterans.
“The lower rate among the Marines was not so much a surprise in that it had been seen in many studies before, but those all had few Marines,” Weisskopf explained. “So seeing it in this much larger population really confirmed that finding and left that as a bit of a puzzle as to why they seem to be at lower risk.”
When looking at rank, the researchers found that officers experienced higher rates of ALS than enlisted personnel. Male officers had a 64% higher rate of ALS than male enlisted personnel. For women, a similar pattern emerged, with female officers showing a 72% higher rate of ALS than their enlisted counterparts. Differences between branches were most pronounced among younger veterans, those ages 17 to 61, and tended to shrink in the oldest age groups.
“The higher rate among officers was a bit of a surprise,” Weisskopf noted. “Because there are differences in ALS by branch and rank, it suggests that there is likely something specific to military experience. Given the higher risk among those in the Air Force, Navy, and Coast Guard, and officers we are considering how to probe those groups more specifically now.”
Despite these relative increases across certain branches and ranks, the researchers emphasized that the absolute risk to any individual remains low. “It’s important to realize that ALS is still relatively rare. So any single person’s overall risk is small, even if elevated because of military service,” Weisskopf said. “Nonetheless, it is hugely impactful for those who get it, so we want to figure out why some people get it and some don’t so we can both try and prevent occurrences and also better understanding how it develops can give us insight into possible therapeutic avenues.”
Surprisingly, the study found that a longer length of military service was associated with lower rates of ALS. This runs contrary to the idea that more time in the military means more exposure to risk factors. The authors suggest a few possible explanations for this pattern. Jobs with high exposure to risk factors might simply be associated with shorter service commitments.
Alternatively, veterans who serve longer might be more likely to seek treatment at private civilian clinics rather than veteran hospitals after retirement, meaning their ALS diagnoses would not appear in this dataset. The higher rates among Air Force, Navy, and Coast Guard veterans suggest that specific occupational hazards in those branches, such as exposure to jet fuel, aircraft exhaust, or radiation, might play a role in developing the disease. The higher risk for officers is also a point of interest, as enlisted personnel generally face more physical strain and chemical exposure.
Officers often experience different stressors and tend to have higher levels of education. Some previous studies have indicated that people with higher education are more likely to be diagnosed with ALS, which might partly explain the difference. If the risk is tied to unique features of an officer’s environment, identifying those factors could help protect future service members.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. Veterans generally qualify for veteran healthcare based on service-related disabilities or specific environmental exposures. If the same exposures that increase the risk of ALS also make someone more likely to use this healthcare system, this could skew the results. To limit this issue, the researchers required all participants to have been in the health system for years before their diagnosis.
Weisskopf also highlighted a specific caveat regarding the findings for the Marine Corps. “Maybe that lower rate among Marines may not necessarily mean they are truly at lower risk,” he pointed out. “There are epidemiological reasons why we might see that if in fact they are at higher risk but that higher risk happens sooner after their military service. This is just speculation at the moment, but we are trying to see if we can address that question.”
The study also faced missing data, with rank information unavailable for over 900,000 male veterans. Because ALS is a rare disease and women make up a smaller percentage of the veteran population, the small number of cases among women made it difficult for the researchers to draw firm conclusions about branch differences for female veterans, as many comparisons did not reach statistical significance. The researchers also lacked genetic data, though they noted it is unlikely that genetic differences alone could explain the specific patterns seen across branches and ranks.
Moving forward, the research team hopes to identify the exact occupational hazards involved. “We are trying to get more granular on the military experience than just branch and rank,” Weisskopf said. “It has turned out, though, to be much harder than we thought to link military service data (DOD) with post service health data (VA).”
The study, “Association of Military Branch and Rank With Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis Incidence Among United States Veterans,” was authored by Andrea L. Roberts, Alexandre D. Vilela Braga, Ian W. Tang, Ran S. Rotem, Lauren R. Moo, Donald R. Miller, Steven D. Shirk, and Marc G. Weisskopf.

UK reviews NATO flying schools for flight training
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
15:00:34 BST
23:00:34 KST

Britain is regularly examining NATO and international military flying training schemes as it looks at the quality, cost and output of training new fast-jet pilots, according to a parliamentary answer.
The work was set out in response to a written question from Labour MP Luke Akehurst, who asked what analysis had been carried out of training systems operated by NATO allies to identify opportunities to improve value for money and pilot output within the UK Military Flying Training System.
Armed Forces Minister Louise Sandher-Jones said the UK regularly assesses opportunities through three multinational training arrangements.
She said: “The UK undertakes regular analysis of NATO flying training system opportunities via participation in the NATO Flying Training Europe High Visibility Project, the Euro-NATO Joint Jet Pilot Training system and the International Flying Training School.”
NATO Flying Training Europe is intended to increase cooperation between allied countries over military aircrew training, while the Euro-NATO Joint Jet Pilot Training system provides multinational fast-jet pilot training. The International Flying Training School is another route through which the UK can examine training approaches used alongside international partners.
Sandher-Jones said the results from those arrangements are assessed against several measures before being considered against the requirements of the UK combat-air force.
She said: “Output is reviewed for quality, safety and value for money to ensure the Combat Air requirement is met for new Fast Jet Pilots.”
The answer indicates that the UK is not assessing its flying training system solely against domestic arrangements, but is using participation in multinational programmes to compare the way new fast-jet pilots are trained and the results those systems produce.

Drones spotted near British military bases almost daily — media
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
13:57:00 UTC
22:57:00 KST

Drones spotted near British military bases almost daily — media
The Independent stated this, according to Ukrinform.
According to the publication, around 340 drone-related incidents were recorded at or near UK Ministry of Defence sites over the course of a year. In 2025, there were 250 such incidents — twice as many as the previous year, when 126 incidents were recorded.
The UK Ministry of Defence did not provide details about whom it suspects of being behind the incidents. However, experts say hostile actors operating on behalf of Moscow or Tehran could be responsible.
Tobias Ellwood, a former Conservative defence minister and former military officer, said the sharp increase in recorded drone incidents suggests that the British armed forces are being regarded "as a target." He added that the government is "asleep" to such threats.
"At the moment these are just rogue drones, and they're passive, but it's not a huge step to then add a kinetic dimension to them to make them introduce lethality. All this points to the fact that we are not taking the rise in threat levels that our European cousins are addressing seriously at all," he said.
Ellwood said Russia and Iran are "100 percent" responsible for many of these incidents.
"They are absolutely active in Britain in plotting, mapping, and then recruiting useful idiots to prosecute this targeting. It could be criminal gangs as well, but they would then be supported by Russia. Russia is by far the obvious culprit here... It's not China's style. They tend to do things in a different way," he said.
At the same time, the UK Ministry of Defence said the increase in recorded incidents reflects improvements in reporting systems, better drone-detection technology, and greater awareness among military personnel.
Minister for the Armed Forces Louise Sanderson-Jones told The Independent that the government is extremely serious about the threat posed by hostile drones to defence sites. She said the authorities are investing in counter-drone systems and giving military personnel new powers to disable drones that threaten defence facilities.
"In February, we established new restricted airspace areas over 44 critical defence sites in the UK. This autumn, we will introduce restricted airspace areas over a further 160 sites," she said. "By the end of the year, the Armed Forces Bill will become law, giving our personnel the power to take out drones – whether in the air, on the ground, or in the water – posing a threat to any defence site without the need for assistance from the police."
She also said that since taking office, the government has quadrupled spending on counter-drone capabilities. Under the Defence Investment Plan, GBP 750 million has been allocated to counter-drone systems and to protecting the British armed forces both within the UK and while deployed overseas.
As Ukrinform reported, the First Sea Lord and Chief of the Royal Navy, Sir Gwyn Jenkins, said that Russia is "testing Britain's vulnerabilities" and could attempt to damage the country's transatlantic cables on the first day of a conflict.

Pro-Palestinian French MEP accuses interior minister of fueling drug smear
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
13:56:14 UTC
22:56:14 KST

Pro-Palestinian French MEP accuses interior minister of fueling drug smear
French MEP Rima Hassan has filed a formal complaint against Interior Minister Laurent Nunez, accusing him of helping fuel false drug allegations against her.
The prominent pro-Palestinian lawmaker was detained in April as part of an investigation into alleged “apology for terrorism” over a since-deleted social media post. While searching her belongings, police found suspicious substances, prompting a separate drug-possession probe and media reports that synthetic drugs had been discovered on her person. The drug probe was dropped after laboratory tests found no synthetic drugs, but not before the story drew widespread media attention.
Hassan filed her court complaint against Nunez on Friday after a French investigative news magazine called Complement d’enquete alleged that the minister had discussed the suspected drugs incident with reporters before laboratory tests had been completed.
Hassan and her lawyer, Vincent Brengarth, lodged the complaint with a special French court that handles cases involving government ministers. Brengarth accused Nunez of breaching investigative secrecy.
He also said the minister’s alleged role in the leak reinforced Hassan’s defense team’s long-held view that the wider proceedings against Hassan were “politically motivated.” Following the Complement d’enquete report, Hassan’s left-wing La France Insoumise (LFI) party accused Nunez of media “manipulation” and demanded his resignation.
Nunez told a National Assembly hearing on Thursday that he had “not organized any leaks.” He acknowledged discussing Hassan’s case informally with reporters but said they already had the information and had merely approached him for comment. He maintained that he had “urged caution” during the exchange.
Hassan is a prominent advocate of the Palestinian cause both in France and in the European Parliament and has joined humanitarian flotillas seeking to reach Gaza by sea and challenge Israel’s blockade. She has faced more than 20 legal proceedings and numerous police summonses in France, and is due to return to court next month over the social media post that led to her April detention.
The post quoted Kozo Okamoto, a Japanese Red Army member convicted for his role in the deadly 1972 Lod Airport attack carried out on behalf of the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine. In a Friday interview with Complement d’enquete, Hassan insisted that the post was not intended as an “apology for terrorism,” but to discuss Palestinian resistance in its historical context, including the revolutionary left’s past support for the Palestinian armed struggle.
Hassan and LFI previously characterized the legal scrutiny surrounding her as “politico-judicial harassment.” Five UN special rapporteurs have raised concerns with the French government over aspects of Hassan’s treatment, including her detention and alleged leaks to the media.
In her interview, Hassan denounced what she called the authorities’ “political and judicial obsession” with her and accused Nunez of using his position “to directly attack a political opponent.” She claimed the minister had “knowingly” disclosed the information while “fully aware of the political and media fallout.” Hassan also said more than 500 articles had been published about her case since April, particularly the illegal-drug claim, adding that “the damage is enormous.”

Fear and anger in South Africa as bodies of nine women found: What we know
Police examining ‘all possibilities’ as women in Ekurhuleni, Johannesburg, fear murders could be linked.
The bodies of nine women have been found in South Africa’s Ekurhuleni municipality over the past two months, prompting police to investigate potential connections between the crimes.
The apparent murders, which bear similarities, have shaken the country, long plagued by high rates of crime and femicide and sparked fears that one or more offenders could strike again.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Haitian gangs release 13 captives after mass kidnapping in Kenscoff
- list 2 of 3Taliban release two detained UN staff members in Afghanistan
- list 3 of 3South Africa’s chrome riches fuel a deadly underground economy
President Cyril Ramaphosa, who urged men to play a greater part in preventing violence against women and girls, has ordered the police to leave “no stone unturned” in their pursuit of justice.
The rate at which women are killed in South Africa is five times higher than the global average, according to figures from UN Women.
Here’s what we know so far:
When was the latest killing?
South African police made their latest discovery on Thursday, September 17 , when they found the body of a woman in Dawn Park on the outskirts of Johannesburg in Ekurhuleni municipality.
Local police said the unidentified, partially clothed woman, believed to be around 30, had been stabbed and dumped before being discovered.
Police said she may have been killed at another location before her body was moved to the park.
She is the ninth known woman to be killed in similar circumstances since July 17 .
Where were the other bodies found?
All the murdered women were found in Ekurhuleni municipality in the greater Johannesburg area.
The first five bodies were found in the Kempton Park area. The others were found in separate locations 25-35km away.
Dawn Park, where the latest body was found, is about 30km south of Kempton Park.
Do we know who the victims are?
Of the nine women whose bodies have been discovered, only four have been identified, according to local media.
The battered and burned body of Dineo Motapane, a 38-year-old mother of two, was discovered this week in a residential area of Ekurhuleni.
The body of 28-year-old Gracious Nkomo, also partially clothed, was found on September 10, having been dumped on the R21 highway in Kempton Park.
Last week, 38-year-old Elizabeth Moselakgomo was also found dead in Kempton Park. Local media reported that her young daughter alerted the police when she failed to return from a run.
Itumeleng Kekana, 32, was a shopkeeper. Her bruised and partially clothed body was found dumped on a bridge in July, 17 days after she was last seen by family members.
Five of the women have not yet been identified.
Are the killings related?
Police say they have not established whether the crimes are connected or if they were committed by one or more perpetrators.
However, police are probing potential links after noting similarities in the ages of the victims and the conditions in which they were found.
All are believed to have been in their 20s or 30s and some were found either naked or partially clothed, according to police. Some of the bodies also had similar bruising.
As local women voice fears of a serial killer, Fred Kekana, police commissioner of the Gauteng province where Ekurhuleni is , cautioned against hastily coming to conclusions.
“Investigators are considering all possibilities, including the possibility of multiple suspects or separate perpetrators,” said Kekana. “Police are comparing the evidence, timelines, locations, victim profiles and circumstances of each case before reaching conclusions.”
Are there any suspects?
At least one suspect has been detained by police.
Deputy police commissioner Tebello Mosikili said the suspect appeared in court on Wednesday and would remain in custody. Police received information suggesting the suspect was not a South African national and were working to verify that, Mosikili said.
Acting national police commissioner Puleng Dimpane also said police were looking into a person of interest, but it was unclear whether she was referring to the same suspect.
Gauteng premier Panyaza Lesufi said whoever is responsible had effectively “declared war against the state” and expressed confidence that police would solve the case.
“We’ll get them,” he told South African media. “And I have trust in the law enforcement agencies.”
What else have police said?
Police have urged the public to report any information they believe could assist the investigation and offered a reward of 400,000 rand ($25,000) for information leading to an arrest.
Police have also advised women in the area to be on heightened alert and to avoid walking or running alone near Kempton Park, where some of the bodies were found.
The National Shelter Movement of South Africa (NSMSA), which funds shelters for women and children affected by gender-based violence, said women already take extensive precautions for their safety and that authorities should not put the onus on women to prevent violence.
“Safety messaging should not imply that women can prevent violence simply by making different choices,” the organisation told Al Jazeera. “The responsibility for violence lies with perpetrators, while the responsibility for protection lies with society and the state.”
“We are not dealing with an issue of women who are not vigilant,” added Philisiwe Gabela, an official with the country’s Commission for Gender Equality.
President Ramaphosa last month called on men in South Africa to take a stand against gender-based violence and femicide by signing a virtual pledge.
He has argued that perpetrators of sexual assault and domestic violence are predominantly male, so men must hold each other accountable, challenge harmful patriarchal norms and report abuse of women to the police.
How has the public reacted?
The killings have triggered widespread fear and anger about gender-based violence, which South Africa has one of the world’s highest rates of.
“I am feeling a lot of fear and paranoia, especially for us with daughters,” Ekurhuleni area resident Nomgqibelo Tshabalala told Reuters.
Between 2020 and 2021, an average of 5.5 out of 100,000 women in South Africa were killed by intimate partners, according to the South African Medical Research Council.
South African police recorded 9,782 reported rapes between January and March this year and 12,590 sexual offences. That amounts to roughly 108 reported rapes every day. It is widely known that many women do not report rape because of the fear of stigmatisation or reprisals.
Princess Eurika Mogane, a commissioner at South Africa’s Commission for Gender Equality, told Al Jazeera the latest killings reflect the broader crisis facing South African women. “This is a war. It feels like individuals are being hunted,” she said.
The UN South Africa said the killings are not “isolated tragedies”.
“They reflect the persistent and deadly violence faced by women and girls in South Africa.”

Drone sightings briefly shut Luxembourg airport
September 19, 2026
Luxembourg authorities are investigating drone sightings that forced the country's main airport to temporarily suspend flights overnight, Prime Minister Luc Frieden said on Saturday.
Frieden said Luxembourg was working with its NATO allies following the incident, which comes amid heightened European concern over suspected hybrid attacks linked to Russia.
What happened at Luxembourg airport?
National carrier Luxair said more than 1,800 passengers were affected, with 17 incoming flights diverted to airports including Brussels, Paris and Frankfurt.
Flights resumed on Saturday, although Luxair warned that delays and knock-on disruption could continue.
The airport said the closure was a precautionary measure to protect passengers, airline crews, airport employees and aircraft.
Frieden stressed that it was too early to determine who was responsible.
"We are analyzing the situation," Frieden told a televised press conference after an emergency meeting with the country's defense and interior ministers.
Have other drones been spotted?
Frieden said "potentially larger drones" had also been observed in Luxembourg's airspace in recent days.
"This is new for Luxembourg, but it is not completely new for our neighboring countries," he said.
Unauthorized drones have previously been detected near sensitive sites elsewhere in Europe, including Belgium, Germany and Denmark.
"We will ensure, together with our partners, that we can guarantee the security of our populations," Frieden said.
European governments have repeatedly warned of Russian-linked hybrid activities since Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Such incidents have included suspected sabotage, cyberattacks and unauthorized drone flights.
There is currently no evidence establishing who was responsible for the Luxembourg sightings.

AAP questions names missing from voter list

NEW YORK – US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and China’s Vice-Premier He Lifeng will lead talks on trade and other pressure points on Sept 20 in New York ahead of next week’s summit between the leaders of the world’s two biggest economies.
The negotiators will lay the groundwork for a high-profile meeting between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping on Sept 24 in Washington.
Bessent and He last met face-to-face near Seoul four months ago, just days before Trump visited Beijing in May.
Energy disruptions from the Iran war, the artificial intelligence boom, and trade and investment are likely to top the agenda, as both sides work to maintain stability in a tariff truce that expires in November.
Adding urgency for US officials to extend the deal are Nov 3 midterm elections where inflation is a persistent voter concern.
The US is “at a stage with China where efforts to try and transform this relationship and strengthen it are no longer top of list”, said Wendy Cutler, senior vice-president at the Asia Society Policy Institute.
The objective is more about “trying to keep things stable, keep things from escalating and try to, in practical terms, keep the trade truce that was reached in Busan in place”, she said.
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer will also attend talks, according to a statement from his office.
“The Trump Administration will continue to pursue balanced trade with China by monitoring the implementation of recent commitments, optimising trade in non-sensitive goods, and improving market access for American farmers, manufacturers, and workers,” he said in the statement late on Sept 18.
An announcement of new US tariffs over allegations of trading partners’ excess manufacturing capacity has been delayed until after the meeting, according to people familiar with the matter.
“Both sides want to avoid another flare-up, and relative stability in the relationship is likely to continue,” Nicole Gorton-Caratelli, Adam Farrar and Maeva Cousin of Bloomberg Economics wrote in a research note this week. “But as the US rebuilds its tariff wall, the risk of renewed escalation remains.”
The US and China have been working to reduce levies on American energy and agricultural products, Bloomberg reported earlier, part of a broader initiative to ease barriers on US$30 billion (S$38 billion) worth of products from each side under the Board of Trade mechanism launched earlier in 2026.

Chinese exports to the US have rebounded in 2026, showing the limits of Trump’s tariffs but also reflecting a surge in demand for AI-related electronics produced by China.
The New York talks are taking place ahead of the United Nations General Assembly meeting held in the city later next week.
Bessent and He have held a series of discussions over the past 18 months, mostly in a third country to portray a sense of neutrality. Whether the meeting in New York signals greater trust or merely convenience given the UN meeting, it also suggests the next round will be in China for the sake of reciprocity.
Bloomberg reported earlier this week that Chinese officials were considering BYD for a possible business delegation joining Xi at the summit, a potentially provocative move given Trump’s tariffs on Chinese-made electric vehicles.
Trump has suggested he might be willing to allow a Chinese car company to build in the US, if it did so with American workers.
One Chinese official familiar with planning for the meeting said China’s top issue would be Taiwan, particularly a planned US weapons sale.
Easier discussions will be held around tariffs and agricultural products like soya beans, while AI, cars, technology and e-commerce will feature on the agenda, said the official, who asked for anonymity to discuss private conversations.
The official added that China would offer more permits for rare earths as a bargaining chip, without disclosing details on what Beijing would seek in return.
Maintaining flows of Chinese rare-earth magnets was a priority for Trump when he agreed to a truce in 2025. Since then, China’s monthly exports of the critical industrial components have been running substantially below the levels that prevailed before Beijing imposed export controls in April 2025.
In recent weeks, AI has rapidly emerged as a new fault line between the US and China.
‘Fear-mongering’
Washington has restricted China’s access to advanced chips and accused Chinese firms of developing their own domestic models by “distilling” capabilities from American tech.
Beijing has pushed back on calls from US tech leaders to pace AI development in the interest of safety, with the country’s Foreign Ministry dismissing such moves as “fear-mongering” and state media denouncing them as “self-serving”.
“As the No. 1 and No. 2 superpowers in AI by a lot, it behooves all of us to put up guardrails, to have close communication,” Bessent told reporters earlier in September.
In a statement to Axios this week, he said “we are open to discussions on avoiding shared risks and avoiding bifurcation of our two systems”.
The US moves, Beijing says, are designed to contain its rise, and China refuses to let Washington take the lead on writing the rules for AI.
A more immediate threat to both economies is the energy shock, and the White House has stepped up pressure on Iran and its trading partners. China provides Tehran with an economic lifeline as the biggest buyer of Iranian oil.

====================================================================================================

'I am pro-Abraham': Meet the unlikely allies risking everything for peace with Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
13:49:33 UTC
22:49:33 KST

In much of the West, asking someone about the weather is about as inconsequential as small talk gets. In parts of the Middle East, however, even a conversation about the weather with someone across the border can cross a legal line. In countries where contact with Israelis is criminalized or restricted, a seemingly harmless exchange can carry the risk of imprisonment or execution.
The Abrahamic Movement was founded on the idea that these communication barriers can be challenged. Bringing together Israelis and people from across the Muslim world, the movement seeks to build relationships across religious and national divides, drawing on their shared Abrahamic heritage.
With artificial intelligence and international travel more accessible than ever, forms of diplomacy once largely reserved for governments and the wealthy are increasingly within reach of ordinary people, which is perhaps why the movement has grown so rapidly in recent years.
The Jerusalem Post spoke with Tom Wegner, CEO of the Abrahamic Movement initiative and author of The Abrahamic Revolution, as well as several members of the group, some of whom risked their freedom and potentially their lives by speaking with an Israeli journalist about their desire for peace.
Wegner originally started the group in 2019, though it did not gain momentum until after October 7, 2023, when 1,200 people were killed by Islamists.
Wegner realized that something had to change and reached out to the diverse contacts he had built over years of working in the IDF’s District Coordination and Liaison unit in Jericho, where he facilitated coordination between Israel and the Palestinian Authority’s police; as a spokesperson for former prime minister Ehud Barak; and as a spokesperson for the Peres Center for Peace.
Telling them that “the regional configuration is not working for us,” Wegner explained that the region’s destabilization had been apparent long before Hamas’s invasion. The massacre of the Yazidis, the civil wars in Yemen and Iraq, and the conflicts that followed were all evidence that something was not working compared to the seemingly functional Western world.
Shared Abrahamic identity
Though Europe seems peaceful compared with the often volatile Middle East, Wegner highlighted that the West has not always enjoyed such stability. Before the formation of the European Union, Europe experienced civil uprisings, invasions, and two world wars, resulting in hundreds of millions of deaths.
Wegner attributed much of that shift toward peaceful coexistence to the development of a European collective identity. That identity “wasn’t coerced on the people. It is not about oppressing someone to fit your narrative, but of creating an umbrella identity, which means that the French can continue to eat frogs and the Greeks can continue to break plates. The Protestants can remain Protestants, and the Catholics can remain Catholic, but everyone is part of a bigger story,” he explained.
The Abrahamic Movement seeks to create that same sense of collective identity in the Middle East, based on a shared Abrahamic heritage.
“The world has missed, to some extent, that 100% of the people involved in this conflict – whether a secular Jew, an Orthodox Jew, a very religious Muslim, a liberal Muslim, an ex-Muslim, a Christian Arab, a Druze, or an Alawite – agree on the Abrahamic narrative. Meaning, we all agree that we came from Abraham,” he said.
This shared heritage, he added, means it is important to view the conflicts as fighting among cousins and families rather than through the Western-centric lens of occupiers and colonists.
The idea that conflicts can be solved simply by drawing lines on maps, Wegner said, is too Western, too managerial, and too simplistic to address conflicts rooted in identity. Rather, he argued, the solution lies in creating a broader “in-group,” limiting the conflict that can arise from in-group and out-group social dynamics.
The Muslim Brotherhood’s opposition
Whether it is soccer hooligans in the UK, gangs in the United States, or ethnic groups in the Middle East, the same in-group versus out-group dynamic can contribute to conflict, with people defining themselves in opposition to those they see as belonging to another group, Wegner argued.
The concept is well established in social psychology, with research showing that in-group identification can contribute to out-group prejudice, stereotyping, and discrimination, creating conditions that can deepen hostility between groups.
Beyond creating a shared in-group identity, it is also imperative to create an identity that is oppositional to the Muslim Brotherhood and its Shia alternatives, like Hezbollah, Wegner insisted.
The Islamist identities are currently all-consuming, he said. The Muslim Brotherhood and Shia groups such as Hezbollah have no mainstream counter-ideology for the average individual living in a Muslim country and are therefore more effective in their recruitment.
The all-encompassing Islamist movements and their various branches provide thought leaders, media, education, healthcare, employment opportunities, social circles, community, and everything an individual could ever need. Wegner explained that all these factors can draw people toward an extreme ideology when no opposing ideology balances it out.
The idea of “Abrahamic Islam,” true to the Quran in its acknowledgment that the Children of Israel will return to the promised land (Surah Al-Isra, 17:104), “enables Muslims to remain loyal to their original religion,” he said, adding that this new ideological approach could be the driving force in finally ending Israel’s wars against extremist groups.
“Losing your honor in this part of the world is worse than losing your life. When it comes to Arab and Muslim society, you’re better off losing your life than losing your honor,” he said, highlighting that Hezbollah, Hamas, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, and every other enemy of Israel face the choice to die in battle as a martyr or sacrifice their honor by surrendering to Israel.
“If we understand that killing all the radicals is not a very good or solid plan, then we should ask ourselves what the way out is. And over here, the Abrahamic Movement represents a way out for many reasons.... It implies that this is common ground, and when you come to common ground, that’s not surrendering,” he said. “That’s an identity that both of us can live with, without losing our honor.”
‘The Quran: A Zionist document’
Wegner believes that Jews “missed the Quran,” overlooking the wisdom it could offer and its potential to help Zionists communicate with people in the region in terms they can understand and accept.
Familiarity with the Islamic holy text, he said, has allowed him to win heated debates with Islamist scholars and bring large numbers of people closer to accepting the humanity of Zionists and their place in the region.
“The Quran is a Zionist document,” he claimed, recounting how heated debates often cool when he can cite Quranic verses in support of his position.
Though many seek to counter Islamists by relying on passages they believe undermine Islamic teachings, including frequently citing the Prophet Muhammad’s marriage to Aisha bint Abi Bakr, such arguments will never be fruitful and are no way to conduct diplomacy, he argued.
Instead, he pointed to the Quran’s numerous references to the Children of Israel, or the Jewish people, as a basis for engaging with Muslims on terms rooted in a text they recognize as authoritative.
In Surah Al-Ma’idah (5:21), Moses tells the Children of Israel to enter the holy land that God prescribed for them. In Surah Al-Isra (17:104), the Quran instructs the Children of Israel to live in the land until the end of days, while Surah Yunus (10:93) states that God settled the Children of Israel in a blessed place and provided them with good provisions.
“If we really want to speak with the Muslim world and create some sort of dialogue, the whole approach of saying ‘Muhammad was a pedophile,’ or all that jazz that basically tries to contradict Islam at face value, is not relevant. It’s not helping anyone,” he insisted. “It’s only creating more animosity and tension.
“We can probably get better results if we speak to our cousins the way cousins speak to each other, focusing on our shared heritage and the things that are common to us.”
Peace in the Middle East is often painted as a pipe dream, and many might call Wegner idealistic for his ambitions. But the Abrahamic Movement has gained tens of thousands of supporters and now has more than 20 branches across the Muslim world – including in countries that criminalize communication with Israelis – thanks solely to the efforts of volunteers and without funding.
Several members readily volunteered to speak with the Post about why they were so invested in peace despite the potential cost. One Pakistani member, in particular, insisted he did not want to speak anonymously, despite concerns about potential risks to his safety.
‘I am not pro-Israel; I am pro-Abraham’
Khurram Ali Raza, chairman of the movement’s Pakistan branch, insisted that the Post use his name despite repeated warnings that doing so could put him in danger.
While Pakistan does not have a specific law criminalizing contact with Israeli citizens, Islamabad does not recognize Israel, and Pakistani passports explicitly state that they are valid for travel everywhere except the Jewish state.
In a country where people are still lynched for accusations of blasphemy, Raza remained confident about his safety, despite acknowledging that his advocacy for normalization with Israel had already cost him a great deal.
Sharing several articles he had written for his website, Faith and Freedom News, about his desire for peace, Raza said he had already been investigated by Pakistani authorities, who initially appeared to suspect that he was working for Israel. He said the unfounded suspicions led to his imprisonment for four months in a jail where he said the conditions were “hell.”
“Somehow, I made them understand that I am doing this for peace, harmony and tolerance among these three religions, not for intelligence agencies or anything else,” he said. “I am not pro-Israel; I am pro-Abraham, and if you are pro-Abraham, the first religion is Judaism.... We are like brothers. We are from one family and one home.”
The conditions of Raza’s four-month detention, spent in a cramped room without a fan or light, have continued to affect him, but they have not deterred him from carrying out his work with the movement as openly as he can.
Despite being free, Raza said, it is impossible to access his website in Pakistan without a VPN, suggesting an unofficial block on his publications to prevent the masses from accessing them.
In his personal life, close relatives have also urged him to keep his distance, fearing that his work could have consequences for the wider family.
The lack of education in Pakistan, Raza argued, has led to many accepting without critical thought what they have been told about Jews and acting with hostility to those seen as part of an out-group.
According to Pakistan’s Education Ministry, the country’s current literacy rate stands at only 62.3%, meaning an estimated 60 million people remain illiterate.
Asked why, given all that he has suffered, he would continue to speak out in favor of a country he has never visited, Raza said that one day he will stand before God and answer for everything he has done in his life, and that he would be proud to answer for his efforts to promote peace and tolerance.
‘Iraq can benefit from establishing peace relations’
In May 2022, the Iraqi parliament passed the “Criminalizing Normalization and Establishment of Relations with the Zionist Entity” law, with 275 of 329 lawmakers voting in favor. The law imposes severe penalties, including life imprisonment or the death penalty, for a range of activities involving normalization or relations with Israel or Israelis.
Under Article 7, promoting Zionist or Masonic ideas, whether through public speeches, conferences, publications, or social media posts, is punishable by death or life imprisonment.
In July 2025, the Karkh Criminal Court in Baghdad sentenced a man to life imprisonment for promoting the “Zionist entity” on social media. According to Iraq’s Supreme Judicial Council, he had posted photos and videos supporting normalization with Israel, while Hebrew-language books and newspapers were seized from his home.
Despite the apparent risks of holding such views, speaking with the Post, and participating in the Abrahamic Movement, the Sunni scholar Abu Musa Al-Iraqi said he believes it is in Iraq’s interest to normalize ties with Israel.
“Iraq can benefit from establishing peace relations to prevent extremism and ideological and cultural terrorism from taking root among religious extremists, as well as to end this unjustified conflict,” Al-Iraqi, who used his alias, told the Post. “We can send messages of peace to future generations of Jews and Muslims. We do not want to pass this hostility on to them, but, rather, establish social and economic relations and communication to develop the land and reject the divisions created by extremists for narrow personal interests.”
Working closely with Iraq’s Sunni and Sufi communities, Al-Iraqi has had opportunities to study Islamic and Abrahamic texts. Through this research, he said, he came to understand that the conflict between Jews and Muslims “is not a genuine one.”
“Islam respects Judaism, but some Quranic texts and their meanings have been distorted and interpreted outside the context in which they were formulated, and misrepresented by those who are ideologically corrupted and do not want there to be a relationship or communication between Judaism and Islam, for purely political purposes,” he explained, adding that he understands Islam to be an extension of Judaism.
Though his research may have provided a clearer understanding of Islam, it was not well received in Iraq. Many newspaper articles Al-Iraqi sent to the Post showed individuals affiliated with the Popular Mobilization Forces, Hizb ut-Tahrir, and other Islamist groups complaining about an “Israeli influence network within Iraqi territory.”
Hizb ut-Tahrir even published a statement in June complaining of the “increasingly active” Abrahamic Movement’s presence in Iraq, saying it is largely viewed “as an extension of normalization with Israel.”
Except for Wegner himself, none of the Abrahamic Movement’s members or leaders interviewed by the Post have had the opportunity to visit Israel.
The movement faces no shortage of obstacles, from laws restricting contact with Israelis to Islamist groups that have openly opposed its activities.
There is no guarantee that personal relationships will translate into political change, or that large numbers of people will embrace the concept of Abrahamic Islam.
Still, movement members continue to risk their freedom, safety, and livelihoods in the hope of ending a conflict that predates the establishment of the Jewish state and, for many, living memory.
