Mike Huckabee on Iran, Hezbollah, Saudi Arabia and Israel’s US relationship - interview
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
13:49:25 UTC
22:49:25 KST

For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee is not a conventional diplomat. A Baptist pastor, former Arkansas governor, presidential candidate, and television host, he came to the post after decades in American public life and an even longer relationship with Israel.
He also came with a style of his own. Huckabee can move from geopolitics to Scripture to a homespun analogy without much warning. He is direct, sometimes blunt, and rarely sounds as though his words have made a preliminary stop at the State Department diplomatic-language desk.
When Huckabee joined me at The Media Line studios, I began with Iran. Despite the damage inflicted on Tehran and its military capabilities, Iran could still move toward nuclear capability, threaten shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, and exert influence in the Red Sea through the Houthis. There are also concerns about what the Houthis might do next against Saudi Arabia.
Huckabee's thoughts on Iran
Where, I asked, does Huckabee think Iran and its regional proxies stand today?
“The good news is, thanks to President Trump, in concert with Israel, Iran is at their weakest point in 47 and a half years,” Huckabee said. “They’re weaker militarily, they’re weaker economically, and they’re growing weaker by the month.”
Whether that weakness eventually produces regime change is another question.
“Will it lead to regime change? We can only hope,” he said.
Huckabee rejected the idea that confronting Iran is chiefly Israel’s problem.
“A lot of people, particularly in America, may think, well, what does that have to do with us? It has everything to do with America, because the ultimate target has always been the United States.”
President Donald Trump said he had decided that Iran could not be allowed to possess nuclear weapons, enrich uranium, or control shipping lanes through the Strait of Hormuz.
“It’s a process, but it is a process that I believe is working.”
What about the Iranian people? I asked where they stood now and whether another popular uprising was possible.
Huckabee said Iranians seeking to challenge their government face a basic problem: They are largely unarmed.
“At some point, I do believe we’re going to see another uprising,” he said, adding that perhaps next time the people could be “better prepared, armed, and be able to truly resist” a government he expects to be weaker still.
Lebanon presents Washington with another problem. With UNIFIL preparing to leave, the question is whether the Lebanese Armed Forces can extend state authority into the south, prevent a security vacuum, and confront Hezbollah at the same time.
Huckabee believes it can, but not overnight.
“Incrementally, they can. I don’t think it’s going to be the flip of a switch,” he said. “They’re going to have to grow into the role of being the only army, the only security force.”
Hezbollah, he noted, remains active and is trying to rebuild after being badly weakened by Israel. As long as Iran can continue financing and arming it, Huckabee said, Hezbollah will remain a threat.
Huckabee says he has considerably less patience with UNIFIL
“UNIFIL is going to go out of business—way overdue for that to happen,” he said. “It’s been a totally ineffective entity.”
“I can’t say that I can point to one specific way in which UNIFIL has been instrumental in making Lebanon freer and better.”
When I pressed him on the timetable months or years? he answered, “It could be years.”
But Huckabee said his experience traveling between Jerusalem and Washington during talks over Lebanon had shown him “extraordinary progress.” One of the most important developments, in his view, was Lebanese recognition that Israel does not want Lebanese territory.
“They don’t want to annex one meter of Lebanese property. They don’t want to be there. They want to go home,” he said.
Israeli reservists, he said, are exhausted and want to return to their families, but Israel will not leave its northern communities exposed to renewed rocket, missile and drone attacks.
Huckabee said he longs for the day when the Lebanese army is strong enough to secure the area itself: “The Israelis can go home, the Lebanese will be at home, and there will be no Hezbollah.”
We also spoke about the new joint defense agreement involving Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan, which pledges to treat an armed attack on one as an attack on all. With three important US partners building their own collective security framework, I asked whether Washington sees that as a welcome development and what it means for the wider regional balance.
“It’s a wait and see,” Huckabee said.
These are sovereign countries entitled to make agreements they believe serve their interests, he said. All three have reasons to be concerned about Iran, while the arrangement could also be intended to protect them from the Houthis or other armed groups.
What he had not encountered was alarm in Washington.
“I never certainly saw or heard any anxiety in Washington that, ‘Oh my gosh, this is a terrible thing.’ I don’t think that anyone saw it that way.”
Would Israel help Saudi Arabia if the kingdom came under attack?
“I don’t know. I mean, that’s the honest answer. I don’t know.”
Huckabee said Israel would welcome a security agreement with Saudi Arabia and would like to see the kingdom join the Abraham Accords. He also pointed to existing military and intelligence contacts.
For what normalization can achieve, he looks to the United Arab Emirates.
“The UAE is the gold standard, the model of how this has all worked,” he said, pointing to gains in tourism, travel, trade and technological cooperation.
“I hope the Saudis will look next door and say, you know, this is working out pretty well for the Emirates. Maybe we ought to go the same path.”
Few issues are more closely associated with Huckabee than the territory Israelis generally call the West Bank and much of the international community calls the West Bank. He has strongly defended Israelis who live there, but he has also condemned recent attacks on Palestinians and described those responsible as terrorists.
Is Israel doing enough to stop terrorists
“Israel is increasingly aware that this has to be dealt with and dealt with in a very strong way,” Huckabee said.
He did not back away from his choice of the word terrorism.
“When you frighten people into changing the way they live because of things that you do to them, you don’t have to murder them, but you do terrorize them into being afraid to come out of their homes, being afraid to go shopping, being afraid to go to a place of worship,” he said. “So it’s unacceptable, whoever does it.”
At the same time, Huckabee stressed that those responsible represent a very small fraction of the Israeli population in the territory. He called them a “tiny, tiny sliver” and said many do not even live there.
“There are 500,000 Israelis living in Judean Samaria, living peacefully,” he said. “They don’t want to burn an olive tree. They don’t want to torch a mosque.”
I asked what more Israel should be doing.
Investigations and arrests need to be followed by real penalties, Huckabee said, particularly for offenses such as burning mosques, stealing livestock or taking over someone’s home.
“They need to be arrested,” he said of repeat offenders. “They need to spend a few nights, a few weeks, maybe a few months in jail.”
Huckabee confronts Tucker Carlson, antisemitism in American politics
Our conversation then moved to a different source of friction over Israel: the changing American political debate.
Huckabee recently encountered Tucker Carlson at Ben-Gurion Airport and challenged several of Carlson’s assertions about Israel. Carlson has since argued that Israel is driving the war with Iran for its own regional interests while US interests are being sacrificed.
I asked Huckabee whether similar arguments about Israel are now converging from opposite ends of the American political spectrum—and how worried he is about the long-term implications for the US-Israel relationship.
“I’m very concerned about it because it’s based on things that are fundamentally not true,” he said. “Tucker Carlson’s allegations about Israel are off the mark.”
Huckabee also rejected accusations of genocide and apartheid and claims that Israel is unsafe or unfair for Christians.
“As a Christian living in Israel, I find that utterly offensive and totally factless,” he said.
He has known Carlson for years and said he does not understand what has changed.
“This is not the same person I once knew and once worked with,” Huckabee said.
With the US midterm elections approaching, I asked whether events in the Middle East would have much effect on American voters.
Probably less than domestic issues, Huckabee said. He then turned to the Democratic Socialists of America and what he sees as the radicalization of part of the American left. He cited liberal commentator Bill Maher as an example of someone who has also criticized that movement.
“The Democrats historically, they’ve been different than the Republicans, but they haven’t been crazy,” Huckabee said.
He was equally unsparing about calls for socialism, saying replacing the American economic system with one that he believes has repeatedly failed is more than a conventional political disagreement.
Another subject has become impossible for anyone in the news business to avoid: artificial intelligence.
Huckabee warns about the dangers of AI
At The Media Line, we spend considerable time sourcing, vetting, and explaining information. That becomes more complicated as AI makes fabricated images, voices, and claims easier to produce and harder to detect. Technology leaders themselves have warned about the potential consequences.
What did Huckabee make of it?
“AI is like fire,” he said. “It can cook your food and warm your house. It can burn your house down and kill you.”
“How do you use it? That’s the question.”
For Huckabee, the danger is not theoretical. He pointed to his own long-running lawsuit against Meta, which he said stems from AI-generated material that damaged him professionally when he was hosting a television program in the United States.
“I saw firsthand what AI can do in creating perceptions, images, the misuse, the abuse of one’s name, image, and likeness,” he said. “And it has to be brought into some level of responsibility.”
Does that mean government regulation?
Huckabee is wary.
“I’m always hesitant to say I’d like to see the government get involved because the government usually messes up whatever they touch,” he said.
One possibility, he suggested, would be for the major AI companies themselves to establish ethical norms, much as other professions have developed standards without having every rule imposed by government.
“There was a sense of self-governing, self-regulation,” Huckabee said. “Maybe that’s the answer.”
Huckabee speaks on upcoming anniversary of Oct. 7
With the anniversary of Oct. 7 approaching, more than 1,000 pastors are expected to come to Israel for events organized by Christian and Jewish groups. Antisemitism, meanwhile, has risen rather than receded.
Can visits like these make a difference?
Huckabee hopes they can remind people of the scale of what happened on Oct. 7.
He translated the attack into American terms, asking his audience to imagine an assault from Tijuana into San Diego that, adjusted for population, left 40,000 Americans dead in one day and another 10,000 taken hostage.
“Ask ourselves as Americans, what would we do? How would we respond?”
He also invoked Sept. 11, 2001, and the lasting changes it brought to American life after the deaths of nearly 3,000 people.
“Twenty-five years later, our whole world changed in the United States because of that,” he said. “Scale that up 10 times plus, and it’s hard to even fathom what the response would be.”
I saved a different kind of question for last.
Huckabee is a Baptist pastor who spent more than a decade in the governor’s office and now serves as America’s ambassador to Israel. He has lived in the worlds of faith, politics, and diplomacy—three places where people can look at the same set of facts and come away insisting on very different versions of reality.
Is truth actually attainable? And how do you know when you have found it?
“Truth is objective. Perceptions are subjective,” Huckabee said.
Three people can stand on a street corner, witness an accident, and each see something different, he said. Their perceptions may differ, but that does not change what actually happened.
“The truth is not what I think. It’s not what I feel. It’s not what I believe. It’s what is.”
That, Huckabee said, is something younger people in particular need to learn in an age when opinion and fact are increasingly difficult to separate.
“What we have to do, especially among younger people, is to force people to move beyond what I think, what I feel, what I believe, and get to what is the absolute concrete fact upon which then I can feel, believe, and think.”
He left it there.
“Without objective truth that from any angle looks the same, we are in real trouble.”

US approves possible F-35 Saudi deal despite Israeli push to link normalization, sale - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
13:49:22 UTC
22:49:22 KST

The US State Department’s announcement on Thursday that it is advancing the sale of 48 F-35 aircraft to Saudi Arabia represents far more than a massive arms deal worth $24.3 billion. For Israel, it highlights a concerning diplomatic shift: one of Washington’s most valuable security leverage tools with Riyadh is now moving forward on its own track, without Saudi Arabia first being required to normalize relations with Israel.
The State Department approved the possible sale of 48 F-35A Lightning II aircraft, alongside 49 Pratt & Whitney F135 engines, communications and encryption systems, electronic warfare capabilities, simulators, training, spare parts and logistical support.
The move does not yet constitute a final contract. The announcement is a stage in the US arms sale process, and a legally required review period in Congress has now begun. In Saudi Arabia’s case, the official review period is 30 days.
The administration is presenting the deal as part of efforts to strengthen Saudi Arabia’s ability to confront current and future threats and deepen its joint operational capabilities with the United States and regional partners. The official announcement explicitly stated that the deal “will not alter the military balance in the region.”
In the United States, Israel’s qualitative military edge is enshrined in law. The statement touches on the core of Israel’s concern: Israel is currently the only country in the Middle East operating the F-35, in its Israeli configuration, the F-35I “Adir.”
US law requires the administration to ensure that arms sales to other countries in the region do not harm Israel’s “Qualitative Military Edge,” meaning its qualitative military advantage. The requirement was codified in legislation in 2008 and requires significant regional arms deals to be examined through the Israeli security lens as well.
The political price Israel sought for the F-35 deal
The Trump administration approved the sale of advanced F-35 aircraft to Saudi Arabia. Israel sought a diplomatic price.
However, Jerusalem’s concern is not only technical or related to air capabilities. In November 2025, Israeli officials said that Israel did not fundamentally oppose Saudi Arabia receiving F-35 aircraft, provided the deal was part of full normalization between Riyadh and Jerusalem.
“We told the Trump administration that supplying F-35s to Saudi Arabia should be contingent on Saudi normalization with Israel,” an Israeli official said at the time.
Another Israeli official warned that providing the aircraft to Riyadh without receiving diplomatic concessions would be a “mistake” and a move that would work against US interests.
That link did not materialize. Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman said during his visit to the White House last year that he was interested in Saudi Arabia joining the Abraham Accords, but conditioned progress on the creation of a “clear path” toward a two-state solution.
The gap between Riyadh and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government on the Palestinian issue has remained. Despite that, the F-35 track continued to advance.
This is the central difference between the deal Israel hoped to see and the deal as it currently appears: Jerusalem wanted the stealth aircraft as part of a broader regional strategic package centered on normalization. Washington, at least at this stage, is not waiting for such an agreement before moving ahead.
China concerns surrounding the Saudi F-35 sale
Jonathan Ruhe, a specialist in US strategy at the Jewish Institute for National Security of America (JINSA), told Walla that in his view, the F-35 deal should not move forward in its current form before two central issues are resolved.
The concern is not merely theoretical. The New York Times reported two days ago that US intelligence officials warned in internal assessments that China could obtain F-35-related technology through espionage in Saudi Arabia or through its security and technology ties with the kingdom.
One report by the Pentagon’s intelligence agency addressed, among other issues, Chinese access to Saudi bases and Saudi use of Chinese communications infrastructure. Reports on Thursday’s deal also noted that expanding security ties between Riyadh and Beijing are among the concerns surrounding the sale.
Ruhe’s second concern directly relates to Israel.
“The entire F-35 program is intended to support US-led collective defense,” he said. “America needs to demonstrate leadership in integrating Saudi Arabia into a new regional security architecture, and Riyadh also needs to show that it is a committed partner before it can receive F-35 aircraft.”
According to Ruhe, Israel’s qualitative military edge must remain part of the equation.
“Israel’s QME is a central factor in this regional integration, and it needs to be reflected in any possible F-35 deal with the kingdom,” he said.
Ruhe added that the United States has significant leverage in the matter.
“The United States has leverage here, because it can offer Saudi Arabia much more than China can,” he said.
Even if the deal is completed, a significant question remains over the exact capabilities that will be transferred to Riyadh.
The aircraft intended for Saudi Arabia are expected to be less advanced in several areas than Israel’s F-35I aircraft, partly as part of the US effort to preserve Israel’s qualitative military edge. Israel also benefits from the ability to integrate unique Israeli systems into its aircraft.
The issue became more complicated after US President Donald Trump publicly said that Saudi Arabia would receive advanced aircraft similar to Israel’s. Secretary of State Marco Rubio reassured Netanyahu and told him that Saudi Arabia would receive a downgraded version and that the United States remained committed to preserving Israel’s qualitative military edge.
Therefore, even after the State Department announcement and assurances regarding reduced capabilities for Saudi Arabia, key details remain undisclosed: which capabilities will be included in the aircraft, what restrictions will be placed on their deployment and access, and what Israel will receive to ensure that its advantage is maintained.
But on the diplomatic level, a significant development has already taken place: the F-35, which Israel wanted to see as part of the price Saudi Arabia would pay for joining the Abraham Accords, is moving toward Riyadh even as normalization itself remains stalled.

Classified F-35 aircraft components disappear after diverted to Hong Kong from Australia - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
13:49:22 UTC
22:49:22 KST

A shipment of sensitive components for the F-35 stealth fighter jets, which was on its way from Australia to the United States for repairs, was unexpectedly diverted to Hong Kong and disappeared.
The incident raised concerns that China may gain access to the highly classified technology of sophisticated US weapons, Politico reported Friday.
According to three sources familiar with the details of the case, the shipment left Australia headed for the United States. However, the flight was diverted en route to Hong Kong. It is unclear who currently holds the classified components or whether they are being transferred to Chinese authorities
A broker handled the shipment for Lockheed Martin, the maker of the F-35. The Pentagon confirmed that some of the components were missing. The Defense Department’s F-35 Joint Chiefs of Staff said it was “aware of the issue with the shipment of unserviceable F-35 Lightning II components” and that it was working with US authorities and industry partners “to recover the components, investigate the incident, and institute safeguards to prevent a similar incident from occurring again.”
According to two of the sources who spoke to Politico, the shipment included one of the aircraft’s cockpit canopies. The canopy is not just a transparent covering that protects the pilot, but a key component of the F-35’s stealth envelope.
China is trying to obtain more information about US aircraft
It is coated with a thin, transparent layer of radar-absorbing material that helps reduce the aircraft’s signature and hide it from enemy radar systems.
Access to the canopy could allow a rival country to examine its materials and production methods, compare them with information already collected through intelligence means, and even attempt to reverse-engineer the technology.
“It’s no secret that China is aggressively trying to obtain information about the F-35 through electronic espionage and other means. Even if they already had specifications or other information about the component, having a real item can provide them with additional information and verify or refine what they’ve already learned,” said JJ Gertler, former member of the House Armed Services Committee and a military aviation expert at the Congressional Research Service.
The previously undisclosed incident led to a series of briefings for staff members of key national security committees in Congress. Representatives from the State Department and the Pentagon held the first briefing in June, and additional briefings are expected in the coming weeks, according to Politico’s sources.
The transfer of components to Hong Kong is of particular concern in Washington due to China's tightening control over the city in recent years. Chinese national security laws give Beijing authorities extensive influence over what happens in Hong Kong and the ability to access equipment within its borders.
US State Department declined to comment
The Chinese Embassy in Washington said it was unaware of the incident. The US State Department declined to comment. Lockheed Martin said it could not discuss the status of shipments for security reasons, but stressed that it complies with all US regulations for the transfer of aircraft components. “Our teams handle each shipment with the utmost care and safeguards to ensure the integrity of the F-35 program and the security of our allies,” the company said.
The F-35 supply chain is a complex global system that relies on facilities in many countries to manufacture, transport, and repair parts. There are maintenance centers for the aircraft in Australia, but none of them are yet capable of repairing the cockpit canopies. That is why the canopy had to be shipped to the United States.
The countries participating in the program, including the United States, Britain, Australia, Denmark, Norway and Poland, use a shared global pool of spare parts. The components remain the property of the US Department of Defense until they are installed on the aircraft, but it is Lockheed Martin and not the Pentagon who manage information about the parts’ movements.
A 2023 report by the US Office of the Comptroller found that more than a million F-35 spare parts had gone missing in the five years prior to its release. The report said the Pentagon could not verify the loss of parts worth tens of millions of dollars because Lockheed Martin and prime contractors held the relevant information.

Economic Watch: Border highway unlocks new growth along China's frontier
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
21:47:13 CST
22:47:13 KST

CHANGCHUN, Sept. 19 (Xinhua) -- In early autumn, Chen Mo, a self-driving tourist from Hangzhou, pulled into a themed rest stop along National Highway G331 in northeast China's Jilin Province.
Setting off from Dandong in neighboring Liaoning Province, he planned a seven-day journey along the border road to Hunchun in Jilin, hoping to experience Korean ethnic customs, pick local mountain produce and take in the riverside scenery along the way.
"I used to think border areas were just places to pass through," Chen said. "Now, they are worth staying for."
Stretching 1,240 km across Jilin, G331 runs along the province's border, skirting the Changbai Mountains and tracing the Yalu and Tumen rivers. The route passes through 10 county-level areas and links 216 border villages, 12 border ports and 45 scenic attractions rated AAA level or above. Parts of the route were once narrow, winding and difficult to navigate, making many border villages and attractions hard to reach.
After years of upgrades, the Jilin section fully opened to traffic in September 2025 and has since drawn a growing stream of travelers to the region. During the 2025 Mid-Autumn Festival and National Day holiday -- the first major holiday after the road opened -- traffic volume along the route topped 307,000, up 410.82 percent year on year, with a daily peak of 50,100.
Ji'an, the first stop in Jilin for travelers arriving from Liaoning along the route, was once a key departure point for the Chinese People's Volunteers as they crossed the Yalu River to fight in the War to Resist U.S. Aggression and Aid Korea (1950-1953). The city boasts a wealth of revolutionary sites, many of which once lay off the beaten track.
Now, the G331 is bringing these areas within easier reach for tourists. The city has renovated historic sites, upgraded study trails and improved visitor services, linking them with border landmarks to create routes that combine revolutionary history, border sightseeing and self-driving travel.
"I brought my child here by car to experience history firsthand," said visitor Wang Junjun. "Seeing the border landscape and the Yalu River up close made the trip both meaningful and memorable."
At the eastern end of G331's Jilin section, Hunchun is seeing another type of longer stay. The city, Jilin's only land-port city open to Russia, has attracted more Russian visitors as travel between the two countries has become easier under visa-free policies. Passenger traffic through Hunchun Port reached a record high of 754,000 in 2025.
Traditional Chinese medicine and wellness services are becoming a particular draw for Russian visitors. Acupuncture, moxibustion and massage are among the treatments gaining popularity, with some visitors shifting from brief trips to longer wellness stays and opting for short-term therapy lasting seven to 10 days.
"I was worried about the language barrier, but everything went smoothly," said a visitor from St. Petersburg after an acupuncture session in Hunchun. "The doctor also showed me some simple stretches I could do at home."
The growing flow of visitors is also creating opportunities for local residents. An Guangri, a retired soldier in Fangchuan Village in Hunchun, converted an idle farmhouse into a border-themed homestay.
"Since the highway opened, we've seen more self-driving tourists, as well as visitors from Russia and the Republic of Korea," he said, adding that during the peak season, rooms are often booked two weeks in advance.
For Wu Meihong, the changes along G331 offered her a reason to come home. She returned to Qushui Village in Tumen in 2023 and, with her sister, renovated an unused old house into a rustic countryside cafe. Her social media videos of daily village life drew viewers, some of whom later came to visit.
"Once the road opened, more tourists came, and I realized there are just as many opportunities back home as in the city," she said.
The changes are reshaping local industries as well. As more visitors arrive, villages along the border are moving beyond simply selling raw produce, instead developing new products and experiences for tourists.
In Baoshan Village of Linjiang, blueberries have been grown for more than a decade. Poor mountain roads once made fresh fruit difficult to transport, resulting in losses and limited sales. With better road access, tourists can now enter the village to pick berries, while cold-storage facilities and processing have helped expand the business beyond fresh fruit.
Dried blueberries, jam and wine are sold to visitors and shipped nationwide online. The industry now brings the village more than 10 million yuan (about 1.5 million U.S. dollars) in additional annual income, boosting per capita income by over 20,000 yuan.
Similarly, in Nanping Township of Helong, six border villages have joined forces to develop local specialties with tourists in mind. Soybean paste, jujube juice and forest honey -- once sold only locally -- are now packaged uniformly as tourism souvenirs and promoted through both livestreaming and in-person sales events.
"In the past, we sold whatever we produced. Now we think about what visitors want," said Ji Huadong, a local official.
Gao Yun, an official with the Party School of the Jilin Provincial Committee of the Communist Party of China, said better connectivity can help turn scattered tourism resources and local specialties into new sources of local growth.
"Developing border tourism routes and high-quality tourism products can meet visitors' diverse needs while driving the growth of related industries and the broader regional economy," Gao said.
The benefits can extend beyond the economy. As folk traditions and traditional crafts become part of tourism and generate income, local communities have greater incentive to preserve and pass them on, creating a virtuous cycle between cultural preservation and development, experts said.
What is happening along the G331 in Jilin is also part of a wider effort to improve transport links in China's border regions. China will advance the high-quality development of transport corridors and support opening-up and development in border regions during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), according to the Ministry of Transport.
Over the next five years, China plans to fully connect and upgrade three major highways -- the G219 along the western and southern frontier, the G331 along the northern border and the G228 along the coast -- as part of a "golden outer ring" running along the country's land borders and coastline. Together, they will stretch more than 26,000 km.
Ma Jiangbo, deputy director of the China economic research center under the China Institute for Innovation & Development Strategy, said the three corridors will link land and sea routes, turning once-remote border areas into new frontiers of opening-up.
"Improved road networks can lower cross-border logistics costs, helping resources from border and coastal regions reach wider markets, and promoting a more balanced industrial layout," Ma added.
As dusk settles over the villages along G331, homestays light up. Travelers sit in courtyards sampling local food, while villagers prepare specialties to sell the next day.
For places that travelers once merely passed through, the road now offers more reasons to stay -- and gives the communities along it more to build upon. ■

21:46:52 CST

BEIJING, Sept. 19 (Xinhua) -- China firmly opposes unilateral sanctions that lack authorization from the United Nations and a basis in international law, as well as so-called "secondary sanctions" targeting third countries, a spokesperson for China's Ministry of Commerce said Saturday.
The remarks came in response to a question about the United States signing the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 into law on Sept. 18 (U.S. Eastern Time). The legislation strengthens sanctions against Russia, extends sanctions related to Iran, and authorizes tariffs of up to 100 percent on certain third countries that import Russian oil or natural gas.
China has always conducted normal economic and trade cooperation with countries around the world on the basis of equality and mutual benefit, the spokesperson said, adding that such cooperation targets no third party and is not subject to interference or coercion by third parties.
China will closely follow subsequent U.S. measures and reserves the right to take all necessary steps to firmly safeguard its national sovereignty and development interests, as well as the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese companies, the spokesperson said.
The spokesperson called on the United States to work with China in the same direction and maintain stable economic and trade relations through dialogue and consultation, while contributing to maintaining the global trade order and the security and stability of global industrial and supply chains. ■

Asian Games open in Nagoya after challenging build-up
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
21:46:24 CST
22:46:24 KST

by sportswriters Cao Yibo, Yue Chenxing and Huang Haoran
NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 19 (Xinhua) -- The 20th Asian Games opened in Nagoya, Japan, on Saturday after a challenging buildup marked by accommodation shortages, transportation problems, heavy rainfall and other logistical issues.
Under the slogan "Imagine One Asia," the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games mark Japan's third time hosting the event, following Tokyo in 1958 and Hiroshima in 1994.
Unlike previous Asian Games, Aichi-Nagoya did not build a traditional Athletes' Village. Instead, organizers opted to use existing hotels, a cruise ship and temporary container-style huts, citing cost control and a desire to avoid leaving behind underused infrastructure after the Games.
The approach came under scrutiny as the number of participants rose beyond initial expectations. Organizers had originally planned accommodation for around 15,000 people, while the final number of athletes and officials approached 17,000. Some delegations reported delays in room allocations and credential activation, while concerns also arose from room assignments and the distance between accommodation and competition venues.
The OCA defended the overall accommodation strategy, saying the priority was to provide athletes with suitable accommodation, transportation, food and other services while ensuring infrastructure investments remained useful after the Games.
The final days before the opening were also affected by torrential rain in the Nagoya area, which disrupted transportation and led to evacuations in some areas. Some Games facilities were affected by water leaks, adding another challenge for organizers shortly before the ceremony.
Against that backdrop, the opening ceremony provided a chance to shift the focus back to sport.
Chinese flagbearers, men's basketball player Hu Mingxuan and women's boxer Wu Yu, led the Chinese delegation in the parade at Mizuho Athletic Stadium, receiving a warm welcome from the stands.
China has sent 815 athletes to compete in 369 events across 38 sports at the Games, including 36 Olympic champions such as three-time Olympic table tennis gold medalist Sun Yingsha and Olympic champion divers Chen Yuxi and Wang Zongyuan.
The delegation has an average age of 24, with 548 athletes making their Asian Games debuts. Athletes born after 2005, including 13-year-old swimmer Yu Zidi and 17-year-old sprinter Chen Yujie, account for 27 percent of the team.
In his speech, Olympic Council of Asia (OCA) President Sheikh Joaan Bin Hamad Al Thani expressed his gratitude to the Aichi-Nagoya 2026 Organizing Committee and the Japanese Olympic Committee for hosting the Games, while also thanking the volunteers, sponsors and media partners involved in the event.
Addressing the athletes, Sheikh Joaan said: "While the world is too often divided by conflict, they remind us that sport remains a powerful force for peace, understanding, and friendship among nations."
"They carry with them the hopes of their families and friends, of young people in their communities and their NOCs," Sheikh Joaan stated, adding, "To each and every one of you: the entire continent is behind you. Give everything you have. Hold nothing back."
Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games and Asian Para Games Organizing Committee (AINAGOC) President Hideaki Omura said the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games carried forward the spirit of the Tokyo and Hiroshima Games, emphasizing the power of sport to bring people together across borders.
"Sports have the tremendous power to bring people together across languages, cultures, and national borders," Omura said, adding that the Games embody the hope that people will "unite as one, and move forward together toward the future."
The torch relay, carried by local runners through Aichi Prefecture, was shown in a video before the flame entered the stadium. Six former or active Japanese athletes then passed the flame under the spotlight, with the final torchbearers, father and son Shigenobu Murofushi and Koji Murofushi, both former Asian Games hammer throw champions, lighting the main cauldron.
The cauldron was designed in the shape of Nagoya's iconic kinshachi, or golden tiger-fish ornaments.
The cultural performance was built around the theme of a "Harmonic Heart Beat," beginning with the sound of a heartbeat and violinist Taro Hakase's performance of "Legacy 2026," accompanied by 240 citizen dancers, heart-shaped drones and light and laser effects.
The program then showcased Aichi-Nagoya's traditional culture and manufacturing heritage before returning to the theme of a harmonious heartbeat bringing people together across Asia. ■

Atlas Portföy also reported payment delays at a money market fund.

The SPK set a three-month liquidation period, which it can extend. The affected funds are closed to purchases and redemptions through both TEFAS and other distribution channels.
The Central Bank pledged to increase funding through one-week repo auctions and reduce collateral haircuts. The banking regulator also temporarily eased capital rules for listed banks buying back their own shares.
The Financial Stability Committee described the fund problems as “temporary and manageable” on Sept. 17 and pledged measures to ease the liquidity squeeze and prevent contagion.
Treasury and Finance Minister Mehmet Şimşek said on Sept. 18 that the difficulties were confined to a limited number of funds, with 90 percent of the market functioning normally.
“There is no widespread systemic risk,” he said. “We have quarantined the troubled segment.”

International Press Institute calls for justice over journalist Viktoriia Roshchyna's death
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
16:44:00 EEST
22:44:00 KST

International Press Institute calls for justice over journalist Viktoriia Roshchyna's death
The International Press Institute (IPI) has called on Russia to release journalists imprisoned on politically motivated charges and hold accountable those responsible for the death of Viktoriia Roshchyna, who was tortured to death in Russian captivity.
Source: International Press Institute, marking the second anniversary of Viktoriia's death
Details: IPI said 16 journalists have been killed while carrying out their professional duties in Ukraine since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion. Viktoriia Roshchyna was the first media worker to die while unlawfully imprisoned in Russia.
IPI Executive Director Scott Griffen said: "Viktoriia Roshchyna paid the ultimate price for her dedication to ensuring the stories of her fellow citizens living under occupation were heard by the world. Her death shed light on the brutal treatment Ukrainian journalists can face at the hands of Russian authorities. IPI will keep demanding justice for Viktoriia, and we call on the international community to press for the release of every journalist Russia is holding."
The organisation said that, as of August 2026, 27 Ukrainian journalists remained imprisoned in Russia, most of them on politically motivated charges of "terrorism" or "espionage".
In several cases, the Russian authorities have brought no public charges and refuse to acknowledge the detentions. As a result, the media workers are effectively being held incommunicado, cut off from the outside world.
Although Russia and Ukraine regularly conduct prisoner-of-war exchanges, civilians held by Russia are released far less frequently.
Background:
- Viktoriia Roshchyna began working in journalism at the age of 16. During her career, she worked for several Ukrainian media outlets, including as a freelance contributor to Ukrainska Pravda. In 2022, she wrote a series of reports from Russian-occupied territories, including Crimea, Donetsk Oblast and devastated Mariupol.
- Viktoriia went missing in August 2023 in Russian-occupied Enerhodar, where she was working on a report about Russian torture chambers. It was not until May 2024 that Russia admitted to having detained Roshchyna. The Russian Ministry of Defence sent a letter confirming this to her father, Volodymyr Roshchyn.
- Several months later, the Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War learned that the 27-year-old Viktoriia had died in Russian captivity. Viktoriia died on 19 September 2024, the same month that Russia agreed to include her in the next prisoner exchange list.
- Russia delayed the repatriation of Roshchyna's body, which was only returned in February 2025. Her body bore numerous signs of torture and ill-treatment. Russia returned the body with some internal organs missing, apparently in an attempt to conceal evidence of crimes.
- On 8 August, a funeral was held in Kyiv for Viktoriia Roshchyna. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy posthumously awarded the Order of Freedom to Roshchyna on 2 August. In September 2025, she was posthumously honoured with the American Oxi Courage Award for bravery.
- In October 2025, IPI posthumously named Viktoriia a World Press Freedom Hero for her courageous reporting on Russia's occupation of Ukraine. She was also awarded a prize by the Czech human rights organisation People in Need.
- A team of 45 journalists from 13 international media outlets, including Ukrainska Pravda, also joined forces to investigate Viktoriia's journey to Russian-occupied Zaporizhzhia Oblast, the circumstances of her disappearance and the torture she endured before her death.
Read the findings of the investigation: The Viktoriia Project: the story of the captivity and torture endured by journalist Viktoriia Roshchyna and thousands of Ukrainians imprisoned by Russia

All EU sanctions linked to Russia's war may expire as France, Slovakia seek to delist oligarchs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
13:43:46 UTC
22:43:46 KST

All EU sanctions linked to Russia's war may expire as France, Slovakia seek to delist oligarchs
President Volodymyr Zelensky clutches his head next to French President Emmanuel Macron at the European Political Community (EPC) summit in Moldova, June, 1, 2023. (Kay Nietfeld/picture alliance via Getty Images)
All of the EU's 3,000 sanctions against individuals helping Russia's war effort could be extinguished overnight if Brussels, Paris, and Azerbaijan fail to find a compromise by Sept. 21, EU diplomats told the Kyiv Independent.
The EU is set to renew the sanctions against Russia-linked individuals on Sept. 21. The package accounts for about half of the EU's total sanctions listings.
Given that Russia has not changed its behavior towards Ukraine since 2022, the vote to renew sanctions against those helping Moscow was supposed to be a formality.
But starting with former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban, some leaders have tried to use such votes to extract concessions from the EU, because any sanctions decision requires unanimity.
This time, Slovakia launched a push to delist two oligarchs, Mikhail Fridman and Alisher Usmanov.
But the push to delist Usmanov gained a second supporter – France.
France did not respond to a request for comment, and Slovakia declined to comment.
While Slovakia has not backed down, EU and national diplomats have told the Kyiv Independent that they "would have agreed by now," were it not for France's involvement.
And President Volodymyr Zelensky has criticized the idea of lifting sanctions on the two men.
"This is definitely not the time to lift sanctions, definitely not the time to shield Russian oligarchs from sanctions, and definitely not the time for Europe to give Russia any gifts," he said.
Following the latest, unsuccessful meeting of EU ambassadors on Sept. 18, one national diplomat painted the situation in stark terms.
"On Monday we will either delist nobody, delist two people, or delist 3,000," they said.
What's so special about these people?
One of the sanctioned individuals, Mikhail Fridman, is a co-founder of the Russian conglomerate Alfa-Group and a member of Russian President Vladimir Putin's inner circle.
Investigative reporters revealed in May 2023 that subsidiary Alfa Insurance provided insurance for vehicles used by Russian forces in Ukraine. The company has also reportedly serviced the Main Office of Special Programs, which is responsible for guarding Putin.
Alisher Usmanov, meanwhile, is a Russian-Uzbek businessman who made his fortune in metal and mining operations following the collapse of the Soviet Union. He was referred to as "one of Putin's favorite oligarchs" in the EU's original 2022 sanctions decision.
Exactly why these two names are the recurring favorites for de-listing from EU sanctions is not clear, although both have repeatedly disputed the claim that they have close ties to the Kremlin.
Slovakia, and Hungary also requested the delisting of Fridman and Usmanov in March.
That attempt was unsuccessful, but France's joining the push to delist Usmanov has increased the pressure.
The Financial Times first reported that Paris wants to delist Usmanov because Azerbaijan has made it a condition to release two prisoners with French nationality.
Reuters reported that an Azeri diplomat confirmed they want Usmanov to be delisted, but denied trying to influence decision-making.
And national diplomats from six different countries confirmed the FT's claim to the Kyiv Independent.
The French Foreign Ministry's website says that travel to Azerbaijan is "not recommended, unless there is a compelling reason."
"French nationals, including dual nationals, whether resident or passing through, are exposed to a risk of arrest, arbitrary detention and unfair trial in Azerbaijan," the website reads.
But why Azerbaijan is trying to negotiate a prisoner swap with France to delist an Uzbek-Russian oligarch over any of its own sanctioned citizens or companies remains unknown.
Reuters reported that its Azeri diplomatic contact described Usmanov as a "renowned philanthropist and public figure."
What can Europe do?
Meanwhile, the French government has remained silent on Azerbaijan's detention of the two French nationals.
An EU diplomat explained to the Kyiv Independent that the bloc is responsive to the wishes of the specific country in such hostage situations, and that often countries ask for a more discretionary approach.
A second EU official confirmed that hostage negotiations almost always take place in private, telling the Kyiv Independent that they find media scrutiny rarely helps such things.
One national diplomat said that such scenarios are very difficult for the victim country, which has to be seen to be doing everything possible to help bring their nationals back home.
Even so, behind closed doors frustration is building.
Multi-hour meetings of EU ambassadors have failed to reach anything resembling a compromise, and after the latest such meeting on Sept. 18, national diplomats vented their frustration, saying that there was "no progress at all."
The 25 EU countries against delisting Usmanov and Fridman show little readiness to compromise.
In July, EU countries agreed to grant an exemption to the Greek shipping company Dynagas, that would allow it to continue transporting Russian Arctic LNG. At the time, some feared it would open a Pandora's box of new exemption requests.
Now several officials have used the phrase "Pandora's box" again about the Franco-Slovak request, which they fear would cement the trend of granting exemptions, and seriously hurt EU credibility.
"France needs to tell Azerbaijan bilaterally that it’s a no-go to convince 25 other countries to shift their positions that dramatically and that Azerbaijan will have to shift its demands," one diplomat fumed.
The option of letting all 2,960 listings expire, for many, is simply unthinkable.
One potential compromise suggested by yet another EU diplomat could be to extend the sanctions for six months rather than one year, but that risks simply kicking the can further down the road, specifically to just one month before France's presidential election.
Most expect France somehow to drop its demand and begin talks with Baku about other ways to secure the release of its citizens.
Note from the author:
Hi, this is Chris Powers. Thanks for reading this article. The EU is a famously complicated beast to understand, but for Ukraine, it has also never been so important.
Whether it's Russia sanctions, fighting corruption, keeping Ukraine's finances in the black, or the process of joining the EU itself, many Kyivan roads eventually pass through Brussels.

NEW DELHI: The Congress on Saturday said the only way to counter a “bully” was to “resist him forcefully”, after US president Donald Trump signed into law a legislation expanding sanctions on Russia and Iran and giving Washington new tariff powers targeting major buyers of Russian energy.AICC general secretary Jairam Ramesh made the remarks in a post on X after Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 on Friday. The White House said the law authorises and expands sanctions, tariffs and prohibitions on Russia and extends existing sanctions on Iran.“The only way to counter a bully is to resist him forcefully,” Ramesh said.The legislation gives the US president authority to impose tariffs of up to 100 per cent on goods from countries that meet specified criteria linked to purchases of Russian crude oil or natural gas and sanctions evasion. It also targets Russian officials, financial institutions, defence networks and the country’s so-called “shadow fleet”.
The measure does not automatically impose a 100 per cent tariff on any specific country, with the law giving Trump discretion over its implementation.
Earlier on Wednesday, Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge said the threat of up to 100 per cent US tariffs on Indian goods showed the government’s foreign and trade policies had “miserably failed”.
He said, “The threat of up to 100 per cent US tariffs on Indian goods shows how the Modi govt's foreign and trade policies have miserably failed.” Kharge also claimed the government had agreed to a trade framework expanding US access to Indian agriculture, alleging it “mortgag[ed] the interests of our farmers”.The legislation comes as India continues to face questions over its purchases of Russian energy. The ministry of external affairs said New Delhi’s energy sourcing decisions are guided by national interest.MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal earlier said meeting the requirements of India’s 1.4 billion people remained an “imperative”.“When it comes to energy sourcing, it is based on our national interest. We have said that meeting the energy requirements of our 1.4 billion people is an imperative that we have to follow. And we continue to buy energy from diversified sources,” Jaiswal said.
On the new US law, Jaiswal said India had already conveyed its concerns to senior levels of the US administration.“As we have stated, at senior levels of the US administration, we have conveyed the implications that this legislation could have on India's energy security, for international energy markets, and for the overall bilateral relationship. I don't have anything further to add at this point,” he said.The White House said Trump signed the legislation on September 18. The law extends the Iran Sanctions Act for five years and expands measures against Russia’s energy and financial sectors.

NEW DELHI: Karnataka chief minister DK Shivakumar on Friday announced that Tulu, spoken in the state's Dakshina Kannada and Udupi districts, would be recognised as an additional administrative language in the region, fulfilling a long-standing demand."Today, we have decided to make Tulu applicable to Udupi and Dakshina Kannada districts and declare it the state’s second additional administrative language," Shivakumar told reporters after a marathon cabinet meeting in Mangaluru.According to a cabinet note shared by the chief minister’s office, Tulu would be Karnataka’s "second additional administrative language" in Dakshina Kannada and Udupi.The 2011 national census recorded more than 18 lakh native Tulu speakers in Karnataka, whose population was recorded at over six crore at the time. New Zealand Must Learn Drone Warfare From Ukraine, Ex-Minister Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
13:39:00 UTC
22:39:00 KST

New Zealand should invite Ukrainian military specialists to train its armed forces in drone operations and absorb tactical lessons from the war against Russia, former New Zealand Defense Minister Ron Mark said in an interview with United24.
Mark stated that the New Zealand Defence Force (NZDF) has an “immense amount to learn” from Ukraine’s rapid battlefield innovation, arguing that formal technological, military, and intelligence cooperation with Kyiv directly serves Wellington’s national security interests.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“When Russia launched its full-scale war, New Zealand sent its soldiers halfway around the world to help train Ukrainians,” Mark said. “Today, it is time to flip the script and bring Ukrainian training advisors and assistants to upskill our forces in the art of drone warfare.”
Mark, 72, who served as defense minister from 2017 to 2020, traveled to Kyiv on his sixth trip to Ukraine since the start of the 2022 full-scale invasion, operating as a private citizen to deliver humanitarian aid and conduct advocacy.
Frontline experience
Mark noted that direct observation of combat sectors across Ukraine highlighted how rapidly unmanned systems have altered traditional military concepts.
While early stages of the conflict were characterized by conventional trench combat reminiscent of World War I, Mark explained that the rapid introduction and mass deployment of loitering munitions, first-person view (FPV) drones, and automated reconnaissance platforms have fundamentally changed operational dynamics.
Poland Joins European Coalition on Ballistic Missile Defense
The former defense minister emphasized that Ukraine’s asymmetric successes extend into the maritime theater, pointing to how the Armed Forces of Ukraine neutralized major combatants of Russia’s Black Sea Fleet using uncrewed surface vessels (USVs) and long-range missiles despite lacking a conventional naval surface fleet.
Mark questioned whether Western nations should continue prioritizing conventional, capital-intensive defense assets when lower-cost autonomous systems have demonstrated decisive strategic utility.
“We’re talking about replacing our frigates, but why do that when Ukraine has proven the Black Sea Fleet can be neutralized without a conventional navy?” Mark said.
Russian espionage allegations
Mark’s advocacy for deeper defense cooperation follows diplomatic tensions between Wellington and Moscow.
In late July, New Zealand’s Security Intelligence Service (NZSIS) cast doubt on claims made by Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) that Wellington had recruited an espionage asset inside the Russian Federation.
The FSB claimed it arrested a Russian citizen in the southeastern city of Khabarovsk who had proactively contacted the NZSIS and passed sensitive state data.
The NZSIS responded by reiterating its longstanding policy of not commenting on operational matters, noting that Russian state media cannot be regarded as a reliable source of accurate reporting.
New Zealand Prime Minister Christopher Luxon similarly declined to comment, adhering to the convention governing intelligence matters.
Foreign affairs analysts noted that New Zealand, an active member of the Five Eyes intelligence-sharing alliance alongside the US, the UK, Canada, and Australia, has maintained extensive sanctions against Russia over its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, with Russian allegations likely designed to discredit Wellington’s diplomatic and security alignment with Kyiv.

The Sudanese army on Saturday recaptured the strategic al-Jamama area in North Kordofan state in southern Sudan from the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), military sources told Anadolu.
“Army forces and allied troops managed to take control of the al-Jamama area northeast of the city of Sodari in North Kordofan after defeating the RSF fighters,” the sources said.
The sources said army forces and their allies were advancing in the area and along the North Kordofan axis while pursuing RSF troops.
Members of Sudan's Joint Forces also posted videos on social media claiming their capture of al-Jamama.
The Sudanese government has not officially announced the capture of al-Jamama, while the RSF did not immediately comment on the report.
Al-Jamama is a commercial hub and a key area linking El Obeid, the capital of North Kordofan state, with the city of Al-Dabbah in Northern State.
The development came a day after the army announced that its forces had taken control of 11 areas in North Kordofan, marking its biggest recent advance.
On Sept. 6, the army also announced that it took control of the city of Hamrat al-Wiz in Jabra al-Sheikh locality of North Kordofan state.
Since late July, the army has taken control of large areas of North Kordofan after recapturing Bara, Jabra al-Sheikh and Umm Sayala and securing a main road linking Bara with Omdurman, west of the capital Khartoum.
The RSF had controlled al-Jamama and established its presence in areas west and northwest of Sodari and along a major export road from the early months of the conflict.
The three Kordofan states — North, West and South — have witnessed clashes between the army and the RSF since October 25.
Sudan has been embroiled in a war between the army and the RSF since April 2023, killing tens of thousands of people and displacing around 13 million others, according to UN and international estimates.

====================================================================================================

Trump’s battle to rename the Kennedy Center has put its future at risk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
13:30:48 UTC
22:30:48 KST

It was born with the world premiere of Leonard Bernstein’s Mass. “Young people will come here and they will see this cultural centre,” Rose Kennedy, the mother of slain US president John F Kennedy, said at that opening night gala. “They will carry some of these ideas back to their different communities.”
More than half a century later, the potential death knell came just after 4.30pm on Tuesday with a perfunctory announcement on the public address system: “The centre is now closed to the public. Please exit the centre by way of the Hall of States.” Soon barricades had been erected and security guards were blocking access.
The John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts in Washington DC, once filled with the buzz of audiences and children, had fallen as silent as a mausoleum. Now a high stakes legal battle is under way to prevent Donald Trump from taking a wrecking ball to the building that is both national arts complex and living memorial to the 35th president.
The current White House occupant, incensed that courts have prevented his name being added to the Kennedy Center, told reporters this week: “I think that the Trump administration should certainly have recognition. Because frankly, if we don’t do that, it’s going to close. It’ll end up being ripped down.” On social media, Trump declared the venue “destined to doom” without his intervention.
The once unthinkable threat became more thinkable when an Agence France-Presse photographer took a picture of Trump aboard Air Force One, holding a placard with ominous red text: “Kennedy Center DEMOLIS...” The rest of the word was obscured by the plane’s window frame. Below was a big picture showing a yellow heavy construction vehicle scooping rubble from a torn-down building.
Trump has no legal right to demolish the facility, which was established by Congress. Critics say he is acting out of spite because he cannot get his way. Kerry Kennedy, the former president’s niece , said: “Like a child who can’t play with a toy, he wants to stomp on the toy. But this is not a toy. This is the living memorial to a slain president.
“It would be like adding the Trump name to the Trump-Lincoln Memorial or the Trump-Jefferson Memorial or Trump-Tomb of the Unknown Soldier. The courts have spoken, he cannot demolish it, he cannot put his name on it and he should be focused instead on his job.”
The Kennedy Center did not respond to requests for comment.
The 100ft structure opened in 1971 on the banks of the Potomac River. Since then it has presented ballet, children’s theatre, comedy, contemporary dance, hip-hop, jazz, international festivals and educational programmes. The annual Kennedy Center Honors have hosted past presidents and a who’s who of US arts and culture.
Trump seized control of the facility in February 2025, claimed its finances were in dire straits and fired board members who did not align with his “vision for a Golden Age in Arts and Culture”. Deborah Rutter, the centre’s president, was ousted and replaced by Ric Grenell, a Trump loyalist and former ambassador with no experience in arts management.
An initiative created in 2020 to promote anti-racism and community outreach was shut down and its 10-person staff dismissed. Citing “drag shows specifically targeting our youth”, any programming perceived as “woke” was purged. It was a commercial disaster as audiences, performers and philanthropists deserted the centre in droves.
Lawyer Norm Eisen, who has litigated against the administration’s attempts to impinge on institutional independence, said: “He slapped his name on there and destroyed the lifeblood of the Kennedy Center: audience and artists.”
In January, the Kennedy Center hosted the world premiere of Melania, a documentary about the first lady, with the Trumps in attendance. Three days later, the president announced that he would be closing the facility for two years for $257m repairs and renovations.
The Trump-appointed board backed the move and also voted to rename the venue the “Trump-Kennedy Center”. Trump’s name was duly added to the exterior marble facade, before the US district judge Christopher Cooper intervened and ruled that only Congress has the authority to rename the memorial. The name was removed but the result remains hidden by giant scaffolding and tarpaulins.
Asked about Trump’s motivations, Eisen of Democracy Defenders Action added: “You would need an authority in abnormal psychology to get the answer to that question but he appears to have developed an obsession because he’s not used to hearing the word no.”
On Tuesday this week, Judge Cooper again ruled that the Trump administration could not put a new Trump sign on the Kennedy Center’s facade or rename its plaza for the president “without Congress’s blessing”.
Hours later, the centre’s board voted to close the facility for two years, citing the need for $257m of repairs and renovations. The centre’s executive director, Matt Floca, ordered an immediate seven-day emergency closure, citing “acute risks to public safety resulting from continued structural deterioration”.
But Democratic congresswoman Joyce Beatty and Senator Sheldon Whitehouse allege that the closure is a “pretext” to hide a financial “death spiral” caused by artist boycotts and dwindling ticket sales.
In an interview on Friday, Whitehouse, the top Democrat on the environment and public works committee and an ex-officio member of the Kennedy Center board of trustees, said the events represented three phases of Trump’s assault on the complex.
“One is what I call the mob bust out gone wrong, in which they tried to take over and run the Kennedy Center, give themselves and their friends big contracts, charge expensive goodies to Kennedy Center accounts, do political favours using Kennedy Center facilities for Trump allies, and that was extremely damaging to the business of the centre,” he said.
“Then they moved into the renaming fiasco and that seems to have struck a lethal blow to the centre’s business model – a predictably damaging blow that they failed to consider at all. Now they’ve moved into a third stage in which they are threatening the actual destruction of the Kennedy Center if they don’t get their renaming.”
Whitehouse added: “It has gone from bad to worse but the through line in all of this is that these trustees are under a legal duty to put the welfare of the centre itself first and, if they fail in that duty, they create a legal environment in which courts can and ultimately likely will step in to make sure that the centre is run lawfully.”
The legal battle intensified on Thursday, when Judge Cooper issued an order requiring the Kennedy Center to give at least 30 days’ notice before making any major physical changes to the building, including demolition.
Whitehouse said: “There’s a contrast between the thuggery and bullying world in which you could countenance a threat to tear down the Kennedy Center if your name doesn’t go on it and the actual legal world in which actions have to be approved by a board that has a fiduciary duty to put the welfare of the institution first. Those two are irreconcilable at this point.”
Still, Trump ordered the demolition of the White House East Wing to make way for a ballroom, despite opposition from preservationists and questions over the administration’s authority to proceed without Congress. He is now threatening to cancel the renovation of the Kennedy Center, and warning of its possible demise, if his name is not restored to the building.
Chris Raleigh, an organiser the Hands Off the Arts movement, which is mobilising grassroots resistance, said: “That’s what you do when the hostage takers can’t get what they want. There comes a point where the hostage is inconvenient. Look at it: the people who have fought back have pushed Trump to the brink here.
“In no way at all is he winning. His name is not going up on the building. There is somebody in the White House every day who says, before they walk in that building, ‘Oh god, please don’t let there be another Kennedy Center story today.’”
Raleigh added: “Everyone in Trump’s life should be telling him: ‘You gotta to get out now. This is not going to help you.’”
And even if the current peril passes, it will be difficult to restore the centre to its former glories. On Friday it laid off about a dozen staff, the Washington Post newspaper reported.
Michael Kaiser, who led the centre from 2001 to 2014, warns that even a two-year closure will be damaging. He said: “When you don’t have audiences and you don’t have donors participating for two years, those individuals go elsewhere. When you have no staff, even if there’s a time in the future where we can return to a more sense of being normal, it’s not going to be so simple to reopen a building of this size and complexity.”
Some critics see the attack on the Kennedy Center as part of a broader assault on institutions and freedom of expression. On Friday, Trump announced that the media outlets CNN, MS Now and Politico would be banned from the White House and, with health secretary Robert Kennedy Jr standing behind him in the Oval Office, railed against the Kennedy Center again.
To Kerry Kennedy, who has worked in the human rights arena for 45 years, the president is a “petty tyrant”. Asked to consider the possibility of the Kennedy Center being lost, she reflected: “It would be devastating for my family because we love Uncle Jack but in the end Trump is not going to hurt my family. He is hurting our country and he’s hurting our world and he’s giving permission to tyrants everywhere to shut down arts centres and silence critical voices.”
On Friday evening thousands of protesters gathered outside the Kennedy Center in view of the marble facade that remained concealed by scaffolding and tarpaulins. The speakers included a drag queen.
Against the setting sun, protesters beat drums and waved signs that read: “Keep your tiny hands off our Kennedy Center”; “You’re no Jack Kennedy”; “Our center not DJT’s”; and “Wicked starring DJT”.

Britain deepens nuclear ties with France and Australia
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
14:30:28 BST
22:30:28 KST

Britain is deepening its nuclear relationships with the United States, France and Australia, with the Northwood Declaration recognising that there is no extreme threat to Europe which would not prompt a response by both Britain and France, according to the annual update to Parliament published this week.
The declaration, agreed in July 2025, reaffirmed and strengthened what the update describes as longstanding nuclear cooperation between the two countries. On the AUKUS partnership, the update records an important development in February this year when HMS Anson docked at HMAS Stirling near Perth.
The United States is described as Britain’s closest defence ally, with the relationship underpinned by long-standing cooperation on all nuclear matters including policy, operations and technology.
The practical expression of that relationship runs through the missile system, since Trident and its supporting systems fitted to the Vanguard class are manufactured in the United States, with Britain having bought title to a number of missiles drawn from a shared pool of assets under the 1963 Polaris Sales Agreement as amended for Trident in 1982. The system is operated independently by both the Royal Navy and the United States Navy.
The warhead fitted to those missiles is sovereign to Britain, with the Mk4A design maintained by AWE at Aldermaston, which also leads development of the replacement warhead, Astraea. Wes Streeting writes that the increase in investment across the enterprise “sends a clear signal of our commitment to global security, and to our Allies”, with the deterrent remaining declared to the defence of NATO.
The update states that nuclear deterrence is the cornerstone of NATO security and that the independent strategic nuclear forces of the United Kingdom contribute significantly to the overall security of the alliance, a declaration maintained since 1962.

Märt Meesak: Only devoted die‑hards will keep working in the food service sector
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
13:30:00 UTC
22:30:00 KST

Märt Meesak: Only devoted die‑hards will keep working in the food service sector
Eating out is not a luxury, and only the true fanatics of the foodservice sector — those who have not yet given up — will continue operating, writes Märt Meesak.
ERR recently published an extensive overview of the state of Estonia's foodservice industry. Nearly every month, if not every week, brings news of restaurants closing. The reasons are always the same: costs exceed revenue. Estonia has the highest VAT on food and dining out in Europe after Denmark — roughly twice the EU average.
What makes me especially disheartened about the arguments coming from leading politicians is the claim that "the strongest will survive," or that eating out is a luxury. Even worse is the suggestion that the sector is not a significant part of Estonia's economy, so why worry about it. In reality, the entire sector is speeding toward a crisis — if it isn't already there.
The tourism sector is one of the most beneficial for the state. A functioning tourism industry brings in foreign money through visitors, who also pay taxes on everything they consume here (VAT, labor taxes, alcohol excise, fuel excise).
Thanks to tourism, many other businesses get work: laundries, courier companies, security firms, cleaning companies, farmers, manufacturers. The list is long, because the economy is a system of connected vessels. Tourists also take taxis, rent cars, and so on. All these companies provide jobs and pay taxes.
Eating out should not be a luxury, as some politicians imagine. In a normal society that aims to grow a healthy middle class, eating out should be the rule, not the exception. Dining out offers people culinary experiences, healthier eating options, and a way to relieve stress.
It is certainly healthier for an office worker to eat at least one warm meal a day rather than snack on store‑bought ready food. Stepping out of the office during a stressful day is already beneficial, and going out in the evenings is good for mental health. We talk about Estonia's mental‑health problems, yet we prevent people from improving their well‑being in a natural way. Eating out is also a social activity — in the internet age, meeting people face‑to‑face and feeling happy is irreplaceable. That's how we climb higher on happiness indexes.
The sector employs professionals trained in Estonia's public education system — funded by taxpayers. They work with passion to create something exciting. The fact that people can work with heart and offer something good to others is a value worth preserving. And there are many more reasons.
But the situation is serious: no business is a social project — it must be profitable. Unless we want to return to Soviet‑era canteens. Too often, foodservice business owners work 24/7, and their health and well‑being matter too. Doing this work at zero profit — or even at a loss — is not sustainable. And so doors close. It's nice to provide jobs and pay taxes, but the owner must also receive some benefit.
Profit margins in the foodservice sector have collapsed to near zero. According to the Estonian Hotel and Restaurant Association's 2026 data, average profitability has fallen from four percent to about one percent.
Politicians' counterarguments against lowering VAT have been predictable. They claim that a VAT reduction would not reach consumers, and that restaurateurs would pocket the difference as huge profits. Let's break that claim down.
The sector's annual turnover is under one billion euros (it fell 1.6 percent last year). Estonia has roughly 2,500–3,000 active food‑and‑drink establishments. That means an average annual turnover of €300,000–€400,000 per business (about €25,000–€33,000 per month). With a one‑percent profit margin, the average annual profit is €3,000–€4,000 euros — about €300 per month.
Even if we optimistically use the former four‑percent margin, the situation is still bleak. A four‑percent margin means €14,000 profit per year — €1,166 per month. In many establishments, the owner works behind the stove or counter, meaning this is essentially their monthly income.
Compare that to Estonia's average salary, which is over €2,000. The imbalance and unsustainability are obvious. And if the owner wanted to pay themselves a salary, social tax and unemployment insurance would reduce it further — leaving around €600.
Show me a government official willing to work around the clock for that amount. The owner must take full financial responsibility, pay all employees on time, and transfer all state taxes down to the second.
Even if part of the VAT reduction stayed with the business, it would not be a crime if the owner could earn €1,000 instead of €600. The business could regain investment capacity, improving working conditions for employees. If the business does better, wages rise — which benefits the entire economy. And when Estonia's economy improves, tax revenue increases.
Let's not kill off a sector that provides so much value we often don't notice at first glance. Only the "crazy ones," the devoted die-hards, remain in the catering sector — everyone else has already given up. Let's support our people and our businesses.
--
Editor: Kaupo Meiel, Argo Ideon
