Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
According to one source, the prospective meeting would bring together Dmitriev – a key confidant of Putin and chief executive of Russia’s sovereign wealth fund, the Russian Direct Investment Fund (RDIF) – alongside AfD federal co-leaders Alice Weidel and Tino Chrupalla.
Prior to the imposition of sweeping Western sanctions following Moscow’s 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Russian supplied more than half of Germany’s natural gas consumption and over one-third of its crude oil imports, establishing deep industrial and commercial ties that Berlin has worked to unwind over the past four years.
Prospective trilateral format and pre-conditions for talks
The source noted that the bilateral gathering is contingent on a preliminary peace framework being agreed upon between Ukraine and Russia prior to the meeting.
Putin Claims Readiness to Restore Relations With Europe
Organizers envision expanding the initiative into a trilateral dialogue connecting the AfD, Russian leadership, and representatives from the US. Several neutral or non-Western locations have been evaluated as potential host venues for the summit, including the United Arab Emirates, India, and Israel.
The diplomatic outreach reflects the AfD’s longstanding foreign policy platform, which demands an immediate cessation of German defense assistance to Ukraine, the removal of international economic sanctions against Moscow, and the swift restoration of bilateral energy transit across the Baltic Sea.
Cross-party backlash and accusations of betrayal in Berlin
Reports of the planned consultations triggered condemnations across Germany’s governing and opposition political establishment, with senior lawmakers from both the Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and the Alliance 90/The Greens denouncing the move as an act of political betrayal.
According to ntv, Michael Kellner, a prominent member of the Bundestag for the Greens, warned that re-establishing energy dependencies with Moscow would jeopardize the nation’s economic and democratic security.
“Germany must not become dependent on Russia again,” Kellner told German news channel ntv. “We must not repeat the mistakes of the energy crisis. It cost us €50 billion. We must not seek to return to that. This would be a betrayal. Putin is using the AfD for his own purposes.”
Senior CDU foreign policy lawmaker Roderich Kiesewetter echoed the criticism, warning that reopening energy corridors would isolate Germany within NATO and the EU.
“The AfD stands on Russia’s side and is ready to betray both Ukraine and Germany,” Kiesewetter stated. “Russia uses energy, including Nord Stream, as a hybrid weapon for military objectives. Resuming the operation of Nord Stream would be a disaster for European security and would lead to Germany’s isolation.”
Kiesewetter added that such consultations also risk exerting pressure on specific domestic political factions within Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democrats that have quietly advocated for a pragmatic return to purchasing discounted Russian hydrocarbons.
Merz’s defense commitments amid rising domestic populist pressure
The controversy arrives amid acute domestic political friction following regional state elections in Saxony-Anhalt, where the AfD achieved a historic triumph by capturing nearly 44% of the vote and falling just three seats short of an outright legislative majority.
Speaking at an Arctic security summit in Rovaniemi, northern Finland, Chancellor Friedrich Merz acknowledged that opposition to Berlin’s military and financial backing for Kyiv had become a primary electoral catalyst for AfD voters. However, the German leader reiterated that his administration will not alter its strategic commitments to Ukraine.
Merz emphasized that a Russian victory in Ukraine would carry “unpredicted and unprecedented consequences for all of us, including Germany,” insisting that European democracies cannot divorce immediate security imperatives from domestic political turbulence.
“That’s the reason why I’m standing here very firm, very clear, and not willing to go back one centimeter,” Merz stated, having previously ruled out any form of political cooperation or coalition agreements with the AfD at both regional and federal levels.

World Insights: Greater BRICS expands cooperation, amplifies Global South voice
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
18:27:05 CST
19:27:05 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 19 (Xinhua) -- Twenty years after its inception, BRICS has grown from an economic grouping into a broader platform for cooperation, with an expanding membership and a widening agenda spanning development, technology and global governance.
Following the recently concluded BRICS Summit in New Delhi, scholars said the grouping is opening up more opportunities for Global South countries to cooperate and increase their voice in global affairs.
FROM EXPANSION TO DEEPER COOPERATION
The BRICS cooperation mechanism was formally launched in 2006, with the first summit held in 2009. The grouping has since expanded its membership and cooperation agenda.
Today, BRICS members account for nearly half of the world's population, around 30 percent of global GDP and one-fifth of global trade.
"BRICS has not only expanded in membership but also deepened the scope of cooperation," said Mikatekiso Kubayi, senior researcher at the University of Johannesburg, pointing to areas such as energy, culture, transport, technology and security.
Marcus Vinicius De Freitas, visiting professor at China Foreign Affairs University and senior fellow at the Policy Center for the New South, a Moroccan think tank, described BRICS as an invaluable mechanism for managing differences and turning common interests into practical cooperation in an increasingly multipolar world.
"China is the driving force behind BRICS, yet its leadership is more consensual, reflecting its win-win perspective in foreign policy and global trade," he said.
A STRONGER COLLECTIVE VOICE
As BRICS has grown, so too has its potential to give developing countries a stronger voice in shaping global governance.
Gan Tian Loo, vice president of the Malaysia-China Public Relations Association, said BRICS countries have built consensus over the past two decades in responding to challenges including financial crises, the pandemic and unilateralism.
He said recent proposals place greater emphasis on contributing to discussions on global governance and promoting the equal application of international rules, an issue of particular relevance to the Global South.
"Acting collectively in discussions on global governance reform could give Global South countries greater bargaining power than pursuing such calls individually," Gan said.
Kubayi said this emphasis on the Global South reflects the original objectives of BRICS, including strengthening the voice of developing countries and promoting access to development instruments for developing and least developed countries.
"His continuous reference to the Global South is important because that's the whole purpose of BRICS in the first place," Kubayi said, referring to Chinese President Xi Jinping's remarks on BRICS cooperation.
At the summit, Xi called on BRICS to be a pioneer in advancing innovation-driven development, a pioneer in upholding peace and stability, a pioneer in facilitating mutual learning between civilizations, and a pioneer in reforming and improving global governance.
Julia Roknifard, senior lecturer at Taylor's University in Malaysia, said such initiatives could help build consensus among Global South countries through practical cooperation.
"Through the day-to-day support of each other in tech, health security, agriculture and other areas between BRICS full members, partner countries and the wider Global South, that is how they can strengthen their collective voice and influence," she said.
TURNING CONSENSUS INTO ACTION
As BRICS enters its third decade, the focus is increasingly shifting toward implementation.
Kubayi highlighted the five initiatives proposed by Xi for greater BRICS cooperation: open source and inclusive AI, trade and investment facilitation, digital industry cooperation, intelligent manufacturing cooperation, and science and technology talent development.
He pointed to AI as a field in which emerging economies want not merely to adopt new technologies but also to help shape how they are developed and governed.
"They should actively participate in shaping international frameworks and standards concerning AI safety, ethics, interoperability and governance," said Luan Camargo, executive director of the Institute for Brazil-China Business Research.
Economic cooperation is another area where such efforts are taking shape.
In Brazil, Maria Elena Rodriguez, deputy director of the BRICS Policy Center and professor at the Pontifical Catholic University of Rio de Janeiro, deems China a crucial partner for Brazil's ecological transition, including through investment in areas such as electric vehicles, photovoltaic equipment and green steel.
Camargo said sustainable development and innovation require peace and effective governance, while lasting multilateral partnerships also rely on people-to-people exchanges.
For BRICS, the next stage will therefore be measured not only by further expansion, but also by whether existing consensus can be translated into practical cooperation.
With China set to assume the BRICS chairmanship in 2027, Kubayi voiced hope that the Chinese chairmanship will give fresh impetus to translating the grouping's expanding agenda into action.
"We would expect a BRICS group that is a bit more buoyant about cooperation next year. That is clearly the agenda being placed on the table," he said. ■

SYDNEY, Sept. 19 (Xinhua) -- A shark that fatally attacked a swimmer at a beach in Western Australia (WA) on Friday will be caught and killed, the state fisheries minister said on Saturday.
A 63-year-old man was swimming at Sorrento Beach in the northern suburbs of the WA capital of Perth on Friday morning when he was attacked by a great white shark.
An emergency search was launched by sea and air for the victim, but he was declared deceased later on Friday.
Responding to the attack, Minister for Fisheries Jackie Jarvis on Saturday said she has issued a catch and kill order for the shark.
Capture gear was deployed on Friday and beaches in the area remained closed to the public on Saturday while authorities continued searching for the shark and the man's body.
Jarvis said it was the first time in 10 years that a catch and kill order had been issued for a shark in WA, but said that a widespread cull of sharks was not appropriate.
She said that deploying more drones to spot sharks along the state's coastline was under consideration. ■

More US troops died in Iran war than Pentagon disclosed – WaPo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
10:26:47 UTC
19:26:47 KST

More US troops died in Iran war than Pentagon disclosed – WaPo
The number of US service members who have died while deployed in the Middle East since the start of the Iran war is higher than the Pentagon’s public tally, the Washington Post reported on Friday, citing military sources. The Pentagon’s public casualty database may be missing as many as five military fatalities, according to the report.
As of Friday, the Pentagon’s Defense Casualty Analysis System (DCAS) listed 18 US military fatalities, including deaths from hostile and non-hostile action since the Iran war began on February 28.
Five sources, however, told the outlet there have been at least 22 military fatalities, while a sixth put the toll even higher, saying 23 service members have died since the war began. Not all of the additional deaths were directly tied to the conflict, the official said, but involved US personnel stationed in the Middle East amid the ongoing hostilities. Three US contractors based in the region have also died since combat operations began, the official added.
It is unclear whether the discrepancy was intended to downplay the war’s toll or stemmed from administrative procedures for classifying military deaths.
The US administration’s casualty accounting already faced scrutiny in July, when the Pentagon briefly removed four Iran war deaths from its public tally during a since-failed ceasefire – three troops killed in an Iranian missile strike on a US base in Jordan and another killed the next day during a controlled detonation of an Iranian drone in Iraq. The Pentagon blamed a data-processing error after the removals drew congressional scrutiny. The deaths later reappeared alongside some 207 wounded personnel, but under “Overseas Contingency Operations” rather than Operation Epic Fury, the administration’s name for the Iran war.
Separately, the Pentagon said two US service members have died in the Middle East since February on missions unrelated to the war. Sgt. Devin Seibel was killed in a training accident in Irbil, Iraq, on May 31, while Maj. Sorffly Davius died after an unspecified medical emergency in Kuwait on March 6. Neither is named in DCAS, despite dying at bases attacked by Iranian forces.
The Washington Post said the Pentagon declined to address its questions about the discrepancies.
Commenting on the report on X, US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth vehemently denied its authenticity, calling it “a complete LIE.”
“This is DISGUSTING and FAKE… Shame on the Washington Post – they’re worse than Iranian state media,” he wrote.

An increasingly unpopular war
Despite US President Donald Trump insisting the war has been a success – even claiming at times that “Americans aren’t against the war” – polling indicates growing public opposition. A September Reuters/Ipsos poll found 28% support Trump’s approach to Iran, while 62% disapprove.
The war has also deepened divisions in Congress ahead of the November midterms. Congressional Democrats have overwhelmingly opposed the conflict, making its multibillion-dollar cost and economic fallout – including gasoline prices approaching $5 a gallon – campaign issues. They have also pledged to investigate the Pentagon’s handling of casualty notifications if they retake the majority.
While most House Republicans have voted to block anti-war resolutions, some GOP lawmakers have broken ranks, backing bipartisan efforts to invoke war-powers restrictions or halt funding for the conflict. Representative Thomas Massie (KY) also moved this week to force a House vote on impeaching Hegseth, alleging he violated the War Powers Resolution of 1973 by pursuing hostilities without congressional authorization.
The war has cost the US $43.6 billion through September 3, including $28.1 billion in munitions expended, according to CENTCOM figures shared with lawmakers and the media on Friday. The total excludes extensive damage to US bases across eight Middle Eastern countries. Senior military officials reportedly warned Hegseth last month that prolonged large-scale operations against Iran were unsustainable.
Trump, however, insists the war will end soon, telling reporters last week it would likely stop immediately after the midterms. He told Axios on Thursday that he faces “a big decision” over whether to restart major combat operations to end the conflict.
Iran, meanwhile, has refused to cave to Trump’s threats, with Parliament Speaker and top negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf warning earlier this month of “faster, heavier and more painful” retaliation against further US aggression. On Friday, Tehran showcased a new volunteer force that will receive limited military and emergency training to support the IRGC. IRGC chief Hassan Hassanzadeh told state broadcaster IRIB that over 600,000 people had registered, with more than one million expected to undergo training.

Cambodia launches 30-mln-USD initiative to reduce e-waste in 5 years
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
18:26:46 CST
19:26:46 KST

PHNOM PENH, Sept. 19 (Xinhua) -- Cambodia's Ministry of Environment has launched a 30-million-U.S.-dollar initiative to improve electronic waste management and accelerate the country's transition to a circular economy, according to a joint press release on Saturday.
The five-year project is supported by 26 million dollars in co-financing from the Cambodian government and private partners, alongside a 4-million-dollar grant from the Global Environment Facility (GEF).
Developed in partnership with the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), the initiative aims to curb pollution and optimize resource use throughout the electronics value chain.
The initiative is projected to directly safeguard over 200,000 people by establishing safer working environments and reducing exposure to hazardous waste.
Additionally, the project targets a 27,000-tonne reduction in greenhouse gas emissions, the containment of toxic materials like mercury and persistent organic pollutants, and the prevention of more than 20,000 tonnes of pollutants from entering the environment.
"Our goal is to move from a linear 'take-make-dispose' model to a circular economy, one that values resources, reduces waste, and protects our people and environment," said Chuop Paris, secretary of state at the Ministry of Environment.
Enrico Gaveglia, the UNDP resident representative in Cambodia, highlighted the striking scale and pace of the country's growing electronics consumption.
With an estimated 24 million electronic devices in use across the nation in 2024, Gaveglia emphasized that end-of-life waste systems must keep pace. He noted that enhanced capabilities and strict safeguards are critical to protecting workers and local communities from toxic substances and unsafe recycling practices.
"This initiative supports the shift toward safer, practical systems that protect public health and strengthen the foundation for a more sustainable and resilient economy," he said.
Claude Gascon, interim CEO and chairperson of the GEF, warned that managing the environmental footprint of electronics will become increasingly difficult without robust systems.
"Addressing e-waste requires changes in how markets operate, alongside clearer policies and standards that support safer and more sustainable practices," he said. "This initiative is an important step toward building that foundation in Cambodia." ■

Researchers uncover gene driving blood cancer drug resistance
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
18:26:21 CST
19:26:21 KST

MELBOURNE, Sept. 19 (Xinhua) -- Researchers in Australia have uncovered a previously unknown gene that helps lymphoma cells resist a widely used blood cancer drug, along with several genes that accelerate lymphoma growth.
Researchers used a new CRISPR activation tool called Partita with a mouse model of aggressive lymphoma. Partita is a "library" that allows every gene in the mouse genome to be switched on individually in cellular and live models, according to a statement released Saturday by Australia's Olivia Newton-John Cancer Research Institute (ONJCRI).
Traditional CRISPR allows scientists to easily delete specific genes and assess their roles, while newer CRISPR activation enables specific genes to be switched on, offering insights into their roles in cancer and other genetic disorders, according to the study published in Science Advances.
Lymphoma comprises more than 80 subtypes and is the most common blood cancer in adults.
The team found that activating the gene Irx5 enabled cancer cells to survive treatment with venetoclax, a widely used blood cancer drug, by quietly boosting levels of a different survival protein.
A significant challenge in cancer care is treatment resistance. By identifying genes responsible for treatment resistance in tumors, researchers can develop new therapies to silence these genes and boost the efficacy of existing treatments.
The team also used Partita in live mice and identified Runx2, Runx3 and Csf1r as genes that accelerate the growth of MYC-driven lymphoma when activated.
"Currently, MYC-driven lymphomas are challenging to treat, and Partita helped find cancer-promoting genes that could be switched off to slow or stop tumor growth in these cancers," said study senior author John Eddie La Marca, a postdoctoral researcher at ONJCRI. ■

Trump claims son repaid Russian oligarch who funded wedding festivities
US President Donald Trump said Friday that his eldest son had repaid a Kremlin-linked Russian businessman who funded two days of lavish wedding celebrations in the Bahamas, after the gift raised questions over foreign influence and ethics.
US President Donald Trump said Friday that his eldest son had reimbursed a Kremlin-linked Russian businessman who paid for two days of wedding celebrations in the Bahamas in May.
Donald Trump Jr. and Bettina Trump confirmed on Monday that their "dear friend" Umar Kremlev "very generously hosted two incredible nights".
The lavish gift sparked questions about ethics and foreign influence.
"It's totally allowed but as I understand it, he paid him back," Trump said when an AFP reporter asked him in the Oval Office if it had been appropriate for his son to accept the gift.
"I guess a friend of his gave him a wedding party. That's very common, I've heard of many people giving wedding parties. I've given many parties."

Pressed on the fact that Don Jr. had not previously mentioned paying back Kremlev, Trump replied: "When I heard the story, I asked about it and he said 'No, I'm paying him back, Dad,' and that was a while ago, so I've heard he's paid him."
The wedding payment first emerged after the ProPublica investigative website reported that Kremlev footed the bill for the parties, paying hundreds of thousands of dollars.
Trump said at the time that he did not know Kremlev. He did not attend the wedding, saying he was too busy with talks on the Iran war.
Don Jr. and Bettina Trump had confirmed the gift in a joint Instagram post in which they defended it.
"It's unfortunate that something so personal and happy can be recast as something political or sinister simply because of who someone is or where they come from," the post added.
Kremlev is head of the International Boxing Association (IBA), with which the International Olympic Committee severed links after repeated warnings over financial governance and ethical concerns.
Russian President Vladimir Putin presented Kremlev with the "Order of Friendship" award in April 2026, according to an IBA press release, which featured a photo of Putin and Kremlev shaking hands.
The IBA website also featured photos of Donald Trump Jr. on stage with Kremlev at an event in Istanbul in September 2025.
ProPublica posted a group photo from the wedding that it said showed the top of Kremlev's head.
According to Russian investigative media outlet Proekt, Kremlev is a Tajik native who worked as a mid-level boxing promoter and cultivated links with the Federal Protective Service (FSO), whose role is to protect high-level officials in Russia.
Kremlev is also a member of the pro-Kremlin Night Wolves biker club, it reported.
The Night Wolves rode en masse to Ukraine's Crimea peninsula just after it was annexed by Russia in March 2014, and members have also fought side by side with pro-Russian separatists in eastern Ukraine.
During his first term, President Trump faced an investigation into alleged collusion between his 2016 election campaign and Russia, which the Republican billionaire branded a "witch hunt".

Russia is trying to sell the world an image of a great power, but “global leadership” exists only in Kremlin statements — intelligence
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
13:25:46 EEST
19:25:46 KST

Russia is trying to sell the world an image of a great power, but “global leadership” exists only in Kremlin statements — intelligence
Kyiv • UNN
Only 26% of respondents in 34 countries support Russia’s leading role in the world. 42% consider it a serious threat to their countries.
Moscow is trying to sell the world an image of a great power without which, supposedly, it is impossible to resolve international problems; however, “global leadership” exists only in Kremlin statements. This was reported by the Foreign Intelligence Service of Ukraine, as reported by UNN.
Details
Russia is trying to sell the world an image of a great power without which, supposedly, it is impossible to resolve international problems. However, the results of a survey conducted in July–August 2026 in 34 countries commissioned by the Rockefeller Foundation show a different picture. Only 26% of respondents are prepared to view Russia’s leading role in world affairs positively. Half of respondents view such leadership negatively. In developed countries, support for Russia’s role is just 13%
It is noted that what is even worse for Moscow is that a significant part of the world perceives Russia not as a leader, but as a threat. On average, 42% of respondents called it a serious danger to their own country. In Poland, the figure is 78%; in Norway and Sweden, 73% each; in the United Kingdom, 67%; and in France and Germany, 64% each.
Particularly telling is the gap between Europe’s perception of Russia and Russia’s own view of itself. For years, the Kremlin has tried to impose the notion of the Russian Federation as a state that sets the rules of international politics. Instead, in a significant part of Europe, it is viewed primarily as a source of military threat
Russian propaganda traditionally tries to compensate for its isolation in the West with claims of support from the countries of the Global South. But here, too, the picture is far from the Kremlin’s version. In developing countries, only 40% of respondents are prepared to view Russia’s leading role positively. In other words, even there Moscow does not secure majority support for its claims to global leadership.
The Kremlin can call Russia a “center of power” and claim to be shaping a new world order as much as it likes. Outside Russia’s propaganda bubble, these ambitions have little public support. For a significant part of the world, Russia is neither a model of development nor a desirable global leader, but a state from which threats and conflicts are expected
Previously
With the start of the main stage of voting in the pseudo-elections to the Russian State Duma, Russian propaganda launched a large-scale information campaign, attempting to create the illusion of a mass “patriotic upsurge” in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine.

Michael Marra elected as Scottish Labour leader
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
10:24:47 UTC
19:24:47 KST

Scottish Labour’s new leader Michael Marra has backed the development of the Rosebank and Jackdaw oil and gasfields in the North Sea in one of his first acts after being elected, calling for a “more rational” approach to energy policy.
On Saturday, the MSP for North East Scotland won a near two-thirds majority to lead the party in Holyrood, becoming Scottish Labour’s 11th leader. He replaces Anas Sarwar after his shock decision to resign in July to join Andy Burnham’s new government as a trade minister.
Dundee-born Marra said he would urge the British prime minister to back both fossil fuel projects despite warnings over their environmental impact. Neither is covered by the ban on new licences for drilling in the North Sea because their applications were already in the system when the Labour government took power, and there is growing expectation that ministers will approve the Jackdaw gasfield in the coming weeks.
“I want Rosebank and Jackdaw to be approved,” Marra told reporters shortly after his election. “It’s the biggest issue in my region in terms of people’s voting intention. We need to have a more rational policy position that delivers for the Scottish economy and Scottish jobs.”
In his acceptance speech at the Dynamic Earth science museum in Edinburgh, Marra said he would spend time reconnecting with Scottish voters after a bruising defeat in this year’s elections.
“May hurt so much because we know the SNP didn’t deserve a fifth term in power. But the truth is Scotland didn’t think we would be much better,” he said.
“Scots know what we are against. They can’t tell you what we are for. And that vacuum was filled by the poison, racism and bigotry of Reform. We must be clear in our values. We must lead with our values,” he said.
“For a decade now, Scotland has gotten weaker. We must reconnect with the country if we are ever to form a government in Holyrood to face these historic challenges.”
Marra faces an uphill battle to reverse the party’s fortunes in Scotland. While 37 Labour MPs from Scotland sit in Westminster, the party has lost seats at every Holyrood election since devolution in 1999.
In May, the party suffered its worst ever results – winning just 17 seats as the SNP retained power. Labour has as many seats as Reform in Holyrood, just two more than the Scottish Green party and five more than the Conservatives.
In a subdued campaign with few policy differences between candidates, both Marra and his main rival, Joe Fagan, were criticised for struggling to outline the circumstances in which Scotland should be allowed a second independence referendum.
Marra said that he thought the party had become overly focused on middle-class voters in Scotland, and vowed to build a broader electoral coalition that was centred on the needs of the country.
When asked again about the level of public support that would mean Scotland should have a second independence reference, Marra said the SNP’s failure to get an outright majority in Holyrood in May signalled that it was not a priority for voters.
“The people of Scotland do not want a referendum right now. We will continue to make the case for a stronger Scotland in a changing UK. It’s imperative to me that we are not in this for the status quo. I’m in this to make sure that we can see a stronger Scotland,” he said.
In total, 6,751 votes were cast in the leadership election, representing 49.43% of the Scottish Labour party membership. Fagan won 2,485 votes, while Marra won 4,266.
Dr Eric Shaw, a research fellow at the University of Stirling who co-authored The Strange Death of Labour in Scotland, said the party had to reconnect with working-class voters to win back support.
“The party is facing three main issues: the continued salience of independence, the association between Scottish Labour and Labour in Westminster, and the erosion of Labour’s historic base in Scotland. The plight of the party is reflected in the fact that Labour did better among the professional middle class than it did in the working class in the most recent election.”
Dr Ewan Gibbs, a lecturer in economic and social history at the University of Glasgow, said the new leader had to ask difficult questions about who the party was meant to represent in Scotland.
“We are approaching 20 years of failure with the government in Holyrood if we look at the performance of public services, educational attainment, ongoing income and wealth inequality in Scotland. But Scottish Labour isn’t a party that seems equipped to mobilise that opposition and disappointment at the moment.”

From Human Reasoning to Belief: An Empirical Account
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
10:23:00 UTC
19:23:00 KST

Joshua Mugg’s book, From Human Reasoning to Belief: An Empirical Account draws on a vast empirical literature to develop and defend a single-process theory (SPT) of human reasoning against popular dual-process theories (DPT). In the second half of the book, it leverages its SPT to help explain various empirical results from belief and belief formation.
DPTs have cropped up in virtually every part of psychological and neural science (Evans & Stanovich, 2013; De Neys, 2021). They distinguish between Type-1 processing, which is often described as “fast”, “intuitive”, “automatic”, etc., and Type-2 processing, which is often described as “slow”, “reflective”, “controlled”, etc. The labels ‘Type-1’ and ‘Type-2’ are fashionable today because they maintain neutrality on different characterisations of the distinction. The common commitment, as Mugg points out, is that the distinction, whatever it is, “is supposed to cut cognition itself in two” (19).
However, Mugg notes that DPT has been engaged in a steady retreat for decades. At first, DPT was associated with massively conjunctive claims, like that cognition itself was cut into two, where one side consisted of processes that are fast and intuitive and automatic, etc. and the other side consisted of processes that are slow and reflective and controlled, etc. Mugg notes that these are most charitably interpreted as statistical, clustering claims (a laSamuels, 2009). This is often known as “Standard Menu” DPT.
Decades of functional dissociation studies have called this view into question: it’s proven easy to find processes that are fast but reflective, slow but intuitive, etc. So, dual-process theorists have retreated to what I’ll call “Essentialised” formulations of DPT: cognition itself is cut into two, where one part has one property, and the other part lacks that property. For example, Evans suggests that Type-1 processing doesn’t involve working memory, while Type-2 does (Evans & Stanovich, 2013). Since Essentialised DPT makes no clustering claims, it is quite resistant to functional dissociation studies.
The retreat from Standard Menu DPT to Essentialised DPT is cause for concern, though. It is reminiscent of what Lakatos (1970) calls a “degenerative” research program. It started off making many specific predictions, which were then falsified. In response, DPT has protected its core theoretical commitment (that cognition itself is split in two) by reducing the empirical content of its auxiliary hypotheses (rejecting conjunctive claims about Type-1 and Type-2 processing), resulting in fewer, less specific predictions (as in Essentialised DPT). (To be clear, I’m not saying that DPT is degenerative—just that it’s reasonable to worry it is.)
The apparent degeneracy of Mugg’s target, DPT, puts him at a significant advantage since he aims to defend a particular instance of single process theory (SPT), which he calls the “Soundboard Account of Reasoning”. Unfortunately, I worry that his account squanders some of its advantage: the first half of the book presses objections against DPT that seem to be mutually inconsistent, and then halfway through the book, Mugg shifts his focus from human reasoning to belief. The beleaguered DPT will live to see another day, I suspect.
Chapter 1 lays out some of Mugg’s starting commitments. He endorses Craver- and Khalidi-style weakenings of Boyd’s account of (natural) kinds (Boyd, 1991; Craver, 2009; Khalidi, 2023). He endorses the view that belief is a kind in this sense—i.e., it is individuated (at least partly) by a cluster of functional properties. It’s a bit difficult to tell from this stage why all this matters, but I think this chapter was meant to provide connective tissue between Chapters 2 and 3 (which focus on cognitive architecture) and Chapters 4–6 (which focus on belief).
Chapter 2 is more focused. Most of this chapter is dedicated to reviewing experimental literature on DPT. His review does well to highlight DPT’s (apparent) degeneracy—although the Lakatosian framing is mine, not his. Consistent with my Lakatosian framing of DPT’s problem, though, Mugg opts to present its problem in the form of a dilemma.
The first horn is Standard Menu DPT. It is rich in empirical content, so it makes bold, testable claims. The problem is just that these claims are widely disproven. Standard Menu DPT is interesting but empirically inadequate, then. The second horn is Essentialised DPT. It rejects the inadequate empirical content of Standard Menu DPT, but at the cost of explanatory power. Essentialised DPT is empirically adequate, but uninteresting (non-explanatory).
Even if we think Essentialised DPT is a retreat from Standard Menu DPT, it isn’t obvious that this is untoward in any way. Rejecting clustering claims is probably a good idea. Why not think, as Evans & Stanovich (2013) clearly seem to, that Essentialised DPT is a disciplining of Standard Menu DPT’s excesses? It’s not enough to say, as Mugg does, that this retreat “reduces the explanatory power of DPT” (31). Giving up some explanatory power for a lot more plausibility and empirical adequacy might be a perfectly acceptable bargain for DPT.
However, it seems like Mugg wants to say that Essentialised DPT has no explanatory power at all. At one point, for example, he complains how “it becomes unclear how to test these nuanced versions of DPT” (33). At another point, he even says that “the Logical Intuition Model renders itself compatible with the results at the cost of making the theory explanatorily and predictively inert” (35–36). If true, this is a serious problem. No amount of plausibility and empirical adequacy would be worth that much sacrifice in explanatory power.
Suppose Mugg is right. Essentialised DPT has no empirical content. All that’s left to it would be two bare claims about type-individuation: (a) some processes have a property-like access to working memory, while others don’t and (b) that property difference is sufficient for them to be different types of processes. Mugg appears to disagree with the latter claim, since he goes in for clustering accounts of types, such that we can change the type a cognitive process belongs to only by making sufficiently large changes to sufficiently many of its properties.
If that’s right, then Mugg’s disagreement with Essentialised DPT is metaphysical, not empirical. But then it’s strange that Mugg attempts to give an empirical argument against DPT at all (via inference to the best explanation). We can expect an empirical argument to work against Standard Menu DPT (since it has empirical content), but it shouldn’t work against Essentialised DPT. If Mugg does want to disagree with DPT on empirical grounds (as seems to), then he’d need to clearly attribute empirical content to DPT.
Chapter 3 introduces Mugg’s Soundboard Account of Reasoning. His account is centred on a metaphor: that reasoning has a soundboard architecture that is modulated with knobs and switches. Put literally, reasoning is such that it can be adequately characterised by dynamical functions over independent parameters, continuous (“knobs”) and/or discrete (“switches”). It’s the independence of the parameters that distinguishes this view from Standard Menu DPT (which maintains clustering and hence, dependence between the parameters).
As Mugg notes in Chapter 2, though, most dual-process theorists today endorse Essentialised DPT. By itself, though, the Soundboard Account is fully consistent with Essentialised DPT, which agrees that the parameters are independent. Essentialised DPT just insists on an additional commitment—that one parameter is privileged, such that changing the value of that parameter (but not any other parameter) makes a type-difference to the whole reasoning process (this works best if the parameter is discrete).
Mugg anticipates this worry:
One might think that I am…retaining diachronic Type 1 and Type 2 processing, which really makes the Soundboard Account a specific version of default-interventionist DPT. This is not so. Initial responses (as a category) and subsequent responses (as a category) will be too heterogeneous on the Soundboard Account to constitute kinds or serve as helpful constructs because the properties on the Standard Menu crosscut one another on my account, even for initial settings. (43)
However, this response begs the question against Essentialised DPT, which rejects that initial responses must have a different cluster of properties than subsequent responses in order to belong to different types of processes.
I think it would have been better if Mugg had just granted the metaphysical claim that default vs. intervening processing would be different types if the former were diachronically separated from the latter (perhaps by a discrete event like metacognitive control), and then he could insist that the empirical evidence suggests there is no discrete distinguishing event like this, and hence, there is no type-difference between default vs. intervening processing. For example, Grayot et al. (forthcoming) press an empirical objection like this against my proposed formulation of Essentialised DPT (Rumana, 2023).
Chapters 4–6 take a significant turn. Mugg stops critiquing DPT and starts critiquing various accounts of belief formation: Chapter 4 criticises Spinozan accounts of belief formation, Chapter 5 criticises conventional explanations of implicit bias results, and Chapter 6 criticises doxastic involuntarism.
In personal correspondence, Mugg has clarified that he meant to show that we “can indirectly test competing accounts of belief by tying them to cognitive architectures”.[1] As such, his Soundboard Account is meant to provide a standard by which to arbitrate different accounts of belief. Since many accounts of belief draw support from outdated formulations of DPT (like Tamar Gendler’s account of aliefs), I think he’s quite right that support for these accounts can be undercut by reiterating criticisms against these forms of DPT. Therefore, I would encourage readers (especially readers interested in belief and belief formation) to read Chapters 4–6 in light of this.
Nevertheless, the book itself provides a different (and less plausible) justification for these chapters: “my aim in [Chapter 3] was not to argue for the Soundboard Account, but merely to build the theory. My argument for the theory will come as an inference to the best explanation [in Chapters 4–6]” (61). My review will take the book at its word that the Soundboard Account draws its justification from the content of Chapters 4–6 (especially since no other justification is provided for it, at least relative to Essentialised DPT).
I doubt the content of Chapters 4–6 can justify the Soundboard Account, though. First, Mugg himself admits that (at least some of) the accounts he criticises could also be couched in terms of his Soundboard Account (65). That seems true for all the accounts. Prima facie, that might seem like a problem for Mugg: if the Soundboard Account is equally compatible with all accounts of belief formation, how could confirming any account of belief formation confirm the Soundboard Account? One would start to worry that this is a real-life case of Clark Glymour’s (1980) tacking problem.
Mugg endorses Elliott Sober’s (1999) contrastive account of confirmation (fn. 4, p. 15), so perhaps he could forestall this objection by taking his explanations of belief formation to confirm his Soundboard Account against DPT, but not to confirm the Soundboard Account tout court. If that’s right, then confirming his account of belief formation can confirm the Soundboard Account against DPT only if his account of belief formation is better accommodated by the Soundboard Account than by DPT. Mugg suggests that it is, but he only considers the Standard Menu DPT (whose empirical inadequacy is already well-known).
Again, though, Essentialised DPT seems equally capable of accommodating accounts of belief formation, since empirical explanations of belief are neutral to type individuation. Thus, it’s hard to see how various explanations of belief formation can help arbitrate the disagreement between SPT and DPT. As a result, Chapters 4–6 may read like a long digression if you, like most dual-process theorists today, are more interested in the viability of Essentialised DPT (and if you take the content of these chapters to be justification for the Soundboard Account against DPT).
Chapter 7 tries to wrap everything up. It’s clear from this conclusion that the focus of the book has shifted from human reasoning to (various observations about) belief (and its formation). I’m left thinking that the title “From human reasoning to belief” should be taken as a literal description of the book’s focus. Perhaps, it’s unfair that my review hasn’t been more willing to follow this shift. I do expect this book can inspire a reader with interests in both belief and human reasoning to see the explanatory relationships between them. Either way, this book does not provide the sustained critique of DPT and empirical argument for the Soundboard Account that it promises.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – Taiwan and the US for the first time co-sponsored a Global Cooperation and Training Framework workshop in Kosovo, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs said Saturday.

IT Coalition allocates over €1.8B to support Ukraine’s Defense Forces
The Ministry of Defense reported this, according to Ukrinform.
“The IT Coalition is marking its third anniversary. Over this period, Ukraine and 17 partner countries have joined forces to strengthen communications, cybersecurity, IT infrastructure and digital systems used by the Defense Forces,” the Ministry said.
According to the Ministry, partners have allocated €1.85 billion to support Ukraine through the IT Coalition over the past three years.
The largest share of the funding – €728 million – has been used to procure broadband radio communications equipment. Another €445 million has been allocated for satellite communications. Partners are also providing equipment for tactical-level command posts, supporting cybersecurity units of the Ministry of Defense and the Armed Forces, and helping develop data centers, cloud infrastructure and tactical networks.
IT Coalition partners also support the Army+, Reserve+, DELTA, Impulse, SAP and other digital defense systems.
The partners have funded training in international cybersecurity standards for more than 1,200 participants, as well as nearly 200 vouchers for SANS Institute courses. They also support innovative projects, including Drone ID, and are testing their technological solutions in Ukraine, particularly in the field of communications.
For 2026–2027, the Coalition will focus on providing secure radio and satellite communications, resilient IT infrastructure and cybersecurity.
As reported, Estonia has pledged €3.5 million through the IT Coalition to provide Starlink systems to Ukraine and strengthen its IT capabilities amid the war.
The IT Coalition is one of the Capability Coalitions within the Ukraine Defense Contact Group, also known as the Ramstein format. It supports the Armed Forces of Ukraine and the Ministry of Defense in IT, communications and cybersecurity.
The IT Coalition currently includes Belgium, Denmark, Ireland, Iceland, Spain, Italy, Canada, Latvia, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Germany, the United Kingdom, Finland, Sweden, Japan and Ukraine. Estonia and Luxembourg are the coalition’s leaders.

The State Duma election, the first since Russia launched its full-scale war in February 2022, is widely expected to see the ruling pro-Putin United Russia party retain its dominance in Russia’s tightly controlled political system.
Most anti-war candidates were excluded from the ballot before voting across Russia’s 11 time zones got under way, after the Supreme Court ruled in August that the liberal Yabloko party, which wants a ceasefire in Ukraine, breached electoral rules, something it denied.
Some Yabloko candidates, however, are still contesting single-member constituencies, which account for half of the 450 seats in the Lower House of Parliament. The party has traditionally polled in the single digits.
On Sept 19, the authorities said the online voting system in Moscow was subjected to a strong attack overnight, but that the situation was under control.
The attacks were continuing, Central Election Commission (CEC) chairwoman Ella Pamfilova was cited as saying by state media, but all were being successfully repelled.
Russia’s digital ministry said it registered a sabotage attempt on communication lines in the country’s Far East, but that the attack was thwarted, and all communication had been restored, state media reported.
President Vladimir Putin earlier accused Ukraine of trying to interfere with the vote, without providing evidence.

Deflating Mental Representations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
10:18:00 UTC
19:18:00 KST

I found this book illuminating. A font of fresh ideas, it challenges the currently dominant Representational Theory of Mind and develops an alternative account of mental states and processes that is worthy of close attention. I was not in the end persuaded by its main claims, but I came away feeling that I had learned a lot in thinking about those claims and evaluating them. The book also offers some ancillary benefits, such as an outstandingly clear account of the nature and scope of computational cognitive science.
The principal claim of the Representational Theory of Mind can be expressed as follows:
RTM: A wide range of mental items (including every propositional attitude, every concept, and every perceptual state) constitutively involve mental representations that are directed on, or represent, objects, properties, events, or states of affairs.
Adherents hold that RTM captures a key architectural assumption of folk psychology and contemporary cognitive science, and they advocate a robustly realistic reading of it, according to which the mind really is populated by mental representations, and representations really are the objects over which the cognitive processes postulated by folk psychology and cognitive science are defined. Contemporary versions of RTM allow that mental representations can take many forms—sentences, images, simulations, maps, place cells, and so on—but they agree that representations of all these kinds bear forms of the generic relation X represents Y to portions of extra-mental reality. Most advocates seek to naturalize this relation by explaining it reductively—that is, without using any semantic, intentional, or normative concepts. It is acknowledged on all sides that a fully satisfactory reduction has yet to be found, but many advocates think that a successful reduction is gradually emerging in the current literature (e. g., Neander, 2017; Shea, 2018).
Egan’s main objection to this picture is that attempts to explain the relation X represents Y are never naturalistic in the advertised sense. They aim to honor the intuition that each representational vehicle has a unique content, but there are always multiple candidates for the role of content, and selection among them is determined pragmatically—that is, by the explanatory interests of the relevant theorist—rather than naturalistically. Consider, for example, Neander’s attempt to show that a certain representational vehicle V in the toad’s optic tectum represents the complex of low-level properties moving worm-shaped object rather than a higher-level ecological property such as nutrient (Neander, 2017). In making her case, Neander points out that attributing the lower-level content to V better serves the purpose of describing the causal process that supports the toad’s feeding behavior. After all, experiments show that a toad will gobble up any moving worm-shaped object it perceives, regardless of whether the object is nutritious.
It follows that the properties moving and worm-shaped are triggers of the process that eventuates in V, and that nutrient makes no proprietary contribution to the process, but is merely co-instantiated with the properties that actually do the causal work. As Egan points out, however, a biologist whose dominant theoretical interest is in explaining the toad’s survival and flourishing in its ecological niche would have an equally strong reason to say that the vehicle V represents nutrient or a niche-equivalent property such as toad food. On what basis could a representationalist philosopher or scientist decide between these two competing hypotheses about the content of V? Egan’s answer appears to be that there are no naturalistic facts that provide such a basis. Rather, preference for one hypothesis over the other can only be justified by context-dependent pragmatic considerations, and in particular, by the explanatory goals of the person making the choice. Someone interested in explaining how the toad’s perceptual system works would prefer the moving worm-shaped object hypothesis, while someone interested in explaining how the toad manages to survive would prefer the nutrient hypothesis. This being so, she concludes, neither claim “will naturalize content in the advertised sense, inasmuch as the content attributed has a pragmatic rationale” (28).
According to Egan, then, representata are not determined naturalistically. Prima facie, this thesis calls the naturalistic credentials of the whole representationalist enterprise into question. Intuitively, however, representationalist explanations of behavior can be extremely illuminating and may even be conceptually necessary, given that naturalistic explanations in terms of neural states and processes are likely to be forbiddingly complex. Can Egan’s anti-naturalist conclusion be reconciled somehow with this observation about the value of representationalist explanations? She thinks it can. Her account of how this is possible begins with a distinction between a scientific theory proper and a gloss that scientists add to the theory.
To illustrate, in the case of the prey-catching behavior of the toad, a theory proper would consist of a naturalistic specification of a physical process involving a mechanism M in the toad’s brain that takes visually acquired information about a distal stimulus S as input and yields a protrusion of the toad’s tongue as output, where S is the target of the protruded tongue. A representationalist gloss on M would designate a state R of M as a mental representation and would add that R represents the external stimulus S. The gloss would therefore make contact with key components of the causal process running from S to the protruded tongue, and could therefore be said to track or model an illuminating physical explanation of the toad’s prey-capturing behavior.
But the gloss would not be unique. One possible gloss would claim that R represents S as a moving worm-shaped object, and another would claim that R represents S as a nutrient. Since, according to Egan, the physical facts of the case would be neutral between these two interpretations of them, we have an example of how representationalist glosses can have explanatory value without being naturalistically determined. A choice between them could only be motivated by the explanatory goals of scientists providing the glosses.
After providing an eagle’s eye view of her proposal in the first half of the book, Egan turns in the second half to examining representationalist accounts of three prominent cognitive domains, arguing in each case that it would be a mistake to view the account as literally true, but maintaining that each account is illuminating when understood to be a representationalist gloss on a set of physical facts. The domains are propositional attitudes, bodily sensations, and visual experiences. Unfortunately, space limitations preclude discussion of Egan’s views about more than one of these domains. I will focus here on what she has to say about propositional attitudes, but her ideas about bodily sensations and visual experiences are different and no less worthy of consideration.
Egan’s proposal about attitudes is complex, but for purposes of this review it can be simplified as follows. Consider an agent who possesses a functional architecture that conforms to the requirements of folk psychology. Thus, the agent has internal states that are linked to each other, and to external stimuli and types of behavior, by a system of causal relations that meets those requirements. Suppose also, however, that the agent only weakly realizes folk psychology because the states in question are individuated purely in terms of causal relations, with intentional contents playing no role. Given this restriction, it can’t be literally true that the states count as beliefs and other intentional states; but even so, we can use terms like “belief*” and “desire*” in describing the agent, provided that we thereby mean only that the so-designated states have the causal roles attributed to beliefs and desires by folk psychology. Egan would, I think, regard a theory of the agent that is guided by these assumptions as a theory proper of the agent’s mind. (Egan does not use starred terms like “belief*,” but they are useful tools for streamlining the exposition. Their use is warranted because we are considering a functionally defined structure with states that meet the causal conditions specified by folk psychology, which assigns differentiating causal roles to the class of beliefs, the class of desires, and so on.)
As I interpret Egan, a gloss on this theory would take the form of a function F mapping sentences of a spoken and written language to the agent’s belief*s, desire*s, and so on. The mapping would associate sentences with attitude*-states in such a way that inferential relations defined over the sentences would correspond uniquely to causal relations among the belief*-states and desire*-states. Thus, for example, if the F-images of sentences of the following forms were belief*-states:
If P, then Q.
P
those belief*-states would have a strong tendency to cause the belief*-state corresponding to Q under F. Here the sentences would have truth conditions and syntactic properties in the literal sense, but their images under F would not.
To appreciate that the theory proper we have been considering admits of multiple representationalist glosses, we need only recall that representational contents are not uniquely determined by causal relations. This is shown, for example, by the causal chain problem, which points out that if a mental state has one external cause, then it has many. In more positive terms, it is shown by the fact that friends of representationalism like Neander and Shea find it necessary to supplement appeals to causal relations with appeals to more complex properties in analyzing the relation X represents Y. (Readers of Neander and Shea will remember that Neander appeals to information functions in analyzing this relation, and that Shea appeals to stabilized task functions. (Neander, 2017; Shea, 2018)) Now as we saw, the internal states specified by our theory proper are individuated purely by causal relations to each other, to external stimuli, and behavior. It follows that if we want to map sentences with determinate truth conditions onto our agent’s attitude*s, we will have to make a choice among possible mappings that is not determined by the causal facts. Egan would say that pragmatic considerations provide the only possible basis for such a choice.
I have several reservations about the foregoing components of Egan’s position.
First, I worry about her initial argument that it is pragmatic considerations rather than naturalistic factors that determine the acceptability of hypotheses about representational contents. As becomes apparent on inspection, the argument presupposes that representationalism is committed to the following two theses:
(1) There is just one representation relation binding mental states to representata.
(2) Pairs of hypotheses about content like these:
(i) Mental state S represents the property-complex moving and worm-shaped object.
(ii) Mental state S represents the property nutrient.
are in competition to specify the unique representatum of a given mental state.
Given these presuppositions about the commitments of representationalism, a naturalistic version of representationalism would have to provide a naturalistic basis for choosing between the two hypotheses. As Egan sees the situation, however, there is no such naturalistic basis for choice. On her view, the principal difference between the hypotheses has to do with what they can be used to explain: the first hypothesis contributes to explaining how a visuo-behavioral mechanism works, and the second hypothesis contributes to explaining how the toad survives in its niche. Accordingly, giving preference to one of the hypotheses depends on the explanatory goals of a philosopher or toad scientist, which means that it depends on contextual pragmatic factors.
I have concerns about this argument because I see no reason to think that representationalism is committed to (1) and (2). It seems entirely compatible with the spirit of representationalism to allow that there are two or more representation relations linking internal states with properties of external objects, where each of these relations can be explained in naturalistic terms. To accommodate the case at hand, for example, we might distinguish between causal mechanism representation and ecological significance representation, perhaps explaining the first in terms of the teleo-causal apparatus that Neander presents (2017), and the second in terms of the ecological apparatus that Millikan constructs (1989). (Both of these proposals are fully in keeping with the requirements of naturalism.) It follows from this that hypotheses like (i) and (ii) are not in competition. Indeed, they can both be true, provided that they are understood to be concerned with different representation relations. To be sure, if a theorist chooses between them, the ground of her choice will no doubt be pragmatic, having to do with her explanatory interests, but she could choose both if her interests were sufficiently broad. After all, they can both be true. Moreover, there is nothing special about a situation in which a scientist bases a choice between true hypotheses on explanatory interests. That is in fact how scientists generally proceed when confronted with pairs of true hypotheses, and they do so without in any sense deflating their theories. (Representational pluralism is advocated at length in Hill, 2022.)
Second, I have apprehensions about Egan’s treatment of propositional attitudes. One reason for worry is that she assumes without explanation that the natural language sentences that model functionally defined belief*-states and desire*-states have a full share of meaning, including truth conditions. It seems that if the idea of mental states with representational contents is problematic, the idea of syntactically individuated sentences with truth conditions should be equally problematic. Also, functions like the function F cited five paragraphs ago are not well defined. As we saw, given an inference involving premises P1,…,Pn and conclusion C, F is supposed to map these sentences onto belief*-states B1,…,Bn+1 just in case B1,…,Bn cause Bn+1. But there will be many sets of n + 1 belief*-states that meet this weak causal condition.
Egan’s deflationary account of the representational contents of beliefs is quite different than her accounts of bodily sensations and perceptual experiences. The present concerns about the former account do not apply to either of the latter. However, the earlier point about multiple representation relations would seem to raise general questions about the motivation for Egan’s deflationary project as a whole.
REFERENCES
Hill, C. S. (2022). Perceptual Experience. (Oxford: Oxford University Press).
Millikan, R. G. (1989a). “Biosemantics,” Journal of Philosophy 86: 281–97.
Neander, K. (2017). A Mark of the Mental: In Defense of Informational Teleosemantics. (Cambridge, MA: MIT Press).
Shea, N. (2018). Representation in Cognitive Science. (Oxford: Oxford University Press).

Swiss commodities association rejects windfall tax on profits

Unknown Publisher

Swiss commodities association rejects windfall tax on profits
Suissenégoce, the association of Swiss companies active in the commodities trade – primarily oil – and in maritime transport, rejects any suggestion of additional taxation on the profits of companies in the sector.
“Taxing profits more heavily is not a good idea, because companies already pay a huge amount in taxes – we’re talking about hundreds of millions of francs,” says Secretary General Florence Schurch in an interview with the AWP news agency. “Finance Minister Karin Keller-Sutter even said that the government had been able to balance its budget thanks to tax revenue from Geneva [where many traders are based].”
In her view, companies in the sector “are rewarded for the work they do, but they are by no means responsible for what happens in the world, nor for the price at the petrol pump, which also depends on refining costs, transport costs, exchange rates and excise duties.”
More
Report sees key role for Switzerland in commodities trading
The interview also touched on the context of tensions in the Middle East, with the drastic reduction in oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz and, more recently, through the Strait of Bab el-Mandeb, which has been blocked by the Houthis.
“In Switzerland, there is no risk of a shortage, thanks on the one hand to our strategic reserves and on the other to the fact that we are a country that can absorb price rises more easily than others. When oil is less accessible in certain parts of the world, the role of traders is to source supplies from other countries, such as Norway, Africa or the United States. The risk lies rather in a rise in prices, because there is less oil available.”
“It is impossible to say how high prices might rise because one cannot predict unforeseeable events,” said Schurch. “Prices depend on the market and are subject to random and variable factors.”
“Even more than the rise in prices itself, it is the duration of this increase that causes problems. Fortunately, under the law, our country has oil reserves. And if Switzerland were to buy it on the market at high prices, it could do so,” she added.
Furthermore, if fuel prices were to become too high, Schurch said the government has complete freedom to lower fuel taxes.
“It must be borne in mind that 50% of the price of petrol comes from taxation,” she added.
With regard to the Cressier refinery, which supplies around 30% of the country’s fuel, the government has authorised a drawdown from the reserves.
“These strategic reserves are precisely intended to be used in the event of a problem,” said Schurch. “The federal authorities have acted as envisaged in the event of an extraordinary situation – which is what we are seeing today, as various factors have come together. In particular, the water levels in the Rhine are too low for ships carrying fossil fuels to be fully loaded. Drawing on these reserves was the simplest solution.”
More
Iran-US: the stakes of disruption at Hormuz for Switzerland
“This episode clearly demonstrates the need to have refineries within the country, as well as our gas reserves,” she said.
As far as transport routes are concerned, the situation is complicated.
“In the Persian Gulf, traders are transporting oil by lorry across the entire Arabian Peninsula to reach the Red Sea and find ships, as the pipeline running through Saudi Arabia has currently been hit by bombing. All this obviously drives up prices, because it involves a massive logistical operation and entails high insurance costs.”
“People often wonder why companies trading in raw materials make such high profits, but they are far less aware of the fact that, thanks to them, the Swiss population has no supply problems and will be able to keep warm this winter,” concluded Schurch.

The US spent a month approving Germany’s transfer of 10 Patriot missiles to Ukraine
Kyiv • UNN
Germany received US approval to transfer 10 PAC-2 GEM-T missiles worth $29.6 million to Ukraine only after a month. The munitions may be enough for one massive attack.
It took the United States a month to approve the transfer to Ukraine of 10 PAC-2 GEM-T surface-to-air missiles for Patriot systems from Germany. Berlin submitted the request back on August 14, but received authorization to re-export the American missiles only a month later, Defense Express reports, writes UNN.
Details
The total cost of the 10 missiles is $29.6 million. PAC-2 GEM-T missiles have a range of up to 160 km and are primarily intended to counter aircraft and cruise missiles.
The delay is related to the U.S. procedure for the re-export of weapons: the U.S. Congress has 30 days to review the proposed transfer and the ability to block it.
The transfer could have been approved faster
Defense Express points out that U.S. legislation provides for an Emergency Waiver mechanism, which allows the transfer of weapons to be expedited in the event of an emergency. However, it was not applied to these missiles.
PAC-2 GEM-T missiles have limited capabilities against ballistic missiles compared with the newer PAC-3 MSE. They do not use the principle of direct kinetic interception but destroy the target with a warhead explosion near it.
According to Defense Express, in the best-case scenario, 10 such missiles may be enough for Ukraine to repel one massive attack. The publication also points to a severe global shortage of ammunition for Patriot systems.

Greenland, Denmark say Trump deal won't compromise sovereignty

Greenland, Denmark say Trump deal won't compromise sovereignty
COPENHAGEN – Denmark and Greenland on Sept 19 said any agreement with the United States would not compromise Greenland’s sovereignty, after US President Donald Trump said the deal would give Washington “permanent control” over the Arctic island’s security, leaving its precise scope unclear.
The US, Denmark and Greenland said late on Sept 18 that they had reached an agreement for the US to develop a significant military presence on Greenland, while prohibiting US adversaries from building their own bases on the island.
Key details of the agreement have not been made public, including the scale of US military presence in the self-governing Danish territory and whether any formal power over foreign policy and resources would be ceded to Washington.
Denmark and Greenland expressed hope that a deal, which is expected to be signed during the UN General Assembly next week, would end months of uncertainty triggered by Trump’s threats to seize control of Greenland.
“Next week could be a good week - for Greenland, Denmark, and the United States,” Denmark’s Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen said in a statement posted on Facebook on Sept 19.
“A time of uncertainty will hopefully give way to a binding agreement that strengthens security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic, and thereby our shared security within NATO and Europe - while respecting the (Danish) Kingdom’s red lines,” he said.
But some residents in Greenland’s capital Nuuk expressed scepticism about closer ties with Washington.
“The US should not control Greenland. I think it’s better if we have cooperation with NATO,” said Jakob Ludvigsen, 65.
“Trump should stay far, far, far away from Greenland,” Marianne Hansen, a 71-year-old retired chef, told Reuters in Nuuk. “He should not expect our children and grandchildren to become Americans in the future.”
Denmark and Greenland have repeatedly insisted that Washington respect the sovereignty of the Danish kingdom and accept that Greenland is not for sale.
Trump’s vision for Greenland deal
Trump said on Truth Social on Sept 18 that under a deal, “the United States will FOREVER have the complete ability to do what is necessary in Greenland in order to secure and defend the security of Greenland, and the United States of America.”
The deal “gives the United States permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland”, Trump said, adding that no adversary would ever be permitted to have a base or military presence in Greenland, or make sensitive investments there, without Washington’s express written approval.
Trump made the announcement after Reuters exclusively reported that the US and Denmark were closing in on a deal.
“This is probably not the end of President Trump’s ambitions for Greenland and certainly not the end of US strategic interest in the territory and its resources,” said Mikkel Vedby Rasmussen, a political science professor at the University of Copenhagen.
If Copenhagen cedes any formal authority to Washington, it raises the question in Greenland of whether “this is the beginning of replacing the colonial relationship with Denmark with a colonial relationship to the United States,” he said.
Greenland’s Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen said in a Facebook post on Sept 19 that the proposed deal “recognises the sovereignty and territorial integrity of our Kingdom and the right of the Greenlandic people to self-determination.”
Trump’s threats, which peaked in January, triggered a diplomatic crisis that strained relations within NATO and pushed Denmark and Greenland into negotiations aimed at defusing the pressure.
A NATO spokesperson on Sept 19 said the alliance welcomed the agreement, which would “help advance security, stability and cooperation in this vital region.” REUTERS

Dutch destinations: Check out the highs and lows of Maastricht
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
10:12:45 UTC
19:12:45 KST

Dutch destinations: Check out the highs and lows of Maastricht
Molly Quell
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
One of the oldest cities in the Netherlands, Maastricht lies in the southern part of the country, close to both the Belgian and German borders. It is no wonder that the founding treaty of the European Union was signed there, nor that the Belgian (and French) influence has created a food mecca.
No one can quite agree on its exact origins. Celts lived in the area at least as far back as the 5th century BC, and the Romans showed up about 600 years later to build a bridge over the Meuse River that now runs through the centre of the city. Maastricht played a vital role in the Carolingian Empire and the Holy Roman Empire, and its location made it quite coveted between the 16th and 18th centuries. Many of those fortifications are still standing.
It was the first Dutch city to be liberated by the Allies during World War II. Half-century later, the city hosted a series of councils that led to the signing of the Maastricht Treaty, which paved the way toward the establishment of the European Union and the euro.
Maastricht is now home for 125,000 people, including many of the students studying at nearby Maastricht University.
Five things to do
Enjoy the city’s long and storied past with a historic walk.
Start at the Vrijthof, the main square where Dutch conductor André Rieu holds his summer concert series and which turns into a Christmas market in the winter.
Vrijthof is home to the majestic Basilica of Saint Servatius, where Maastricht’s patron saint Servatius is said to have died in 384 AD. A stone church was built over his grave in the 6th century which has been gradually expanded to the looming structure you see today.
You can loop past Our Lady, Star of the Sea (Sterre der Zee), a popular pilgrimage site, and see the famous wooden statue of Mary that dates to the 15th century.
Walk under the Helpoort (Hell’s Gate), the oldest city gate in the whole of the Netherlands, and then stroll through the Stadspark. On a nice day, you can join the many students who spread out a blanket and enjoy a few beers in the sun.
The part is also home to a number of sculptures and art installations. You can walk along the city walls and even see a statue of the fourth musketeer d’Artagnan. The leader of King Louis XIV’s elite corps of gentlemen, died in battle in 1673 during the French siege of Maastricht and archaeologists recently announced they may have discovered his skeletal remains under the floorboards of a nearby church.
If you want to go deeper into history, go underground
 You can tour the caves of Mount Saint Peter, a collection of limestone quarries which date back to the 13th century. During World War II, they were used to safeguard arms and valuables from the Germans, including The Night Watch by Rembrandt van Rijn which was removed from its frame and rolled into a cylinder.
You can also walk through the casemates (kazematten), defensive corridors that run under the city. These structures are unique in the Netherlands, as the groundwater level is too high in other parts of the country.
Visit a bookstore
 The 700-year-old Dominicanenkerk has quite the history. Along with serving as a house of worship, the church has been used as a warehouse, an archive, a printing house, and even a place to store bikes. Napoleon used it to store equipment and military personnel while invading the region in the 1790s.
It was converted into one of Europe’s most unique bookstores following a restoration project in the mid 2000s. If that’s not enough, you can also check out De Tribune, which was named the best literary bookstore in the Netherlands in 2024.
Shop til you drop
 Maastricht is known for its shopping and the city is filled with boutiques, art galleries, vintage shops and more. The Rechtstraat is just one of many lovely shopping streets. On Wednesday and Fridays, the city holds a market with Friday wares more orientated towards clothing. On Saturday, hundreds of vendors turn out for the antiques market.
Go to the other extreme
 Just outside Maastricht, you can find the highest point in the Netherlands. At a little over 322 metres tall, the Vaalserberg might merely be considered an average hill in other countries, but for the Netherlands, that’s a mountain.
It’s also home to Drielandenpunt, a three country-point where the borders of Belgium, Germany, and the Netherlands meet. Its lookout towers offer great views of the surrounding region.
Where to eat
Limburgse vlaai is the local delicacy and a must have on any trip to Maastricht. It’s not quite a pie and it’s not quite a pastry, but it’s definitely delicious. De Bisschopsmolen currently has no less than nine on the menu at their bakery and cafe. If you’d like to try your hand at making your own, they also host vlaai workshops.
The Onze Lieve Vrouweplein has a collection of outdoor cafes where you can enjoy a coffee or a beer.
If you want a fancy meal, look to L’Auberge. This lovely restaurant sits in the former stables of Château Neercanne. For an even fancier meal, the companion Restaurant Château Neercanne. For a real treat, you can stay at the hotel.
Cycle outside of the city and have lunch at Grand-Café Buitengoed Slavante. The country estate has a great breakfast menu and you can also take a walk on the grounds.
Another great lunch option in the city is the hip, Marres Kitchen. It’s in the same building as the museum Marres, House for Contemporary Culture so enjoy some art at the same time.
Where to stay
For a boutique experience, try Townhouse Hotel Maastricht. It also offers apartments if you’d like to eat your vlaai at home. Kruisherenhotel is the only five star hotel in the region. It’s housed in a 15th century monastery along the Kommelplein and each one of its 60 guest rooms features unique art and decor. The the Easy Hotel is a clean and cheap choice.
How to get there
The train stops practically in the middle of the city and you can walk in along a beautifully landscaped boulevard. It’s about three hours from Amsterdam. The drive is a bit shorter, at 2.5 hours, depending on the traffic.
Anything else
Keep in mind that Maastricht is south of the river and therefore deep into Carnival territory. Andre Rieu’s summer concerts are extremely popular and thus make it impossible to find hotels and parking.
