China, Iran, Israeli groups weaponize AI for first-of-their-kind social media influence campaigns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
08:26:44 UTC
17:26:44 KST

Iran, China, and groups from Israel used artificial intelligence to operate thousands of fake accounts, creating first-of-their-kind AI-powered influence campaigns across social media, according to an investigation published by The New York Times.
The countries and firms used AI to intensify the scale of online campaigns beyond what verified human users could organically achieve, US officials told the NYT.
The firms reportedly turned to Chinese “open-source” AI models, which users can download and modify for custom purposes. The firms then used those open-source models to create “agents,” bots with the autonomy to operate software and complete tasks on their own without constant prompting.
The New York Times explained that once hundreds of those AI agents were let loose on the internet, they autonomously opened networks of fake accounts on platforms such as Instagram, Facebook, X/Twitter, and TikTok.
The AI agents then rapidly populated the fake profiles with false information relating to politics and current events.
First time Chinese models were used like this
US officials told the NYT that these instances marked one of the first times AI agents from Chinese-produced models were used to handle every stage of an online influence campaign, from creating new fake accounts to coordinating messaging and framing online.
Unlike proprietary AI models, the open-source models were manipulated by developers to allow the agents to evade safeguards designed to verify users and prevent the manipulation of online discourse, the US officials added.
The US intelligence community, along with cybersecurity experts, looked into the groups behind the AI-powered campaigns and traced those efforts back to state-backed Chinese and Iranian groups, as well as to Israeli campaigns stemming from two private firms.
Kyle Crichton, a fellow at the Georgetown Center for Security and Emerging Technology who studies AI and cybersecurity, told the NYT that “Agent-led campaigns” will likely become more common as the technology spreads.
“Agents can be fairly sophisticated, and so in addition to just scale, they have an ability to blend in and look more like a human user,” he said.
The investigation was published in the wake of other major technology news, as AI leaders warned of the risks of developing AI too quickly and without proper safety measures. These warnings followed public concern over recent stories of AI models going rogue and hacking other companies.
In a report last month, Meta said it had seen a “technically significant development” of bad actors using AI for malicious purposes.
AI is now “embedded within automated systems that can produce, adapt, and distribute content with minimal human intervention,” Meta added.
The investigation also traced AI-agent campaigns back to Israel
The report mentioned that IntelEye, a Tel Aviv-based company founded by former NSO Group employees, operated roughly 1,000 AI-powered fake accounts on social media to manipulate political discourse around the upcoming Israeli elections.
The company used DeepSeek, a Chinese open-source AI model, to create its agents. According to the investigation, the bots then published content both supporting and opposing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
IntelEye disputed claims that its work was intended to influence online discussions, stating the company was conducting a defensive research experiment to expose weaknesses in AI systems.
“IntelEye does not operate influence campaigns,” co-founder Maor Sellek told the Times. “Our work with DeepSeek was conducted for defensive research and testing, to understand how models with insufficient safeguards could be misused and to improve detection of that activity.”
Sellek said IntelEye bought 10,000 social media accounts and handed over control to autonomous AI agents, though he added that only about 1,000 of the accounts were operational.
The agents used the accounts to leave comments on posts to boost engagement, although Sellek said they were not very successful.
Meta told the New York Times that the vast majority of the AI-powered agents set up on Facebook and Instagram by IntelEye, other companies, and state-backed groups had been removed by its automated detection and verification systems.

In the kitchen with Henny: Celebrating in the sukkah
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
08:26:34 UTC
17:26:34 KST

Rosh Hashanah just ended, and already we’re planning our Sukkot menus. Just three days ago, there was no room in my fridge for one extra carrot, and now there’s almost nothing in there except for carrots. The irony!
And the cycle will continue over the next couple of weeks. Even for Yom Kippur, when we don’t eat, the supermarkets are packed with people buying food for before and after the fast. Again, the irony.
But Sukkot is something I look forward to all year. I love Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, with their days of prayer, reflection, and forgiveness, but there is something so special about sitting in a cozy sukkah, surrounded by guests, both spiritual and physical, and simply taking in Hashem’s love and kindness.
Sukkot is a time of real joy, and after all the planning, cooking, and preparing, I can’t wait to sit down in the sukkah and celebrate.
Arugula Salad with Maple Dressing
Besides being beautiful, this salad is perfect for this time of year. The maple dressing and candied pecans give it a touch of autumn, while the mangoes are perfectly sweet right now.
You can use arugula, baby leaves, spinach, or a combination of whatever greens you like. As always, adapt it to fit your own culinary style and what your family enjoys.
Yields 6 servings
4 cups arugula (rocket)
3 cups mixed baby leaves
3 small cucumbers, thinly sliced
1 ripe mango, peeled and thinly sliced
1 apple, thinly sliced
½ cup candied pecans, roughly chopped
¼ cup sunflower seeds or pumpkin seeds, optional
Dressing:
¹⁄³ cup olive oil
2 Tbsp. maple syrup
2 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice
1 Tbsp. apple cider vinegar
½ tsp. salt
Black pepper, to taste
In a small bowl or jar, combine the olive oil, maple syrup, lemon juice, apple cider vinegar, salt, and black pepper. Whisk or shake well until combined. Set aside, or refrigerate until ready to use.
Place the arugula and baby leaves on a large serving platter. Arrange the cucumbers, mango, and apple over the greens, then sprinkle with the candied pecans and sunflower or pumpkin seeds, if using. Drizzle the dressing over the salad just before serving and toss gently.
Crispy Potato Cups
I don’t know why, but I always associate the sukkah with finger foods. Maybe it’s because we’re going up and down the stairs between the apartment and the sukkah, and I’d rather not carry large pans filled with hot liquid, or maybe it’s simply because finger foods are fun and the sukkah has such a fun feel to it.
When I saw the idea of making potato cups using just a potato, I thought, this sounds easy enough. I’m giving you a ground beef filling here, but you can really be as creative as you want.
For a vegan option, try mashed sweet potato or butternut squash. For a dairy version, fill them with sautéed veggies, mushrooms, and onions, and top with shredded cheese.
I love recipes that can be adapted to fit different meals. You can prepare a batch of the potato cups ahead of time and then fill them with whatever works best for the meal you’re serving.
Yields 12 potato cups
Potato cups:
12 small potatoes or 6 large potatoes, plus 1 large potato for the meat filling
2-3 Tbsp. olive oil
½ tsp. paprika
1 tsp. garlic powder
1 tsp. salt
½ tsp. ground black pepper
Oil spray, for greasing
Ground beef filling:
2 Tbsp. olive oil
2 large onions, diced
400 grams ground beef
1 red pepper, diced
¼ cup chopped fresh parsley or cilantro (coriander)
2 Tbsp. tomato sauce or BBQ sauce
½ tsp. salt
¼ tsp. ground black pepper
1 large cooked potato, reserved from the potato cups
1 egg
Place the potatoes, with the skins on, in a large pot and cover with water. Bring to a boil and cook until soft and easily pierced with a fork. Drain and let cool enough to handle. Set aside 1 large potato for the meat filling.
Preheat the oven to 200°C/400°F. Grease a 12-cup muffin tin or ramekins very well with oil spray. Place one small potato, or half of a large potato – skin side down, into each muffin cup or ramekin. Using the bottom of a small glass, press each potato down and up the sides of the muffin cup, leaving the center hollow. Use a spoon to gently smooth and shape the potatoes into cups.
In a small bowl, combine the olive oil, paprika, garlic powder, salt, and black pepper. Brush the mixture generously over the inside and edges of each potato cup. Bake for 15-20 minutes, or until the edges begin to brown and crisp. Remove from the oven and allow the potato cups to cool in the muffin tin.
Meanwhile, heat the olive oil in a large frying pan over medium heat. Add the onions and sauté until soft and caramelized. Add the ground beef and cook for about 5 minutes, breaking it apart with a wooden spoon as it cooks. Add the red pepper, parsley or cilantro, tomato sauce or BBQ sauce, salt, and black pepper. Continue cooking for another 5-7 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the beef is cooked through and the pepper has softened.
Peel and mash the reserved cooked potato, then stir it into the meat mixture until everything is well combined.
Reduce the oven temperature to 180°C/350°F. Spoon the meat filling into the potato cups and bake for about 20 minutes. Allow the cups to cool for a few minutes in the muffin tin before carefully removing and serving.
Breaded Veal Chops
Whenever I see breaded veal chops, I immediately think of my mother. She didn’t make them often, which is probably part of why I remember them so well, but when she did, I loved them.
Years later, on one of our visits to New York, our cousin Lisa, on my husband’s side, took us out to a meat Italian restaurant in Manhattan that she knew we liked. I spotted breaded veal on the menu, and, all of a sudden, that memory came rushing back. I ordered it, and it came with creamy mashed potatoes and was smothered in fried onions. It was every bit as comforting and delicious as I remembered.
Veal chops are not something you see very often here, but around the holidays they tend to show up more at the butcher. So if you spot them, pick up a few and make these easy breaded veal chops for one of your Sukkot meals. The crispy coating and fried onions make them feel festive without being complicated.
Yields 4 servings
4 veal chops
1 cup potato starch or wheat flour
2 eggs, beaten
2 cups unseasoned bread crumbs
¾ tsp. salt
½ tsp. ground black pepper
2 Tbsp. granulated garlic
½ tsp. paprika
½-¾ cup oil, for frying
1 large onion, sliced into rings
Prepare three shallow plates. Place the potato starch or flour on the first plate. On the second plate, place the beaten eggs and season with ¼ tsp salt and a dash of black pepper. On the third plate, combine the bread crumbs, granulated garlic, paprika, ½ tsp salt, and ½ tsp black pepper.
Heat the oil in a large frying pan over medium heat. Dip each veal chop first into the potato starch or flour, then into the egg mixture, and finally into the bread crumbs, making sure it is well coated on all sides.
Place the breaded veal chops in the hot oil and fry for 8-10 minutes on the first side. Flip and fry for another 8 minutes, or until golden and crisp on the outside and cooked through.
While the veal is frying, add the onion slices to the same pan. Fry until golden and crisp, removing them as they are ready.
Transfer the veal chops to a serving platter, scatter the crispy onions over the top, and serve warm.
Cookie Crust Brownies
I feel very blessed that I get to cook with my students at Midreshet Darkaynu on Wednesday evenings. Last year, one of the students, Atara, asked if we could make these triple-layer brownies that she loves. I was a little skeptical at first because they sounded complicated, but they really weren’t.
We divided the group into two. One group prepared the chocolate chip cookie crust while the other made the brownie batter. And what goes in the middle? Oreos. That part was simple enough!
We spread the cookie dough into the pan, arranged the Oreos on top, and then poured the brownie batter over everything. It was such a fun dessert to make together, and even more fun to eat.
Because these brownies are so rich, they’re not something I would make all the time, which is exactly why I think they’re perfect for Sukkot. It’s a festive dessert, a little over the top, and definitely one that feels like a celebration.
Yield: 20-24 brownies
Cookie layer:
¹⁄³ cup brown sugar
¹⁄³ cup granulated sugar
¹⁄³ cup oil
1 egg
½ tsp. vanilla extract
1½ cups flour
1 tsp. baking soda
½ tsp. salt
¹⁄³ cup chocolate chips
20 Oreo cookies or other chocolate sandwich cookies
Brownie layer:
½ cup oil
250 grams chocolate
1 tsp. vanilla extract
3 eggs
1 cup sugar
¾ cup flour
¼ tsp. baking soda
½ tsp. salt
Preheat the oven to 175°C/350°F. Line or grease a 23 x 33 cm. (9 x 13-inch) baking pan.
For the cookie layer, mix the brown sugar, granulated sugar, egg, oil, and vanilla until well combined. Add the flour, baking soda, and salt, and mix until a dough forms. Add the chocolate chips and mix until evenly incorporated. Press the cookie dough evenly into the bottom of the prepared pan, then arrange the Oreo cookies in a single layer over the cookie dough.
For the brownie layer, place the chocolate and oil in a small saucepan over low heat and stir until melted and smooth. Remove from the heat and set aside to cool slightly. In a separate bowl, mix the eggs, sugar, and vanilla until combined. Slowly add the melted chocolate mixture, stirring as you pour. Add the flour, baking soda, and salt, and mix until smooth.
Pour the brownie batter over the Oreo layer and spread evenly. Bake for about 30-35 minutes, or until the brownie layer is set and a toothpick inserted into the brownie portion comes out with moist crumbs.
Allow the brownies to cool completely before cutting into squares.
I HOPE you found some of these recipes exciting and that they’re getting you into the festive Sukkot mood. Although we still have Shabbat Shuva and Yom Kippur in the coming days, Sukkot will be here before we know it.
It’s such a meaningful time of year, filled with reflection, prayer, and forgiveness, and hopefully giving us the ability to move forward with more understanding, connection, and unity.
I want to take this opportunity to wish you a year filled with good health, laughter, and joy. May it be a year of coming together, of feeling more connected to one another, and of enjoying many festive meals together with the people we love.■
Henny is a kitchen coach who teaches women how to meal plan and cook so they get dinner on the table and prepare for Shabbat and hag on time. To book her for one-on-one coaching or an exciting food workshop: www.inthekitchenwithhenny.com

Yom Kippur through the centuries: The prayer books that preserve centuries of Jewish history
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
08:26:33 UTC
17:26:33 KST

From a World War II soldier’s mahzor (prayer book), to manuscripts from the Cairo Genizah, to a recently reunited prayer book from Portugal, the National Library of Israel’s impressive collection of prayer books and other holiday-related items immeasurably enhances our appreciation of the High Holy Days.
Dr. Chaim Neria, the NLI’s curator of the Haim and Hanna Solomon Judaica Collection, was excited to share a bevy of Yom Kippur-related artifacts, including rare prayer books, from its vast archive. It holds millions of items, both physical and digital, including books in Hebrew and those on Jewish topics; Jewish journals and magazines; Hebrew manuscripts; personal archives; and Jewish music.
In an interview with The Jerusalem Post, Neria explained how the NLI came to house thousands of prayer books, noting that “it fits into the overall mission of the library.”
He shared the extent of the library’s commitment to assembling a “very deep and broad” collection; ideally, it will include “every book printed about the Jewish people – and eventually have the best documentation of the Jewish people since the invention of printing.”
One reason the NLI has such a large collection of prayer books is that they were widely produced. “People needed them, and used them,” he noted. He even playfully pointed out that given their popularity, a printer would be making a “safe bet” if he produced prayer books.
The mystery of the Jewish soldier who fell on Yom Kippur, 1944
Neria began our tour by sharing a relatively “new” prayer book, where careful research and detective work by the NLI solved a mystery of a Jewish soldier in the US Army who fell on Yom Kippur, 1944.
A particularly peculiar two-volume Yiddish and Hebrew prayer book, printed in New York in 1942 by Ziegelheim Press, a publisher who had immigrated from Vienna to Manhattan before World War II and continued his work from the Big Apple, showed up at the NLI with many unanswered questions.
It contained the following inscription in Dutch with some Hebrew: “In memory of our son, David Meyer Wald, of the American Army. September 27, 1944 – Yom Kippur 5705, who fell in the liberation of Holland. May he rest in peace in the cemetery of Margraten, Plot Nn, row 9, grave number 222.
“Zelg and Hania Wald. Please commemorate his soul.”
The prayer books were apparently donated in memory of an American Jewish soldier initially buried in a cemetery in Holland. Researchers learned that David Meyer Wald was one of 8,288 soldiers buried in the American military cemetery near the village of Margraten, in southern Holland.
They later pieced together key aspects of his life: he was born in 1923 in Timkovichi, now in today’s Belarus. His family immigrated to the United States in 1938 and settled in Pittsburgh, PA. He served in the 325th Infantry Regiment, a unit belonging to the US Army’s 82nd Airborne Division, and was killed in Holland in 1944.
Wald was initially buried in Holland and re-interred in 1949 in Montreal.
Researchers at the NLI were puzzled about the prayer book until they discovered in 2007 that a Torah scroll was dedicated in memory of the same deceased American soldier by his parents. It was donated to the synagogue closest to his burial place in Holland. The Walds also donated two prayer books and perhaps other books to the NLI at the same time.
It is still unclear exactly how the books reached the NLI, or why it mistakenly contained another label – the Jewish Cultural Reconstruction, Inc., often abbreviated as JCR, which worked after the Holocaust to save books stolen by the Nazis during the war from Jewish libraries and from private collections across Europe.
Yet one thing was clear: the books were donated in memory of a Jewish soldier who gave his life fighting the Nazis and who died – on Yom Kippur – “for the sanctification of God’s name,” as stated on his gravestone in Hebrew.
This is a case, Neria noted, “in which one mahzor opened an entire story of an American soldier who died while liberating the world from evil. It gives new meaning to Yom Kippur, Jewish history, and the Israel experience. The story is very touching and unique.”
A remnant of one of the oldest Yom Kippur prayer books in existence
Neria took our tour further back in time – to the Cairo Genizah, which contains hundreds of thousands of complete Jewish documents and fragments of documents, including holy books, letters, and business and legal documents. They were all discovered in the attic of a synagogue in Fustat (the ancient city of Cairo) in the mid-1800s.
Neria explained the centrality and importance of the city. “Cairo was the center of Jewish activity, partially because it was a city where many merchants and rabbis arrived; it was a religious center and also a center for commerce.” The synagogue in Cairo was similarly important in the history of nusach (traditional wording and music).
Among the treasures in the genizah is a fragment of a page from an ancient Yom Kippur prayer book. It was written in the late 11th or early 12th century by a scribe named Hillel Ben-Eli, a cantor from Baghdad who immigrated to Egypt and worked as the official scribe of the Cairo rabbinical court.
Certificates in his handwriting appeared between 1066 and 1108. He is one of the most important scribes whose writings were found in the genizah. The prayer book from which this fragment comes is the oldest in the NLI’s collections, and one of the oldest in the entire world.
Those familiar with the Yom Kippur liturgy may recognize the name of Rabbi Eliezer Kalir, one of the greatest poets in Jewish history. On one side of a page from the genizah is a paragraph from a piyut (liturgical poem) by Rabbi Kalir called “Please Answer My Whisper.”
According to Neria and his team, in the third line, one can make out the Hebrew words “[Honi] hamulat kodesh, umehallelim behadarat [kodesh]” (“[My riches] are holy noise, and they praise in [holy] splendor”). On the other side are prayers related to the Yom Kippur service in the ancient Temple.
Neria explained the importance of the poets who wrote the poems that have made their way to prayers we recite on various holidays. They include slihot (penitential poems and prayers read before Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur), kinot (elegies on Tisha B’av), and yotzrot (liturgical poetry read before the “Shema” on four designated torah portions).
“They even wrote new piyutim for each Shabbat.”
The discovery of the piyut from the genizah shows that, nearly 1,000 years ago, Jews gathered in synagogues and recited prayers similar to the ones that we recite today. And we are still familiar with these piyutim.
The Lisbon Mahzor that wandered the world
Neria completed our tour of the library’s prayer book gems by sharing one from Lisbon, produced in the period just after Jews were expelled from Spain.
“This was a very unique moment in history,” noted Neria, since the Jews had just been expelled from Spain and were briefly permitted to live in Portugal before also being expelled from there as well.
King John II of Portugal recognized a personal opportunity that would also benefit his country if he allowed tens of thousands of Spanish Jews to settle in Portugal, as the Jews possessed commercial skills and an important trade network.
Soon after, things began to worsen for Jews living in Portugal. There were new restrictions, Jewish children were seized and shipped to Portugal’s colonies, and families had to pay large sums to renew their right to remain in Lisbon. Often, Jews faced forced baptism.
Many of the Jewish community’s manuscripts – precious works of art – disappeared; others were smuggled out of the country.
The Lisbon Mahzor eventually reached the Jewish community of Aleppo and was guarded alongside the famed Aleppo Codex. The three-volume prayer book contained all of the liturgy for the Jewish year: one volume for daily prayers, and two others with the festival services for Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur.
In 1957, one volume of the Lisbon Mahzor was given to then-president of Israel, Yitzhak Ben-Zvi by the Jewish community of Aleppo, where it remained in the archives of Yad Ben-Zvi.
The whereabouts of the other two volumes remained a mystery until recently, when the missing volumes appeared in the catalogue of the Kedem Auction House. When the NLI learned of their availability – and knowing their incredible importance – it appealed to acquire them directly without public auction.
They claimed that they were treasures belonging to the Jewish people. The purchase was made possible with support from the Haim and Hanna Solomon Judaica Foundation, and the Zukier family.
All three volumes have now been reunited at the NLI and are accessible online.
Neria couldn’t contain his excitement as he showed off these treasures.
“This is why the National Library is here, to tell us about our roots and traditions – from 2,000 years after the piyutim from the Cairo Genizah were written (and read until today on Yom Kippur), to a soldier who died on Yom Kippur, with his parents’ words continuing to move us! This is a living tradition!”

Wine talk: The grape and the word
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
08:26:30 UTC
17:26:30 KST

Wine guys love wine to the depth of their being. To them, it is more than a drink.
It’s not just fermented grape juice or liquid grapes. Wine can be a window into all kinds of worlds. These include agriculture, archaeology, economics, gastronomy, geology, history, politics, religion, technology, and peoplehood.
It gives insight into the “people of Israel” and the “places of Israel,” from the first sprouting of the Jewish people in biblical times to the start-up Israel of today. Above all, we like to talk about wine and share experiences to enthuse others… and be enthused.
Wine also has a wide-ranging literature. You only have to see the number of wine books in a wine lover’s private library to understand what is obvious to me: wine is aspirational. We love to read about wine, learn about it, and immerse ourselves in the wine stories of others. Some of us like to read about wine and talk about it as much as drink it.
In the next few months, some books will be published that should be on every wine professional’s and wine lover’s bookshelf.
Hugh Johnson’s Pocket Wine Book
Hugh Johnson’s Pocket Wine Book, edited by famous wine writer Margaret Rand, is the largest-selling wine book in the world. It is not new. The first one was published in 1977.
Englishman Hugh Johnson is the world’s most famous and prolific wine writer. He remembers James Mitchell saying to him: “You know, Hugh, everything anybody really needs to know about wine could go into a little book like this…” and pulling out his diary. (Once there really was something called a pocket diary!) This was the invention of the Pocket Wine Book, published by Mitchell Beazley, and it has continued every year since then.
The Pocket Wine Book is a mini-reference book for anyone who buys wine – in wine stores, restaurants, or on the internet. It is a comprehensive up-to-date annual guide that has retained its popularity despite the accessibility of online information.
Hugh Johnson never believed in giving wines scores, but he does rate wineries from one to four stars.
Explanations are in brief note form and in British understatement, though the experts contributing cover the world. The book is close to being a kind of Michelin Guide for wine, with information about wineries and wines, grape varieties, matching food to wine, and the best values and vintages.
Even Israel gets a mention. Where else will you find a ranking of 45 Israeli wineries ranked by an international book? The entry includes large commercial wineries, small wineries, and boutique wineries; some kosher, others non-kosher. It also gives a heads-up about new-ish, tiny wineries of interest, which are below the radar.
Included are wineries owned across the spectrum: from haredi (ultra-Orthodox) to liberal Jews, right-wing settler wineries from the Central Mountains Region to left-wing kibbutz wineries, Israeli Arabs, and Christian Monks. This is part of why I say “Wine is the beautiful Israel.” Wine represents the rich mosaic of Israelis and the Land of Israel.
In Israel, we act very loudly in wine. We are active on social media like a wine giant. So it is a wake-up call to see our relative importance. In the Pocket Wine Book, Israel is part of the Eastern Mediterranean Region, and we are allocated a total of one and a half pages.
At the beginning, Israel did not feature at all, but slowly and steadily we found a voice. We were first mentioned in the 1980 edition, but it was only a few lines. The Golan Heights Winery was the first Israeli winery to be awarded stars in the late 1990s and the first to be awarded three stars. Domaine du Castel was the first to be awarded four stars in 2008.
In the new book, there are three Israeli wineries with four stars outright, and another three which earn two or three to four stars. Hugh Johnson’s Pocket Wine Book 2027, published by Mitchell Beazley, was released last week.
The World Atlas of Wine
IT WAS IN 1971 that Hugh Johnson wrote the first The World Atlas of Wine. He believed that wine was liquid geography. The publisher, James Mitchell, was interested in the idea of matching precise cartography to viticulture. Hugh Johnson liked the idea of mapping the main vineyards and vineyard areas.
It took him two years of travel, research, and writing, and it became a classic. Other editions followed. It was reprinted four more times between that first edition and 2001. Each time, the content advanced considerably as the wine world expanded in terms of quality and awareness.
In the early 2000s, Jancis Robinson MW, today’s most famous wine critic, joined him as co-author. This certainly made the ultimate dream team. Three more editions were published, and they are not reprints. The texts are rewritten, and the maps are updated, and they somehow manage to squeeze in all the new wine information that has come to light since the last edition.
Israel used to feature in the World Atlas alongside our neighbors in a page headed “Eastern Mediterranean.” From the eighth edition published in 2019, we were honored with our own full page and map! This is repeated in the ninth edition as well, except the maps and texts have been totally updated to take into account changes in the last seven years.
The ninth edition of The World Atlas of Wine by Hugh Johnson, Jancis Robinson MW, and Julia Harding MW will be published on September 24, 2026.
The most serious tome in the wine lover’s library is The Oxford Companion to Wine edited by Jancis Robinson MW. This is the one wine professionals studying for the WSET Diploma or Master of Wine use as a textbook. It is the ultimate in wine expertise and scholarship, and it covers every aspect of wine, written by the relevant world experts in every field.
The contract for the first edition was signed in 1988, and after years of graft, it was published in 1994 to acclaim throughout the wine trade. It won every book prize possible.
Since then, there have been four new editions. The latest is the fifth edition, which was published in 2023. It has more than 4,000 entries from over 250 global experts and is over one million words in total. The subjects of particular interest to us are “Israel” and “Kosher,” each of which has its own entry.
Any wine professional, expert, or connoisseur will have this book and is likely to purchase each new edition as soon as they come out. The fifth edition of The Oxford Companion to Wine is edited by Jancis Robinson MW, Julia Harding MW, and Tara Q. Thomas, and published by Oxford University Press.
If The Oxford Wine Companion is too academic for your needs, there is a new wine encyclopedia being published which is geared more to the wine lover. This is The Encyclopedia of Wine: A Definitive Guide to the World of Wine, edited by David Williams and published by Dorling Kindersley, which will be released in October.
An alternative is The New Sotheby’s Wine Encyclopedia by Tom Stevenson and Orsi Szentkiralyi, published by National Geographic. Both are excellent, comprehensive, and bulging with information. The only difference is that the Dorling Kindersley book is brand new and up-to-date. The Sotheby’s book was published in 2020.
So if you are buying a present, it is a better bet to choose the newer book. However, both are thoroughly recommended. All the books recommended are available from the publisher, bookstores, or Amazon.
The Bible of Israeli Wines
THOSE INTERESTED in wine books on Israel have a smaller choice in English, but there have been a few I picked up over the years that I still have and occasionally refer to.
The first one was The Bible of Israeli Wines by Michael Ben Joseph, published by Modan Publishing in 2002. I know the author as Mimi. He is in his 90s and still occasionally attends tastings. He wrote the first serious wine books in Hebrew that brought many into the wine world in the 1990s.
The book is way out of date, but it is like a time capsule of Israeli wine at that time. Furthermore, some of it still reads well. I still dip into it occasionally. If you find a copy in a book sale, it is a worthy purchase.
The next book worth having is The Ultimate Rogov’s Guide To Israeli Wines published by Toby Press. The late Daniel Rogov, a food and wine writer initially for The Jerusalem Post and later Haaretz, was Israel’s most important wine critic. He published his annual wine guide, and I still return to it.
It is useful for checking out winery stories and when certain wines were launched. However, if you only have one, it would be the last edition before he passed away, published in 2012. The best bet is a secondhand bookshop.
Then there is a series of publications of The Wine Route of Israel, with its striking green vine leaf cover. It was edited by Eliezer Sacks and published by Cordinata. The last English edition was in 2015. The essays, including a comprehensive history of Israeli wine, are still relevant. The sister book Wine of Israel, also by Sacks, was published in 2020 by Cordinata.
Both of these may be found at winery visitors’ centers, and Cordinata still has a few.
Wine Journey: Israeli Adventure
THE NEWEST and most up-to-date book is Wine Journey: Israeli Adventure by Itamar Gur, Guy Haran, David Silverman, and Roni Saslove. It is a paperback that was first self-published in 2021.
It proved popular, and an updated edition was printed in 2025. This format is practical and primarily for tourists, but there is a lot of information about Israeli wine, too. The book may be found in winery visitors’ centers or can be purchased online: www.israeladventure.wine
For a fun read, I recommend two books that cover two Israeli success stories. The Golan Heights Winery celebrated its 40th anniversary in 2023, and Domaine du Castel had its 30th year in 2022. These are Israel’s two most famous wineries, and the stories will warm the cockles of your heart.
Golan Heights Winery: Forty Years of Quality, Innovation and Authenticity and Domaine du Castel: The Biography are still available (if you are quick) at the relevant winery visitors’ center. Both books are self-published, and they have something else in common: they both won major awards at The Gourmand Awards, the Oscars of cookery and wine books.
These are the wineries that Israel put on the international wine map. Wine lovers, Zionists, or anyone interested in Israel will enjoy a good read and an insight into the Israeli wine industry.
In case anyone is in the know, I can confirm some involvement of sorts in many of the publications mentioned, but that is not relevant, and I make the recommendations on merit alone.
What I will claim ownership of is the ultimate Israeli wine book that was written but not published. I had a formal agreement to write a book with a major international specialist wine publisher. The book was to include Cyprus, Lebanon, and Israel, which was a unique approach and an exciting joint venture.
Unfortunately, Israeli and Jewish academics, artists, scientists, and authors are experiencing tough times due to Israel’s image abroad. Boycotts, cancellations, and unpleasantness are the order of the day.
After the work had been completed, the agreement was canceled – retroactively, to my surprise, regret, and disappointment. I was told verbally that it was because of Israel’s image. This is where we are. The book on Israeli wine has been written. Let’s hope we can find a way amid the opposition to get it published. Until then, invest in a wine book.
Dive in! Happy reading! ■
The writer is a wine trade veteran and winery insider turned wine writer, who has advanced Israeli wines over four decades. He is referred to as the English voice of Israeli wine. www.adammontefiore.com

The surprising history of Kol Nidre: How Yom Kippur’s legal formula became a sacred anthem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
08:26:16 UTC
17:26:16 KST

The iconic Kol Nidre theme – with its distinct modal inflections, expressive leaps, and solemn cantorial contours – has accomplished something rare in Jewish liturgy: it crossed the threshold of the synagogue into secular culture. For centuries, this ancient melody has fascinated everyone from classical composers and avant-garde musicians to film directors and pop artists.
Yet, the tension at the heart of Kol Nidre is striking. Fundamentally, the text is not a poetic prayer or a plea for mercy; it is a dry, legislative formula written in Aramaic for the annulment of personal vows. How did a dry legal disclaimer become bound to the most emotionally charged melody in the Jewish calendar?
“The text for Kol Nidrei dates from the eighth or ninth century, and already then it was controversial,” explained Cantor Eliyahu Schleifer, professor emeritus of Sacred Music and former director of the School of Sacred Music at Hebrew Union College in Jerusalem, who is one of the world’s foremost authorities on Jewish liturgical music. “The primary dispute was whether or not one can annul future vows.”
He noted that during the Middle Ages, the text initially referred to the year to come: “From this Yom Kippur until the next Yom Kippur which comes to us for good.” However, because scholars debated whether future vows could legally be absolved, many communities shifted to referring only to past vows: “From the past Yom Kippur until this Yom Kippur.”
“But nowadays,” Schleifer observed, “we refer to both past and future vows: ‘From the past Yom Kippur until this Yom Kippur, and from this Yom Kippur until the next Yom Kippur which comes to us for good.’”
That legal flexibility came at a heavy cost. In the Middle Ages, antisemites weaponized the formula, claiming that in the Kol Nidre prayer – one of Judaism’s holiest – Jews absolved themselves of any and all agreements and promises. This false pretext led to the systemic imposition of the humiliating “Oath More Judaico.”
The struggle over Kol Nidre’s legal text
In response, during the 19th century, leaders of the nascent Jewish Reform movement attempted to alter or drop the text entirely.
As Schleifer noted, “In early 20th-century American Reform prayer books, the text for Kol Nidre was omitted altogether.”
Instead, the rubric simply read “The Kol Nidre Chant,” and the organist or choir would perform the traditional melody without the Aramaic words. In other non-Orthodox traditions, alternative German psalms were substituted for the original legal formula, or cellists were brought in to perform Max Bruch’s famous instrumental fantasy on the theme as part of the service.
The text was only widely reinstated among non-Orthodox communities during the rise of Nazism in Europe, as Jews reclaimed their ancient liturgy under the ethos of “this is how our forefathers prayed.”
While Sephardi traditions feature a wide variety of regional recitatives and chanting styles – differing from community to community and cantor to cantor – the Ashkenazi melody developed into a single, widely standardized theme across Europe.
It is categorized as one of the “Mi-Sinai” tunes – traditional Ashkenazi melodies so deeply revered that oral legend attributed their origin to divine revelation at Mount Sinai. In reality, its roots are a complex tapestry woven in 15th- and 16th-century Germany.
ACCORDING TO Schleifer, the theme represents a synthesis of Ashkenazi biblical cantillations (derived from the haftarah), virtuoso cantorial improvisations, and secular medieval German folk songs sung by Minnesängers, German poet-musicians.
Historical records show how early rabbinic authorities shaped its performance.
“Our teacher, Rabbi Ya’acov Ben-Moshe Levi Moelin (the Maharil), one of the greatest rabbinic figures of the late 14th and early 15th centuries, described a traditional theme that is recited three times, with the cantor increasing his voice each time,” Schleifer noted. “Theologians still debate whether he meant increasing dynamic volume or raising the pitch by melodic steps. Today, cantors do both.”
However, whether the Maharil was referring to the exact melody sung today remains doubtful. Without musical notation from the 14th century, musicologists believe the early medieval theme likely differed from the modern version.
The melody was first transcribed in print in Berlin in 1765 by Cantor Aharon Beer, but it was Louis Lewandowski in 1871 who formalized the standard choral and cantorial arrangement known worldwide today.
How Kol Nidre’s melody conquered the secular world
The emotional gravity of the Ashkenazi theme inevitably attracted non-Jewish and secular classical composers.
The most famous adaptation remains the 1880 fantasy for cello and orchestra, Kol Nidrei, by the Protestant German composer Max Bruch. Bruch transcribed the theme directly from Jacob Abraham Lichtenstein, cantor of the Old Synagogue in Berlin.
Though scholars like Leon Botstein note that Bruch was drawn to the piece primarily as a folk music enthusiast rather than a philosemite, his composition permanently etched the melody into the classical music repertoire.
Decades later, Arnold Schoenberg created his own modern and deeply spiritual Kol Nidre (Op. 38). For Schoenberg, who had converted to Christianity before formally returning to Judaism as the Nazis rose to power, the piece was a deeply personal act of repentance.
Schoenberg embedded texts from Lurianic Kabbalah alongside the traditional prayer. He also subscribed to a popular myth: that the theme originated among Sephardi Conversos singing secretly in cellars during the Spanish Inquisition.
“That legend has no historical basis,” Schleifer clarified. “If it were true, you would hear the theme in Sephardi synagogues today. Schoenberg’s work is derived entirely from Ashkenazi cantillations.”
Myths surrounding classical masters and the melody extend even further back. Rumors have long persisted that Ludwig van Beethoven quoted the Kol Nidre motif in the Adagio of his String Quartet Op. 131.
“In comparison with the actual theme of Kol Nidre,” Schleifer reflected, “I don’t believe that to be true.”
Beyond the classical canon, Kol Nidre migrated into 20th-century popular culture. It was recorded by pop crooners like Perry Como, adapted into psychedelic rock (such as The Electric Prunes’ 1968 track “Kol Nidre”), and featured prominently in cinema – from Al Jolson in the groundbreaking 1927 film The Jazz Singer to Neil Diamond’s 1980 remake.
Why has this specific melody crossed so many cultural boundaries?
Beyond its connection to Yom Kippur’s theme of repentance, Schleifer believes the answer lies in its core musical architecture.
“The theme came to symbolize the fate of the Jewish people,” he reflected. “It begins in a solemn minor key, but ultimately transitions into the major scale – symbolizing a profound sense of hope and salvation at the end of days.”

Archaeologists discovered a mysterious Roman burial with the body placed face down

Archaeologists discovered a mysterious Roman burial with the body placed face down
Kyiv • UNN
A burial with the body face down and four glass vessels was discovered in the necropolis of ancient Salona. The reason for the ritual has not yet been established.
Archaeologists in Croatia have discovered an unusual Roman-period burial in which the deceased was placed face down in the grave. Several glass vessels were found alongside the remains, including an unusually shaped perfume bottle, Croatia Week reports, according to UNN.
Details
The burial was one of 16 recently examined in the western necropolis of ancient Salona—the capital of the Roman province of Dalmatia. The excavations are being conducted by specialists from the Croatian Institute for Nature Protection and the Croatian Academy of Sciences and Arts.
In the grave containing a body placed face down, archaeologists found three glass bottles and a small glass vessel. One of the perfume bottles was made in the shape of a date.
Unusual burial among cremated remains
The find is particularly notable because most of the other nearby burials examined contained cremated remains. In 12 graves, the remains were placed directly in the ground; in several others, ceramic urns were used, while in one case archaeologists discovered a stone urn.
In another burial, a glass bottle, a bone needle, and a ceramic oil lamp were found together with the cremated remains.
Researchers have not yet determined why one of the deceased was buried face down. Such burials differ from standard burial practices and may be of particular interest for further research.
Overall, archaeologists have already examined more than 150 graves on the territory of the necropolis of ancient Salona.

Leonardo DRS to power South Korea’s newest destroyer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
08:22:30 UTC
17:22:30 KST

- Leonardo DRS will supply the electric propulsion system for South Korea's KDDX destroyer, the Republic of Korea Navy's first full-electric-drive surface combatant.
- The six-ship KDDX program, led by Hanwha Ocean, is valued at roughly $5.7 billion, with the lead ship due by 2032.
Leonardo DRS will build the electric propulsion system for South Korea’s next-generation KDDX destroyer, the company announced, supplying technology for what will be the Republic of Korea Navy’s first full-electric-drive surface warship.
DRS signed the contract with Doosan Enerbility, which will work alongside the American company to build the ship’s complete power and propulsion system, covering everything from the prime movers that generate power to the propellers that turn it into thrust. DRS is providing its 100-Series permanent magnet propulsion motors paired with matching variable-frequency drives, hardware the company says is built to be more compact and power-dense than older electric drive systems. Hanwha Ocean is building the lead ship under a separate contract with South Korea’s Defense Acquisition Program Administration.
Electric propulsion lets a ship dedicate more of its power to sensors and weapons rather than the mechanical drivetrain connecting engines directly to propellers, an arrangement that matters more as warships add power-hungry equipment. “Our advanced electric-propulsion technologies are designed to deliver the power capacity, efficiency, reliability and adaptability required for advanced radars, advanced EW systems, directed energy systems, the charging of unmanned vehicles, the launch of drone swarms and other increasingly power-intensive mission capabilities,” said John Baylouny, president and chief executive officer of Leonardo DRS.
The KDDX program is South Korea’s first indigenously designed and built destroyer class, intended to fill the gap between the Navy’s 4,200-ton KDX-II destroyers and its larger KDX-III Sejong the Great-class Aegis ships, while replacing the aging three-ship KDX-I Gwanggaeto the Great class. The full program covers six destroyers of roughly 6,000 to 7,000 tons and about 155 meters (509 feet) in length, at a total program cost estimated near 7.8 trillion won, or roughly $5.7 billion. South Korea’s Defense Acquisition Program Administration awarded Hanwha Ocean the detailed design and lead-ship construction contract in July 2026, worth about $580 million, after the company narrowly beat rival HD Hyundai Heavy Industries in a competitive scoring process that followed more than two years of delay over how the contract should be awarded. The lead ship is due for delivery by 2032, with the remaining five ships following by around 2036.
The destroyers are planned to carry mostly Korean-made systems, including a domestic combat management system, Hanwha Systems’ integrated mast, a dual-band active electronically scanned array radar, and Korean vertical launch systems. Propulsion for the class appears to combine gas turbines with the new electric drive system: GE Aerospace said on Sept. 1 that it would supply 12 LM2500+G4 marine gas turbines across the six ships, with Hanwha Aerospace manufacturing engine components, assembling the turbines, and providing local support.
DRS’s role builds on a longer relationship with the Republic of Korea Navy. The company has supplied hybrid electric drive systems for 20 anti-submarine warfare frigates across the Navy’s FFX Batch II, III and IV programs over more than a decade, and has scaled similar propulsion technology for the U.S. Navy’s Columbia-class submarine program. “For more than a decade our systems have supported Republic of Korea Navy FFX II/III/IV frigates, and we have demonstrated the ability to scale our electric-propulsion technology for the most demanding naval applications, including the COLUMBIA-class submarine program,” said Jon Miller, senior vice president and general manager of Naval Power Systems at Leonardo DRS.

Turkiye’s banking watchdog has revoked the operating licence of Iranian lender Bank Mellat’s branch in the Turkish city of Istanbul.
“It has been decided to revoke the operating licence of Bank Mellat, Head Office in Tehran, Istanbul Turkey Central Branch,” read the decision by the Banking Regulation and Supervision Agency (BDDK), published in the Official Gazette on Saturday.

The regulator said the decision was taken under a clause of Turkiye’s banking law allowing a bank’s licence to be revoked or withdrawn if its continued operation is deemed to pose a risk to depositors’ rights or to the security and stability of the financial system.
Bank Mellat has been subject to Western sanctions for years over accusations that Tehran was pursuing a nuclear weapon under the cover of a civil nuclear programme.
Those sanctions were lifted as part of a landmark 2015 deal between Tehran and world powers to curb Iran’s nuclear ambitions. However, the United States unilaterally pulled out of the agreement in May 2018, reimposing economic sanctions on the country.
Bank Mellat was hit by further US and Gulf sanctions in 2019 after being named as one of 25 entities linked to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).
The Turkish notice did not cite the US measures or specify operational issues.
Earlier this month, the US Treasury Department imposed sanctions on a small Turkish investment bank and two subsidiaries over alleged ties to Iran.
The Treasury Department accused Golden Global Yatirim Bankasi Anonim Sirketi (Golden Global Bank) of facilitating “tens of millions of dollars’ worth of transactions for the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps-Qods Force” and providing the Iranian government with banking access to move its funds internationally.
Golden Global Bank has denied the accusations.

EU urges US to reconsider visa denial to Palestinian delegation for UN meeting
BRUSSELS – The European Union said on Sept 18 it regretted Washington’s decision to deny visas for the second year running to Palestinian officials seeking to attend the UN General Assembly, urging a rethink.
The US State Department said this week it was refusing to grant visas to Palestinian leader Mahmoud Abbas and other members of his delegation ahead of next week’s meeting in New York.
“We regret the decision to extend the denial of entry visas for members of the Palestinian delegation for a second year in a row,” said Anouar El Anouni, a spokesman for the EU’s diplomatic service.
“In the light of its existing headquarters agreements with the UN and its obligations as host state, we urge the United States for this decision to be reconsidered.”
The administration of US President Donald Trump denied visas for the Palestinian delegation also in 2025, forcing Abbas, a regular at the UN General Assembly, to address the body of global leadership by video.
The General Assembly voted 152-3 on Sept 17 for Abbas to be able to appear virtually once again in 2026.
As it stands, only members of the Palestinian mission to the UN will be able to attend the meeting, which begins on Sept 22.
On Sept 18, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres expressed regret at Washington’s decision, adding that he was concerned about its impact “on the ability of the State of Palestine to participate fully in the work of the United Nations”.
The US and Israel have objected to the Palestinian Authority’s (PA) historical payments to families of imprisoned or slain Palestinians, including those who carried out attacks against Israelis.
The PA recently reformed this system, allocating welfare payments to families on a needs basis rather than political affiliation or prisoner status.
The US State Department said Washington also opposed Palestinian “actions to internationalise the Israeli-Palestinian conflict including through the International Criminal Court and International Court of Justice, seeking to bypass negotiations through seeking unilateral recognition”.
It accused the Palestinians of “continuing to pay stipends to terrorists and to glorify acts of terrorism and terrorists in public pronouncements and school textbooks”.
The US is at odds with the 142 UN member states that recognised a Palestinian state at the United Nations in 2026.
The decision to deny Abbas a US entry visa comes as violence by Israeli settlers against Palestinians has escalated in recent months in the West Bank. AFP

Alleged Lukashenko henchman to appear again before a Swiss court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
08:15:00 UTC
17:15:00 KST

Alleged Lukashenko henchman to appear again before a Swiss court
A man alleged to be a member of a Belarusian special forces unit is due to appear before the cantonal court in St Gallen on Tuesday. The 48-year-old Belarusian is alleged to have been involved in three murders on behalf of Alexander Lukashenko’s regime.
The Belarusian man had already appeared before Rorschach District Court in the autumn of 2023. The trial attracted international attention and was covered on site by around 30 journalists from Switzerland and abroad, as well as several human rights organisations.
In his asylum application in 2019, the defendant stated that, acting on behalf of the regime of President Lukashenko, he had been involved in the murders of three opposition politicians in 1999 – including the former Minister of the Interior, Yuri Zakharenko. He had also described the crimes in detail in various media outlets.
A first for the Swiss justice system
The complaint was filed by two daughters of opposition politicians who disappeared at the time, as well as Trial International, a non-governmental organisation (NGO) based in Geneva.
Legally, the case centres on the offence of enforced disappearance, which has been enshrined in the Swiss Criminal Code since 2017. The relevant section of the law is based on a UN convention. Under this, a person can be prosecuted in this country even if the offence was committed abroad. This is the first prosecution of its kind in Switzerland.
Acquittal at first instance
The prosecution had sought a three-year prison sentence for the accused before the district court, one year of which was to be suspended. However, the court of first instance acquitted the man in full. The presiding judge explained that certain accounts were simply absurd. The facts of the case had not been proven. The defendant had repeatedly contradicted himself, both during the asylum proceedings and during questioning by the public prosecutor’s office and in court.
More
He can’t go home: a Belarusian author on lost roots and life in Switzerland
It was possible, the judge said, that the defendant had sought to influence his asylum decision favourably with his dramatic accounts. It had, however, been proven that the defendant had been sentenced to several years’ imprisonment in Belarus in the 2000s for bribery. The man was not a suitable key witness against the regime in Belarus.
The prosecution, however, considered that the accused was a proven member of a special unit responsible for making opposition figures “disappear”. The man had provided details of the crimes that only insiders could know.
The tall defendant, who has been physically impaired since an accident, did in fact admit in court that he had helped carry out orders to abduct and shoot people at the time, but that he had not committed any murders himself. He apologised to the victims’ bereaved families.
Public prosecutor did not appeal
This case marked the first time ever that a possible crime commissioned by the authoritarian regime of Alexander Lukashenko in Belarus had been discussed in court. Following the acquittal at the time, the lawyer representing the two bereaved families expressed his disappointment to the Keystone-SDA news agency. He said the court had failed to recognise the significance of this case.
The lawyers lodged an appeal and are seeking a conviction for multiple enforced disappearances before the St Gallen cantonal court. The public prosecutor’s office did not appeal against the first-instance verdict, a spokesperson explained to Keystone-SDA.

US explains what is limiting Patriot missile supplies to Ukraine

US explains what is limiting Patriot missile supplies to Ukraine
Amid problems with supplying interceptor missiles for Patriot systems, US Ambassador to NATO Matthew Whitaker has said that the main issue is a lack of adequate production capacity.
Source: Whitaker in an interview with Radio Liberty, as reported by European Pravda
Details: Whitaker stated that the United States and its NATO allies are working to find available Patriot interceptor missiles for Ukraine.
He said they are working very actively through the PURL initiative The Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) programme allows NATO allies to finance purchases of US-made weapons for Ukraine. , which also provides Ukraine with Patriot PAC-3 interceptor missiles. The ambassador noted that demand exceeds supply and that the US and its allies will have to look deeply for ways to ensure Ukraine could defend itself in winter.
In response to a question about the main problem with missile supplies, Whitaker indicated that allies' contributions to PURL are sufficient.
Meanwhile, the ambassador pointed to a lack of adequate production capacity.
Whitaker stressed that this means existing stocks are insufficient for the current situation in the world. He added that an even more important factor is the global security environment, as the world has become more dangerous.
The ambassador believes the solution is to combine several measures at the same time, including expanding production capacity both in the US and in Europe.
He also said he is working on opportunities for joint production, both with Ukrainians and with NATO allies. Whitaker noted that they are taking a broader look at integrated air and missile defence, adding that some combination of all these measures was needed.
Background:
- Negotiations on additional US supplies of Patriot missiles to Ukraine have been ongoing for a long time, while US President Donald Trump's position on the issue has changed repeatedly.
