Germany news: Campaigns wrap up in two state elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
06:54:00 UTC
15:54:00 KST

Germany news: Campaigns wrap up in two state elections
Published September 19, 2026last updated September 19, 2026
What you need to know
- Elections campaigns are closing in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin ahead of elections on Sunday
- The elections are particularly in the spotlight as a gauge of the strength of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, which won a recent state election by a landslide
- A port union has warned that seaports are at significant risk of cyberattacks and sabotage
- The famous Oktoberfest opens in the Bavarian capital, Munich
- Annual anti-abortion marches are to take place in Berlin and Cologne, with some Catholic bishops expected to participate
Here is a roundup of the top headlines from and about Germany on the weekend of September 19-20, 2026:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.
Anti-abortion protests held in Cologne, Berlin
Protests against abortion and assisted suicide took to the streets of the German capital Berlin as well as the western city of Cologne on Saturday, in protest dubbed "March for Life."
Police said some 2,200 took part in Berlin, whereas no figures on the Cologne protests were immediately available. Catholic bishops were among those attending.
Meanwhile in both cities, pro-choice protests were also held.
Abortion in Germany is banned but women are allowed to carry out the measure if the first 12 weeks of the pregnancy have not yet concluded. They are however obligated to hold consultations first, and the abortion can only be held at least three days after such consultations.
Exceptions are naturally if the pregnancy poses a risk to the woman's health.
WATCH: Holocaust survivor on 'very dangerous' AfD Saxony-Anhalt win
Charlotte Knobloch, a Holocaust survivor and one of Germany’s most prominent Jewish community leaders, has voiced her alarm at the Alternative for Germany's (AfD) landslide victory in the Saxony-Anhalt state election.
Speaking to DW, she warned that some Jews are once again considering leaving Germany, saying years of efforts to rebuild trust after the Holocaust are being undermined. Knobloch described the rise of the far-right party as a serious threat, urged mainstream politicians to confront extremism more forcefully and called for greater engagement with young people.
Her comments come amid renewed concerns about antisemitism, political polarization, and reported death threats against her.
Far-right AfD holds final rally before Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania election
The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party held on Saturday its final rally in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, ahead of the Sunday vote in the eastern state.
Ulrich Siegmund, the party's winner in Saxony-Anhalt two weeks ago, addressed a rally of some 1,000 AfD supporters in Schwerin, according to police estimates.
He said that what happened in Saxony-Anhalt, where the AfD won but without an absolute majority, was also possible in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
The latest ZDF Politbarometer poll puts the AfD in the eastern state one percentage point behind the Social Democrats (SPD); at 36% and 37% respectively. Next is the Left Party (Die Linke) at 9%, then the CDU at 6% and the Greens at 5%.
The AfD rally was also attended by the party's candidate in the state, Leif-Erik Holm, who echoed previous remarks that the election "should serve as a signal that this government must finally go." Several other AfD leaders have repeated the same calls since the results of the Saxony-Anhalt state vote.
The far-right party's final rally of the campaign also saw some 350 counter-demonstrators, according to police. No incidents were reported.
Merz schedules CDU meeting with all party leaders to discuss election results
In an unusual measure, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz will convene the Christian Democratic Union leadership on Sunday to discuss the results of the state elections in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin.
Unlike in previous state elections, Merz has invited the entire party executive committee to a formal meeting at 5:00 p.m. (1500 GMT) at the CDU headquarters in Berlin. The committee includes some 25 members, either electees or representatives by virtue of their offices.
Due to attend are the eight influential CDU premiers who backed him ahead of the election.
Compounding pressure has befallen the conservative chancellor since the state elections in Saxony-Anhalt earlier this month, which saw the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) narrowly missing out on an absolute majority, while Merz's CDU secured half their previous result.
Polls for the upcoming votes are also grim, with the CDU threatened with the prospect of falling below the 5% threshold needed to enter parliament.
In the capital Berlin, where CDU is currently in power, polls suggest the conservative party is in a neck-and-neck race with the socialist Left Party.
Germany's Carsten Breuer to become NATO's Military Committee chairman
Germany's highest ranking military officer, General Carsten Breuer, will be the next chairman of NATO's Military Committee, after being voted into the role on Saturday.
"The support of the chiefs of defense of our NATO allies means a great deal to me. The alliance faces major challenges - for our security and peace in Europe and beyond," Breuer, who is also Germany's chief of defense, told German news agency DPA.
The position is considered among NATO's most influential ones.
Breuer succeeds Italian Admiral Giuseppe Cavo Dragone and will take over as of July 2027.
Breuer was competing for the position against Canada's Chief of Defense General Jennie Carignan. Had she been elected, she would have become the first woman to head the committee.
Cologne opera house reopens after 14-year redo
Cologne's cultural complex, which includes the city's main opera house, theater and children's opera, has finally reopened after renovation works that extended for some 14 years.
"With the reopening of our theaters, we are giving the city back a central place of meeting, inspiration and artistic freedom that belongs to all people of Cologne," Mayor Torsten Burmester said.
The western German state's opera house dates back to 1957, with the theater coming shortly after in 1962.
Since 2012, renovations on the pair commenced with an original budget of €250 million (roughly $287 million) that has somehow multiplied nearly three fold as the years rolled on.
The final price tag on the refurbishments stood at around €800 million.
In the 14 years it took to get the job done, Cologne's opera and theater houses had to relocate to other venues.
Celebrations of the reopening include music, dance, as well as other hands-on activities. On Sunday evening, the opening ceremony will conclude with a concert at the opera house.
Kremlin envoy offers economic cooperation to AfD
A senior Kremlin envoy has offered Russian help with Germany's energy supply in cooperation with the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, which has been widely criticized for its perceived links with Moscow.
The remarks by Kirill Dmitriev, Russian President Vladimir Putin's envoy for international economic cooperation, come as voters are set to go to the polls in the northeastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania on Sunday, with the AfD locked in a close race with the ruling Social Democrats (SPD).
"Mecklenburg-Vorpommern will thrive again when affordable, reliable Nord Stream gas returns through joint work with AfD," Dmitriev wrote on X, using the German name for the state.
"Lower energy bills, more jobs and higher growth," he continued.
"No more German energy and industrial suicide," he added, responding to response to a post by AfD co-leader Alice Weidel calling for political change in the state.
Moscow has in the past offered to resume supplying Germany with cheap gas through the Nord Stream pipelines in the Baltic Sea if sanctions over its invasion of Ukraine are lifted.
The AfD has argued that cheaper Russian energy would benefit the German economy and has called for Russian gas supplies to Germany to resume.
However, critics say that Germany's previous reliance on Russian gas made it prone to energy blackmail from Moscow, while buying it would also serve to fuel Moscow's war machine.
Sunday's state election will have no direct bearing on the issue, with Russian pipeline gas subject to European Union sanctions.
Only one of the original four Nord Stream pipeline strands remains intact following explosions that damaged Nord Stream 1 and 2 in 2022. The remaining strand is not in use.
Oktoberfest opens as Munich mayor taps first beer keg
Crowds rushed onto the Oktoberfest grounds in the southern German city of Munich shortly after the gates opened on Saturday.
Some visitors ran toward the beer tents to claim the best seats after waiting for several hours. Members of the first group in line said they had arrived at 7 p.m. on Friday with camping chairs, sleeping bags and emergency blankets.
Beer could not be served until the official opening ceremony at midday, when new Munich Mayor Dominik Krause of the environmentalist Greens tapped the first keg with the traditional cry of "O'zapft is" — Bavarian dialect for "It is tapped."
"Hop" over to our story for more about the opening of Oktoberfest.
Driver seriously injured in collision with plane at Munich Airport
The driver of a car operated by a cleaning company has suffered serious injuries in a collision with a plane engine at Munich airport overnight and has been flown to hospital by rescue helicopter, police said Saturday.
The car struck both the engine and then a passenger staircase, a police spokeswoman said, saying that the driver might have been affected by a medical problem before the crash.
The accident, which occurred at around 3. a.m. local time (0100 GMT), is being analyzed to determine the exact cause.
There was never any danger to other people, police said, and flight operations were unaffected.
No scheduled flights are permitted at Munich Airport between midnight and 5 a.m.
Germany's Carsten Breuer seeks to chair NATO Military Committee
Germany's highest-ranking soldier, General Carsten Breuer, is standing as candidate for the post of chair of the NATO Military Committee at a vote to take place on Saturday in Copenhagen.
The post is currently held by Admiral Giuseppe Cavo Dragone of Italy.
Breuer, 61, will contend against General Marie Annabelle Jennie Carignan, who is currently Chief of the Defence Staff in Canada.
Breuer himself is the current inspector general of the Bundeswehr, or German armed forces.
The winner of the vote would take over leadership of the NATO Military Committee from July 2027.
The head of the committee is seen as the most influential person in NATO alongside the Supreme Allied Commander Europe (Saceur), a position currently held by General Alexus G. Grynkewich of the US Air Force.
High-profile Jewish representative calls for AfD ban
Charlotte Knobloch, the former president of the Central Council of Jews in Germany, has reiterated her call for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) to be banned.
"A lot about the AfD reminds me today about the path the Nazis took to power," the 93-year-old Knobloch told the daily Augsburger Allegemeine.
She said the party "teems with Jew-haters and extremists" — something she said had already existed before, "but once, such parties disappeared from the scene very fast."
This would not be the case with the AfD, she said: "It has broad support in the population, not least with young people."
The party spouts hatred, including "hatred of Jews," she said.
"Unfortunately, no one has managed to clamp down on it so far, so it needs to be banned," she said, even if this is "perhaps difficult legally."
Knobloch called on voters in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania on Sunday to "read the newspaper, listen to the radio and watch TV; then you can't help seeing that the AfD is a profoundly anti-democratic party."
She also warned that Jews in Germany were "literally under fire once more," with much reminding here of the 1920s and early 1930s.
"There is hatred of Jews from right, from left and from the Muslim milieu," she said.
Knobloch herself was recently the target of a death threat following the AfD's landslide victory in the state of Saxony-Anhalt two weeks ago.
Police raid home of aide to AfD top candidate in Berlin
Police this week searched the home of an aide to the top candidate for the Alternative for Germany (AfD) at Sunday's election in Berlin, Kristin Brinker, media reports have said.
Responding to the reports, Berlin prosecutors said the police had been investigating suspected violations of laws governing the use of explosives and weapons.
According to the prosecutors, the police found no evidence to support those suspicions in the September 15 search but did turn up other items of potential criminal interest.
Reports in the Bild and Berliner Zeitung dailies said the investigators had found Nazi relics and drugs in possession of the 48-year-old aide.
In comments to the Bild, Brinker appeared to downplay the significance of the police finds.
"I never had any indication that he was of that bent. He is simply a collector," she said.
Growing sabotage risk at Germany's seaports — association
German ports on the North and Baltic Seas are facing growing risks to their security, a port association has said.
"The threat situation for German seaports has intensified considerably," Florian Keisinger, the managing director of the Association of German Seaport Operators (ZDS), told the Welt newspaper.
Keisinger said that as major hubs, ports were likely targets for cyberattacks, espionage and sabotage.
Norman Zurke, the managing director of the UVHH, an association representing the interests of employers at the port of Hamburg, told the paper that he felt cyberattacks were the main danger.
"However, the entire logistics sector is also already affected by sabotage," he said.
He said that protecting critical infrastructure was a state responsibility and called for more investment by the federal government in protective measures for the port.
Bundeswehr to hold Hamburg drills
From September 24 to 26, the German armed forces, or Bundeswehr, will be holding drills in Hamburg, entitled Red Storm Charlie, as they have in previous years.
Among other things, they will be cooperating with authorities at the port to rehearse responses to possible crisis situations and procedures for transporting troops and materiel to other locations via the sea.
Last year, some German navy corvettes were sabotaged at a Hamburg shipyard. State prosecutors investigated two employees over the incidents but have so far failed to find any culprits.
Oktoberfest set to begin in Munich
The world-famous Oktoberfest will kick off in Munich on Saturday with a traditional ceremony where the city's mayor taps a first barrel of beer — the liquid focus of the event.
New Munich Mayor Dominik Krause of the Green Party will open the 191st edition on the Theresienwiese festival grounds in the center of the Bavarian city at noon (1000 GMT).
Read this DW preview for everything you need to know about Oktoberfest 2026.
Campaigns wrap up ahead of Sunday elections
Parties vying for power in Sunday's elections in two German states are wrapping up their campaigns with several events.
In the northeastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) and the leftist environmentalistGreen Party are both holding large rallies.
In Berlin, the center-right Christian Democrats (CDU) of Chancellor Friedrich Merz and the left-wing populist Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) will also be staging big events.
Other parties concluded their campaigns on Friday.
Many voters undecided
This comes as a large proportion of voters in both states seem unsure about who they will cast their ballot for.
According to the "Politbarometer Extra" survey by public-service broadcaster ZDF, 21% of voters in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and 23% in Berlin remained undecided as of Thursday evening.
In Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, a tight contest is expected between the AfD and the center-left Social Democrats (SPD), while the Greens are polling around the 5% needed to enter the state parliament at all.
The state is currently governed by a SPD-Left coalition under Premier Manuela Schwesig of the SPD.
In Berlin, surveys show the CDU in a neck-and-neck race with The Left party, while the BSW could fall below the 5% parliamentary threshold.
Berlin's government currently consists of a coalition between the CDU and the SPD under CDU Mayor Kai Wegner.
Merz's future at stake
Results from the elections could have repercussions at federal level, with Merz's political future under debate after his CDU's drubbing at the hands of the AfD in state elections in Saxony-Anhalt two weeks ago.
Surveys in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania have shown the CDU polling at just 6%.

Switzerland Adopts Security Strategy to Counter Hybrid Threats
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
06:54:00 UTC
15:54:00 KST

The Swiss Federal Council has approved a comprehensive new security strategy aimed at bolstering national defense capabilities, safeguarding critical infrastructure, and preparing the country against hybrid and standoff attacks amid deteriorating European security conditions driven by Russia’s war against Ukraine.
According to Anadolu Agency on Sept.18, the Swiss government stated that the global security landscape has grown increasingly volatile and unpredictable.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Bern has identified escalating great-power rivalries, regional armed conflicts, the degradation of the international rules-based order, and a surge in hostile cyber operations and foreign influence campaigns as primary catalysts for the policy overhaul.
Swiss authorities underscored that an end to Russia’s military aggression against Ukraine remains nowhere in sight, while hybrid threats targeting European democracies continue to multiply and intensify across physical and digital domains.
Partner defense cooperation
The updated blueprint sets out 10 strategic goals and 46 specific operational measures. Under the framework, Switzerland plans to substantially elevate the resilience of state institutions, the domestic economy, and civil society, while systematically curbing critical external dependencies.
The strategy prioritizes reinforced protections for the civilian populace, constitutional bodies, and vital supply networks.
A central pillar of the new posture involves expanding conventional defense capabilities. The document mandates that the Swiss armed forces must maintain operational readiness to deter and counter potential armed aggression, directing defense planners to establish pre-arranged cooperative mechanisms with partner nations well before an active crisis erupts.
US Approves $2.68B Air Defense Equipment Sale to Ukraine
Federal authorities stressed that special focus must be directed toward the threats deemed most probable in the contemporary threat environment, specifically state-sponsored hybrid warfare, long-range standoff strikes, and transnational organized crime networks.
Implementation of several strategic measures has already commenced across federal departments. The State Secretariat for Security Policy (SEPOS) will oversee and coordinate execution of the blueprint, with the Swiss Federal Council scheduled to receive its first comprehensive progress report by the end of 2028.
Alignment with EU sanctions
The adoption of the defense blueprint marks another milestone in Switzerland’s calibrated departure from strict historical neutrality in response to Moscow’s aggression on the continent.
In recent years, Bern has moved in lockstep with the EU to implement consecutive economic sanctions targeting Russia’s military-industrial complex, energy revenues, and banking apparatus.
The Swiss government has enacted a total ban on the purchase and import of Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG) in February, aligning domestic regulations with the EU’s 19th sanctions package to curtail fossil fuel revenues financing the Kremlin’s war effort.
Alongside the energy restrictions, Swiss authorities prohibited domestic financial intermediaries from providing cryptocurrency services to Russian nationals and legal entities, while barring transactions involving ruble-backed crypto assets.
Bern has also expanded its statutory export control lists to restrict shipments of specialized industrial metals and advanced manufacturing components utilized in Russian weapon systems and domestic fuel production.

Russia’s elections are more than political theatre
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
06:46:17 UTC
15:46:17 KST

Russia’s elections are more than political theatre
For the Kremlin, parliamentary elections remain a mechanism for political participation, feedback, renewal and legitimacy.
Russia’s parliamentary elections offer an excellent opportunity for a new round in the information war between the West and Russia. Western politicians, experts and journalists have been given yet another convenient occasion to tell their target audiences that democracy has long ceased to exist in Russia; that the federal parliament, like any other representative body, in practice determines nothing in Russian life; and that all genuinely important decisions for the country are made not even by the government but exclusively in the Kremlin, by an extremely narrow circle of individuals accountable to no one.
Therefore, in the view of many critics of the Russian authorities, elections in Russia need not have been held at all: their outcome was predetermined by Kremlin political strategists and, in any event, will have no significant impact on the country’s future.
And yet even the most biased outside observer could hardly fail to notice the obvious: the Russian authorities made consistent and persistent efforts to ensure that these elections attracted the highest possible participation and were conducted successfully under current electoral law. For at least the past several months, the country had experienced heightened political activity.
Leading politicians and state officials constantly reminded the electorate of the importance of the coming elections. Governors of politically “problematic” regions were urgently allocated additional subsidies. Payments to certain categories of public-sector employees and pensioners were hastily indexed. And inevitable but unpopular or painful decisions for the public – for example, the forthcoming significant nationwide increase in housing and utility tariffs – were postponed until after the elections.
Even possible shifts in Russia’s position on the conflict with Ukraine and future relations with the West were often linked in public and political discussions to the results of the September elections, which were supposedly meant to “untie the hands” of the Russian leadership, although there were very different, sometimes diametrically opposed, views about how exactly the leadership would use these “untied hands”. In any case, it must be acknowledged that the Kremlin did not take the easy path of its opponents in Kyiv, who simply postponed the 2024 Ukrainian presidential election until better, “postwar” times, despite clear discontent and muted grumbling from part of Ukraine’s political class.
What is going on here? Why should the Kremlin invest so much energy and so many resources in what is often interpreted outside Russia as little more than an unconvincing simulation of genuine political competition? Why launch a new full electoral cycle while a large-scale military conflict has yet to end, when the normal boundaries of peacetime political democracy tend, one way or another, to narrow?
It is difficult to suppose that holding elections in Russia is driven solely by Kremlin strategists’ obsessive desire to impress, at all costs, either their external opponents or their partners abroad. As for the former, they would not change their views about the nature of the Russian political system, even in the hypothetical event that the elections ended in a complete triumph for the radical opposition and a crushing defeat for all pro-Kremlin candidates. Such a scenario would most likely lead to endless speculation about yet another “cunning Putin plan”, intended to mislead a credulous Western public and conceal the consistently authoritarian nature of Russia’s political regime.
As for the latter, it is hard to imagine that the leaders of Iran, North Korea, Belarus or China are seriously concerned about the state or future of Russian democracy. The political systems of their countries, like those of many other foreign friends and partners of Russia, to put it mildly, do not entirely conform to the classical standards of Western liberal democracies. It is doubtful that Kim Jong Un, Alexander Lukashenko or, say, Mohammed bin Salman, or even Donald Trump, would suddenly decide to offer Vladimir Putin wise advice on how to organise polling stations properly and count votes.
It is hardly likely that the Kremlin felt an urgent need to erect elaborate and expensive but not especially durable scenery on the Russian political stage when the reaction of the potential audience to the forthcoming theatrical production was known in advance. It seems more logical to assume that the Russian authorities need elections not as cosmetic decoration for the façade of their political system, designed to attract the indifferent gaze of an outside observer, but as a quite effective and, above all, much-needed mechanism for maintaining dialogue between the authorities and society in the difficult geopolitical and socio-economic conditions of autumn 2026.
First and foremost, the Russian authorities are fighting hard for a high turnout, creating the most comfortable possible conditions for their voters to cast their ballots. This is no accident. A high turnout is convincing evidence of the population’s continued political activity and of the fact that Russian society has not descended into political apathy and wholesale cynicism. The idea of active civic participation is far from an empty phrase for the country’s leadership. In this sense, even a vote against the main “party of power”, United Russia, is clearly preferable to the alternative of a significant part of the electorate conspicuously choosing not to participate in the elections.
No less important, the authorities need the election results as a barometer of current public preferences, something even the most accurate opinion polls or in-depth sociological research cannot replace. Contemporary Russia undoubtedly has its own, albeit relatively narrow, political spectrum of “systemic opposition” parties reflecting the differing interests and expectations of various social, economic, age and regional groups. The constantly changing balance of power between these parties must, one way or another, be taken into account by the authorities when determining the future priorities of their strategy.
For example, relative success for the Communist Party, A Just Russia and candidates from other left-wing parties would be a signal that the authorities should pay more attention to social programmes, the fight against economic inequality and social polarisation, and to countering the many remnants of “wild capitalism” left over from the 1990s. Conversely, a large number of votes cast for the New People party and other right-wing candidates would provide grounds for accelerating structural economic reforms and creating additional opportunities for the private sector, including small and medium-sized businesses. Strong electoral results for the Liberal Democratic Party would indicate growing nationalist tendencies in Russian society. The authorities may respond to such political signals in different ways, but they cannot ignore them and must therefore read shifts in public sentiment correctly.
Moreover, it can be assumed with a considerable degree of confidence that the State Duma elections will, one way or another, lead to substantial changes in the composition of not only the lower house of the Russian parliament but also Russia’s federal government. Following the elections, significant personnel changes are likely to take place in the executive branch – both at the federal level and at other levels. Such personnel changes, in turn, will make room for fresh ideas, innovative programmes, unconventional projects and proposals. There is a clear demand for renewal in Russian society today. Parliamentary elections are one way of responding convincingly to this demand without calling into question the stability of the state’s overall strategy or its senior leadership.
The Duma elections are the first parliamentary elections held during the special military operation, during which Russian society has changed considerably. In a sense, they can be called a large-scale political experiment whose outcome remains difficult to predict with precision. For example, it is still difficult to determine with confidence which political force will be supported by the majority of people who have participated in the special military operation or who remain on the line of contact. No less uncertainty remains regarding the likely political preferences of many residents of the new Russian regions, for whom the September elections will be their first State Duma election in their new status.
Such an experiment probably carries a degree of risk for the Russian leadership. Nevertheless, the leadership appears prepared to take that risk, not without reason viewing elections not only as an important but as an indispensable mechanism for public confirmation of its continuing political legitimacy.

Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania: SPD seeks to fend off AfD
September 19, 2026
Stretching along Germany's Baltic coast, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania is known for the tourist draws of Rügen and Usedom, the quiet island of Hiddensee with the grave of playwright Gerhart Hauptmann, and the historic universities of Greifswald and Rostock, among the oldest in the country. The state is also shaped by its industrial heritage, including its shipyards and the vast nuclear power plant at Lubmin, built in former East Germany and closed in 1995.
Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania is Germany's most sparsely populated federal state, with a population of just 1.57 million at the end of 2025. The unemployment rate in the structurally weak state stands at 8%, above the national average. At roughly 6%, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania also has by far the lowest share of foreign nationals of any of Germany's 16 federal states.
For many former East Germans, the state is associated with long summers spent at campsites and holiday resorts along the Baltic coast. It is also home to 16 national parks, more than any other federal state in Germany, and to the Mecklenburg Lake District, centered on Lake Müritz.
Yet this federal state was also the scene of some of the earliest violent attacks on asylum-seeker accommodations following German reunification. Images of burning housing blocks in Rostock-Lichtenhagen in August 1992 were broadcast around the world. That year, the number of asylum seekers in Germany reached a provisional peak of 440,000, fueling heated debates across the country.
In August of that year, hundreds of far-right rioters attacked a residential building in Rostock that housed around 100 people from Vietnam. The building was set on fire as some 3,000 local residents applauded the attackers. Miraculously, no one was killed, though many people were injured. It was the worst outbreak of racist violence in Germany since the Second World War.
Incumbency advantage may help Manuela Schwesig
Former Chancellor Angela Merkel had her electoral district in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. For around 28 years, the state has been governed by the Social Democratic Party (SPD) in coalition with various partners.
Most recently, it has been led by the popular state premier and former federal minister Manuela Schwesig. The 52-year-old heads a coalition with the socialist Left Party. Schwesig stands a good chance of ensuring that this remains the case after the election on September 20.
Schwesig, who for a long time trailed the far-right populist Alternative for Germany party (AfD) by a wide margin in the polls, has been campaigning on the slogan "The woman against blue" — a reference to the AfD's party color.
In a televised debate with AfD lead candidate Leif-Erik Holm just over ten days before the election, the state premier described the AfD as "the most dangerous party for our country, for the economy, for social welfare, and also for us women." Addressing Holm directly, she added: "You are talking the country down."
Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania is not an AfD stronghold
Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania is the only eastern German state where the domestic intelligence agency has not classified the AfD as "confirmed right-wing extremist."
The center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU), the party of Chancellor Friedrich Merz, is polling at a historic low, the lowest in any German state. A poor showing in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania could further fuel debate over the increasingly unpopular chancellor. The environmentalist Greens are also fighting to remain in the state parliament, with support hovering around the 5% threshold for representation.
With a vote distribution like this, it is highly unlikely that a majority could be assembled to elect AfD lead candidate Leif-Erik Holm as state premier. After all, every party with a realistic chance of entering the state parliament has ruled out any cooperation with the AfD.
The party's lead candidate, Leif-Erik Holm, deliberately cultivates a down-to-earth image. At campaign events, he draws on his experience as a radio host, including with the public broadcaster NDR. A member of the Bundestag for the Alternative for Germany (AfD) since 2017, he repeatedly taps into widespread dissatisfaction with the government, the economic slowdown, and the comparatively difficult social conditions in the structurally weak and sparsely populated northeast.
Holm cannot match the popular SPD state premier, Schwesig, in head-to-head comparisons of the leading candidates. But the AfD's support in the polls, neck and neck with the SPD, underscores just how deeply divided Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania remains.
Governing the coastal state is unlikely to become any easier in the years to come.

Maharashtra TET paper leak: Employees hid question papers in shoes, paid Rs 8,000 each
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
06:45:40 UTC
15:45:40 KST

File photo: Thane Police arrest three in connection with TET paper leak case
NEW DELHI: The Maharashtra Teacher Eligibility Test paper allegedly walked out of an Agra printing press hidden inside shoe insoles, with two employees paid Rs 8,000 each to smuggle out the confidential examination material, according to a chargesheet filed by Thane City police.The chargesheet, filed before a Bhiwandi court on Friday, names 18 accused, including alleged mastermind Bijendra Gupta, and lays out how investigators traced the leak from the printing press to those allegedly trying to sell the papers in Maharashtra. Sixteen accused have been arrested, while two others, Ashok Sav and Prakash Misal, remain absconding, police said.
How the papers allegedly got out
According to the chargesheet, the leak was traced to Mahim Patran Pvt Ltd, an Agra-based printing press tasked with producing the confidential TET examination material.
Between June 15 and 17, two employees and a former staffer allegedly concealed folded question papers inside their shoe insoles while leaving the premises. Security guards frisked their clothes but allegedly did not check their footwear, allowing the papers to be taken outside, the chargesheet said.The state had prepared four separate sets of question papers for the two TET papers to maintain confidentiality and allow one set to be selected on examination day.
Investigators allege that all four sets were nevertheless taken out of the press.The employees were allegedly paid Rs 8,000 each and promised land plots in Agra in return for stealing the papers, according to the chargesheet.
Leak exposed a day before exam
The racket came to light on June 27, a day before the TET was scheduled to be held. Deputy commissioner of Police Pavan Bansod received information that three men were allegedly trying to sell question papers to a Bhiwandi resident.Police then laid a trap using decoy personnel in Kongaon and detained the suspects, recovering four sets of question papers. Officials of the Maharashtra state council of examination later verified that the seized material matched the actual TET paper.
The examination, scheduled for June 28, was subsequently postponed.Police have booked the accused under provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita relating to cheating, criminal breach of trust and criminal conspiracy, along with Maharashtra laws dealing with examination malpractice. A special investigation team is probing the case.Investigators have identified Gupta, a former coaching-class teacher, as the alleged mastermind. Police said he had previously been implicated in another examination paper leak in Odisha.The chargesheet cites money trails, technical evidence and the recovery of an original question paper from the Bihar residence of a relative of Gupta as evidence in the alleged supply chain. Police said a supplementary chargesheet would be filed as the investigation continues.

The war is exhausting Russia’s economy – the budget deficit is growing, reserves are dwindling, and debt is becoming more expensive – AP
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
09:41:16 EEST
15:41:16 KST

The war is exhausting Russia’s economy – the budget deficit is growing, reserves are dwindling, and debt is becoming more expensive – AP
Kyiv • UNN
Russia’s economy has almost stopped growing, while the budget deficit has reached 2.8% of GDP. Reserves are dwindling, and bond yields have reached 17%.
The Russian economy is increasingly feeling the consequences of enormous military spending: economic growth has nearly stalled, the budget deficit is growing, and available reserves are shrinking. At the same time, economists do not yet see signs of an imminent financial crisis or economic collapse, Associated Press reports, writes UNN.
Details
After growing by more than 4% in 2023–2024, the Russian economy has slowed sharply. The Russian government forecasts growth of only 0.6% this year; the economy contracted in the first quarter and recovered only slightly in the second.
The mood among Russian consumers is also deteriorating. The Levada Center's consumer sentiment index fell to 94 points in the summer, compared with 116 in the spring and summer of 2025. A figure below 100 indicates that negative assessments predominate.
The deficit is growing, reserves are shrinking
One of the main problems is the state of Russia's budget. As of the end of July, its deficit had reached 2.8% of annual GDP—almost twice the initial plan for the entire year.
Available funds in the reserve fund have fallen to approximately 1.6% of GDP. As a result, the Kremlin is increasingly forced to borrow money from Russian banks.
At the same time, servicing such borrowing is expensive. According to Janis Kluge, an expert at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs, interest rates on Russian bonds reach 17%.
Budgetary stress is intensifying doubts about how long Russia will be able to continue the war
Additional pressure is being created by high interest rates, which the Central Bank of Russia is maintaining to combat inflation caused, in particular, by military spending. This is hitting civilian businesses the hardest because, unlike defense companies, they do not have privileged access to credit.
Loans from Russian banks have become another source of financing for the defense industry. Such debts are not directly reflected in budget deficit figures.
Despite the accumulation of problems, economists do not expect an immediate collapse of the Russian economy. High oil revenues still allow the Kremlin to finance the war, but the current model is gradually increasing the country's debt and budgetary burden.

Day of Countryside Living organizer says rural life best suits active people
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19

Day of Countryside Living organizer says rural life best suits active people
Reve Lambur, the lead organizer of Day of Countryside Living, said that anyone interested in rural life should definitely go meet the vibrant communities who are eager to welcome new residents.
Rural living is best suited for active people, because there are so many opportunities to create something new yourself, she added.
"There are two ideas behind organizing Day of Countryside Living. One is to show that living in the countryside is very pleasant, and to give people who have thought about moving there a chance to see what the local community is like — whether there is work, whether there is housing," said coordinator Reve Lambur.
The second idea is to show local residents what their municipality looks like. "Maybe new people have moved in — it's a chance to introduce them to the community, and for the community to feel proud of their municipality, to see that it's such a great place to live," Lambur said.
This year, 26 rural municipalities are participating. "In previous years, the municipality itself had to be the main contact point, but this year communities could take the lead as well, so we wouldn't take away the opportunity from communities that are actively looking for new residents," Lambur said.
The pandemic, she noted, encouraged many people to move to the countryside — and stay. "Many of them are families with children, because rural living is safe. The downside is that services aren't always close at hand. Families definitely need a car. When visiting communities, you can ask directly about the pros and cons of living there," Lambur explained.
"You don't just move into a house — you move into a community. That's the message of the day. Rural life suits active people. There are so many opportunities to create and do things yourself, to become a spark‑person — someone whose actions matter to others," Lambur said.
This year's Day of Countryside Living will take place on September 19.

Paramount may finally buy Warner Bros. for $110 billion this weekend – Reuters
Kyiv • UNN
Paramount is negotiating with U.S. states over a $110 billion deal with Warner Bros. Discovery. The conditions include monitoring CNN and theatrical distribution.
Paramount may reach an agreement as early as this weekend with the U.S. states seeking to block its $110 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery. Possible settlement terms include independent monitoring of CNN content and commitments regarding the number of films released in theaters, Reuters reports, citing sources, according to UNN.
Details
After information emerged about a possible agreement, Paramount shares rose by nearly 7% in over-the-counter trading, while Warner Bros. Discovery shares rose 8.4%.
California and 11 other states filed a lawsuit against the deal in July. They claim the merger would create a media giant capable of raising prices for films and television content. Federal regulators in U.S. President Donald Trump's administration previously approved the deal.
CNN, HBO and "Harry Potter" could come under Paramount's control
If the deal is completed, major media and entertainment assets would come under one corporate roof, including CNN, HBO, the "Harry Potter" franchise, "The Daily Show" and the rights to broadcast NFL games.
Paramount CEO David Ellison views the combination of the two major Hollywood studios as a way to strengthen the company's position amid years of changes in the market and competition from Netflix and Disney.
One of the most sensitive issues remains CNN's future. Ellison's critics previously accused him of changing CBS News' editorial policy in favor of Trump and expressed concern about how CNN's operations might change after the acquisition of Warner Bros.
Paramount has also promised to pay Warner Bros. shareholders $7 million for each day after September 30 if the deal has not been completed by then. Therefore, settling the dispute with the states by the end of the month would allow the company to avoid significant additional costs.

Denmark’s plan to send foreign prisoners sentenced to deportation to a prison in Kosovo has been delayed again.
The 300 prison places are now expected to become available at the end of 2027 at the earliest and possibly not until the beginning of 2028, Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen informed the parties behind the agreement Friday.
“I have been informed by the Danish Prison Agency that the construction of the prison in Kosovo is delayed, so the prison places can at the earliest be put into use at the end of 2027 and possibly not until the beginning of 2028,” Wammen said in a written statement to Ritzau.
Denmark reached a political agreement in 2021 to lease 300 prison places in Kosovo to reduce pressure on Danish prisons.
When the agreement with Kosovo was finalized, the first foreign nationals sentenced to deportation were expected to begin serving their sentences there in early 2023.
The latest delay means the prison could open about five years later than originally planned.
Wammen said the project remains an important priority for the government so “we can relieve pressure on the Danish prisons and get criminal foreign nationals sentenced to deportation out of the country.”
“It must happen as quickly as possible, and I naturally would have very much liked for us to have long since begun sending inmates there. Therefore, I am of course far from satisfied that the project is further delayed,” he said.
According to the Ministry of Justice, authorities in Kosovo have now emptied the prison of inmates.
An agreement with a contractor was signed in July, and the renovation work is expected to take about a year.
The project has previously been delayed by the approval process in Kosovo’s parliament, where opposition parties did not support international agreements.
Danish prisons have faced overcrowding for years, adding pressure to make the Kosovo prison places available.
The number of people injured in traffic accidents in Denmark increased in 2025, while the number of deaths fell slightly, according to new figures from Statistics Denmark.
Police recorded 2,832 people as injured or killed in traffic accidents during the year, an increase of 313 compared with 2024.
The number of traffic deaths fell from 145 in 2024 to 143 in 2025.
Denmark has now recorded fewer than 200 traffic deaths a year for 10 consecutive years. This is well below levels seen between 1965 and 1973, when more than 1,000 people were killed in traffic each year.
Of those recorded in 2025, 1,732 were seriously injured and 957 suffered minor injuries.
The number of injured road users increased across almost all forms of transport, with mopeds the exception.
Injuries among people riding electric bicycles increased from 173 in 2024 to 211 in 2025. Nearly three-quarters of those injured in this group were aged 45 or older.
The police figures do not show the full number of people injured on Danish roads because they only cover accidents reported to police.
Hospital emergency departments keep separate records of traffic injuries. In 2024, they registered 29,589 injured people, more than 1,000 above the previous year’s figure.
Denmark will bring forward and increase a military aid package for Ukraine to DKK 1.8 billion, days after a Russian frigate fired two flares toward a Danish military helicopter.
Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen of the Moderates and Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus of the Social Democrats announced the decision Friday after a meeting of the Danish Parliament’s Foreign Policy Committee.
Most of the money will go toward air defense systems produced in Ukraine. The support had been requested by Ukraine.
Løkke described the incident involving the Danish helicopter as a “severe Russian provocation.”
“If they think they can provoke us into being restrained with our support for Ukraine, then they are mistaken,” he said.
Ukraine has faced difficulties defending itself against Russian ballistic missile attacks because of shortages of suitable air defense missiles, including Patriot missiles produced by the United States.
The decision follows an incident Monday involving a Danish Air Force Fennec helicopter and a Russian frigate in international waters off Gedser in southern Denmark.
The Danish Defence said the helicopter was carrying out routine photographic surveillance of the Russian vessel when the frigate fired two flares toward it. One passed close to the helicopter.
According to Bruus, the Russian ship did not establish radio contact with the helicopter before firing the flares.
NATO has described the incident as an “irresponsible Russian act.”
“This fits into a pattern we are seeing around Europe, where Russia is escalating and constantly testing boundaries. It serves the purpose of shaking our unity and our support for Ukraine, and that must not work,” Løkke said.
Denmark summoned the Russian ambassador following the incident. Russia has said the Danish helicopter acted “provocatively.”
“If the Russians think that they can rattle us by doing this kind of thing, then our counter-response is that we will step up our support for Ukraine faster than we had intended,” Bruus said.
The captain of the Russian frigate has since received an award from Russia for his actions, according to the Danish report.
Denmark has been a major supporter of Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022. However, since December, Denmark has announced only one other major aid package in addition to Friday’s package.
The Danish Ukraine Fund, which has financed much of the country’s support, has almost run out of available money. Further support would therefore require politicians to find funding elsewhere.
So far, much of Denmark’s support has been financed through the government’s projected future fiscal surplus.

Denmark plans to raise the fine for repeated violations of residency requirements to 100,000 DKK, Housing Minister Jacob Mark of SF, the Socialist People’s Party, told Jyllands-Posten.
The current maximum fine for a second violation is 20,000 DKK, meaning the proposed penalty would be five times higher.
“Cheating on the residency requirement is destructive to smaller towns and small island communities,” Mark said.
“When a citizen buys a house, but chooses not to live there, the consequence is that lovely towns in beautiful surroundings turn into ghost towns, the local grocery store closes, and community life and neighborhood spirit die,” he said.
Owners of homes intended for year-round use must ensure that the property is inhabited for at least 180 days a year. If they do not live there themselves, they can rent it out for permanent residence.
Under current rules, a first violation can lead to a fine of up to 10,000 DKK, rising to 20,000 DKK for a second offense.
Municipalities set the detailed rules for different types of housing. Holiday homes are generally exempt, while some properties can be designated as flexbolig, allowing a year-round home to be used as a holiday home.
Several island municipalities, including Samsø, Ærø, Fanø, Bornholm, Læsø and Langeland, have previously called for stronger monitoring powers. They want to be able to check water and electricity use weekly when they suspect violations, rather than monthly.
Mark said he has invited the island municipalities and Landdistrikternes Fællesråd, an organization representing rural areas in Denmark, to discuss possible additional measures.
Bus and light rail tickets in Aarhus will cost 15 DKK from 2027 under a new municipal budget agreement approved Thursday evening.
Aarhus Municipality will allocate 35 million DKK a year from 2027 to lower ticket prices, TV 2 Østjylland reported.
A consultancy firm had estimated that introducing 15 DKK tickets across the municipality could cost 122 million DKK, although the figure was uncertain.
Mayor Anders Winnerskjold of Socialdemokratiet, Denmark’s Social Democratic Party, argued that the actual cost would be lower, and the City Council agreed.
The budget agreement also notes that the national government plans to introduce free public transport for people under 22. Aarhus expects that measure to cover part of the cost of the cheaper local tickets.
Since March, residents have already been able to buy 15 DKK tickets on three bus routes as part of a trial.
The municipality has said the trial is intended to show how cheaper fares affect passenger numbers and what changes may be needed if more people choose public transport.
The experience will also be used in planning for a permanent price reduction and for making sure buses and the light rail can handle more passengers.
Frie Grønne leader Sikandar Siddique has been removed from Copenhagen City Council after authorities ruled that he does not meet the requirement of living in the municipality.
The City Council approved the decision Thursday, following a long dispute over Siddique’s residence.
Siddique has called the case a “miscarriage of justice” by “the system” and said it had been influenced by Zionists, meaning supporters of the Jewish national movement and political ideology. Several parties rejected those claims during Thursday’s meeting.
“I believe that it is quite damaging when an election is called into question by Sikandar Siddique’s statements, but also so-called experts,” Lord Mayor Sisse Marie Welling of SF, the Socialist People’s Party, said before the decision was approved.
Before the November 2025 municipal election, Siddique registered a move from Herlev to Copenhagen so he could run in the capital.
Copenhagen Municipality later cancelled his residence registration, citing, among other things, an unusually low electricity bill and a lack of documentation showing purchases near his registered Copenhagen address.
Siddique appealed, but the Ministry of Research, Education and Digitalization upheld the municipality’s decision on September 8.
His seat will now go to Frie Grønne’s first alternate, Asham Agha Nadeem, meaning the party keeps its mandate.
Frie Grønne received nearly 7,000 votes in the election, including more than 3,000 personal votes for Siddique. Nadeem received 612 personal votes.
Denmark’s oldest living person, Kirsten Schwalbe, has entered the list of Europe’s 10 oldest living people, TV Midtvest reported Thursday.
Schwalbe turned 112 in March. She was born in Salling in 1914, a few months before the outbreak of World War I, and grew up with nine siblings.
She married her first husband in 1938 and had three children. Today, she lives in her own home in Struer.
Schwalbe has previously said that genetics may partly explain her long life. Four of her nine siblings also lived past the age of 100, she told Berlingske in 2024.
She has also said that mood plays an important role in living a long life.
Europe’s oldest living person is British woman Ethel Caterham, who is 117 and is also the world’s oldest living person.
Schwalbe is not yet among the world’s 20 oldest living people, according to TV Midtvest.
Meanwhile, a man in Costa Rica, Jose Flores, claims to be 119 years old. His age has not yet been confirmed, and specialists are reviewing documents to determine his date of birth.

Three Danish government ministers from Moderaterne, the Moderates, want schools to stop using Aula, the digital platform used for communication between schools, daycare facilities and families.
Ministers Monika Rubin, Christina Egelund and Jakob Engel-Schmidt made the proposal in a joint interview with Berlingske. They have not proposed an alternative to Aula.
“An IT system has been created that sucks so much oxygen out of the school and the classroom that it is harmful to our children’s well-being and learning,” Engel-Schmidt said.
Aula was introduced in 2019 to replace Skoleintra. Danish public schools and public and self-governing daycare facilities have access to the platform, where students, parents and employees can receive and share information.
Rubin told DR that the amount of communication on the platform had become excessive.
“More communication is not always better communication. 10,000 messages are sent on Aula per minute between half past seven and nine in the morning. It has gotten out of hand,” she said.
According to Berlingske, Egelund said answering parents’ questions is not a core task of Denmark’s public schools.
The proposal follows the latest PISA study, an international assessment of 15-year-old students’ performance in reading, mathematics and science, which showed a decline among Danish students.
Other government parties have expressed skepticism about removing Aula.
Nanna Bonde, education spokesperson for SF, the Socialist People’s Party, one of Denmark’s governing parties, suggested guidelines for the platform could be introduced instead, according to DR.
Apartment sales in Copenhagen fell sharply in August, while several other parts of Denmark saw more houses change hands than a year earlier, new figures from Boligsiden show.
A total of 390 owner-occupied apartments were sold in Copenhagen Municipality in August, 36 percent fewer than in the same month last year.
It was also the third-lowest number of apartment sales recorded in Copenhagen for an August since Boligsiden began collecting the data in 2011.
“Significantly fewer owner-occupied apartments are being traded in Copenhagen, and there has been a clear shift in the otherwise hectic pace that we have seen for a long time in Copenhagen,” said Birgit Daetz, communications director and housing economist at Boligsiden.
Across Denmark, apartment sales were 20 percent lower than in August 2025.
Overall housing sales also fell slightly during the first eight months of the year compared with the same period last year, after seasonal changes are taken into account.
Brian Friis Helmer, personal economist at AL Sydbank, said the apartment market was largely responsible for the decline, while sales of houses and holiday homes remained strong.
Boligsiden recorded more sales of detached and terraced houses than a year earlier in South Jutland, West and South Zealand, North Jutland and Funen.
House sales fell in Copenhagen, the Copenhagen suburbs and North Zealand.
“Now, we see the activity spreading to other parts of the country to a greater extent,” Daetz said.
A Lego model of the Danish royal yacht Dannebrog has been sold at auction for 60,000 DKK after spending 28 years at Legoland in Billund.
The model was sold Wednesday by auction house Bruun Rasmussen for twice its estimated price of between 20,000 and 30,000 DKK.
Legoland said the proceeds will be donated to the Mary Foundation, which works to combat social isolation.
“We think it could be nice to donate the money to the Mary Foundation, now that it is the royal yacht ‘Dannebrog’ that we have had up for auction,” said Jan Mouritzen, head of Legoland’s model department.
Bruun Rasmussen specialist Line Hjorth Langkjær said the model’s history at Legoland and the royal yacht’s place in Danish history had helped increase interest.
It is the first time Legoland has auctioned an original model from Miniland, where landmarks are recreated in miniature using Lego bricks.
The original Dannebrog model contains about 25,000 bricks. It was replaced after a new Copenhagen Harbour area opened in Miniland in July with an updated version made from 225,000 bricks.
The real Dannebrog serves as the official and private residence of the Danish royal couple and other members of the royal family during summer cruises and official visits overseas.
The Mary Foundation was established by then-Crown Princess Mary in 2007. The foundation said the donation will support efforts to combat bullying among children and loneliness among young people.
A patient at Landssygehuset in Tórshavn underwent surgery for an inguinal hernia on Wednesday while the surgeon performing the procedure was in Aabenraa, southern Denmark.
The operation used robot-assisted telesurgery, with the surgeon controlling a robot in the Faroe Islands from an office in Aabenraa.
It was the first time the technology had been used for an operation in Denmark and between two public hospitals in the Nordic region, Sygehus Sønderjylland, the Southern Jutland hospital, said in a press release.
Chief physician Jan Krzak said the operation had a “highly satisfactory result.”
“We have started out with a few selected patients with an uncomplicated inguinal hernia. The first step was to document whether the technology, safety, communication, and cooperation functioned stably in practice,” Krzak said.
The operation is part of a project examining whether telesurgery could eventually provide treatment to patients who live far from major medical facilities.
Elinborg Mortensen, chief physician at Landssygehuset in Tórshavn, said the technology could be particularly useful in the Faroe Islands, where many patients currently have to travel long distances for hospital treatment.
“Therefore, it is interesting for us to investigate whether new technology can bring some of the expertise closer to the patients in a safe and controlled manner,” Mortensen said.
A full surgical and anesthesia team was present with the patient in Tórshavn throughout Wednesday’s operation. The team was ready to take over if the technology or connection failed.
Robot-assisted telesurgery has previously been used internationally, including for operations performed remotely between London and Gibraltar.
The ferry between Thyborøn and Agger in northern West Jutland ran aground Wednesday morning, TV Midtvest reported.
No one was injured in the incident, ferry operations manager Andreas Groth told the broadcaster.
All ferry services have been suspended for the rest of the day, according to the operator’s website.
It is not yet clear what caused the ferry to run aground.
The coastal rescue service is at the scene, and divers are expected to inspect the ferry, TV Midtvest reported.
There is currently no indication of when ferry services will resume.
The ferry can carry around 22 passenger cars and about 100 passengers. It normally runs once an hour between Agger and Thyborøn, with the crossing taking about 10 minutes.
The route is owned by Lemvig Municipality and Thisted Municipality and carries around 145,000 passengers a year.
The ferry is about 45 meters long and 11 meters wide.
Novo partners with Anthropic to develop drugs faster
Danish pharmaceutical company Novo has entered into a partnership with US technology company Anthropic to use artificial intelligence in the discovery and development of new medicines.
Novo said it will use Anthropic’s Claude Science AI model to examine what the company described as “central challenges” in drug research.
The agreement is part of Novo’s wider use of artificial intelligence. The company already works with OpenAI and Amazon on AI, according to Børsen.
Novo CEO Mike Doustdar said the partnership reflects the company’s “ambition to become the world’s most AI-driven healthcare company.”
“By joining forces with Anthropic, we will strengthen our research and development organization and advance our mission to deliver new, transformative healthcare solutions to people living with chronic diseases,” Doustdar said.
Novo, which is behind medicines including Ozempic and Wegovy, said it plans to use Anthropic’s AI models to “scale AI across the entire company.”
Claude will also be used to develop software internally.
As an initial step, Novo plans to test Claude Science in specific research and development workflows.
Novo told Reuters in May that it aims to use AI to reduce the time it takes to bring new medicines to market.
Russian captain honored for flares at Danish helicopter
The commander of a Russian warship that fired two signal flares at a Danish military helicopter Monday has received an award for his actions, according to the Russian Ministry of Defense.
The ministry said Wednesday that two flares were fired to prevent what it described as a “provocation,” Reuters reported.
Russia identified the vessel as the Soobrazitelny and described it as a corvette, a relatively small and lightly armed warship. The Danish Armed Forces have described it as a frigate. According to TV 2, Russia and NATO countries use different classifications and standards for warships.
The Russian ministry said the vessel was carrying out “operations in neutral waters,” according to Russian media outlet Tass. It did not specify what those operations involved.
The ship’s commander was praised for his response during the incident, which the ministry said caused the Danish helicopter to leave the area shortly afterward.
The Danish Armed Forces said Monday at 11:02 p.m. that one of the Air Force’s Fennec helicopters had been fired at with pyrotechnics in international waters off Gedser.
According to the Danish Armed Forces, the helicopter was conducting routine photographic documentation of the Russian vessel at the time.
Russian Ambassador to Denmark Vladimir Barbin has previously described the helicopter’s actions before the flares were fired as “provocative.”
He said the helicopter had carried out “dangerous manoeuvres” and that the Russian vessel had been unable to establish contact with it. He also said the communication problem was on the Danish side.
Danish Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus, a member of the Social Democrats, rejected that account.
“I trust the Armed Forces. The fact is that there are plenty of ways to contact such a helicopter via radio and other things,” Bruus said.
“There was no contact before these flares were fired, and that should have been done.”
Train traffic resumes between Skanderborg and Aarhus after disruption
Train traffic between Skanderborg and Aarhus has resumed after a stopped train blocked the line Wednesday afternoon.
DSB, Denmark’s national rail operator, said shortly before 2 p.m. that trains were running according to schedule again.
Rejseplanen, Denmark’s national journey planner, showed that some trains had been canceled and several others were heavily delayed.
“There may still be longer travel times and isolated cancellations until train staff are in place again,” DSB said.
Passengers delayed by more than 30 minutes may be entitled to compensation under DSB’s travel time guarantee.
Travelers delayed by 30 to 59 minutes can receive 50% of the ticket price back. Delays of 60 to 89 minutes qualify for 75%, while delays of 90 minutes or more qualify for a full refund.
Passengers can choose between a ticket for a new journey on the same route or a cash payment.
Applications for compensation can be submitted through DSB’s travel time guarantee scheme.
