Economic Watch: AI takes spotlight at China-ASEAN Expo
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
14:14:48 CST
15:14:48 KST

People visit the sales area of AI-related products during the 23rd China-ASEAN Expo in Nanning, south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, Sept. 18, 2026. AI-related products have taken center stage at the ongoing 23rd China-ASEAN Expo, which attracts more than 3,400 companies from China, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and beyond. (Xinhua/Cao Yiming)
NANNING, China, Sept. 19 (Xinhua) -- When Vietnamese visitor Doan Minh Thao stepped into an exhibition hall of the 23rd China-ASEAN Expo here on Friday, he got interested in an artificial intelligence (AI)-powered eyewear that can provide real-time translation in over 40 languages, including Vietnamese.
With the help of this gadget, developed by a Chinese company, he managed to have unimpeded verbal communication with exhibitors at the venue.
AI-related products including these smart glasses have taken center stage at the ongoing Expo, which attracts more than 3,400 companies from China, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and beyond.
FROM CONCEPT TO REAL BUSINESS
"Last year, AI was mostly for show. This year, it is driving sales," said Wang Jicai, secretary-general of the China-ASEAN Expo Secretariat.
In exhibition halls situated in the downtown area of this southern Chinese city, embodied AI robots, exoskeleton medical equipment and AI-enabled wearables attracted crowds of curious visitors, while unattended coffee booths and ice cream stands served customers with nimble robotic arms.
As some companies display fancy hardware at the Expo, others showcase AI-driven systems for sectors ranging from finance, healthcare, transportation and agriculture to production management and water treatment.
China and ASEAN, trading partners that saw bilateral trade volume top 1 trillion U.S. dollars in 2025, have been organizing this major trade and investment event for more than two decades. And for this year's Expo, which runs from Sept. 17 to 21, special emphasis was placed on the AI sector.
According to organizers, the Expo's "AI marketplace" features about 500 products from more than 70 companies, allowing visitors to test and buy products on-site.
In the meantime, a China-ASEAN AI application cooperation center has cataloged more than 1,000 potential AI scenarios, set up offices in Vietnam, Laos and Malaysia, and backed over 30 cross-border projects.
AI ENABLES BROADER COOPERATION
"What inspires me most is seeing that AI is not limited to the technology sector. It can also serve as an enabler for education, healthcare, tourism, industry, public services, agriculture and the development of economic zones," said Dyah Wahyu Ermawati, director of investment and integrated license services office of Indonesia's East Java province.
"There are very broad opportunities for cooperation," the Indonesian official said to Xinhua Thursday when attending the 2nd China-ASEAN AI Scenario Application Matchmaking Session organized in Nanning alongside the Expo.
China and ASEAN, already each other's biggest trading partner, are seeking to strengthen and upgrade cooperation in a wide range of sectors. The progress in digital technologies including AI has facilitated cooperation and enhanced efficiency.
In Laos and Cambodia, for example, a platform developed by local partners together with an enterprise from China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region has started to use satellite imagery, drones and ground sensors to optimize tropical crop cultivation.
Apart from precision agriculture, cooperation in AI applications can also include fields like smart logistics, manufacturing automation, financial technology, urban management and cross-border e-commerce, according to exhibitors and seminar speakers at the Expo.
AI BRINGS GREAT OPPORTUNITIES
As China and ASEAN advance high-quality economic cooperation under the framework of the China-ASEAN Free Trade Area 3.0 Upgrade Protocol, signed in October 2025, AI has emerged as a new frontier for win-win cooperation.
During a China-ASEAN business and investment summit held here on Thursday, a collection of case studies on China-ASEAN AI cooperation was released, showcasing a range of practical achievements.
The cases include 31 practical AI cooperation projects between China and ASEAN, covering all 11 ASEAN member states and sectors such as infrastructure, intelligent manufacturing and smart logistics.
"I think there's a lot of optimism that we will be benefiting from this collaboration with AI," Secretary-General of ASEAN Kao Kim Hourn said to reporters Thursday on the sidelines of the Expo. It is not only for the economic sector; it cuts across all sectors of the society, he said.
The secretary-general said there are great opportunities to capitalize on the potential of AI and the digital sector. Regarding AI cooperation, he called for adequate rules and regulations and advised against stifling innovation and creativity. ■

NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 19 (Xinhua) -- China's women's basketball team made a dominant debut at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games on Saturday, routing Thailand 111-46 in its group opener.
China opened the game with a 12-1 run, establishing a 33-14 lead by the end of the first quarter following a three-pointer from Chen Yujie. Six Chinese players scored in double digits. Guard Yang Shuyu led the team with a game-high 21 points, adding seven rebounds and five assists. Luo Xinyu and Chen Yujie contributed 16 points each, while Chen Mingling finished with 15 points and nine rebounds.

Yang added that the team is in high spirits and showing no signs of fatigue from consecutive games. "The team has multiple lineups and different tactical approaches. We will present different things depending on different opponents," Yang said.
China will face its second group opponent Indonesia on Monday. ■

Austrian parliament speaker calls for mutual learning, fair cooperation between Europe, China
China

VIENNA, Sept. 19 (Xinhua) -- Europe should abandon an anxious mindset toward China's development and instead pursue mutual learning and fair cooperation, said Walter Rosenkranz, president of Austria's National Council, or the lower house of Parliament.
In an interview with Xinhua, Rosenkranz said China has achieved leaps and bounds in many fields, notably in renewable energy. "The EU and China must continue to deepen their cooperation while operating within a framework of fair rules," he said.
European national legislatures, he said, should take the initiative to build fair and reasonable frameworks for cooperation, helping various sectors in Europe and China eliminate perceptual biases, deepen practical cooperation, and achieve complementary strengths and common development.
Noting that he recently led a delegation to China, which was his first visit to the country since taking office as president of the National Council, Rosenkranz said Austrian political parties share broad consensus and a strong willingness to deepen exchanges with China.
During the visit, the delegation not only experienced China's long and profound history and culture, but also witnessed the vitality of China's modernization drive, he said.
This year marks the 55th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic relations between China and Austria. Rosenkranz said friendship between the two countries has been deepening since the establishment of diplomatic ties.
Since the 1990s, there have been more than 60 exchanges between the national legislative bodies, Rosenkranz said.
Looking back on the 55-year history of exchanges, Rosenkranz said Austria and China cherish peace, consistently uphold multilateralism and the norms of international law, and remain committed to promoting peace through cooperation and pursuing development through win-win outcomes.
The two countries share compatible development concepts and have long worked together under the framework of the United Nations to contribute to world peace and development, while deepening cooperation in multiple fields, including the economy and culture, with fruitful results, he said.
More than 650 Austrian companies are currently operating in China, fully demonstrating the strong vitality of Austria-China cooperation, he added.
Rosenkranz said the current international situation is marked by intertwined changes and turbulence, with challenges such as climate change, artificial intelligence governance and regional conflicts emerging one after another. The legislative bodies of Austria and China could further deepen dialogue and cooperation, build consensus on governance, improve cooperation rules, and contribute wisdom and strength to addressing global issues.
Looking to the future, Rosenkranz regards young people as the main force of future cooperation and the inheritors and promoters of friendship between the two countries.
Deeper youth and cultural exchanges, he added, could strengthen the foundation of people-to-people ties and give the friendly strategic partnership between the two countries fresh momentum.■

Switzerland has changed its national security strategy because of Russia’s war against Ukraine and hybrid threats
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
09:13:20 EEST
15:13:20 KST

Switzerland has changed its national security strategy because of Russia’s war against Ukraine and hybrid threats
Kyiv • UNN
Switzerland has approved a security strategy with 10 objectives and 46 measures. The country will prepare for hybrid attacks and a possible armed assault.
Switzerland has adopted a new national security strategy that provides for strengthening the country's defense capabilities amid Russia's war against Ukraine, cyberattacks, and other hybrid threats. The document contains 10 goals and 46 specific measures, Anadolu Agency reports, writes UNN.
Details
The Swiss Federal Council stated that the international security situation is becoming increasingly unstable due to rivalry among major powers, armed conflicts, and the weakening of the international order.
The document paid particular attention to Russia's aggression against Ukraine. The Swiss government noted that an end to the war is not yet in sight, while the number of cyberattacks, influence operations, and other hybrid threats is increasing.
Switzerland will prepare for a possible armed attack
The strategy identifies three main areas – increasing the resilience of the state, economy, and society; protecting the population and critical infrastructure; and strengthening the country's defense capabilities.
The government considers hybrid and remote attacks, as well as organized crime activities, to be the most likely threats. At the same time, Switzerland must be capable of effectively countering an armed attack as well.
To this end, the country plans to create the necessary military capabilities in advance and expand cooperation with partner states.
Implementation of the strategy will be coordinated by the State Secretariat for Security Policy. The Federal Council is to receive a report on the implementation of the planned measures by the end of 2028.

The US nearly started a war with China over an erroneous AI-generated report – CNN
Kyiv • UNN
The US prepared to intercept a Chinese vessel based on a false report about a nuclear cargo. The AI error was discovered before the operation began.
In the spring, U.S. military personnel prepared to intercept a Chinese vessel based on an intelligence report claiming that the ship was carrying components for a nuclear program. Shortly before the operation began, it was discovered that the analyst had prepared the document using artificial intelligence, which had misidentified the cargo, CNN reports, citing sources, writes UNN.
Details
The incident occurred in the spring amid the war with Iran. An intelligence report circulated among U.S. military personnel contained information about a Chinese vessel in the Middle East that was allegedly carrying components linked to a nuclear weapons program.
The information was taken so seriously that the U.S. military began planning to intercept the ship. According to CNN sources, armed U.S. service members were preparing to board it, while military aircraft were already in the air.
The error was discovered before the operation began
Only shortly before the planned interception did officials decide to examine in greater detail the report prepared by an analyst from the U.S. Special Operations Command.
It then emerged that artificial intelligence had been used in preparing the document, and that the chatbot had incorrectly identified the materials being carried by the Chinese vessel. CNN was unable to establish what was actually on board.
According to one of the network's sources, the report about the cargo was "completely false."
This nearly started a war
The U.S. military operation against the Chinese vessel could have caused a serious escalation in relations between Washington and Beijing and potentially developed into an armed confrontation between the two countries.

AfD surge in eastern Germany makes some immigrants question whether they still belong
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
06:08:36 UTC
15:08:36 KST

AfD surge in eastern Germany makes some immigrants question whether they still belong
- Many Syrian immigrants in eastern Germany feel increasingly unwelcome as the far-right AfD party gains support and anti-immigrant sentiments rise.
- The AfD, advocating immigration restrictions and "remigration", is poised to become the largest party in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, stirring fear among migrant communities.
- Despite hardships, many migrants contribute to the local economy, but concerns about discrimination may lead some to consider leaving their homes in Germany.
AI generated
ROSTOCK, Germany – Shahd Najeeb still remembers the trauma of fleeing ISIS fighters during Syria’s civil war.
More than a decade after finding refuge in Germany, she now fears she may no longer be welcome there.
“When I think about the time we left Syria, I still don’t know how we managed to get through it,” she told Reuters in her home in Rostock, on Germany’s Baltic coast.
“It was like a nightmare.”
Najeeb and her husband, Mahmoud Hmouech, fled their home in Deir al-Zor in eastern Syria and rebuilt their lives in Germany, where he works in a barber shop and she serves meals in local schools. They have two young children.
“We are grateful to the German people for welcoming us and giving us peace and security,” Hmouech said. “The work we do is a small way of showing our gratitude.”
They are among more than 900,000 Syrians living in Germany, most of whom arrived as asylum seekers during the civil war.
But as the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) gains support and migration returns to the centre of political debate, migrants say hostility towards foreigners is growing.
Reuters spoke to 20 people of migrant background in Rostock and the nearby city of Schwerin, many of whom have become German citizens and have lived in Germany for years.
Most said they had encountered more anti-immigrant abuse in recent years, ranging from muttered remarks to demands that they return to their countries of origin.
One woman said a neighbour poured foul-smelling water on her from a balcony.
Their concerns come as the AfD gains momentum across eastern Germany.
In Najeeb and Hmouech’s home state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, in the formerly communist east, opinion polls suggest the AfD is set to become the biggest party in an election on Sept 20.
Earlier in September, the party, which wants to restrict immigration and talks about “remigration” – or sending foreigners back to their home countries – won its first major regional election in Saxony-Anhalt, another eastern state.
Several interviewees, including people working in healthcare, tourism, education and food services, said they would consider leaving Rostock or Schwerin if the climate continued to worsen.
‘This country is for Germans’
Sitting in the family’s small apartment in northern Rostock, where their children’s drawings cover one wall and toys are neatly stacked in corners of the living room, Najeeb spoke as her children, aged six and four, played nearby.
Najeeb, who studied physics in Baghdad and later worked as a jewellery designer in Syria, recalled stopping at a grocery store after collecting her children from school when, she said, an elderly man in a wheelchair shouted “this country is for Germans!”, and that she did not belong in Germany.
“The pain I experienced in Rostock is a new kind of pain that I have never felt before.
“You feel the injustice because you have done nothing wrong. I worked hard to build a life for myself and then someone comes along and treats you like garbage,” she said, her voice cracking.
She recalled her son asking: “Mama, why is he insulting you? What did you do to him?”
Unsure how to explain, she told him the man was perhaps unwell.
Labour force
The AfD began as a eurosceptic party in 2013 and its anti-immigrant tone sharpened markedly after former chancellor Angela Merkel’s decision in 2015 to open Germany’s borders temporarily, admitting around one million migrants and refugees, around a third of them Syrians fleeing the civil war.
Since then, it has grown from a fringe movement into Germany’s most popular party, leading Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s conservatives in national polls.
Leif-Erik Holm, the AfD’s main candidate in the election of Sept 20, says he has “absolutely no objection” to immigration by skilled workers.
He says those who should be deported are the more than 250,000 foreigners who have no legal right to stay in Germany.
But critics say the broader problem is the atmosphere created by rhetoric they say targets foreigners in general.
During a televised debate on Sept 16, Social Democrat state premier Manuela Schwesig accused the AfD of “causing widespread fear with its statements on remigration and workers from different cultural backgrounds”.
“I think it’s terrible that people who work here, who make their contribution and pay their taxes and social security contributions, are afraid and don’t feel at ease,” she said.
During the debate, she and Holm took a question from a design engineer concerned about the risk of losing a valued Moroccan draughtsman because of the racist insults he said he encountered regularly on the street.
Holm said it was “naturally a shame that there’s such a mood”. But he blamed the government for allowing illegal immigration and failing to deport more than a fraction of foreigners formally required to leave the country.
The debate carries economic implications as well.
Around 50,000 people with a migration background work in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
Economists have warned that like other eastern states with low birth rates and an ageing population, it will need more skilled workers.
According to data from Germany’s labour office, around 316,000 Syrian nationals – not including Syrians who have acquired German nationality – work in Germany, most in full-time jobs that pay social security contributions.
Their unemployment rate is above 30 per cent, but data show the longer people stay, the more likely they are to find work.
Figures from 2023 indicate that among those who have been in Germany for seven years or longer, more than 60 per cent have a job.
Many Syrians say they hope to return home if conditions improve. Others, including Najeeb and Hmouech, increasingly see their future in Germany.
Whether the AfD’s rise changes that calculation remains an open question.
Hmouech says he does not want his children to grow up feeling rejected by the society they call home.
“At the end of the day, family comes first,” he said. REUTERS

Only 31% of Russians believe in the fairness of State Duma elections – poll
Kyiv • UNN
T More than half of Russians allow for manipulation in State Duma elections. Nearly half do not consider the parliament independent of Putin.
Only 30.8% of Russians expect the parliamentary elections in the Russian Federation to be held fairly, while more than half allow for manipulation of the voting results. This is evidenced by the results of a survey conducted by the research company ExtremeScan, reports UNN.
Details
According to the study, 32.7% of respondents believe that the election results may be significantly altered. Another 23.5% expect that votes may be added for certain candidates or parties, although, in their opinion, this will not significantly affect the final result.
At the same time, Russians gave a critical assessment of the work of the previous convocation of the State Duma. 40.2% of respondents said that the laws it had adopted since 2021 had brought citizens more harm than benefit. 19.9% of those surveyed hold the opposite view.
Almost half do not consider the State Duma independent of Putin
Another 49% of respondents believe that the State Duma has no real opportunity to disagree with Russian dictator Vladimir Putin on important issues. Only 23.3% are convinced that the Russian parliament has such an opportunity.
The survey was conducted by telephone from September 4 to 10 among adult residents of Russia in all federal districts. At the time the interim results were published, 800 people had been surveyed; the stated margin of error is ±3.5%. ExtremeScan plans to publish the full report, based on a sample of more than 1,600 respondents, after the elections.
Parliamentary elections in Russia are being held from September 18 to 20. These are the first elections to the State Duma since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Parties step up work on candidate lists ahead of March Riigikogu elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
06:02:00 UTC
15:02:00 KST

Parties step up work on candidate lists ahead of March Riigikogu elections
With less than half a year until the Riigikogu elections, Estonia's major political parties are assembling candidate lists and drafting election programs. Some have already begun campaigning, while others will finalize their lists and platforms only in January.
EKRE Ready even for snap elections
EKRE parliamentary group adviser Aarne Mäe said preparations for candidate lists have been underway for some time. "Because of the possibility of snap elections, we have accelerated the process," Mäe said.
"If we proceed at the usual pace, we will hold our internal elections in November, as required by the party statutes. That's when the order of candidates in each district will be determined. The general list will be approved by the party council at the beginning of January," he added.
Social Democrats campaigning for lower food VAT
Social Democratic Party secretary‑general Piret Hartman said their list‑building is also ongoing. "In fact, it started already in spring. Districts will make final decisions on candidates and their order at the end of the year. The general list will be approved at the general assembly on January 16," she said.
Hartman noted that campaigning is already underway. "We are actively meeting people across regions, attending events and organizing activities. At the moment we also have an outdoor campaign in several districts focused on lowering VAT on food. We will roll out larger campaign events in October–November. The election program will be approved at the January general assembly," Hartman said.
Eesti 200 preparing as part of everyday politics
Eesti 200 executive director Anneli Kannus said the party does not treat election preparations as a separate process.
"For the party, politics is everyday work. It's difficult to view election preparation as something separate from ongoing discussions or work in the Riigikogu and government. Plans are made continuously as part of normal activity. Eesti 200's more detailed election plans will be finalized in the coming months," Kannus said.
Center Party gathering proposals from regions
Center Party secretary‑general Anneli Ott said the party is drafting its platform and collecting proposals from regional branches. "We also have ongoing meetings with representatives of various interest groups, both in the parliamentary faction and at the party office," Ott said.
She added that regional branches are currently working on candidate lists in their districts, and the party is waiting for their proposals.
The election slogan will be decided once the main focus of the platform becomes clear. "Today the timeline for lists, the platform and the slogan is still open," Ott said.
Isamaa: Some people don't yet know they'll be candidates
Isamaa secretary‑general Andres Metsoja said preparations have been underway for at least half a year.
"Since spring, various program working groups have been meeting, open to all party members. The last meetings were held this week, and discussions with professional organizations will continue in the coming months. At Tuesday's leadership meeting, we agreed to compile all ideas by the end of September for a full overview. We will also cost our core promises, because the last years under Reform Party leadership have pushed public finances into such deep crisis that promising rivers of milk and mountains of porridge is impossible. We must show how we will fund our commitments," Metsoja said.
Work on candidate lists is happening in parallel. "Many well‑known politicians, community leaders and experts from various fields — including those not previously involved in politics — have agreed to run. It's too early to name names, and certainly there are people in Estonia who don't yet know they will be candidates on Isamaa's list. That's why program work is so important — to communicate Isamaa's vision for Estonia's future and give people the chance to contribute," Metsoja said.
He pointed to the summer mini‑campaign "Eesti asi on parim asi" ("Estonian things are the best things"). "Our regional branches are now carrying that message forward by visiting food producers, industrial companies and other contributors to Estonia's economy," he said.
The main Riigikogu campaign will begin after New Year. "But of course we are ready to present our vision earlier if snap elections are called," Metsoja added.
Reform Party to announce lead candidates in November
Reform Party secretary‑general Kristo Enn Vaga confirmed that work on candidate lists and the election program is underway, with both set to be approved at the January general assembly.
"We will announce our lead candidates during November. The campaign kickoff will be on October 17 at the party council meeting in Tartu," Vaga said.
Parempoolsed began pre‑campaign in summer
Parempoolsed currently have just one party switcher MP, a former Eesti 200 member Kalev Stoicescu, but the party is polling above the electoral threshold. Parempoolsed are also assembling their lists, and their pre‑campaign began in late summer.
"We believe Parempoolsed will have strong lists, and right‑leaning voters will find suitable candidates to support," said party vice-chair Kristjan Vanaselja.
"Unlike parliamentary parties, our campaign resources are limited and taxpayer funding is minimal. We use the opportunity to be visible when advertising is cheaper than during the active campaign period. Parempoolsed will run another short campaign in autumn. The slogan and unified campaign will be unveiled in December–January, when the full program and lists are finalized," Vanaselja said.
The next Riigikogu election will take place on March 7 next year.

'I poured him every beer and said, "Now shut up and let me close the pub"'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
06:01:37 UTC
15:01:37 KST

What do you do about an overdraft, how much do you pay for your home and what dream did you fulfill in the shadow of war? People from across Israel speak candidly about everyday life, before and during the war. This time: the Arwas-Youell family of Even Yehuda.
Pictured: Thomas, 45, Mai, 36, Blue, 5, and Creed, 2.
The home: A rented house. They pay about NIS 14,000 a month.
How did you meet?
Thomas: “I lived about a 45-minute drive northwest of London. One of my rules is that I have to live no more than 30 steps from the local pub, and Mai worked at that pub.”
Mai: “I worked there as a bartender. I moved to England with my parents when I was 14, and at 18 I started working at a pub near where we lived. One Sunday afternoon Thomas walked in and started giving me a hard time. He said, ‘I want a Vedett.’ I opened a Vedett, and then he said, ‘Actually, I want a Guinness.’ I poured him a Guinness, and then he decided he wanted another beer. So I put all the beers in front of him and said, ‘Drink all of them, because you’re paying for all of them, and you’re buying me one too. Now shut up and let me close the pub.’ We’ve been best friends ever since.”
Thomas: “Guinness has to be poured in a very specific way, and she passed the test.”
Best friends?
Mai: “Every night after my shift, I would go over to his place with two pints from the pub, we’d smoke a joint and watch a show on MTV called ‘Yo Momma,’ where rappers battled by insulting each other’s mothers. We would sit there for hours laughing, and then I’d go home. That went on for nine or 10 months.
“Then one night, when I was at his place, I wanted to keep the night going, so we got in the car. Thirty minutes later, I was in a very serious accident. They had to cut open the car to get us out.”
Thomas: “I suffered a head injury. I was in the hospital with a broken neck and broken joints.”
Mai: “After the accident, I helped him through his entire recovery. After about three weeks, we started realizing that something between us was becoming more than friendship. Our first official date wasn’t until about a month after the accident.”
What do you do?
Thomas: “I’m a chef. I grew up with my grandfather, who was a chef in the Royal Air Force, and from the age of 7 I started working with him in kitchens and at events all over England. I caught the bug. By 14 I was already attending culinary college in London, and I completed a three-year program in two years. From the age of 16, I started traveling the world.”
Traveling the world?
Thomas: “My grandfather had saved about £20,000 for me, and he said, ‘Either you get an apartment and work in London, or you travel the world.’ I decided to travel.
“At 16, I moved to Sydney on my own and worked in different kitchens. I would work for three months and travel for three months. I had a rule: If the chef annoyed me or I didn’t like something, I left and moved on to the next kitchen.
“When I returned to London, a Japanese friend from Sydney called and said they were looking for a Western chef to train in sushi in Tokyo for a year and a half, so of course I flew to Tokyo. A sushi master took me under his wing and taught me Japanese techniques.
“At one point, I opened and ran Michelin-level restaurants in five hotels across Southeast Asia. I did that for three years and then returned to London. Six months later, I met Mai at the pub.”
Mai?
“Commitment has never exactly been my strong suit. After we had been together for a while, I moved to Los Angeles. I wanted to be an actress. I told him, ‘I’m leaving. If either of us meets someone else, we’ll call each other and end it properly.’
“We were long-distance for two years, writing letters through the mail, emailing and talking on Skype. There was no WhatsApp back then. My parents actually banned him from coming to visit me because of the accident. They didn’t like him being around. He would come secretly and hide at a friend’s apartment in the building next to mine. Once, my brother showed up unexpectedly and I hid Thomas under the bed.
“It took six years for my family to accept him. When we were already living together in Los Angeles, I heard that a restaurant called BAZAR was looking for a chef who understood Middle Eastern food. I knocked on the door and said, ‘I have someone for you.’ He worked with them for 10 years and opened restaurants for them in Chicago and Istanbul. From there we moved to New York for three years, and that’s where Blue was born.”
Blue?
Mai: “He was hospitalized for a year. He can’t be vaccinated, so he can’t attend regular preschools because anything could put him at risk. That’s where the idea of homeschooling came from. We teach the children ourselves and have a preschool teacher come to the house twice a week.
“It’s not that we didn’t want them in regular frameworks, but because of his health we had no choice. Then Thomas was transferred to work at the group’s restaurant in Jaffa, so we went with it and made aliyah. We’ve been here for three and a half years.”
Israel?
Thomas: “We arrived at exactly the right time, shortly before the war. My grandfather fought in two world wars. If he knew there was a war where I live and I ran away, he would be ashamed of me. So I’m not leaving.
“I love Israel. It’s the only place where people tell you exactly what they think to your face and nobody gets offended.”
Mai: “Adjusting to life in Israel was difficult for me. Coming back after 20 years, dealing with all the bureaucracy in Hebrew and everything being shouted — I was in shock. I felt very lonely. Thomas was working long hours, and I was alone with a small child and postpartum depression. Slowly, we learned how to manage. We didn’t really have a choice.”
What do you do today?
Thomas: “I realized that opening a conventional restaurant right now would be financial suicide. Half the staff could be on reserve duty, the fixed costs are insane and places are constantly shutting down.
“So we developed a different concept: private culinary hosting here in our home, three times a week. We host up to 22 people for a 10- to 12-course chef’s meal. Every month has a different concept. This month, for my birthday, it’s a British menu with an Israeli twist and Japanese techniques.
“We use only Israeli ingredients. For me, it’s critical to support Israeli producers.”
Mai: “People come into our home for the experience, ask questions and take an interest in our story. It’s all very intimate, and it’s simply a lot of fun.”
Financial situation?
Mai: “We’re balanced. We calculate everything carefully and are looking ahead at how to develop the business profitably.”
What do you do for fun?
Mai: “The evenings when we host people here are our entertainment. Beyond that, when we finally have some peace and quiet, it’s a good joint at the end of the day, some music or a TV series, and a chance to breathe.”

====================================================================================================

What we know (and still don't) about Canada's 'associate membership'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
06:00:49 UTC
15:00:49 KST

The idea of making Canada the European Union's first "associate member" has caused a furore. Here's what we know and still don't know.
It's the head-turning, eye-popping announcement of the week: Ursula von der Leyen has invited Canada to make history by becoming the first-ever "associate member" of the European Union.
"We want to bring the relationship with Canada to the highest level possible," the European Commission president said in her State of the Union speech.
The following day, speaking from the same lectern in Strasbourg, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said his country "welcomes" the offer and hailed the dawn of an "alliance for the future".
"Europe and Canada are stronger together," he said.
The back-to-back speeches made international headlines, caused a political furore, inspired countless memes and even caught Donald Trump's attention. But they also left many burning questions unanswered.
Here's what we know – and still don't know – about the splashy idea.
There's just no precedent
The concept of "associate membership" is not envisioned in the EU treaties as such. And since it does not exist on paper, there is no precise playbook that Brussels can follow to make it reality.
A similar dilemma emerged earlier this year when German Chancellor Friedrich Merz proposed making Ukraine an "associate member" of the bloc. This, he said, should grant observer status in the decision-making bodies, gradual access to some EU programmes and mutual assistance in the event of a future attack.
Merz's surprise pitch received mixed reviews from capitals and was rebuffed by Kyiv, which worried the half-in, half-out rank would plunge it into accession limbo.
Commission officials say von der Leyen's vision fundamentally differs from Merz's because it is designed for countries outside Europe's geographic sphere that wish to be politically and economically closer to the bloc.
Brussels is confident the ground-breaking concept can be designed from scratch without the need to revise the EU treaties, a perilous avenue.
Some have suggested that a possible way forward lies with Article 217 of the EU treaties, which holds that "The Union may conclude with one or more third countries or international organisations agreements establishing an association involving reciprocal rights and obligations, common action and special procedure."
Carney, meanwhile, said the set-up should be "open enough that others can join".
It's not enlargement
One thing Carney made sure to stress is that his country would not pursue the conventional full-time membership that Ukraine, Moldova and other candidates are seeking.
According to the treaties, this process is available to "any European State", which means a nation on the other side of the Atlantic would not qualify.
"Canada is not in a position nor seeking to become a full member of the European Union. Therefore, it's a different framework," Carney said after his speech. "It's a framework that is relevant for a country that shares deep bonds with Europe."
Accession is a notoriously cumbersome process that requires candidates to adopt thousands of EU laws and align themselves with the bloc's world-class standards. Each step is subject to unanimity, creating multiple opportunities for vetoes.
Ottawa and Brussels want an arrangement that can be concluded much faster.
But it seems curiosity has been piqued: ahead of Carney's trip to Strasbourg, a poll showed that a whopping 49% of Canadians supported full-fledged EU membership.
The name is TBD
Though the headlines that emerged from Strasbourg all honed in on the striking "associate member" title, Carney did not outright endorse it. Instead, he stuck to his "alliance for the future" moniker, which is less politically charged.
"President von der Leyen used both terms: alliance for the future and associate membership. The nomenclature, the precise nomenclature, is a question for Europe," he said. "What matters is the substance."
For the Canadian premier, "associate membership" carries the connotation of ceding sovereignty to Brussels, something he vowed would not be the case under any circumstance.
"We are looking for partnerships that are complementary, that reinforce our sovereignty, and that's what is on offer here," he said. "Canadians are united that nobody is going to tell us what language we speak. No one is going to dictate our culture or with whom we can strike international agreements."
EU officials have brushed off the semantic clash. For them, the "alliance for the future" is the immediate deliverable and "associate membership" the long-term prospect.
It'll be put to a vote
After von der Leyen extended her invitation, the conservative opposition in Canada criticised Carney for seeking deeper ties with the EU without an electoral mandate.
In response, Carney cautioned the negotiations were still in early stages and committed to bringing the outcome to a final vote in the Canadian parliament.
"We will have a series of debates, I'm sure, in parliament (and) relevant committees. And ultimately, there will be a vote in the Canadian parliament for the final structure of the alliance that we're working on," he said. "It will all roll out transparently."
On the European side, it remains to be seen how von der Leyen's team will advance the novel concept through the legislative cycle. The executive has not yet said which department will supervise the work, though the Secretariat-General and DG Trade appear the likeliest candidates to take the reins.
"We're talking about a very ambitious project here, so this is going to require many services across the Commission. It's going to be a whole-of-government approach if you want to call it that," Olof Gill, the Commission's deputy chief spokesperson, said.
Gill insisted the talks would be carried out in close coordination with the member states, some of which were given a heads-up right before von der Leyen's speech.
"Big changes in the European Union only happen with the say-so of our member states, and that will always be the case," he said.
Ireland, Spain and France are among those who have expressed support for exploring the original idea. A high-level discussion on the matter is not excluded when EU leaders gather in October for a busy two-day summit in Brussels.
Later that month, von der Leyen and Carney will meet in Montreal, Quebec. This will be a chance for both to flesh out what exactly they have in mind.
Economy comes first
Still, Strasbourg already gave us a pretty good idea of the areas that von der Leyen and Carney have set their sights on.
Chief among them is commerce, building on the EU-Canada free trade deal, CETA, which still has to be ratified by 10 member states.
Von der Leyen said the goal should be to establish a "common prosperity and economic security space" encompassing intelligent manufacturing, energy, batteries, artificial intelligence, quantum, cyber, defence industry and the Arctic.
Carney echoed these areas and added broadband connections, semiconductors, liquefied natural gas and hydrogen to the list.
He also made sure to underscore Canada's position as a supplier of critical minerals, which Europe desperately wants to diversify to cut off Beijing's chokepoints.
"Canada has deposits of over 34 critical minerals, and we are among the top producers of the 10 most essential for the world's energy transition," he said.
"Our alliance can help fill Europe's need for reliable supply, Canada's need for advanced processing capabilities and our common objective to build complete value chains."
Another way to deepen ties is for Canada to participate in EU programmes. Canada is already part of the Horizon research platform and the SAFE defence initiative and wants to join the popular Erasmus+ for students and the €90 billion loan for Ukraine.
The four freedoms
Von der Leyen's invitation has raised the question of whether Canada, a country more than 6,000 kilometres away from continental Europe, will one day benefit from the bloc's four freedoms of movement: goods, services, capital and people.
The four freedoms are what make the single market seamless, borderless and effectively invisible. Norway, Iceland, Liechtenstein and Switzerland are the only nations outside the EU that enjoy this unfettered access. In return, they have been asked to apply thousands of EU laws without having a direct say in their approval.
Will Canada go as far?
In his speech, Carney said the burgeoning alliance should aim to enable free movement for young people between the EU and Canada.
"We should deepen our people-to-people ties, allowing our youth to live, work and study where they want on either side of the Atlantic," he said.
Carney also spoke of an "integrated market for financial services to broaden choice and reduce costs for our citizens, improve access to capital for our companies while maintaining our world-leading financial resilience".
Von der Leyen, however, did not mention any of the four freedoms.
The Commission has consistently said the four freedoms cannot be "cherry-picked". Earlier this year, Brussels reportedly rejected a post-Brexit overture from London to secure free movement of goods but not people.
Asked if any of them would be available under the "associate membership", Gill, the spokesperson, neither confirmed nor denied.
"Let's see where these discussions go," he said. "Right now, we have a shared commitment between the European Union and Canada that we want to strengthen our relations for mutual benefit, in our own interests."

Spider season! Ten species you’ll see scuttling across Britain’s carpets and lawns this autumn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
06:00:40 UTC
15:00:40 KST

Summer is at an end, and suddenly spiders seem to be everywhere – in your house, in your garden, in your hair. Fresh webs hang from doorways, walls, shrubs and fence posts, creating invisible obstacle courses. Where do all these spiders come from, what kind are they and what, if anything, should we do about them?
The short answer to the question “Why are there so many more spiders at this time of year?” is: there aren’t. They are just more obvious. Dave Clarke, an ectotherm (“cold-blooded” animal) specialist at the Zoological Society of London, says: “There are more spiders around in the spring, because that’s when they hatch from their egg sacs, and there are hundreds of babies in each egg sac. But they’re small and not very obvious. They grow up during the summer and, at this time of year, they reach their maximum size.” Their webs are also correspondingly larger.
The other reason they are more apparent is that they are finding their way indoors in the desperate search for a mate. Dr Sara Goodacre, professor of evolutionary biology and genetics at the University of Nottingham, says: “The ones you see in your home at the minute, the really big, fat, hairy ones, they’re usually teenage males that are lost – emotionally, geographically – and are just hoping they might find a female so they can continue the life cycle.”
The spider season can be a difficult time for people who don’t like spiders, but a little knowledge about these fascinating creatures can go a long way to promote understanding. Here, then, are the 10 spiders you’re most likely to run into this autumn.
1. House spider (Tegenaria domestica)
One of the species you are likely to find in your home, the house spider ranges from pale to dark brown, with black markings and banded, hairy legs. While the name seems to imply that it thrives only within four walls, that is not the case. “They’re not called house spiders because they have to live in your house,” says Clarke. “It’s just because it’s the commonest species you would see inside the house.” Centrally heated homes are generally too dry and too short of food for most species of spider so you don’t have to feel bad about gently relocating one. “It’s your home,” says Goodacre. “You decide who you share it with.”
If you wish to evict a house spider, trap it gently in an upturned glass and slide a piece of card underneath the glass. At this time of year, it’s probably best to release it somewhere with a bit of shelter – a porch, shed or garage.
2. Cardinal spider (Tegenaria parietina)
The cardinal is the largest spider native to the UK, one of a range of hard-to-distinguish species in the genus Tegenaria that also go by the name giant house spider. The term “giant” is in some cases an exaggeration, but not here: adult cardinal spiders can reach a total leg span of 14cm.
They are allegedly called cardinal spiders because Cardinal Wolsey was terrified of them, or because he was protective towards them, or he thought they were lucky, or something. They are found in the south of England, but not the extreme southwest.
3. Cellar spider (Pholcus phalangioides)
It is also known as the daddy-longlegs spider (its legs are about five times the length of its body), but this can be confusing because the name daddy longlegs is also used for a type of crane fly and for harvestmen, the latter of which are arachnids but not spiders.
Cellar spiders are originally subtropical, but they have spread around the world thanks to indoor living. They spin quite untidy webs and generally hang out in the corners where walls meet ceilings. When disturbed they can gyrate rapidly, turning themselves into a blur which, in theory, is supposed to convince predators that they have vanished.
4. Garden spider (Araneus diadematus)
If you have ever stepped out your back door and walked face first into a spiral spider’s web, chances are it belonged to a garden spider. “They’re one of the most obvious because they tend to sit in the middle of the web,” says Clarke. “I’ve been blundering into loads of their webs in my garden over the last few weeks because they are very good at building them right across the path.”
Garden spiders range in colour from grey-brown to reddish-brown, with a white cross – made up of speckles – on the abdomen. Females are twice the size of males, with a body length of up to 1.8cm.
5. False Widows (Steatoda nobilis, Steatoda bipunctata, Steatoda grossa)
Of the three false widows, two – the cupboard false widow (Steatoda grossa) and the rabbit hutch false widow (Steatoda bipunctata) – are native to Britain. The other, the noble false widow (Steatoda nobilis), turned up here some time in the late 19th century from the Canary Islands. The noble false widow is the one that gets all the bad press: it’s often referred to as “Britain’s most dangerous spider”, a construction roughly as misleading as “Britain’s most earthquake-prone region”. It’s not a competition that is hard to come top in. Medium-sized with a glossy black abdomen, the spider is, in fact, solitary and not in the least aggressive.
False widows can bite, although confirmed cases of them biting humans are rare, and while they are venomous, the common reaction to the bite is similar in severity to a nettle or wasp sting. “But it doesn’t fly like a wasp,” says Goodacre, “so you’d have to try really hard [to get bitten]. The level of hysteria is the worst bit – people feel ill because they’re so worried about the concept of a spider bite.”
You may regard all other spiders commonly found in Britain as essentially harmless. And Britain’s most earthquake-prone region is Perth and Kinross, by the way.
6. Missing sector orb weaver (Zygiella x-notata)
Often found in and around windows, this spider is usually silver-grey with an oak-leaf mark on its back, but it’s easiest to identify by its web: a classic circular pattern with one pie slice missing. This gap is bisected by a single thread, running from the outer edge to the centre, from which the spider can pick up the vibrations of anything landing. “They don’t sit in the middle of their web; they sit hidden on your windowsill,” says Goodacre. “They always sit with one foot casually out, but there’s nothing casual about it – it’s sensing.”
7. Tube web spider (Segestria florentina)
One of the biggest spiders found in the UK – mostly in the south – its body can reach 2.2cm in length. It’s easily identifiable by its iridescent green mouth parts, but only if you can see them: tube web spiders spend most of their time tucked into holes in brick walls or fences, at the centre of their vortex-shaped web, waiting to pounce on any prey disturbing the silken tripwires. “If you’re very careful, you can often get them to come out of their retreat with a grass stem or something like that,” says Clarke. But it won’t work if you just touch it with your finger – they can sense the difference. This spider does have a venomous bite, which is said to be painful but not dangerous, but it’s a very reclusive creature, so you’d have to really bother it to get bitten.
8. Zebra jumping spider (Salticus scenicus)
These little spiders are between 5mm and 9mm long, can jump about 10 times their length, and have been observed taking on prey up to three times their size. Despite their predatory nature, they are among the most adorable of all spiders, thanks to their zebra-stripe markings and their two big, front-facing SpongeBob eyes. “If you see a jumping spider and you look at it, it will look up at you, which is very cute,” says Clarke. For what it’s worth they also have six smaller eyes, distributed down their flanks and in the rear.
9. False wolf spider (Zoropsis spinimana)
This gets its name because of its outward resemblance to wolf spiders. Like wolf spiders, they don’t trap their prey in webs – they go out and hunt it down. It’s also known as a Nosferatu spider, because the markings on its back look like a little vampire face. Normally found in the Mediterranean, the false wolf has only recently arrived in the UK, and is increasingly likely to be spotted in and around London. “This is a species that really wouldn’t survive our harsh winters outside,” says Clarke, “so they do rely on human structures.”
10. Woodlouse spider (Dysdera crocata)
They get their name not because they resemble woodlice, but because they eat them. Their look, in fact, is quite distinctive: reddish orange with a peanut-shaped abdomen, and large enough fangs to penetrate the protective armour of a woodlouse. “People are often quite surprised when they see one because they look quite exotic,” says Clarke. But they’re not rare; just quite demure. “I think they prefer to be hidden away underneath things a lot of the time, rather than running about in the open.”

Nine women in South Africa have been murdered since July. We are being told to be vigilant – but where are the warnings to men? | Nolethu Ndude
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
06:00:39 UTC
15:00:39 KST

When I heard the authorities advising women in and around Kempton Park, the site of a recent spate of femicides, not to walk or run alone, to avoid isolated places and to “remain vigilant”, my immediate response was anger. Remain vigilant. How groundbreaking.
Women are already vigilant. We photograph number plates before entering vehicles. We share Uber details with friends. We phone one another while walking. We watch the driver’s route and notice every unexpected turn. We avoid certain roads, certain times and certain conversations. We scan parking areas before getting out of our cars. We check the back seat. We listen for footsteps. We carry pepper spray where we can. We hold our keys in a way that makes us feel slightly less defenceless.
Women have informal safety systems built into our friendships. “Please let me know when you get home” is not simply a polite farewell. It is a survival protocol.
Yet women are still being killed.
Police are investigating the deaths of nine women whose bodies have been found across the Ekurhuleni district, east of Johannesburg, since July. Some were found naked or partially clothed, and several had visible injuries.
One of the women was Elizabeth “Tsontso” Moselakgomo, a 38-year-old who disappeared after leaving her home in Kempton Park for an afternoon run on 9 September. Her body was found three days later.
Now running must be approached like a security operation. Choose a group. Share your route. Check the time. Avoid quiet roads. Stay where people can see you. Keep one earphone out. Carry your phone. Remain visible. Remain alert. Remain vigilant.
But women cannot “vigilance” themselves out of gender-based violence and femicide.
Where are the instructions to men? Where is the urgent public warning telling them not to harm women? Where is the nationwide mobilisation asking men to confront their friends, brothers and colleagues? Where are the campaigns teaching men that affection does not create ownership and that rejection is not humiliation?
Where is the same relentless attention on perpetrators, effective policing, prosecution and prevention?
The truth is, women are not safe anywhere.
In 2019, 19-year-old University of Cape Town student Uyinene Mrwetyana went to collect a parcel from a post office in Cape Town. She was raped and murdered inside that post office by an employee. Her murder shattered the idea that danger is limited to badly lit streets and isolated fields.
If we must avoid every place where another woman has been attacked or killed, where are we allowed to exist?
We are told to stay indoors, although many women are abused in their homes. We are told not to trust strangers, although women are killed by husbands, boyfriends, relatives and former partners. We are told to choose better, as though abusive men introduce themselves honestly and arrive carrying warning labels.
South African women were killed at a rate of 12.2 per 100,000 in 2022, nearly six times the global rate, according to the UN Office on Drugs and Crime. That figure should stop the country in its tracks. Instead, it becomes another statistic repeated during interviews, marches and annual campaigns.
After protests ahead of the G20 summit in Johannesburg in November 2025, President Cyril Ramaphosa declared gender-based violence and femicide a national crisis. Women had already spent years explaining that it was one.
The issue is not whether government has heard us. It has. The issue is hat actually changes after gender-based violence is declared a national crisis?
Which institutions become accountable? What additional resources are committed? Are police stations properly equipped to act when a woman is reported missing? Are officers trained to respond to survivors with care rather than suspicion? Are investigations adequately resourced? Are protection orders enforced? Are shelters funded? Are survivors protected while cases move through courts?
Who answers when commitments are not fulfilled?
The Commission for Gender Equality has called for an urgent safety audit of the affected areas. It wants attention given to lighting, surveillance, public transport routes, neglected spaces, police visibility and access to emergency assistance. That is necessary.
But the response cannot end at Ekurhuleni’s borders. Women are being killed nationally, therefore prevention strategies must implemented at a national level.
We also need to stop treating every killing as an isolated tragedy with no relationship to the culture around it. Femicide does not begin when a body is discovered. It develops along a continuum.
Through my work with young people, I see why intervention must begin long before violence reaches the criminal justice system. We need sustained education about consent, bodily autonomy, healthy relationships, emotional regulation and positive masculinity.
That is not an excuse for violence. It is part of preventing it.
Men must confront misogyny in their own circles. They must challenge the jokes, controlling behaviour, coercion and entitlement before somebody is dead. Silence is not neutrality. It protects the conditions in which violence thrives.
This responsibility does not belong only to activists, police or women’s organisations. It belongs in homes, schools, churches, workplaces, sports clubs, taxis, universities and friendship groups. It belongs wherever boys learn what manhood means.
I am not arguing that women should ignore immediate safety warnings. I am arguing that those warnings cannot be presented as the solution. There is a difference between sharing information about a specific risk and building an entire response around women limiting their lives.
The state’s responsibility is not to teach women how to stay alive around violent men. Its responsibility is to prevent violence, investigate cases properly, pursue perpetrators and build a country in which women can collect a parcel, go for a run, leave a relationship, take a ride home and simply live.
We have restricted ourselves. We have changed our behaviour. We have remained vigilant. We are still being killed. It is time the authorities, and men, tried something different. Accountability would be a good place to start.

Xiaomi Has a Luxury SUV for $31,000 That All Western Brands Should Fear
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
06:00:00 UTC
15:00:00 KST

If there's one thing that can unite the world in these AI-troubled times, it's everyone's love of SUVs. For decades, the SUV has been the savior of the car world. Accounting for nearly half of all new sales worldwide, this is by some margin the largest segment in the global auto industry.
Sedans? Forget it. Ford doesn't even sell a traditional sedan in the US now. China still likes a sedan. About a third of all Chinese autos are in this form, compared with less than half that for the US. But Chinese carmakers know full well how much we love our chunky SUVs, so they are focusing their efforts to lure the Western world away from familiar marques.
Indeed, Xiaomi has just played its hand in this particular game, revealing the remaining details earlier this month in Beijing—including the all-important pricing—of its coming SkyNomad SUVs. Bentley and Range Rover may well have revealed their flagship electric SUVs, but both will be mightily worried about just how many scalps Xiaomi Auto's SkyNomad SUVs will take from them. If they're not, they should be.
Sedan to SUV
Trucks and SUVs represent more than 80 percent of new vehicle sales in America these days. Marc McGrath, US CEO of the automotive manufacturer Schaeffler Group, tells WIRED that one of the main reasons the company is developing its own solid-state batteries is to properly electrify the power-hungry trucks and SUVs Americans so dearly love. No one wants another F-150 Lightning U-turn.
The shocking success of the Jaecoo 7 is a prime example of SUV supremacy. This Chinese-made ride has enjoyed a staggeringly meteoric rise in the UK, going from an unknown newcomer in 2025 to now being one of the country’s best-selling new cars. Nicknamed the “Temu Range Rover,” it comes in both gas and hybrid flavors, and the company liberally uses the word “luxury” in its marketing, yet the vehicle costs just £29,210 (a little over $39,000).
These 7s are becoming ubiquitous on UK roads. My local Nissan dealer has swiftly dumped the Japanese brand and is now an official Jaecoo dealer, offering not just the 7, but the Jaecoo 5 and 8. I can't think of another auto brand that's enjoyed such a rapid rise.
Other Chinese brands are playing the same tactic in Europe, such as XPeng and BYD, but the big one incoming is Xiaomi Auto, set to launch in Europe in 2027, despite only making its first EV in 2024. Astonishingly, its SU7 Ultra claimed the title of “World’s Fastest Sedan” the very same year.
Far from a Temu pretender, the SkyNomad is not only tech-laden, it's also seemingly high-end, with seating that purports to be “more like an Italian sofa.” The SkyNomad N70 is a five-seater that, especially in its “Stealth Black Edition” guise, looks almost exactly like a Range Rover from the outside, and far more successfully than the Jaecoo.
The larger N90 is a seven-seater that also comes in a “Max Studio” camper version, complete with a pop-up roof. The second row can transform into a bed with one touch of a button—no disassembly, no mattress needed—just 30 seconds from upright seats to a flat, large bed.
The theme of reconfigurable interiors continues. A flat floor, courtesy of the Kunlun platform, comes with sliding rails built in from the front seats to the boot, meaning all (yes, all) the seat sections can move about. The front seats spin a full 180 degrees to face the second row; floor-mounted tables slot between the rows to make for “living-room-style" layouts; the center console can move forward or back at the press of a button; and rear legroom can max out at over 5 feet. In the N90 Max Studio, the pop-up roof lifts 100 mm to open a sleeping loft with 1.8 meters of headroom, along with heated flooring (!), a built-in projector, and a 30-inch projector screen.
An amazing optional extra for the SkyNomad is Xiaomi's version of in-brand car-to-car communications. Essentially, it's a walkie-talkie that runs on cellular network coverage rather than short-range radio, so it's marketed as having “unlimited range” and looks very similar to tech Xiaomi already ships in its phones.
Just stop for a minute and compare what you've just read with the sorts of interior innovations Western brands deliver on flagship models these days. Power doors, multi-point massage seats, relaxation programs with scent sprays, and a central console that moves maybe 10 cm are the typical cutting-edge fare. The SkyNomad makes US and European efforts look, frankly, lazy—right when they desperately need to stop their decline and show they can compete.
There's more. “Full scenario” voice control; customizable head-up display; lidar units, high-definition cameras, and Nvidia's Thor-U chip for level 2-plus autonomous control. A low-voltage power system apparently keeps “sentry mode” drain to under 5 kilometers of range overnight, so the onboard fridge running on 0.72 kWh a day can offer up to 24-hour continuous cooling.
The extended-range plug-in hybrid powertrain combines a 1.5-liter turbocharged internal combustion generator with battery packs and dual electric motors. This ICE engine never drives the wheels, but the SUV can charge from 20 to 80 percent in as little as 18 minutes for a 300-plus-mile electric-only range, or 1,000-mile combined range. Yes, these stats use China’s far more forgiving CLTC cycle, but this converts to about 700 miles using stricter US EPA standards.
Now to the clincher: the price. The maxed-out N90 Max Studio with its camper roof clocks in at RMB 299,900, about $44,700. The entry-level N70 Pro five-seat, rear-wheel-drive model with its movable “Italian sofa” seats, lidar, 14-speaker sound system including subwoofer and headrest speakers, and prodigious range is just RMB 209,900, or just over $31,000—about the same as a 2026 Hyundai Tucson.
Earlier this month, I asked a Western luxury auto CEO what he thought about Xiaomi Auto. He laughed. “They make vacuums, don't they?” he scoffed. I think he'll rue the day he said that. It reminds me of when, in a 2011 Bloomberg interview, Musk laughed when asked if he saw BYD as a competitor. Musk isn't laughing now. Make no mistake, Xiaomi is coming to clean up.

Putin Accuses Ukraine of Sabotaging Peace Negotiations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
06:00:00 UTC
15:00:00 KST

Russian President Vladimir Putin claimed that Ukraine is unwilling to engage in genuine peace negotiations, asserting that Kyiv is actively taking steps to prevent a diplomatic resolution to the war.
Addressing a meeting of Russia’s Military-Industrial Commission on Friday, Sept. 18, Putin alleged that Ukrainian calls for diplomatic engagement are disingenuous, state news agency Interfax reported.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Representatives of the Kyiv regime, the leadership in Kyiv, speak of peace and propose resuming so-called negotiations, but themselves commit such crimes, doing everything to ensure that there is no peace and no negotiations,” Putin claimed.
The Russian leader contended that Moscow cannot be intimidated and insisted that recent Ukrainian actions demonstrate a refusal to negotiate. His remarks follow a series of Ukrainian drone strikes on defense-industrial and refining facilities across western and central Russia, as well as recurring cross-border engagements.
Despite the Kremlin’s accusations, Ukrainian officials have repeatedly presented diplomatic initiatives to end hostilities, including proposals for an unconditional ceasefire and direct leader-level talks.
However, Moscow has consistently conditioned any diplomatic engagement on sweeping political concessions, including international recognition of its illegal annexations and Kyiv ceding control of remaining areas in the Donbas.
US Approves $2.68B Air Defense Equipment Sale to Ukraine
Putin’s true goal
Putin’s assertions contrast with assessments delivered earlier in the week by President Volodymyr Zelensky, who warned that the Kremlin leader remains fundamentally committed to destroying Ukrainian sovereignty rather than settling a localized territorial dispute.
Zelensky stated that Putin’s ambition extends far beyond consolidating occupied frontline territory.
“The problem is that we have to change Putin’s mind,” Zelensky said, responding to US mediation concepts focused on drawing new territorial borders. “He needs Ukraine. He needs Ukraine to be a part of Russia.”
Zelensky emphasized that Kyiv remains prepared for an unconditional cessation of hostilities if Moscow halts combat operations along the existing line of contact, allowing international mediators to facilitate diplomatic talks.
However, he firmly dismissed the concept of a “win-win” compromise promoted by external mediators, arguing that an unprovoked war that has claimed hundreds of thousands of lives cannot yield mutual benefit.
The president reaffirmed his readiness to meet Putin directly if such an encounter could produce concrete progress toward a lasting peace, while reiterating that robust Western security guarantees remain essential to prevent Russia from using an operational pause to prepare future offensives.
Washington weighs pre-settlement economic incentives
The diplomatic impasse arrives amid reports that the administration of US President Donald Trump is exploring preliminary commercial agreements with Moscow before achieving a definitive peace settlement.
Washington is assessing whether concluding bilateral economic deals could signal seriousness regarding a long-term diplomatic reset and incentivize Russian elites to support ending the war. A US official told the newspaper that business agreements could help persuade hardline figures surrounding Putin that Washington seeks a constructive bilateral framework.
The prospective approach would mark a shift from previous US policy, which insisted that commercial ties and economic normalization could occur only after Russia ends its military aggression against Ukraine. Potential areas of cooperation previously raised by Moscow and Washington have encompassed energy partnerships, critical mineral investments, Arctic transit routes, and corporate joint ventures.
During early September discussions in Moscow between Putin and US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov confirmed that talks addressed potential large-scale, mutually beneficial commercial projects alongside conflict settlement concepts.

Live: Hawks and Lions face off for grand final spot to face Dockers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
05:59:51 UTC
14:59:51 KST

Thu, 3 Sept, 8:10 pm, Final score, Dockers 40, Hawks 72
Hawthorn fans rain bottles on umpires after contentious call as Brisbane claims prelim thriller
Furious Hawthorn fans have thrown bottles at the field umpires after Brisbane benefited from a massive late call in their preliminary final epic at the MCG.
After the Hawks had recovered from a 28-point deficit in the early stages of the final quarter, Hugh McCluggage put the Lions back in front from a set shot with 18 seconds remaining on the clock, before Kai Lohmann goalled after the siren to give Brisbane a 20.11 (131) to 19.8 (122) win in front of 97,835 spectators.
McCluggage was awarded a set shot on goal from 30m out on a slight angle after Hawthorn defender Jarman Impey was penalised for holding the ball, a decision that was greeted by deafening boos from the Hawthorn faithful.
The decision, while controversial, appeared to be the correct one, with Impey's left arm free to dispose of the football while being tackled.
"I think this might be the bravest umpiring decision I've seen in my time in footy," Melbourne great Garry Lyon said on Fox Footy's post-game coverage.
McCluggage said he knew the umpires would call holding the ball on Impey after he pinned a single arm.
"I tried to grab a lever [arm] like we're taught," he told Fox Footy.
"We've been taught that you have to try and make an effort to get the ball out if you've got an arm free, so I'll take it."
Hawthorn coach Sam Mitchell was left deeply emotional, and said his focus was on other umpiring calls, particularly a deliberate out of bounds call against Mitch Lewis and a high contact free kick to Dayne Zorko.
"It's probably not the one I'm focused on. There were a couple leading up to it," Mitchell said when asked about the Impey call.
"I'm sure the umpires will assess how they performed in that game in key moments."
The final moments led to ugly scenes after the match, and Mitchell joined former teammate Luke Hodge in condemning the behaviour from the fans.
"The emotion of sport is why we love it so much," he said.
"At the end of the game, part of me wanted to break down in tears, part of me wanted to scream with rage, part of me wanted to throw chairs.
"When you're in the stands, you need to continue to be feeling that emotion, because that's why we love it, but we shouldn't be throwing things on the field. But the passion of the game is why we love it.
"I hope for the vast majority that it was done responsibly."
Nick Watson was outstanding for Hawthorn in the loss, finishing with six goals, while Jack Gunston and Mitch Lewis combined for nine goals between them.
Lohmann's five goals led the way for the Lions, while Eric Hipwood, McCluggage and Charlie Cameron kicked three goals apiece.
Brisbane's win means it will contest Fremantle in next weekend's grand final with the hope a second three-peat in club history after doing so between 2001 and 2003 under Leigh Matthews.
Brisbane veteran Lachie Neale will play against his old side after playing in Fremantle's last grand final appearance in 2013 as a 20-year-old.
